A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

---

WHEREAS Our Parliament stands prorogued to Thursday the Eighth Day of this Instant December: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare. That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued on the said Eighth Day of December, to Tuefdaythe Twenty-fourth Day of January next ensuing: And We have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly: And We do here-

by further declare our Royal Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall , on the said Twenty-fourth Day of January next, be held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give their Attendance accordingly, at on the said Twenty-fourth Day of January next.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the Sixth Day of December, in the Eleventh year of our Reign.

GOD save the King.

MESSAGE from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, Gentleman Uiherof the Black Rod: Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech, from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I HAVE called you together for the necessary Dif* patch of the publick Business, which I hope will be carried on with that Prudence and Expedition, which becomes the Wifdoin of Parliament.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates for the Service of the current Year to be laid before you; and the Readiness which I have always found inyou, to make the necessary Provisions for the Honour, Peace, and Security of my Crown and Kingdoms, leaves me no room to doubt of the same Zeal, Affection, and due Regard, for the Support of my Government, and the publick Safety.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I hope you are met together in a Disposition to lay aside ail Heats and Animosities, which may unnecessarily p rot raft this Session. I am determined, that the Affairs of the Publick shall fufler no Delay or Interruption from me upon any account whatsoever.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House, for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to con* dole with his Majesty, on his and the Nation’s irrepara? ble Loss,by the Death of her most excellent Majesty the Queen; and to assure his Majesty, that this House does always take part in every thingthat nearly concerns and aftefts him; and will, as far as in them lies, with the gre&teft Gratitude, endeavour to soften every Care that Vox.. 2 3.

may approach him; to assure his Majesty, that we will carefully avoid all Heats and Animosities; that we will readily and effectually raise the Supplies necessary for the current Service of the Year; and, as we are truly sensible of the Regard his Majesty has always shewn to the Liberties and Privileges of his Subjects, that we will, as becomes the Reprefeniatives of a grateful People, lose no Ocoafion of testifying our Affection and Zeal for the Support of his Government, and the Preservation of our excellent Constitution; and further to beseech his Majesty, to be careful of his sacred and inestimable Life, on which the Happiness of his Family, and his People, so immediately depends.

Address on the King't Speech*

2 5* — 26°

A. 1757.

double Duty by which we are bound, as affectionate Subjects to your Majesty, and as Representatives of the People of Great Britain; not to pass over in Silence this Ohject of your Distress, and their universal Mourning.

When we refleCi on the amiable private Character of that great Princess, on her personal and domeflick Merit, as an indulgent and instructive Parent, a mild and gracious Mistress, or, with regard to your Majesty, as uniting in one all the different Characters of the moll pleasing, as well as constant, Companion; the most able, as well as the moil faithful. Friend; the most tender, as well the moll observant. Wife; when we reflect on these Circumstances, we mourn her Loss, as the greatest with which your Majesty, and your royal House, could have been afflicted; but when we turn our Thoughts to her great and publick Virtues, her Love of Justice, her Attachment to the Laws and Principles of this wife and happy Constitution, her extensive Charities, her boundless Benevolence, her Succour to Distress, her Favour to Merit, her Lenity to all; when we consider these Parts of her high Character, it is no longer for particular and personal Causes that we grieve, it is a national Loss we lament.

If adueSubmission to superior Authority, and a due Exercise of Power, when committed to her Hands, are the strongest Marks of Excellence in both Parts of Government: and if these justly claim Praise and Admiration, how can we fufliciently praise or admire her Conduct, either in the Presence or Absence of your Majesty ? In the first, we saw the most constant Compliance with your Will; in the last, the true Representation of him, with whose delegated Authority the was veiled; for all her Acts were great, and wife, and good; alternately we beheld her Submission in this Character, and felt her Mildness in the other; and, great as the Distance may seem from Command to Subjection, the Transltion to her was easy; whose Abilities were equal to any Situation, and whole Temper could conform to all; as resigned to the Duties of a Queen Con fort, as capable of the high Office of Guardian of the Realm; as ready to submit, as able to command, and equally an Example to all Sovereigns when ilie ruled, and to all Subjects when fheobeyed.

And though your Majesty’s just and great Concern on this Occasion, would, perhaps, receive no Extenuation from the Comfort your faithful Commons might vainly try to administer, yet, that nothing may be wanting on our Parts, which may contribute to the making your Majesty’s. Government, the Source of our Prof-perity, as easy to yourself, as it has ever been to your Subjects, we do assure your Majesty, that we will not only carefuly avoid all Heats and Animoftties, but will, with the greatest Readiness, effectually raise the Supplies necessary for the Service of the current Year; and, with a Zeal and Affection becoming the Representatives of a grateful People, make all necessary Provisions for the Honour, Peace, and Security, of your Crown and Kingdoms; demonstrating to all the World, that the Support of your Majesty’s Government, and the publick Safety, are constantly our Care; and that we desire nothing more than the Preservation of our wife and excellent Constitution, in the same happy, firm, and envied Situation, in which it was delivered down to us from our Ancestors, and your Majesty’s great Predecessors.

But whiift, hv these means, we endeavour to prevent any additional Disquiet from approaching your Royal Person, we mult beg Leave to lay again before your Majesty the anxious Grief of your whole People, together With their humble and most earned Willies, that your Majesty's known Resolutionmay aid Time in alleviating your Sorrow for that Loss which nothing can repair, and in restoring to your Majesty that Tranquillity of Mind, which can alone free us from the most felicitous FearsforaLife,on which the Happinefsof your royal Family, and of thisaftlicted Nat ion, so immediately depends.

The said Address being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Abcrbrortwck A Petition of the Provost, Bailies, and Town Council, Harbour, Lc. Gf t|ie Burgh Gf Aberbrotho; and also, Ditto. A Petition of the Heritors, in the Neighbourhood of the Burgh of Aberbrothock, and other Heritors in that County, whose Subscriptions and Defoliations are thereto Subjoined;

Were Severally presented to the House, and read; Setting fbrth. That the Situation of the Town of Aberbrothock is such, that a commodious Harbour there mult not only tend to the Advantage of Trade within the Burgh, but be of great Use to Navigation in general, upon the Northern Coast of Scotland: That the old Harbour there, becoming so decayed, that it was hazardous, even for Small Barks, to enter the fame. In 1715 the Petitioners, the Provost, Bailies, arid Town Council, of the said Burgh of

thock, laid the Foundation of a new Harbour, and the Work was carried on for some Years, upon the foie Expence of the Burgh and Inhabitants thereof; whereby they contracted large Debts, and became unable to carry on the Work; which obliged them to apply lor charitable Contributions, for advancing an undertaking so necessary for the Subsistence of the Burgh, and useful to the Trade of other Places:

' That the Money, arising from such Contributions, has been, with the utmost Frugality, laid out in early ing on the Work; and, nevertheless, the Harbour is not yet near perfected, and the Burgh is brought under such Debts, as not only render them uncapa-bleoffinishing this Undertaking, so successfully hitherto carried on, but unable to discharge the Debts already contracted on that Account: That the Town-house and common Prison are old and decayed, and the Streets and Causeways are in so bad Repair, as render them very incommodious, both to the Inhabitants and to Travellers: And therefore, in order to enable the Petitioners, the Provost, Bailies, and Town Council of the Burgh of , to per-

sect the necessary Work, already so far carried on, to repair their Streets, and to pay off the Debts contracted for the publick Service of the Town, and to support their other necessary Expences, which will be further increased, from the Necessity of rebuilding the Town-house and public Prison, praying, That a Duty of Two Penies, Scots, may be granted upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer, that shall be for Sale brewed, brought in, vended, tapped, or fold, within the said Town, and Liber-

ties thereof, payable by the Brewers, Venders,

Sellers, and Tapsters, of the said Ale and Beer, during such Term of Years, and subject to such Regulations, as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Contideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it thall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Brigadier Sir

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called, Mr. William Wild, and Mr. John Woodroff: Who, being severally examined, said. That, the Road mentioned in both Petitions, is about Nine Miles in Length, and that, by Reason of many heavy Carriages frequently puffing through the fame, some Parts thereof in the Winter Seafonare very deep and dangerous to Passengers.

The said William Wild further said, That some of the Parishes through which the said Road leads were, about Two Years since, indicted, on account of the Badness thereof, although the Inhabitants had constantly done and performed their Statute-work, and collected as much or more than they were obliged to raise by Law, and duly laid out the same in amending that Road.

It appeared by the Evidence of those Witnesses, That it is irapoffible for the Inhabitants of all the Parishes effectually to amend the Road now desired to be amended, and to keep the same in good Repair, for the Accommodation of Travellers, unless some further Provision be made for that Purpose.

Sir Robert Clifton, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The said Peter Marlin being asked, What Condition the Town-house and Common Prison were in, he said, That the same were old and decayed; and that the Streets and Catrfeways were in so bad Repair, that the same were rendered very incommodious, both to the Inhabitants and Travellers.

Then an Account of the present Debts, contracted for the publick Service of the said Town, was laid before the Committee; whereby £. 4,925 appears to be due; the Interest of which Debt the annual Revenue of the said Towrn is not sufficient to discharge.

And it appeared to the Committee, That, unless some Power be given to the Inhabitants of the said Town to raise Money, neither the said Harbour, which is very useful to Trade, can be completed, nor the Building of the Town-houseand puibtick Prison, the repair of the Streets, and other publick Works, of the said Town, carried on and finished, and the present Debt discharged.

A Petition of sundry Iron Mailers, in behalf of them- Encouraging selves and others concerned in the Making of Iron in the making Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; *r°n !" setting forth, That the Petitioners are not able to make Dg Iron so cheap as, notwithstanding the present Duties, it is imported from abroad: That the Quantity of British Iron is already greatly decreased, and will soon come to nothing, unless something be speedily done in their Favour: That their Trade employs a Multitude of Poor; supports the Woodlands; whereby Timber is produced for the Navy, and Bark for the Leather Manufacture; and, byfurnilhinga Commodity, which, when imported, is, for the most part, paid in Specie, prevents large Sums from going out of this Kingdom; and that, in their Opinion, Great Britain is naturally capable, and, in time, would be enabled to supply herself with Iron, both in Quantity and Quality, sufficient for all our Pilrposes, excepting Steel only, were but proper Encouragement afforded: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and grant such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Ironmongers and Manufacturers of Iron, in the Towns of Birmingham, Wolverhampton, Stourbridge, and Dudley, and the Parts adjacent, in the Counties of Warwick, Stafford, and Worcester,is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

SI R Francis Child reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of the Vicar of the Parish of St> Leonard in Shoreditch, in the County of Middlesex; and

of others, the Trustees, appointed by an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the Eighth Year of his present Vol. 23.

Majesty’s rteign, intituled, An Act for rebuilding the Parish Church of St.Leonard, Shoreditch, in the Coun

ty of Middlesex; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: "Where the same was read; and is as follows;

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof;

The Petitioners laid before the Committee the Act of Parliament mentioned in the said Petition; whereby it appeared. That the several Funeral Rates and Duties, mentioned in a certain Indenture, bearing Date the 'Eighth Day of April 1735, made between the Vicar of the said Parilli, of the One Part; and the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the same Parish, of the other Part; should be collected, levied, and paid, in the said Parish, for the Burial of any Person, in the manner therein mentioned.

And the Trustees, in the said Act mentioned, are impowered to receive and take the several Rates and Duties contained in the said Indenture; the Whole whereof are to be appropriated for the Payment of certain Annuities, by the said Act granted, for the rebuilding the said Church.

Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee the said Indenture, inrolled in the High Court of Chancery, which appeared to be nothing more than a Deed, under the Hands and Seals of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, to testify and declare, what had been anciently and accuftoraably the several ecclesiastical Rates and Duties, payable on all Accounts, within the said Parilli; fothat not only the Fu-neral Rates and Duties, payable to the Parilli, but like-wife those due to the Vicar, Clerk, and Sexton, are contained therein; by which means the whole Rates and Duties are appropriated for the Purposes of the said Act.

Then the Reverend Dr. Denne, Vicar of the said Pa? ri(h, being examined, said. That it never was his own, nor, in all Probability, could be the Intention of the Parilli, That the Rates and Duties payable to himself. Clerk, and Sexton, lliould be made applicable for the Rebuilding of the said Church; but that the Appropriation of the same proceeded from an Overlight: And, to prove that it was never the Intention of the Parish, he laid before the Committee the Report of the 14th of February 1734> of the Committee appointed by publick Vestry to consider of proper Means for rebuilding of the said Church; which Report was agreed to in publick Vestry; and by which it appeared, That only the Income ar'ifing to the said Parish for customary Fees, or Duties at Funerals, as for Ground, Bells, Palls, SCc. were to be appropriated for the Payment of the said Annuities, to be raised by the said Act.

And the said Dr. Denne farther said, That the Act of the Eighth of his present Majestjr was founded on the said Report.

And that it could never be imagined, That the Vicar of the said Parish should part withfo large a Share of his Living, as near One third Part of it; the Profits of the Living being about £. 140 per Annall which, within

£. 20. arises out from Fees and Offerings; and of that Sum, full Seventy Pounds did arise from Burial Fees, One Year with another: Or that the Sexton and Clerk should part with much the greater Part of their whole Living, which they have done, as the Witness apprehends, as the Act now standsjtherebeingnoDiftinftion made of the Fees due to them, or the said Parish; for that the said Indenture,which comprehends all their Fees, is, in general, referred to by the said Act, which appropriates all of them to the Rebuilding of the said Church.

That by the said Act, it also appeared to the Committee, That in case the said Funeral Rates and Duties should be deficient to pay the Annuities, amounting to

£. 680 per Annum, thereby granted, such Deficiency was

to be i'upplied by an Assessnaent, to be made on all Lands,

Creditors of Hugh Naish, late a Prisoner for Debt, in the Prison of the Fleet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Hugh yaish, having become indebted to the Petitioners, and other Persons, in very large Sums of Money, in order to avoid Payment thereof, and to defraud the Petitioners, and his other Creditors, on the 2qth Day of June 1731, becamea Prisoner for Debt in the Fleet Prison, and there remained, till on or dbout the 23d Day of July 1737; That, by an Act made ill the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, reciting. That several Persons, who were Prisonersfor Debt, chose rather to confftlue in Prison, and spend their Substance there, than discover and deliver up to their Creditors their Estates and Effects, in order to the Satisfaction of their just Debls, it was Enacted, That it should and might be lawful, to and for any One or more of the Creditors of any Prisoner, committed fi nee the ill Day of January 1730, at whose Suit he or flte was detained ifl Prison on the ill Day of January 1736, upon Thirty Days Notice in Writing, to be given to such Prisoner, and the Person in whose Custody he or she was detained, to require the Sheriff or Sheriffs, Gaoler or Gaolers, or Keeper of the Prison, wherein such Prisoner was detained, to bring such Prisoner before the Justices, at their next General or Quarter Sessions of the Peace for their respective County, Riding, Division, City, Town, or Liberty; together with a Copy or Copies of the Cause or Causes of his or her Detainer; and such Prisoner, coming before such Justices,at the said General or Quarter Sessions, should, at the Desire of any One or more of his or her Creditors, at whose Suit he or Hie should appear to be detained, be obliged to deliver in, upon Oath, and subscribe, a Schedule of his or her Estate and Effects, to be veiled, assigned, and equally divided, for the Benefit of his or her Creditors, in such manner, as by the said Act is directed; and that, in pursuance of the said .'ft, on or about the 9th Day of July last, several of the Petitioners, at whose respective Suits the said Hugh Naish then was, and had, from belore the ift Day of January 173b, been a Prisoner lor Debt, in the said Fled Prison, cauftd Notice in Writing to be given to the said Naish, and likewise to the Warden of the Fled Prison, in whose Custody the said H Naish then was, to have the said Hugh Naish brought belore the Justices, at their next G enera 1 or Quarter Sessions of the Peace, which should Vot. 23.

of the said Act; and that the Petitioners likewise caused Notice thereof to be published in the London Gazette, as by the said Act is required; and that the said Hugh Naish was, at the Time of paffnig the said Act of Parliament, seised and possessed of, or entitled to, a real and personal Estate, sufficient to pay and satisfyall the just Debts due and owing from him to his Creditors: That nevertheleft the said Hugh Naish,with Intent to elude the said Act of Parliament, and to cheat and defraud his Creditors of their just Debts, after such Notice to him and the said Warden of the Fleet given, and published in the London Gazette, as aforesaid, escaped out of the said Prison of the Fleet, and fled beyond the Seas, where he now re-fides; so that the Petitioners, and the other Creditors of the said Hugh Naish, are, by such Escape, prevented from obtaining an Assignment of his Estate and Effects, to be divided amongst them, according to the Directions of the said Act of Parliament: And therefore praying.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for veiling the real and personal Estate of the said Hugh Naish, to be assigned and equally divided, for the Benefit of his Creditors, in such manner as the same would have been liable, in case the said Hugh Naish had submitted to the Directions of the said Act for the Relief of insolvent Debtors; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as the House shall think fit.

private Expence, from cutting and felling Hides and Skins, in such Pieces and Parcels as are most fit for the various Artificers using the same in their respective Occupations; which will not only tend to the manifest Injury and Oppression of the Petitioners, but of great Numbers of his Majesty’s industrious Subjects: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation; and that Leave may be given to briDg in a Bill to explain and amend the said Statutes, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the said Collegiate Church came into the Hands of the First Dean and Chapter unfiniffied; and, by Length of Time, and Badness of Materials, became so ruinous, that, in the Eighth and Ninth of William the Third, in regard to its being of ancient and royal Foundation, an annual Sum, for a certain Term of Years, was granted by Parliament, towards repairing the fame, under the Direction of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Lord Chief Justice of the King’s Bench, and the Dean of Westminster, who were appointed Commissioners for that Purpose; and that, by an Act, passed in the Ninth of Queen Anne, a Sum' of Four thousand Pounds per Annum, for a certain Term of Ypars, was granted to the said Commissioners, towards; repairing arid fi milling the said Collegiate Church, and the (Chapels of the fame; and that, in order to the finishipg/of it.gs difefted by Parliament, Sir Wren, the then

Surveyor, formed a Design of ereaing a Spire in the mid-dleTower; a Model of which he' then prepared, and a Draught of which, with the rest of the intended Building, was laid before this House the last Session of Parliament; and that, by Acts, passed in the Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, and Tenth of his present Majesty, the several Sums of Four thousand Pounds, each Year, have been issued and applied towards carrying on the said Work; and an Account how the same has been expended has been annually laid before this House; and that all the Monies, granted as aforesaid, being expended, the said "Works are now at a stand; which the Petitioners fub-mit to the Consideration of the House; acknowledging the Favours already conferred on the said Collegiate Church, as well by the present as by former Parliaments: And praying for the Continuance thereof.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

The House divided.

Horse Ferry, in the City of WeflmuUleto the Town of

other Part adjacent, within the said Parish, may be a more convenient Situation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and determine, either by ascertaining a Place for the Situation of the Bridge, or by such other Methods as the House; shall think proper.

Sir John Norris re ported from the Committee to whom Dover and the Petition of the Commissioners appointed, by virtue of Ry®

the Acts passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Harbourt* Reign of his late Majesty King George, for relloring the Harbour of Rye, in the County of Sussex, to its antient Goodness; and also the Petition of the Assistants, incorporated for the Preservation of the Harbour of , whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, the Warden, and the rest of the said Assistants; were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same wa# read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, purfeant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petitions.

It appeared to your Committee, upon inspecting the Journal of the House of February 25th 1722, That a very full Evidence was, at that Time, given, with regard to the Ufefalness of the Harbour of Rye, and the Benefit arising therefrom to Trade and Navigation; which induced the then Parliament to grant certain Duties, mentioned in an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of his late Majesty, for restoring the said Harbour to its antient Goodness:

But a doubt arising. Whether the Duties, granted by that Act, were applicable to the making a new Cut or Chanel, from Winchelsea Chanel, right out to the Sea, and other Works, the Ufefufness and Conveniency hi generall whereof appeared to yonr Committee, from the Examination taken, and report thereupon made to the House, the 24th of February, in the Tenth Year of his late Majesty King George, an Act then passed, for explaining and amending so much of the said Act, passed in the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty, as relates to the opening a new Chanel from Winchelsea River, and for other Purposes in the said Act meritioned.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners proceeded to acquaint your Committee, how far the Petitioners had, in pursuance of the Powersgranted by the before-mentioned Acts, advanced in the Works intended; and what was (lilt further necessary to be done; for which Purpose they produced a Plan of the said new Cut, and intended Harbour: And then called,

L Mr.

38 mv.-j-j ' FebruariL

Mr. Edward Ruby Who had the Management of those Works underCaptain Pand the Care of them since his Death: And the said Mr. Ruby explained to your Committee the several Works that had been done; and, in particular said, That, at the Entrance from the Sea into the Chanel, there were erected two large Piers of Portland Stone, which were 6a Feet in Length, 27 in Breadth, and 120 Feet diflantfrom each other; and that they are already raised 18 Feet from- the Foundation; and it is proposed to raise them Six Feet higher. He likewise said. That, in the Middle of the said Chanel, there are Two Sluices made, with a large Stone Pier between them, the One of 40 Feet in Breadth, and 22 Feet deep. One of which Sluices is for the Passage of Ships, and to pen up the Water; and the other 34 Feet in Breadth, and of the same Depth, which is for scouring the Chanel, and therefore is narrower than the other, that the Water, which they are plentifully provided with from behind, may pome with the greater Force through the fame, and thereby more effectually carry off what i£ meets, with in its Course.

The laid Edward.Ruby also acquainted yo r Committee, That the Breadth of the Chanel, up to the Sluice, in the Middleof it, was 180 Feet, and from thenceup to the Winchelsea Chanel 140 Feet; and that the Depth

already dug was Eight Feet; but it was proposed, that itfhould be 16 or 18 Feet; which will make the Chanel 22 Feet deep in Water, when the Tide comes in: And that the Earthdug thereout, which will raise the Bank so high as to secure the neighbouring Lands from being overflowed, was laid at such a Dillance, that, if ever it should be thought necessary to make the Chanel wider, it might be easily made 20 Feet wider, on each Side, than it is at present.

He was then asked, What he thought would be the necessary Charge of completing the whole Work: Upon which he laid before your Committee an Estimate thereof, amounting t%£. 26,977, which, he said, was the Ioweft Calculation that could be made.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners proceeded to acquaint your Committee, What Money had been already raised for the Purposes afore-mentioned; and how the same had been disposed of: Upon which,

Mr. Thomas Cooke, Treasurer of Rye Harbour, was called; who produced an Account of the Money transmitted to him, from the Receiver General of the Customs, on account of the Duty granted for the Repair of the Harbour of Rye, from the First of May 1723, to the Firftof May 1737, which amounted to 20,736 igr. lojd.; which Sum had been duly and regularly laid out in the Repair of the said Harbour.

It appeared likewise, by the said Account, That the Treasurer had drawn £.719 8f. 1 id. more, on Account, from the Receiver General; and also that £. 5,600 had been borrowed on the Credit of the Duty granted, and was still due, and carried interest.

The said Mr. Cooke acquainted your Committee, That he had with him the Books from which he had drawn out the above-mentioned Accounts, and also the Vouchers for each Payment, ready to produce, if required.

It appeared to your Committee, That, in the Management and Disposition of the Money, granted and collected for restoring the Harbour of Rye to its antient Goodness, the strictest Care hath been taken, to prevent its being diverted or applied to any other Use or Purpose, than what it was granted for; for that no Money is ever paid, but by the Direction of Eleven Commissioners; the Accounts, for every Article in which Vouchers are produced, are annually examined, and signed by Eleven of them likewise; and afterwards examined and ligned by the Justices of the Peace, at their General Quarter Sessions for the County; and, at all publick Meetings of the Commilhoners, they defray their own Expences.

The Committee then proceeded to examine the Matter of the Petition of the Assistants, incorporated for the Preservation of the Harbour of Dover.

And it appeared. That, in the nth and 12th Year

of King William the Third, an Act passed for the Re- pair of Dover Harbour; and that a Duty of Three Pence per Ton, upon Ships and Vessels therein-described, was granted, for raising a Sum therein mentioned, for repair* ing that Harbour, as being of very great Use and Bene* fit to the Merchants of this Realm, and others, passing through the narrow Seas, to avoid the Dangers of Tem-pells, Pirates, and Enemies, in tiuqe of War; which iaft-tneotipned.Act, and tire Duties thereby granted, were, by. several subsequent Acts, further continued and made payable, till the Firli of May 1727: And the Sum granted by the firli-mehtioned Act proving insufficient forcompleting the said Harbour, and several other Works being found necessary to be done, for securing the ftyne, another Act passed in the Ninth Year of his said Majesty, for completing the Repairs of that Harbour, and for re-lloring the Harbour of Rye to its antient Goodness; by which; ACtthe said Duty of Three Pence per Ton was continued, till the Firli Day of 1744; One Third Part whereof is directed, by the said Act, to be applied towards repairing and securing the Harbour of and the other Two Third Parts are directed to go, and be applied, towards restoring the Harbour of Rye to its antient Goodness.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners for the Preservation of Dover Harbour acquainted your Committee, what had been done, in pursuance of the Powers granted by the before-mentioned Acts, and what was the present Condition of that Harbour, and what is Hill further necessary to be done. It appeared likewise to your Committee, That the Receipts and Payments of all Money received by the Treasurer, are annually examined at a Harbour Sessions, held in the Council House at Dover, and signed by the Warden, or his Lieutenant, and Assistants; and that those Accounts are afterwards laid before the Justices of the Peace for the County of Kent, at their next Quarter Sessions; and Oath is then made before them of the Truth thereof: And that a Duplicate of those Accounts, signed by Seven of the said Justices, is lodged in the Navy Office.

Were feveraDy presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by an Act of Parliament, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for making a con-

venient Dock or Bason at Liverpool, for the Secu-, rity of all Ships trading to and from the Port of Liverpoole, certain Rates, Tonage, and Duties, were granted for the effecting the fame, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, from and after the 24th Day of June 1710; which have been continued by another Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for enlarging the Time granted by the said Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the further Term of Fourteen Years; and that, by the said former Ad, the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Common-council, of the said Borough, and their Successors, are appointed Trustees, and thereby empowered to make such Dock or Bason, and to receive a Fourth Part of the faicl Rates and Duties, thereby also granted, for the Support thereof, so long as the said Dock or Bason shall be continued; and that the said Trustees have, as far as in them lay, carried on such Work, and made such Dock or Bason capable of taking in Ships, and erected and placed proper Land-marks and Buoys, for Direction of Ships into the Harbour, and laid out therein the Sum of Fourteen thousand Pounds and upwards, and been obliged to borrow a considerableSum more at Interest, on the Credit of the said Acts; but that, it is conceived, the same will not answer the good Ends and Advantages thereby intended, without an Addition for the light Ships to lie in, whilst refitting; nor can the Ships, which are outward-bound, and often put back by contrary Winds, and constrained to lie in the open Harbour waiting for a Wind, be preserved, without making of a Pier, which may be conveniently made on the North Side of the Entrance into the said wet Dock or Bason; for want whereof, many Ships, when detained in tire said Dock or Harbour, which often happens, and for a long time together, have been greatly exposed to the utmost Danger; and for tlrat the present wet Dock is found to be too i'mall to contain both the laden and light Ships, till dispatched and fitted out; and that such additional Works cannot be done and perfected, without taking up at Interest a further considerable Sum for that Purpose; and for that the present Term is scarce suficient to raise the Money already taken up and owing at Interest; and that such further Sum can-hot be raised under a long Tract of Time, in the manner appointed by the said several Acts, without a further Enlargement of the said Terms thereby granted, which, when done, will, in a great measure, take away the Hazard and Danger that the Merchant Ships, trading to and from the said Port, are frequently exposed to, and will be for the public Good; and that the setting up of proper Lights round the Bason may prevent, not only the Loss of many Persons Lives, that frequently happen in the Night, but the Running of Goods; and that the enlightening the Streets of the whole Town may prevent many Robberies and evil Practices committed by Persons unknown, who make their Ef-capes by the Favour of the Night: Therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for further enlarging the Time granted by the said several Acts; and for such Term, as by the House shall be thoughtmost meet; and for enlightening round the Bason where the Ships lie; the last mentioned Petitioners farther praying a Provision for enlightening the whole Town, with Power to afiefs the Inhabitants to defray the Expence thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Navigation, Inhabitants, of the Town of Hertford-, and of the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, in the County of Hertford-, and of several Farmers, Mai tilers, and Barge Owners, living in or near the said Towns, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and several hundreds of other Persons, residing near to, and concerned in, the Navigation on the River Leu, running from Hertford to Ware, and from thence to the River of Thames, near the City of London; and of the Governor and Company of the River, brought from

Chadwell, and Amwell, to London; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Navigation of the said River Lea is an antient Navigation, and hath been very useful to the Publick, by conveying great Quantities of Grain and other Goods to and from the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof; and that the Petitioners, the Governor and Company of the New River, have usually taken, and Hill take, great Quantities of Water out of that Part of the River Lea, which runs from Hertford to Ware, for supplying the said Cities, Suburbs, and Liberties thereof, with Water; touching which, many Disputes and Controversies have arisen between the Petitioners the Governor and Company, and the Navigators, and other Persons, concerned in the Navigation on the said River Lea, which have lately been accommodated; and that, although the Settling of such Disputes will be of great Advantage to the Publick, by ascertainingand improving that Part of the Navigation

on the River Lea, running from Hertford to Ware, and will very much improve the Navigation of that Part which runs from Ware to the River Thames, and enable the Petitioners the Governor and Company to supply the said Cities, Suburbs, and Liberties, with good Water, and tend very much to Increase of Trade; yet such Agreement cannot be established and made effectual, without the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaining, preserving, and improving, the Navigation of the said River Lea-, and to enable the said Governor and Company the better to supply the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, with good Water.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of divers Merchants, Planters, and others, Spani(J} . trading to, and interested in, the British Plantations in America, on behalf of themselves, and many others, was seas, presented to the House, and read, - setting forth, That Application was made to this House, in the Year 1716, against the many unjust Seizures and Depredations that had, for several Years preceding, been committed by the Spaniards in America, upon his Majesty’s Subjects, whilst they were carrying on their fair and lawful Trade in those Parts: Upon which Application this HousecamO to a Resolution, " That, from the Peace concluded at " Utrecht in the Year 1713, to this Time, the British " Trade and Navigation, to and from the several British " Colonies in America, had been greatly interrupted, by " the continual Depredations of the Spaniards, who " have seized very valuable Effects, and unjustly taken " and made Prize of great Numbers of Ships and

" Vessels in those Parts, to the great Loss and Damage " of the Subjects of this Kingdom, and in manifest Violation of the Treaties fubflfting between the Two " Crowns And that this House was pieased humbly to address his Majesty thereupon: And that the Spaniards continuing their Depredations on the British Subjects, and no Satisfaction having been obtained for those before committed, a further Application was made to this House, in the Year 1730, complaining of the great Interruptions given by the Spaniards to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom, and their cruel Treatment of the Bril if 1 Subjects: And that this House having again taken this Matter into their Consideration, and examined into the same with the utmost Deliberation,

Game to a Resolution, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, '"That he will be graeiously " pieased to continue his Endeavours to prevent the " Depredations of the Spaniards for the future; to procurefull Satisfaction for the Damages already sustained;

" and to feenre to the British Subjects the fliH and Uninterrupted Exercise of their Trade and Navigation, to and from the British Colonies vnAmerica:"WhichAd-

dress was presented to his Majesty accordingly: And re-prefehtihgto the House, That the Spaniards have paid so little Regard to his Majesty’s most gracious Endeavours, that they have continued their Depredations almost ever since the Treaty of Seoille;and, more particularly fall Year, have carried then* to a greater Height than ever; they having arbitrarily seized several Ships, with their Ef- feflts, belonging to his Majesty’s Subjects, on the High Sestd, in the destined Course of their Voyages to and frOrii the British Colonies, amounting to a very considerable Value r And that the Captains or Matters of feme of the said Ships were, according to the last Advices of the Petitioners, and are, as the Petitioners believe, ait this Time confined by the Spaniards in the West Indies, anti the Crews are now in Slavery in Old Spain, trhere they are moftinhumanly treated; and that that cruel Nat ion make it their Practice to attack and hoard all Merchant Ships they meet with, in the Ameri Seas, unde*- Pretence of searching for Goods, which they deem contraband or not, according to their own arbitrary Will and

Pleasure, contrary to the Law of Nation*, and in manifest Violation of the Treaties subsistidg between the' Two Crowns: And, that, by these unjust and violent Proceedings of the Spaniards, the Trade and Navigation to and from America is rendered veryunfafe and precarious;

insomuch that the Insurance from Jamaica has greatly risen, on these Accounts only: And that, without some speedy and effectual Remedy, the American Trade and Navigation will be, together with the Revenue of the Crown arising therefrom, very much diminished, if not entirely loft: And farther representing to the House, That although his Catholick Majesty has stipulated by the Treaty of Seville, and by the Declaration 1732, relative thereunto, tocause Reparation to be forthwith made to the unhappy Sufferers; yet there is no instance of its having been done; so far from it, that, whilst the British Subjefcts have been amused with vain and fruitless Hopes of Satisfaction, the Spaniards have committed further In-fults and Depredations upon them, and dill continue the same unjust Practices: And that the or Orders

given by the Court of to their Governors in -rica, are only calculated, as the Petitioners, by Experience, have great Reason to apprehend, to evade giving Satisfaction to the British Subjects; for there has never been one of these Cedulas complied with, nor any Governor recalled, nor punished for his Disobedience, as the Petitioners ever heard: And that, for any Nation to affumethe Power of detaining or rummaging the British Ships, upon their lawful Voyages in the American Seas, under pretence of searching for contraband Goods, is, in effect, as the Petitioners conceive, claiming and exercif-ing the foie Sovereignty of those Seas: And that, if the Spaniards be suffered to act in this injurious Manner, to insult the Persons of his Majesty’s Subjects, or to plunder them of their Property, the Petitioners apprehend the same will be attended, not only with a great Obstruction to this valuable Branch of our Commerce and Navigation, but also with Consequences very fatal to Great Britain itself: And therefore, and as the Measures hitherto pursued have proved ineffeClual, praying the House te take the Premises into their mature Consideration, and provide such timely and adequate Remedy, for putting an End to all Insults and Depredations on the British Subjects, as to the House shall seem meet; as well as procure such Relief for the unhappy Sufferers, as the Nature of their Cafe, and the Juliice of their Caule, require: and that they may be heard, by thein-selves and Counsel, thereupon.

A Petition of Samuel Bonham, Christopher AJlley, Ben- pmUh jamin Weal, Joseph Crowchtr, Owners of the Ship Ann Depredation* Galley, Joseph Spademan Master, Burden One hundred " and Thirty Tons, or thereabouts, on behalf of themselves, and the Mariners and Seamen of the said Ship, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Petitioners, on the 4th of December 1728, and since, have delivered to his Grace the Duke of Newcastle,

One of his Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State, Seven Memorials and Petitions, addressed to his Majesty, and Four others delivered at the Council Board; each Memorial and Petition setting forth the great Lofsand Damage the Petitioners have received, by the unjust Capture and Seizure of their Ship Ann Galley, and her Cargo, by the Spaniards, on the 13th Day of June 17 28, in her Way from Guinea to Jamaica, after the Pacification between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain was not only agreed on, but notified to the respective Governments in the West Indies; the same being notified at Jamaica the 3d of June, and at gena, in New Spain, the 1 oth of the same Month: And that the Value of the said Ship and Cargo, with the Freight, He.hath been attested, on the Oaths of the Master, and several of the Officers and People, belonging to the said Ship Ann Galley, when taken by the Spaniards, to be worth Ten thousand Five hundred Pounds Sterling, and upwards; besides the Loss of Interest for that Sum to this Time, being upwards of Nine Years:

In all which Memorials and Petitions, the Petitioners most humbly besought his Majesty’s Favour, Interest, and Protection, in recovering their Loss and Damage from the Spaniards; yet that, notwithstanding his Majesty’s Goodness, in endeavouring, by all peaceable Ways and Methods, to obtain Satisfaction for such their Loss and Damage, it plainly appears to the Petitioners, that those Cedillas are no more than Delusions, and shew of Justice; for his Majesty hath been graciously pleased to fend several Ships of War from , to demand

Restitution at St. Jago de Cuba; and, by his Minister, Benjamin Keene, Esquire, at the Court of Spain, hath made Demand of the said Ship and Cargo, or the Value thereof; and hath obtained several Orders from the King of Spain, and his Minister Don Joseph Patinho, to his Governor and Royal Officers at St. Jago de Cuba -,

One dated at Seville, the 28th of December 1730, One dated the 23d of Februari) 1733; wherein his Catholick Majesty allows the Ship to be an unjust Capture, and orders his Governor, Sc. to cause immediate Restitution to be made, without making any Reply to those Orders: And that, notwithstanding all this, and contrary, as the Petitioners apprehend, to the Second separate Article of the Treaty of Seville, and those made by his Majesty’s Royal Predecessors, and particularly the Fourteenth Article of the Treaty 1670, between England and Spain, and confirmed by the otherTreaties, particu-

larly that of Utrecht in the Year 1713, by which Fourteenth Article it is stipulated, that, if Justice is denied, or unreasonably delayed, it shall be lawful for that King, whose Subjects have suffered, to take any Rules and Methods, according to the Law of Nations, until Reparation be made to the Sufferers: notwithstanding his Majesty’s Goodness, noSatisfaction could be obtained: And that therefore, on the 17th of January 1733-4, the Petitioners again addressed his Majesty in Council; setting

forth

iiGeo. II. 3° Martii. 55

forth the Hardness of their Cafe: And that his Majesty, by the Advice of his Council, the 21st of February >733-4, did signify his Royal Pleasure to his Ministerat the Court of Spain, that he, in his Majesty’s Name, represent to the Catholick King, That his Majesty looks . upon himselfas obliged, by his Failure of Justice, in the West Indies, to his Majesty’s Subjects, to infill, that the Catholick King do forthwith cause Reparation to be made to the Petitioners for their Loss and Damage: On which another Order was forwarded to St. Jago de Cuba, to the Governor and Royal Officers, to make full Recti-tution for the said Loss and Damage; by which the Factors of the Petitioners, about 1734, received out of the Royal Chest at St. Jago, Two thousand Three hundred and Sixty Pieces of Eight, and Two Negro Men; the Value of which doth not exceed Five hundred Thirty-one Pounds Sterling: And that the Petitioners finding that nothing more is ever to be expected out of fheWest Indies, after Nine Years Solicitation and Expence, as appears by their several Letters, the Copies of which have, from time to time, as they came to Hand, been font and delivered at the Council Office, and to the Office 1 of his Grace the Duke of: Therefore, since

his Majesty was graciously pleased to lay the several Memorials and Petitions, relating to this, unhappy Capture before the House, the Petitioners, on the 24th of March 1736-7, brought their Petition into this House, which was read; and, on a Motion made, was ordered to lie on the Table: But that they have neither received, nor have any probable Expedations to receive, from Old or NewSpain, farther Satisfaction, than as before-mentioned, for this their great Loss, which is too severe and heavy for them to bear; and which is attended with this aggravating Circumstance, That the King of Spain hath agreed, that the Capture was unjust, and hath ordered Satisfaction to be made; but at a Place where Experience shews, by repeated Demands and Endeavours, it cannot be obtained: And therefore praying the House to take this their unhappy same into their Consideration; and grant them such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

But that no Relief being had thereupon, the Petitioners again petitioned his Majesty, in the Month of September lait; which was also delivered to his said Grace, and has been fincetransmitted to Mr. Keene; but no Answer being returned thereto, there is no Probability or Expectation of receiving any Satisfaction: And therefore praying the House, as the Measures hitherto pursued have proved ineffectual, to take the Premifes into farther Consideration; and grant such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet: And that the Petitioners may be heard, by . themselves and Counsel, thereupon.

of themselves, and other Persons concerned in the said Manufactures, throughout Great Britain, was presented to the House; and read; setting forth. That the great Quantities of Wool run to foreign Parts, from Great Britain and Ireland, and the great Quantities of Wool-

len Goods completely manufactured, which are exported from Ireland to foreign Countries, contrary to Law, is highly prejudicial to the Trade of this Kingdom, and the principal Cause of the Decay of the Woollen Manufacture: That, by this Means, Foreigners are enabled to work up great Quautities of their own Wool, by mixing it either with English or Irish; without the AlMance of which they could not make several Species of Goods, with which they now supply foreign Markets; and that the Petitioners are truly sensible of the Zeal of this House, and of the Laws already in being, to prevent the said mischievous Practice of exporting Wool, and Woollen Goods, manufactured in Ireland; but find, by fad Experience, that all Endeavours for that Purpose have been hitherto ineffectual: Aud therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to provide such Remedies, as to the House shall seem meet.

And it appeared. That, by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 8 th Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, certain Rate's, Tonnage, and Duties, were granted for the Term of 11 Years, for making a convenient Dock or Bason at Liverpoole; and that the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common-council, of the said Borough, were appointed Trustees, and thereby empowered to make such Dock or Bason, and to receive a Fourth Part of the said Rates and Duties thereby also granted for the support thereof, so long as the said Dock or Bason should be continued or kept up; which Rates and Duties were continued by another Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, for the further Term of 14 Years,1

: The Petitioners then proceeded to shew what had been done, in pursuance of the Powers granted by the afore-mentioned Acts,towards making the said Dock or Bason; and what was still further necessary to be done for the Security of Ships entering into the fame: To which purpose they called,

Mr. Ralph Peters: "Who, being examined, laid, That in making the said Dock, erecting Land-marks, and placing Buoys, for the Direction of Ships entering into the Harbour, upwards of £. 14,000 had been laid out; notwithstanding which, the good Ends and Advantages intended by the said Works were far from being answered: For that the Dock was much too small for the Number of Ships which come there, to lade and unlade in; and the Ships, that are put back by contrary Winds, and couftrained to lie in the open Harbour, waiting for a Wind, were frequently exposed to the utmost Danger, for want of a Pier to secure them from the Violence of the Weather.

He further said, That upwards of £. 4,000 was now owing, and at interest, for the Works already done; and that, to enlarge the Dock, and build the Pier, would cost £. 10,364, besides the £. 1,000 agreed to be given by the Corporation: an Estimate of the Charge of which he produced to the Committee.

Mr. Jonathan Slade, being called, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Peters, with regard to the Smallness of the Dock, and its Unfitness to receive the Number of Ships that come there, as well as the Dangers that Ships, lying in the open Harbour, are exposed to, for want of a Pier; an Instance of which he gave in himself, who had differed £. 40 thereby, very lately: And he further said.

That he had known Ships detained in the Harbour T'hree Months together, and 40 or 50 Sail of Ships at a tin^ driven up and down the River, not being able to get into the Dock; which Inconveniencies and Dangers the enlarging of the Dock, and the Building of a Pier, would greatly remove;. but that the present Term for that it was necessary to have the said Road well repaired, the Duties granted was so far from being answerableto for that it lies near, and leads to and from, Hitchin, those necessary Purposes, that it was scarce sufficient to Hertford, and Ware, Three of the principal Market-

Coal Admea- A Petition of several Persons, whoseNamesare there-furcment. untQ subscribed, keeping Wharfs, and dealing in Coals, in the City of London, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; fettingforth, That by an Act, passed in the Third Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the better Regulation of the Coal Trade, it is enacted, That all Dealers in, and Sellers of, Coals, by the Chaldron, or a lefsQuantity, in the Cities of London and and Ten Miles round the fame, shall conliantly keep and use such a lawful Bushel as is described by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty QxieenAnnc, for ascertaining the CoalMeafure; and that any Persons altering such Bushel should incur a Penalty of Fifty Pounds; and it is by the said Act declared, that every Wharf, Dock, Yard, and other Places therein mentioned, and wherein Coals were fold, should be the Place of Sale; and that the Coals are, and have been, conliantly measured there accordingly, by fuchMeafures as are described by the Acts aforesaid; and that the Petitioners having so done, apprehend, that they were not liable to a Re-measurement of such Coals so measured and fold; but that Coals, when delivered at the Houses of the Buyers thereof, will not, upon a Re-measurement, answer the first Measure, although measured with the same Exactness, by the same Person, and the very same Bushel; whereupon several Prosecutions have been commenced and carried on against some of the Petitioners under a Pretence, that their Coals, when fold, were not full Measure, that the Prosecutor might recover the Penalty of Fifty Pounds; which some of the Petitioners have paid; and that the said Penalty being so large, the Petitioners have Reason to believe, Persons have ordered Coals to be sent to their Houses, and, after secreting some Part thereof, have sent for Meters to measure such Coals again, that there might be a Foundation to commence a Prosecution thereupon: and that, unless the said Act, of the Third Year of his present Majesty be explained, the Petitioners, and all Dealers, and their Families, may be ruined, and have it not in their Power to prevent the fame: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Act of the Third Year of his present Majesty, so far as it relates to the Measuring of Coals, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premiles as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, Nemine contradicente. That the said Petition be rejected.

A Petition of the Heritors, Merchants, Burgesses, Inverness Brewers, Victuallers, and Inhabitants, of the Royal Burgh rio'VII of Inverness, thereto subscribing, was presented to the House, and read; complaining of the Exaction and Misapplication of the Duty of Two Penies Scots, granted by Parliament, on each Pint of Ale and Beer, brewed, vended, and retailed, within the said Burgh, and Liberties thereof, for the Space of Nineteen Years, commencing from June 1719; and alleging. That the said Burgh, exclusive of the Returns of this Gift, has a yearly Revenue of Two hundred and odd Pounds Sterling, which may appear more than sufficient to defray the ordinary and necessary annual Expence of a small Borough; and that the Debts of the said Town, at this Period, do, in several Hundred Pounds, exceed the Extent of the Debt thereof, when this Gift commenced: And that their Ministers, having far above competent Livings, according to the Laws of Scotland, the Managers of this Place begun with making some small Additions thereunto; but allowed the Debts of the Town to increase; not one Two Penies being bellowed on adding to, or repairing, their Churches:

And that there was, before the Commencement of the said Gift, a Harbour for Shipping in the said Town, which, to this Day, is the Harbour frequented, and is well situated, as their River runs; and, by a small Expence, not exceeding Two hundred Pounds Sterling, would have been made abundantly commodious and convenient for more Ships and Trade, than this Place had before or since, or could well look for: And that the other Harbour, devised by the Magistracy, is useless, the Proje&ors having quite mistaken the Situation thereof, both according to the Run of the River, and the ordinary Course of the Winds there for Two Thirds of the Year; and the Mole thereof having Angles, and other irrepa-rableFaults, that make it uniafe for Ships; and, iffinished according to the Design, not capable to accommodate Five Vessels, to load and unload regularly; and that, since its Bason was red, and is almost finished, the Resort of Ships, trading to this Place, is to the old Harbour, as the most safe and commodious; and that the best Use which can.be made of it, is to have Sale made of the Stones that compose it, which the Petitioners believe would return Three hundred Pounds; which Sum, rightly applied, would make the old Harbour good and sufficient: And that the exacting of this Gift has brought a Number of Families to Ruin, anddedroyed the Credit and Circuiustances of the greater Part of the Town: And

that,

that, at the Commencement of this Gift, the Neighbourhood were fond of Dealing with the Inhabitants, and very sure of prompt Payments; but that now it is the lleverfe; there being few Brewers that can have the least Quantity of Barley, from any within Reach of the Town, without Bail; Two Thirds of the Malt Barns being fallen down to the Ground; and the Trade - in Malting, which was a very considerable Branch of the Trade of the Town, being so decayed, that the yearly Return of this Tax, which, immediately after the Commencement of it, extended to betwixt Four and Five hundred Pounds Sterling, if not more, does not now, nor has, for some Years past, exceeded One hundred and Forty Pounds; and that his Majesty’s Revenue of Malt Tax and Excise have decreased proportionably, as this Tax is levied from the Brewers: And that there has been no Account of the Returns, or Application of the Monies, arising from this Tax, exposed by the Magistrates, to the Overseers named in the Gift, lince the Month of 1732: And that the

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition of the Curriers, and other Dealers in Leather, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Merchants trading from Liverpoole Spanish De-to the British Plantations in America as presented to predations the House, and read; setting forth. That Application I^"enc*a was made to this House, in the Year 1728, and again in the Year 1730, complaining against the many unjust Seizures made, by the Spaniards in America, of the Ships belonging 10 his Majesty’s Subjects, whilst they were carrying on a fair and lawful Trade to and from the British Colonies, during the Course of some Years preceding: And that, notwithstanding the said Applications, and all the Endeavours his Majesty has been graciously pleased to make use of since that Time, the Spaniards have been so far from making any Satisfaction for the Losses then complained of, as sustained by the Petitioners, and others his Majesty’s Subjects, that they have continued the said Depredations almost ever since; and, of late, have carried them on to such a Height, as gives great Interruption to the Trade of the British Subjects to those Parts: And that the audacious Practice of the Spaniards in boarding, detaining, and searching, all the British Ships that fall in their Way, in the American Sea, under colour of looking for contraband Goods, the frivolous Pretences on which they carry away, and condemn, as Prizes, many of the said Ships; the barbarous Treatment Sailors meet

with from them in such Cases; together with the extravagant Advance of late made in the Premiums oflD-furance, on account of these Insults; these are such Dif-couragements, as must render the American Trade very precarious; which, without some effectual Remedy, will soon be greatly diminished, if not entirely loft to this ' Nation: And therefore praying. That the House would be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration, and make use of such Measures, as to the House shall seem most fit, not only to put an End to the Insults and Depredations complained of, for the future, but also to obtain such Satisfaction for past LolTes sustained, as the Justice of the several Cafes of the unhappy Sufferers shall appear to deserve.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House to whom the Petition of divers Merchants, Planters, and others, trading to, and interested in, the British Plantations in America, ,on behalf of themselves, and many others, is referred.

That by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of Derwentwaler, and Charles Radcliffe, the said Estates are continued vested in his present Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, with the Appropriation of the Rents, Issues, and Profits, thereof, for the Use and Benefit of the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, according to the Direction of the said Act, for such Uses, and subject to such Incumbrances and Claims, as are contained in the said Act; and that some Doubts have been raised by the Tenants of some of the said Estates, whether any Fine or Sum of Money was due and payable on the Death of the last Lord, he being an Infant at the time of his Death, and not having been seen by the Tenants, or on the Death of every of the said Tenants which ftnee hath happened ;and, as the said Premises are vested in his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, in their politick Capacity, which, in Consideration of Law, never dies, whether the said Tenants ought to do such Acts and Services, and pay such Fines and Sums of Money, on the Death of his present Majesty, or on the Death of any future King or Queen of this Realm, as, by the Tenure of their Estates, founded upon immemorial Custom, they ought to have done, and perfomed, and paid, on the Death of any Lord thereof; and that the said Estates are not vested in his Majesty, and bisSuccessors, for his Majesty’s private Use, but in Trust only.

and that the Interest of the principal Money due thereon is partly at the Rate of Five Pounds for One hundred Pounds, and partly at the Rateof Six Pounds for One hundred Pounds, for a Year; and that it will be a Benefit to the said Hospital to have the Money at a left Rate: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, or rendering more effectual, the said Act, in such manner as the House shall think fit.

That the said Manufactures have been, of late Years, greatly improved, and considerably increased; and, if proper Encouragement was given to the fame, might be brought to equal (which they do now in some Sorts), if not excel, the like Manufactures of foreign Fabrick, imported into Great Britain; whereby the Consumption thereof would be increased at home, as well as extended to Parts beyond the Seas; to the great Benefit of this Kingdom; as some Thousands of useless Hands, who now want Business, might be employed in such Manufactures; and that the said Manufactures now labour under several Discouragements; but more particularly on account of the Drawbacks allowed on the Exportation of foreign Linens and Threads; by means whereof considerable Quantities are sent to Parts beyond the Seas; to the great Hinderance of the Consump-tiou of the Produce and Manufactures of this Kingdom; And therefore praying the House to take

the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Heretors and Freeholders of the County of Perth, North Britain, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, for themselves, and in Name of the other Gentlemen of the County, was presented to the House, and read; letting for*h, That the Manufactures of Linen and Threads in North Britain, and particularly in that County, have, of late Years, by the Encouragement of the Legislature, been greatly improved, and considerably increased; whereby many poor Families have been provided in a comfortable SubfiHence; and that there are several Thousands still living in extreme Poverty, and Burdens to their Country, who might become useful Members of Society, by being employed in the several Branches of thefe Manufactures, if they urere carried on to the Extent they are capable of, by the farther Favour and Affiliance of the Legislature; but that the said Manufactures now labour under several Discouragements; more particularly on account of the Drawbacks allowed on the Exportation of foreign Linen, Threads, Sic.; by means whereof considerable Quantities are sent from henceto the British Plantations, to the great Hiudrance of the Consumption of our own Produce, and thereby likewise the Balance becomes to be greatly in favour of those Countries from whence they are exported, whereas,* if the Consumption at home, and the Markets abroad, were supplied with Linens, Threads, &c. of the Manufacture of these Nations, good Part of that Balance would rest in our Hands, and it would add so much more Wealth to the publick Stock of the Kingdom: And that, as the carrying on of the Linen Manufactures towards Maturity and Perfection is of great Consequence to the Nation in general, so it is of the greatest Moment and tail Consequence to this County in particular, in regard the Product of these Manufactures is the principal, if not the only, Fund the Farmers have left, for paying their yearly Rents to their Mailers, and the Manufacturing of Linen and Threads is the principal Branch of the Trade of the Market Towns in the County; and there are great Quantities of Yarn carried annually out of this Shire, which, if manufactured in the County, would enable the Petitioners to employ great Numbers of idle and poor People; and not only to supply our home Consumption, but also to fend good Quantities of our Linen to Markets abroad; And therefore praying the I lonfe to take the same of the Linen Manufactures under their Consideration, and give such Encouragement thereto, as that they may be carried on with the greatest Vigour, and to the utmoll Extent.

And the said Petitions were severally-ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants of the City of Iwndon, and others, Dealers in the Manufactures of Linens, Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, be received.

Sir John Ttamfden reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of the Clothiers, Makers of Kersies, Plains, and other narrow Woollen Cloths, whoseNames are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other Clothiers, Makers of such narrow Cloths, in the West Riding of the County of was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, in purfnance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee, Three several Acts of Parliament, of the Seve nth and Tenth Years of her Kite Majesty Queen Anne, and also of the First of his late Majesty King George, to prevent several Frauds and Abides committed by the Makers and Dealers in the Woollen Manufactory; which were federally read: And then the Petitioners called,

Mr. Edmund Bothomley: Who being examined, said. That he knows and is very well acquainted with the Trade of the Woollen Manufactory, in the West Riding of the County of York;and that divers Frauds and Abuses

are committed by the Makers and Dealers there, in the Manufacturing of the narrow Woollen Cloths, occasioned by the stretching the said Cloths on Tenters, after the same is taken out of the Mill, which is a great Disadvantage and Prejudice to the fair Trader: And if Searchers and proper Officers were appointed by Law, to prosecute such fraudulent Traders, it will be a Means to prevent the said Frauds being committed.

That if any private Person should give any Information against such fraudulent Traders, in order to have them prosecuted, they would incur the Displeasure of the several Clothiers; and that he has often known the narrow Woollen Cloths stretched Two or Three Yards, and never any Prosecution carried on against any Person for the fame.

Upon the w hole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Bejolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in Force, relating to the narrow Woollen Cloths, are not sufficient to prevent the several Vot. 23.

Frauds and Abides' committed by the Makers and

> Buyers of fitch Clpths.

Hefolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the better regulating the Manufacture of narrow Woollen Cloths, in the West Riding of the County of

York.

The first Resolution, being read a Second time, was agreed to by the Houie,

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating the Manufacturbof narrow Woollen Cloths, in the West Kiding of the County of York:

And that Sir John Ramsden and Sir John Lifter Kaye, do prepare and bring in, the fame.

The Petitioners laid before the Committee an Act, pasted in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for employing the Manufacturers, and encouraging the Consumption of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, by prohibiting the Wearing of Buttons and Buttonholes made of Cloth, Serge, or other Stuffs; which was read: Then the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Clayton: Who, being examined, said. That he computes there are near Thirty thousand People, in the Places mentioned in the Petition, employed in Making of Silk and Mohair Yarn, and Thread Buttons, and Button-holes, with the Needle, and in preparing the Materials whereof such Buttons and Button holes are made; and that raw Silk and Mohair Yarn are the greatest Part of such Materials: That the said Manufacture hath, through the Encouragement from time to time given by Parliament, greatly increased; but, of late, is very much decayed: That it always afforded a great Supply and Relief to the numerous poor Families in the Places before-mentioned, and the Parts adjacent; and is the principal, and almoll only, Manufacture, whereby they are chiefly employed: And that some Sort of Buttons are made at so low a Price as an Halfpenny per Dozen, and not less than One thousand Pound per Week has been paid in the Places aforesaid, by the Traders, to the Button-makers, for the Working of such Materials, which are chiefly purchased from the Turkey Merchants.

Mr RichardDuhorty, being examined, said, That he

is a Trader betwixt the Merchants and the Manufacturers of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, which are bought from the Italianand Turkey Merchants, and East India Company; but the Mohair Yarn from the Turkey Merchants only: He further said, That a great Deal of the Horse-hair, used in Making of Buttons, is imported from Flanders.

Mr. James Lock, and Mr. Henry March, being severally examined, said, That they import large Quantities of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, and that the Woollen Manufactures, and other Merchandizes, the Produce of this Kingdom, are exported to Turkey, in Exchange for such raw SilkandMohair Yarn: ThatNine Parts in Ten of the Goods so exported are Woollen Manufactures: That the Factors and Dealers in London buy such raw Silk and Mohair Yarn from them, which, they believe, are sent to Macclesfield, Stockport, and Congleton, in the County of Chester, and Leek, in the County of Stafford.

They further said, That if there was a sufficient Demand for Mohair Yarn, and other Goods, the Produce of Turkey, they could fend consideraMe Quantities more of Woollen Cloths, and other the Manufactures of this Kingdom, in Exchange for the fame, but that the French export greater Quantities of their Woollen Manufactures to that Country, than the do.

Mr. Samuel Lankford, being examined, said. That there are different Sorts of Buttons, some wove and some covered with Stuff of different Sorts, some Mohair, some of Silk and Mohair, and some of Thread and Mohair, some of Horsehair, and some of Horfahair and Silk; That, of late; and at this Time, narrow Breadths'or Slips have been, and are foil, woven in a Loom, in the manner of Caniblets, Grograms, and other Stuffs, hut of a smaller Breadth; and that, under Colour thereof, as he Delieves, more Buttons are covered with Shreds of Cam-blets, Grograms, and other Stuffs, than.are really woven in such narrow Breadths; and that there is no knowing the Difference betwixt the Button covered with such *3

woven narrow Breadths or Slips, and those covered with the Shreds of Camblets, Grograms, and other Stuffs, without the Cutting of the Cover of the Button from the Mould; several Specimens whereof they produced to your Committee.

He further said. That he believes One Loom will weave as much as Eight or 10 Persons can work with . the Needle, in the same Time; and that they can em-

floy Six or Eight in the Needlework Way, at the same 'rice as One Weaver at the Loom: That working the Buttons in the Needle Way, is chiefly carried on by antient and decrepid Men and Women, and by Children, that are incapable of any other Labour: And that he has seen the Weavers of such narrow Breadths or Slips at Work in the Loom several Times, and never knew or heard of any more than One Breadth at a Time worked in a Loom; and that such Looms are like the Ribbon Looms.

Mr. Jonathan Gurnell, being examined, said.
