The Petitioners then proceeded to shew how much further the said Manufactures are capable of being extended in Britain and Ireland, with proper Encouragement; and what Advantage would arise from it:

But, in order to explain this, your Committee think it proper to state to the House the several Duties now payable upon foreign Linens imported, and the Drawbacks allowed upon Exportation thereof.

There was granted by the Act of Tonnage and Poundage, passed in the 12th Year of King Charles the Second, and continued by several subsequent Acts, a Subsidy of all Goods and Merchandize imported, of the Value of every 20.V. of the same (according as they are rated and valued in the Book of Rates, to which that Act refers). Twelve Pence, and so after that Rate.

And in that Book, Linen, called and Sitejia

Cloth, broad, white or brown, is rated, the Hundred Ells, containing Six Score, at £. xo os. o; Linen, called Hamboro' Cloth, narrow, is rated, the hundred Ells, containing Six Score, at £. 8 os. o and Linens, called Ozenbrighs, the Roll, containing 1,500 Ells, at FiveScore to the Hundred, at £.60: And such of these Linens as were not above Three Quarters and ah Half broad, were to be accounted narrow Linens; and all above that Breadth Were to be accounted broad; and to pay accordingly:

And the Rates there affixed, upon Incle unwrought, this Pound, is zs. 6d.; Incle wrought,theDozenPound, £.8;

Incle Rolls, the Dozen Pieces, containing 36 Yards, £. & os. od.-. Thread, whited-brown, the Dozen Pound, £. 4 os. od.; Raw Linen, Dutch Yarn, the Pound, £.0 1 s. od.: Aud One Moiety of the Subsidies, so to be paid

upon each and every of the said Goods imported, was al j lowed as a Drawback upon Exportation of any of them.

By an Act, passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, afurther Subsidy was granted, and by subsequent Acts continued, upon all Goods and Merchandize imported; to be rated according to the former Rates: And a Drawback of the whole Subsidy was to be allowed upon Exportation of* any of the Goods before enumerated.

By an Act, passed in the 2d and 3d Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, an additional Subsidy was granted, of One-third Part of the several and respective Duties by the said former Acts imposed, or either of thetrt; which Duties have been since made perpetual: And wherp any Drawbacks were made of the whole, or any Part of the said Duties, a proportionable Drawback was to be allowed, by that Act, of the whole Duties thereby granted.

And Mr. Buckannan, being examined in relation to this Matter, said. That the Ojnaburgh Linen pays, upon Importation, 13$. 4 d.upon every Hundred Ells; and the narrow Germany pays the fame, only that the Hundred contains Six Score, which lessens the Duty 20 per Cent.; lor which Reason few , under that

Denomination, are entered inwards; and that, under the Denomination of narrow Germany, no Distinction is made in the Entry between the white and the brown: That the Drawbacks upon Exportation of foreign Cloths in general, on an Average, are about 10 per Cent, and on the brown Sorts about 14 per Cent, j which comes to about 1 fd. per Ell:

That the Prices for Linen used for Cloathing the Negroes, as bought for Exportation here, with the Drawbacks taken off, are, from 5 J to 7 an Ell, and may be reckoned 7 dper Ell upon an Average in general; which is at the Rate of 8*d. for Home Consumption: That, with the Allowance of this Drawback, foreign brown Linens are fold, in the Plantations, between 6 and £.j. per Cent, cheaper than the British or Irish.

And that, without this Drawback, British and Irish Linens would be then fold, near Six per Cent, cheaper than the foreign: And he said, Th'at, with proper Encouragement, sufficient Quantities of Linen might be made in Great Britain and Ireland, in a fewYears time, for the Service of the Plantations, in lieu of the coarse Germany, now used there; and that, he apprehended, if the Drawback was discontinued, 19 Parts in 20 of the Cloth sent to the Plantations would be British and Irish: That, in Scotland, Plenty of Yarn may be spun, proper for making Goods of the Species of brown Linens, for the Plantations, of the same Nature of that which is now made up into Harns and Buckrams; there being great Plenty of Flax and Tow, and great Numbers of Spinners, to spin it into Yarn, who are capable of spinning any fort they fee; That the Reason, why they do ' not make the coarse Sorts, is, because that the Drawbacks of i-f d.perEll, allowed on foreign Linens, causes them to be sold cheaper: And that those Goods are chiefly fit for the Wear of Negroes, and not for Consumption in England:

That, as to the Benefits which would accrue from further extending the Linen Manufacture, he said, That Great Britain and Ireland would, by that means, be able, in time, to supply our Home Consumption, and that of the British Plantat ions, and to undersell the and

French, with respect to their Linens, in foreign Markets;

Being alked, In how long a time this Manufacture could arrive to such a Maturity, as to undersell foreign Linens in the Plantations, he said. He apprehended, in a Year, or a little longer; and that he was confirmed in his Opinion from what had happened formerly, in an Instance which he related to be as follows:

That, about the 10th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, a Duty was laid upon checked, striped, and other Linens imported, and the coarse bi own German Cloth, used for Buckrams and filleting*, were adjudged liable to that Duty; upon which a Manufacture was fct up in Vot. 23.

Scotland, of such a Sort of Cloth, and great Quantities Liiwn were made; insomuch that though, upon Application to Manufacture. Parliament in One or Two Years after, the Duty upon that Species of foreign Cloths was taken off, yet the Peo- , pie in Scotland made so great a Proficiency in their Manufacture, that they have continued it ever lince, and the Germans could never regain that Trade; and he doubted not, but that their success would be the same with regard to the Ojnaburgh Linens.

He was alked. Whether an Increase in One Branch of these Manufactures must not occasion a Decrease in some other

He said. He did not apprehend it would; because there were great Numbers of Hands sufficient to carry it on, who are now unemployed: On the contrary, he thought it would prove an Encouragement to increase the Whole; and his Reason for thinking fowas, because; that then the Weaver, who had Yarn by him, could fell his coarse brown Cloths at Market in Two or Three Weeks, and, by that means, be enabled to keep his fine Cloth on Hand, till the proper Season of the Year for Bleaching: And that, if the presentDrawback was taken off, Persons of Fortune, both in Great Britain and Ireland, would then set up Manufactures of coarse Linens; fit for the Purposes of the Plantations: And he added.

That had foreign Linens, Ten Years ago, beeu imported Duty-free, neither the British or Irish Linens, as he apprehends, would have had any Vent at London Market; nor would there, in that Cafe, have been any Linen Manufacture in Great Britain.

He was then alked. If this Drawback was taken off, how far it might affect the Plantations?

Heanswered, That it might perhaps increase the Price of Linen a little at first; but that it would be such an Encouragement towards the making those Species, that, in Twelve Months time, they would be as cheap, if not cheaper, than ever; and that, as Linens had fallen 10 Cent, within these EightYears, and the Drawback, on an Average upon the whole, was 10 per Cent, they would not be dearer in the Plantations now, supposing the Draw* back taken off, than they were Seven or EightYears ago.

Being alked. To what Value the Linen consumed by a Negro amounted to in One Year; and what would be the Advance of the Price of his Clothing in that time, supposing the Drawback was taken off

He said, That a Negro might consume One or Two Shirts, of about 2 or 3*. Value: But that in many of the Plantations, particularly in the Islands, they are allowed little or no Linen, except those employed in Houses; for that such as labour in the Fields are cloathed with Kendall Cottons, and Woollen Goods:

That in Virginia and Maryland, where the Witness some time resided, the Negroes, who work abroad, wear little Linen, by reason of the Necessity there is of keeping them warm in the WinterSeafon; which makes them choose to have Woollen Cloaths next their Skin, rather than Linen: That their Waistcoats and Hose are thick Welsh or Kendall Cottons, and their Coats coarse Cloths:

And he said. He believed it would have been an Advantage to the Woollen Manufacture, had coarse Linen been dearer, and the Negroes cloathed with Woollen Goods only: That he computed, that Three Yards of the Ojnaburgh Linen is more than sufficient to make One Shirt for a Negro; and that the Advance in the Price of the Cloathing of each, upon a Medium of the W hole, would amount to about 3d. a Head.

Being examined, as to the Quantities of the Ojnaburgh Linens consumed at home;

He said, That he believed the Consumption of the brown Germany was very little; but that of the white

Sort might be near Five Parts in Six of what is imported: That in the Course of his own Business, Five Parts in Six of the Fort ign Linen he exports is brown: And he hath observed, upon the Inspection of Accounts relating to that Matter, That not a Sixth Part of the German Linens imported has been exported to the Plantations.

Being a/ked. If the Reason, that the coarse Sheeting remained on hand, was not owing to its being made of a worse Quality than formerly

He said. That some Part was made worse, to answer the Price the Di apers would give; but that large Quantities were imported of the best Fabrick that ever was made; and that all the inferior Part was fold.

Upon his being a/ked, if he could give a Reason, why Osnaburgh Linens, charged with the Duty, were fold for Home consumption, preferable to Linens of the same Quality?

He said, it was because those Linens had Two Markets; and such as would notfuitthe Home Consumption, might he exported, and allowed the Drawback; and that, he apprehended, Seven Parts in Eight of the Osnaburgh Linens imported, were again exported; and the Drawback upon these Species being higher, in proportion to their Value, than what is allowed on any other Sort of Hamboro' Goods, therefore, if any Quantity of the same Sort of Goods was to be made in Ireland, they miuft be exported, under the Discouragement of that Drawback; but that, be apprehended, the Irish Linens are cheaper than the foreign for Home Consumption; he having been informed, by several retail Drapers, that they get greater Profit by the Sale of them, than ’ Linens.

He was then a/ked, Why the Preference was given to foreign Linens, when Irish Linens are cheaper

To which he answered. That there were several Gentlemen, and Men of Fortune, in , wholesale Dra-

pers, wiio ever did, and ever will, discourage the Sale of our Home Manufactures of Linens; because it is their undoubted Interest so to do: That foreign Linens, being made up in large Package, and Variety of Sortments, Vol. 23.

cannot be easily parted by the Importer, without making the Remainer unfaleable; and, as the Quantities are too large to be bought by any but themselves, they, by being the Purchasers of those large Cargoes, have the Custom of the retail Drapers in London, and the Shopkeepers all over England, for those foreign Goods:

That the British and Irish Manufactures are not made up in this maimer, therefore may be fold in small Quantities by the Importer, without Prejudice to the Sale of the Remainder; so that the wholesale Drapers do not purchase those Manufactures in any Quantities proportionable to what they purchase of the foreign; and they do not scruple to say That they tnuft discourage the one, and promote the other, as much as lies in their Power; for that, /hould the Home-made Linens be in as great Demand as the foreign, the Consequence would be the Loss of their Trade, by reason their Customers would be supplied by the Importer, fts cheap as themselves.

He added farther, That it was for this Reason, that the Sale of the British and Irish Linens were confined chiefly to so narrow a Compass as the retail Drapers in London; and to this Cause it is owing, that a largerStock of Home-made Linens remains on hand, than bath been known before, some having lain unfold Three or Four Years.

Mr. Adair said. That, in Great Britain and sufficient Quantities of Linens, equal to Ofnaburghs, might, with proper Encouragement, be made in a Year or Two’s time, to serve the Uses of the Plantations: That many Persons would then set up the Manufactures of those Linens: And the Witness said. He should hio self undertake to have them made:

That there are Quantities of Yarn spun in Ireland, fit to make Linens to answer the Purpose of those called Crocuses-, and that there are Linens of that Sort made, as well as of Ofnaburghs iand that, in Two Years time,

there might be had Yarn in Ireland sufficient to make Linens to Supply the Plantations; there being large Quantities now spun, and made into Sheeting:

That Encouragement is more necessary to this Branch of the Linen Manufacture than any other, it being the properest to Employ Learners; but, as there is no great Consumption of coarse Linens in , in proportion

to what is exported, there is not the same Encouragement for bringing them to; because no Buyer

will give the same Prices for Linens which cannot be exported, as they will for those they have Two Markets for; and, from this Cause, a Detriment arises to the Home Consumption of other British and Irish Linens:

That he knows but One Merchant Importer, who deals in foreign Linens, that imports any considerable Quantity of Irish; but that there are some few Lineu Drapers, who import Irish Linens as well as foreign.

Being a/ked, if great Quantities of Flax is not annually imported into Ireland He said. There was very little, except in those Years when their own Crops proved Bad: That the foreign Flax was chiefly imported from London; and was, he believed, the Produce of the

East Country: That the Irish Flax is generally the most proper for fine Linen; but that, in all Flax, there is some Part that is coarse; and the Prices of such as is imported vary, according to the Goodness of their own Crops; and that their own Flax is sometimes fold cheaper than any foreign can be imported.

Mr. Armjtrong said, That, of late Years, many Protestant Schools are instituted in several Parts of That the Boys are chiefly trained up in the Cultivation of Land, and the Girls in preparing Flax, and spinning Yarn, proper for the Goods now wrought up into Sheeting: That the Trustees for the Linen Manufactory of Ireland annually distribute Flax feed, and Uteufils made use of in spinning Yarn and Weaving of Linen, to the Value of some Thousand Pounds, by way of Encouragement; and, by means of that A Alliance, the Manufacture is extending into several of the Southern Provinces, which heretofore was carried on in the Northern Provinces only:

Frauds in Cold and Sil.

ver Warts. Sir Francis Child reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Goldsmiths, of the City of London, wa* referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee an Act of Parliament, passed in the 28th Year of the Reign of King Edward the First; whereby it appeared, That no Goldsmith is to make any manner of Vessel, or other Thing, of Gold or Silver, except it be of good and true Alloy; and that no manner of Vessel of Silver is to depart out of the Hands of the Workers, until it be affayed by the Wardens of the Craft, and marked with the Leopard’s Head; which Wardens are likewise thereby irapowered to go from Shop to Shop among the Goldsmiths, to assay their Gold: They then called,

Mr. Joseph Ward, Assay-master of Goldsmiths Hall,

and Mr. Thomas Banks, Clerk to the Company of Gold-

smiths: Who, being examined, said. That, notwithstanding the Powers given by the afore-mentionecfAft, there had been no Searches made for these lati 12 or 15 Years; and that there were no Wardens now living that had ever made a Search: The Reason of this Dif-continuance of Searching was, as they apprehended, and had heard, from the Opposition the Wardens uiuaily met with in executing that Power: And, in order to shew the ill Consequences arising from the Goldsmiths being thereby exempted, in a manner, from the Inspection of the Wardens of the Craft, they called,

Obadiah Welfted, Richard Vincent: Who federally produced to the Committee several Pieces of Plate by them purchased at Shops within the Cities of London and Westminster, foine whereof had no Marks at all upon them; and others, as appeared by the Evidence of the above-named Mr. Joseph Ward, Assay-master, had counterfeit Marks stamped upon them.

The said Mr. Ward being asked, If a Alark could not be taken out of an old Piece of Plate, and put into a new one, so as that the Fraud should not be discovered?

Said, It might be easily done, and in such a manner, as to deceive a Person not versed in the Business; which h’rs Evidence, in this Particular, was confirmed by Mr.

Welfted and Mr. Vincent.

It appeared further, by the Evidence of Air. Welfted and Mr. Vincent, That the several Pieces of Plate, by . them produced, had, since the Parchafe of them, been assayed at the Tower-, and that the same had been found greatly deficient: And they produced to the Committee the particular Deficiency of each Piece of Plate; which was in feme very great, and in others less.

The Petitioners then proceeded to shew what had been the Produce of their Assay Office for feme Years last past; and what the Expence of keeping it: To which

Purpose they called,

Adr. Thomas Banks, Clerk to the Company: Who laid.

That it had formerly been usual for the Com|>any to take Four Grains per Pound Troy, for allaying and marking Silver Plate; felt that, for these 20 Years last past, they had taken Six Grains for large Plate, Six Pence a-piece ferSword Hilts, Three Pence a-piece for Snuff Boxes, and other small Sums of Money for other finall Wares by the Piece. He then produced an Account of the Produce and Expence of the Assay Office, for the 20 Years ending the 29th Efoy of May last past, during which Time the advanced Prices were taken; whereby it appeared, on a Balance for the whole ao Years, that the Company had been in Disburse by the said Office £.950. 17 s.6d. including the Rent for the Aflayer’s House and the Assay Office.

Linen A PETITION of the several Persons, whose Names Manufacture, fl are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, tand many Thousands concerned and employed in the Manufactories of Linen Cloth, wrought Incle, Threads, and Tapes, made in the Borough of Preston, and Parts adjacent, in the County Palatine of Lancqfier, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Manufactures have produced a comfortable Support to many Thousand poor Families employed therein; but that the same now labour under great Discouragements, by reason of the Drawback allowed on the Exportation of the like Manufactures of foreign Fabrick; by means whereof considerable Quantities are annually exported to Parts beyond the Seas; which has greatly prevented the Exportation of the Manufactures of Linen Cloth, wrought Incle, Threads, and Tapes, made in those Parts: And therefore praying the House to take the Vot. 23.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Farmers, Masters, Workmen, and others, of Ashburton,in the County of Devon,

in behalf of themselves, and other Persons concerned, throughout Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the great Quantities of Wool run to foreign Parts, from Great Britain and Ireland, is highly prejudicial to the trading Interest of this Kingdom, and the principal Cause of the Decay of Trade; by which means Foreigners are enabled to work up great Quantities of their coarse short Growth, by mixing it with English or Irish Wool; without the Assistance of which they could not make several Species of Woollen Goods, with which they now supply foreign Markets: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to provide such Remedies as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Freeholders, Serge-makers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Ta-vistock, in the County of Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, ami read; setting forth, That, for a considerable Time past, the Woollen Trade in this Borough and Neighbourhood hath been in a very decaying Condition; which, the Petitioners think, is, in a great measure, owing to the great Number of Spinning Houses which have been, within these few Years past, set up in the Country Villages around the Petitioners; whereby the Dealers in Wool set out certain Quantities to the Poor, to be spun at a very low Price, allotting, instead of Sixteen Ounces to the Pound, Eighteen or Twenty Ounces; which is never brought into the publick Market to be weighed, where there are Scales, and proper Persons to attend to fee Justice done: And that such Dealers frequently, instead of prompt Payment in Money, oblige the Spinners to take Goods at an extravagant Price, by way of Barter, contrary to the Laws now in being; whereby the poor People are much oppressed, and consequently the Yarn not so well spun as it should be, and the Serges not so good as formerly; which hath, of late, occasioned the Returning of many Pieces from abroad; all which do manifellly tend to the Destruction of Trade, the Oppression of the Poor, and the ruin of all Market Towns in that Part of the Kingdom, that depend mostly on the Sale of white Yarn, commonly called white Shute: And therefore praying the House to give such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Wardens and Assistants, and the Lawsrefpcft-rest of the Company of Cordwainers, in the Town of ingtauned Shrewsbury,in the County of Salop, whose Names are Leather-#thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many other Manufacturers of Leather, inhabiting the said Town; and of many other Cordwainers, and other Manufacturers of Leather, living in the neighbouring Market Towns,.Villages, &c. in the said County of Salop, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Petitioners find, by the Votes of this House, that a Petition hath been lately presented by the Curriers of the City of London, and some other Dealers in Leather, therein complaining, that should they be hindered from cutting and felling Leather, Hides, and Skins, in such Pieces and Parcels as they should think proper, it would be highly injurious and oppressive to them, and great Numbers of his Majesty’s industrious subjects; and praying the Consideration of the House; and that Leave might be given to them to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the several Statutes now in Force, and mentioned in their said Petition: And therefore repre-fenting to the House, that not otily the Curriers in and about the Town of Shreivsbury, and other Towns, Villages and Places within the said County of Sabp, Imt al-fofevefal others of them, living in other Cities, Towns,

Boroughs, and other ^Places of this Kingdom, have, for many Years past, endeavoured tofupplantthe Petitioners Trade, and monopolize the Leathern Manufacture to themselves, not only by buying up all Sorts of Leather, which they do not, nor can, manufacture, but all’o by cutting and felling the same in such small Quantities and Parcels, as will only make a Angle Pair of Shoes, Slippers, Clogs, or other such small Article, as well to Journeymen Shoemakers, Clogmakers, and other Journeymen and Workmen in the said Leather Manufacture, who are not Mailers or Freemen of any of the said Trades, to make up into Wares, as also to any other Person whatsoever that will buy the fame, in order to be made up by such the said Journeymen; and thereby such Journeymen are encouraged to work, in a clandestine manner, for their Mailers Customers, when they might fully and conllantly be employed by their said Mailers; and, by that means, the Mailers Work is not only laid afideand neglected, bnt Customers disappointed, and oftentimes the Mailers Goods changed, at the Pleasure of such the said Journeymen, to the great Detriment of the said

Mailers,

Mailers, by canting their Custbihers to leave their Shops: And that the Petitioners apprehend, that a farther Explanation of the said Statutes, or Extension of the Laws how in being, and a further Liberty thereby to be given to the Curriers, to cut and fell all Sorts ofl-eather, Hides, and Skins, in such small Quantities and Parcels as before mentioned, without any Restriction, or other Liberty, than is by the said Statutes already granted, will tend to the utter Ruin of the said Petitioners, and other Manufacturers of Leather, and many Thousands of poor People, who get their Livelihood under them, and the Vert, of the Cordwainers and Manufacturers of Leather in this Kingdom: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into mature Consideration; and that the said Petitioners may have Leave to be heard, either by themselves, or Counsel, what they have to offer against the Allegations contained in the Curriers said Petition, at such Time, and in such Manner, as the House shall please to appoint} or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the said Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

L*orsre(pc&» A Petition of several Master Cordwainers, living jcgtauued within the Town of Birmin, in the County of War- *' trick, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and all others of the same Trade or Pro-session, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Trade or Occupation of the Cordwainers of this Kingdom hath, for several Years, been encroached upon by the Curriers, by their cutting of Leather into Pieces, contrary to the Laws yet in being, till of late deterred from such Practice, by several Prosecutions carried on with Success against some of them: That the cutting of Leather by Curriers, and their felling the same in Pieces, hath been found veiy injurious to the Trade of the Petitioners, and other Master Cordwainers; for their Journeymen or Servants, whoseldotn work in their Mailers Shop, have thereby had constant Opportunities of defrauding their Mailers, by buying Leather from the Curriers, of lefsValue than the Leather put into their Hands by their Mailers to be worked; or converted by such Journeymen, and uling the same instead of their Mailers Leather, which they privately convert to their own Use, to the great Damage, as well of the Customers, as of the Trade of the Petitioners, and other Mailer Cordwainers: That the Petitioners have been informed, that the Curriers had applied to the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for impowering them to cut and fell Leather in any Town or Corporation in England: And that the Petitioners apprehend, that, by the Palfing of such a Bill into a Law, the Cutting of Leather, which is reasonably secured to the Cordwainers by the present Laws, will be almost monopolized by the Curriers; and the Trade of the Petitioners, and all other Cordwainers within Eng, very much damaged; and that many Hundred Families, who now subsist by the Help thereof, will be in great Danger of being totally impoverished: And therefore praying that the Petitioners may have Leave to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

And the said Petitions were severally referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition of the Curriers, and other Dealers in Leather, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, is referred; who are to examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the Hojlife.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The House resumed the adjourned Consideration of the said Report.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to impower Landlords or Leffors, in the Day-time, to break open and enter into any Place locked up, fattened, or otherwise secured, wherein Goods and Chattels, fraudulently or clandeliinely carried away by Tenants, shall be put; and to seize, for Arrears of Rent, such Goods and Chattels.

And the said Clause was twice read, and amended.

Then the said Clause was, upon the Queliion put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to oblige Tenants, who, after having given Notice of*

,their Intention to quit the Premises by them holden, at a certain Time, shall not accordingly at such Time deliver up Possession, to pay an additional Rent from thence^ forward.

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks $ which were filled up; and the Clause amended.

Then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

And the said Clause was once read; and, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

And several Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be

ingrossed.

Mr. Thomas Godfrey, Captain Robert Rogers, Captain Robert Saunders, and Captain JolmThomas, were called; who, being severally examined, said, That it was cuf-toniary for the British Merchants and Factors, residing in several Port6 of Portugal, Spain, and Italy, to raise annually among themselves Sums of Money towards defraying the common and ordinary Ekpence* in Support of their Privileges, the Relief of the diipwreckod and otherwise diltressed Mariners, and for other pious and charitable Uses.

That the British Merchants, residing at , had

accordingly, from a Seufe and Experience of the Cfeful-n^(s of the said Practice, raised Sums of Money, and applied the same to the Purposes aforesaid; but that the Number of Ships coming to the Port of Genoa, and, with them, the Objects of Relief, were, of late Years, so i . , . greatly increased, that it was irnpofiibleto raise Money adequate to such an Increase of Expence, by voluntary Contributions.

They further said, That the Inability in the' British

Merchants to raise such Sums of Money, was attended with particular llardships to the Factory, as well as prejudicial to the Pnbliqk in general; for that the Spaniards were always at Work to seduce the English Sailors to their Service; and tlwit many of them were accordingly got over into the Spenish Service, merely because there was a Want of Relief among their own Countrymen j and their NecefiUy therefore obliged them to embrace it, where they first could get it: A particular Ioftance of this was given by

Captain John Thomas; who said, That, in the Year 1719, be was taken by the Spaniards, and carried to Genoa -, and that Four of his Sailors, for Want of necessary Relief at Genoa, voluntarily entered on board the Privateer that took him.

Regulating Mr. Cholmondeley reported from the Committee to the Cheese whom the Petition offeveral Gentlemen and Land-owners ra e* of and in the County Palatine of Chester, on behalf of themselves and their Tenants, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matterof the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table-: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz. The Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, Benjamin Bruen Esquire, John Rigley, and Richard Lamb, were called: Who, being severally examined, said, That very great inconveniencies and Losses arose to the Farmers from the present manner of Dealing with Factors for Cheese; for that the Factors generally make their Contracts in such a private and clandestine manner, that the Farmers cannot prove the fame; so that the Factors weigh the Cheese, take it away, and pay for it when they please; and the Farmer, though he has agreed on particular times for those Purposes, has it not in his Power tocompel a Performance thereof; and that, though the Factors agree to weigh the Cheese at a particular 18

time, itistifual for them to exceed that time feveraf Months, and the Cheese, in the mean time, loies very much in the Weight, which turns to the very great Loss of the Farmer:

And they further said, That, though the Factors agree to take the Cheese away at a particular time, it is usual for them to exceed that time several Months; and, by reason of the Contract, the'Farmer cannot dispose of the Cheese to any other Person; and if, in the mean time, the Price of Cneefe drops, it is usual for the Factors to leave upon the Hands of the Farmer a great Part of the Cheese contracted for; pretending, that it is damaged; as perhaps sometimes it may; but that, if it had been taken away at the time agreed on, such Damage would have been either prevented, or, if not prevented, would have been the Loss of the FaCior, and not of the — Farmer.

They also said, That, though the Factor agrees on a particular time to pay for the Cheese, he frequently exceeds his time several Months, vv hereby the Farmer fullers very much, and the Landlord is kept out of his Rent.

They further said. That the Factors frequently deal beyond their Commission; and that the Farmers know not One in Twenty of the Mongers for whom the Factors deal; and that many Farmers have been ruined, and others have sustained very great Losses, thereby.

They likewise said, That the Contracts are seldom or never reduced into Writing, and are made in such a private manner, that it is impossible for the Farmer to prove the fame; who therefore is without Remedy: But that/ they apprehend, it would greatly tend to remedy the said inconveniencies, if the Contracts were always reduced into Writing, and the Factors obliged to declare what Mongers they acted for.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Cheese Trade in the several Counties of England and Wales: And that Mr. Cholmondeley, Mr.

Wat kin Williams Wynne, Mr. LeveJ'on Gower, Colonel Cholmondeley, Mr. Crave, Mr. Brereton, and Sir Walter Bagot, do prepare, and bring in, the fame,

Sir Thomas Clarke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Hertford; and of the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, in the County of Hertford-, and of several Farmers, Maltsters, and Barge Owners, living in or near the said Towns, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several Hundred of other Persons, redding near to, and concerned in the Navigation, on the River Lea, running from Hertford to Ware, and from thence to the River of Thames, near the City of London; and of the Governor and Company of the River,

brought from Chadwell and A to London; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners Agents laid before the Committee,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, for the Bringing of the River of Lea to the North Side of the City of London-, and also, an Act, passed in the Third Year of the Reign of King James the First, for the Bringing in of a fresh Stream of running Water to the North Part of the City of London-, and also One other Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of the said King James, for Explanation of thelaft-mentioned Statute; which Aftswereread:

And by the first-mentioned Act, a Power, is given to the Lord Mayor, Commonalty and Citizens, of the City of London,to begin and continue the Laying out of such convenient l imits of Ground, for the Making of a Trench for the said River, at such Breadth, and in such Manner, as is and are particularly described in and by the said Act: And a Power is by the said Act given to the Lord Chancellor, or Lord Keeper, for the Time being, at the Request of the said Lord Mayor, Com-xponalty, and Citizens of the said City, to appoint and authorize, by Comnyfiion under the Great Seal, Sixteen Commissioners; Four to be of the City of,

and the other Twelve to be of the Counties adjoining to the River of Lea -, viz. Four of every of the Shires of Essex, Middlesex, and Hertford, or some of them, not being Citizens of London, using the Trade of Merchandize; which Sixteen Commissioners, or the more Number of them, had thereby full Power and Authority to treat, agree, and compound, with such Num-Jbers of Freeholders and Inhabitants of the said Counties, as to them should seem meet and convenient, for the fcouffhg, cleoofing, repairing, and keeping, the River Lea, from fuph Place where the new River or Cut should have tire Beginning, to the Town of Ware, in such fort, as that the same should be navigable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels;

And, by the Second Act before-meatioped, a Power *9

is given to the Lord Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of London, and their Successors, to make a new d rench for conveying Water from Chadwell and to the

City of London-, and to maintain the same when made; And that they might, from time to time, flop all Breaches at their own Charges, and sufficiently maintain them and make a Recompence to the Party or Parties grieved, for the Damages they should sustain by such Breaches; And that the new Cut, Stream, or River, when fmiflied, should be subject to the Commission of Sewers; and the Scouring, Cleansing, Amending^ and Conservatiou of the new River or Cut, should be at the only Cost and Charges of the Mayor, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of London:

And, by the Act, of the Fourth of King James, the Mayor, and Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, were further empowered to make a Trunk or Vault in the Earth of Brick or Stone, not exceeding Ten Feet in Breadth, for the Passage of the Water from Chadwell and Amwell to London-, which they were for. ever to maintain and preserve.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine Witnesses; and

Mr. Bojlock Toller, being called, said, That he appeared as Agent for the Petitioners the Corporation and Inhabitants of the Town of Hertford, and also for the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, and for the Navigators on the River Lea-, and that he, about Five Years ago, was directed by those Petitioners, to inquire what Right the New River Company had to take so large a Quantity of Water out of the River Lea, as they con-flantly did; and, about Two Years and an Half since, he came to the Knowledge of the fame.

He produced, and laid before the Committee, a Copy of an Order of Council, bearing Date the 2 2d Day Of Septembei' 1669; by which it appeared to the Committee, that several Disputes had formerly been between the New River Company, and the Maltsters and Barge-

mailers of Ware and Hertford, in relation to the Conveying of Water out of the River Lea into the New River; and the Matter in Difference between them having been laid before the King and Council in the Year 1607 and 1668, an Order, dated the 22d of September 1669, was made by the King and Council; a true Copy whereof was laid before the Committee; wherein it is recited.

That the Matter in difference between the Governor and Company of the Corporation of the New River, and the Maltsters and Barge-masters of Ware and Hertford, concerning the Conveyance of Water out of the River Lea into the New River, had, by Order of the 15th of that Month, been appointed to be heard the 2 2d of September 1669; and that the Parties concerned attending accordingly, and being called in with their Counsel, and Two several Reports (One signed by Six of the Referee?, to whom, among other things, the Matter in Difference had been, by Two several Orders of Council of the 16th of October 1667, and the 29th of July 1668, referred to settle the lame, if they could, or otherwise make report to that Board; the other signed by Fifteen Commissioners of the Sewers for the River Lea and the New River, residing in the County of Middlesex, to whom the same Matter had been also referred, by the Order of the 28th of August then last) being read, as also several Depositions of Witnesses, and other Evidences; and by hearing Counsel on both Parties, as also Counsel for the City of London,in behalf of the Navigation of the River

of Lea, and long Debate had thereupon;

His then Majesty, taking iutohis princely Consideration, as well the great Use and Benefit of the Navigation of the River Lea, not only to the City of London and County of Hertford, but also to the adjacent Counties, as the Necessity of l'upplying the City of London with the New River Water, was then graciously pleased,

in Council, to order.

That the Governor and Company of the New River should take away the great Pipes then lying in the River

Lea, and, inllead thereof, should lay Two ieffer Pipes,

the

11 Geo. II.

17* Mar til

the one of Eight and the other of Six Indies Bore, at or near the Places where the great Pipes lay; and to place and contrive them, that they might be constantly served with Water to supply the New River: And if, upon Trial, it should be found, that the Water in the River Lea would not always rife high enough to 611 the said Pipes, that the Governor and Company might, and they were thereby authorized to set up and use a Turnpike, Jetty, or some other Device, to raise and force the Water to the Pipes, whereby they might be render* ed most useful to the New River; yet so, as might not cause Inundation of the Meadow-grounds adjoining, nor retard nor endanger the Vessels that should pass that Way: And thereof all Persons concerned were to take Notice, and to conform themselves thereunto accordingly, as they would answer the contrary at their Peril:

And Mr. Toller further said, That, when he had collected all the Facts together, he recommended it to the Inhabitants of the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and the Navigators, to take the Opinion of some eminent Coun-fel: Whereupon a same was dated; a Copy whereof was laid before the present Lord Chancellor, then his Majesty’s Attorney-general; and anotherCopy before the late Lord Chief Juliice Reeve -, and they both advised. That, as the same was a publick Concern, proper Application should be made to the Legidature; and, thereupon, he waited on the New River Company, from time to time, by Directions of the Persons he was concerned for, that an amicable Agreement might be entered into.

DoCtor Dejegulieis, being called, and examined, said, That, in August 173.5, he was Cent for into the Country, by the Navigators on the River Lea-, but did not know for what Purpose: That, whild he daid there, he measured the Gage, or new-made Indrument, belonging to the New River Company, through which the whole Water passed out of the River Lea-, and found that Indrument to measure Six Feet wide, and Two Feet deep, and the Top thereof to be 28 Indies above the Cill at the Water-house; and then he tneafured the Quantity of Water below the Gage, and found, that, it run about 2,400 Tuu in an Hour, with small Allowance for the Eddies: That, on the 28th of the same Month, he went down again; and, not truding to the 6rd Experiment, he then made several others, in presence of many Persons of the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and of one Mr. Mill,a Gentleman belonging to the New River

Company, who also made a Calculation; and that, aftermaking several large Allowances, He found the Quantity of Water, diverted or taken out of the said River, to be 2,100 Tun per Hour.

He also said, by the Pipes, which were directed to be laid down by the before-mentioned Order of Council, about 200 Tun of Water an Hour would be taken out of the River, the Surface of the Water being jud over the Pipes; but, if the Pipes were square, 250 Tun of Water per Hour would be taken out:

And he further said,' That the Fall of that River is very considerable; and, if a Coirtpensation was given for eroding of Locks, and making other Conveniences for the Navigation, not only that Quantity of Water which is now taken, but Half as much more might be taken without any Prejudice to the Navigation.

Mr. Thomas Petit and Mr. James Barge-

owners, being severally examined, said, That they had known the River Lea^ the one 45, and the other 47 Years; and that there is a great Difference in the Navigating of Boats and Barges now, than when they first used the River;

That formerly they navigated to and from London to . Ware, in a considerable less time than they now do, and at a much less Expence; and the Reason they gave, was because the Lock-keepers cat the Weeds, which makes 4he Waterto run quicker away, and thereby the River becomes more ih.allow; and great Quantities of Gravel and Stones being thrown into the River by the Weir-keepers and Millers at the Weirs, occasions so many Shoals, that they cannot now pais without paying, at Vol. 23.

the several Locks, for Flaibes of Water frequently in the foyer tea Summer Season, by reason great Quantities of Water are ^av^gatl0*< taken out of the River, for the Use of the New River. c’ Company; and, for those Reasons,theWitnesses said; that the Navigation is become very tedious and expensive.

They also said, The Owners of Boats and Barges, and Navigators, had raised amongd themselves the Sum of £. 3,000, which had been expended in removing of Shoals; which, if so large a Quantity of Water had not been taken away, and such Shoals thereby made, they should not have been at so great an Expence: And that, before the Weed6 were cut, and Gravel and Stones thrown into the River, the Boats and Barges, when they got below Waltham Abbey, were frequently towed to Old Ford, without any Obstruction, or the Affiilance of any Weirs; which cannot now be done.

And they likewise said, That there had been, in their Memory, Two Commissions of Seweis taken out, in re* lation to this Matter; and, during the time the Commissioners fat, and executed the Powers given them by those Commissions, the Navigation was carried on much easier, and at a less Expence, than at other times.

And they feveratly added to their Evidence, That if a Fund was established for removing the Shoals, and constant Commission of Sewer established, it would make a double Recompence for the Water now taken out of the River by the New River Company; and that the several Nnifances complained of would thereby be remedied, and such a Quantity of Water as is now taken out, be the better spared.

Mr. Toller, being again called, said. That the River Lea is divided into Two or Three Branches between the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and write again into One Stream a little below Ware Mill; That the ancietft and right Way of navigating Boats and Barges between the said Towns, was, and is, through One of the said Branches, called Manifold Ditch; but the Navigation is now carried on, and has been, for many Years past, rorough another Branch of the said River, called the Mill Stream, running to Mills, and from thence through a Lock or Cistern there, into the main Stream, running to Ware Bridge; but this Navigation is carried on by Agreement between the Navigators and the Owners of Ware Mill, but may be refused by the Owners of that Mill; and, if they Ihotild, the Navigators muff have recourse to their ancient and right Way, through Manifold Ditch; which will oblige the New River Company to pull up their Turnpike or Jetty erefited cross the fame, for conveying the Water they now take, which is now agreed they may take out of the said River Lea -, whereby the Company will be less able to supply the Cities of London and Westminster with the Quantity of Water they now do;

But, that the Company may be enabled to supply the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, the Company have agreed to purchase Ware Mills, and the Lock belonging to thfe fame, with the Stream of Water running to the fame1; and to declare, That! the Stream through the Lock there into the main River,shall be the indisputable right Way for navigating Boats and Barges, for the future, between Hertfordand Ware: And when the fanrie shall be so purchased and declared, the Navigators have; on their Part, agreed to reiintjoilh all their Right and Title to the Navigating of Boats and Barges through Manifold Ditch; by which the Company will hare the sole Use of the Turnpike or Jetty already erected; and will thereby be the better enabled to supply the said Cities of London and Wefminger, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof,

with good fresh Water.

Prohibition A Petition of the Manufacturers -of raw Silk, and of Stuff Mohair Yarn, and Needle-work Buttons, and of the Buttons, &c. Traders and Dealers therein, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rell of the Manufacturers, Traders, and Dealers, as aforesaid, in the Town of Sherborne, and the Parts adjacent, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, through the Encouragement given by-Parliament, from time to time, as occasion required, the Manufacture of Needle-workButtons, hath for many Years been, and now is, the principal Branch of Trade, whereby great Numbers of poor Families in the said Town, and Parts adjacent, have altogether subsisted; and that great Quantities of Stuffs, made of Horsehair, or mixed therewith, and of several otherMaterials, have been woven in narrow Breadths or Slips, and used only for Making and Binding of Buttons and Button-holes, under Pretence that the same are not such Stuffs whereof wearing Garments are usually made, in Evasion and contrary to the Intention of the said Acts; and that Advertisements have been published, and industriously handed about, to encourage the Ufeand Wear thereof; and that some of such late-invented narrow Stuffs, being made mostly of the same Materials with Camblets, Grograms, Barragon, and otherStuffs, whereof wearing Apparel is made, it is impossible, even for the nicest Judge in the Button Trade, to distinguish the Buttons made or covered therewith, from those covered with Camblets, Grograms, Barragons, and other Stuffs, used in wearing Apparel, without first cutting off such covered Buttons from the Cloaths whereon they are set or sewed; and it is therefore very difficult to ground a Prosecution against many Offenders against the present Laws: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that this Hopfe will take the Nature of their same into Consideration; and that the Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for employing the Manufacturers, and encouraging the Consumption of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, by prohibiting the Wearing of Buttons and Button holes made of Cloth, Serge, or other Stuffs, may be so explained and-amended, as that the Petitioners may be relieved in the VoL 23.

A Petition of the Manufacturers of, and Dealers in, woven Buttons and Button-holes made of raw Silk, Mohair Yam, and other Materials, in and about the Cities Buttonl* c of London and Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themfel ves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in case the Bill, now depending before the House, for explaining and amending an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for employing the Manufacturers, and encouraging the Consumption, of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, by prohibiting the Wearing of Buttons and Button-holes made of Cloth, Serge, or other Stuffs, should pass into a Law, it will prevent the Petitioners, and many Thoufartds of his Majesty’s industrious Subjects, manurafturing wbven Buttons and Button-holes made of raw Silk, Mohair Yarn, and other Materials, whereby they now maintain themselves and Families, and be a Means to reduce them to extreme Poverty; the Weaving Trade being greatly lessened in most of its Branches, and they having no other Way of getting a Livelihood; and will be injurious to the Publick, as well as to the Dealers in the said Manufactures: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the B’ll to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for employing the Manufacturers, and encouraging the Consumption, of raw Silk and Mohair Yarn, by prohibiting the Wearing of Buttons and Button-holes made of Cloth, Serge, or other Stuffs, and making the same more erteftual, be read a Second time.

And, being examined, said.

That, by the Works carried on by the Magistrates in and about the New Harbour, it is now made more commodious than before:

That there is a greater Depth of Water in it than in the old Harbour, by Three Feet and more:

That, according to his Judgment, it will take £.2,000 to complete it, according to the Scheme:

That the new Harbour is more resorted to by Ships of Burden than the old Harbour; and the new Harbour is very safe to load and unload in:

That it is capable to contain Ten or Twelve Ships, and believes it will contain Twenty when iinished; and that the old Harbour dannot contain any Ship of 160 Tons, or upwards; and that, for Three Years past, he has not seen any Ship of 100 Tans in it:

That John Reid's Brigantine was hurt in the new Harbour, by falling over against her Heeld, as was re-j>orted, and broke her Ribs on the Pier; but it might be owing to the Negligence of the Pilot Or Seamen *.

That, in or about the Year 1724,30 or 40 Men have been employed, and at Work, in cleansing the old Harbour; which occasioned a considerable Expence:

Mr. George Ro/i, being examined, said, That, by the Works carried on by the Magistrates, in and about the new Harbour, it is now made more commodious than before; which was confirmed to him by the Opinions which he had from moll of the Merchants of in the Conversations he has severally had with them at that Place: That there is a greater Depth of Water in it, than in the old Harbour, by Three Feet and more: That it was but about half completed:

That the old Harbour lies upon Gravel; and, being higher up the River, the Currency thereof is apt to throw up Stones therein; whereas the New Harbour is of a soft oozy Bottom:

That he heard of Complaints made, by reason of an Angle in the Pier of the new Harbour, which was the Fault of the Architect; but that this will be in some Measure remedied when the Scheme is prosecuted and completed; and that, by the Situation of the new Harbour, it is free from the Danger of being filled up with the Gravel carried down by the Floods or Frefhes of the River: That it is built of Free Stone, of Seven or Eight Feet long, laid with their Ends outwards; but, if not-completed, would be of very little Use.

And both Mr. Frafcr and Mr. said. That what they have proved was according to their own Knowledge and Opinion, and also according to the Opinion of Merchants who have been at Sea, and of Seafaring Men, who have seen and known these Harbours.

William Robertfon, being examined, said, That the said new Harbour is, by the Works carried on by the Magistrates, rendered more commodious than before; That it is (bore resorted to by Ships of Burden than the old Harbour, and is very lafe to load and unload in: And further said. That he has lately sent down to a

Ship with Goods, which he ordered to lie at the new Harbour, by reason of its being more commodious; and that it can contain Five or Six Ships to load and unload in.

To prove the Allegations of the other Petition of the Heretors, Merchants, Burgesses, Brewers, Victuallers, and Inhabitants, of the Royal Burgh of Inver~ nej's,thereto subscribing.

They called James Gumming; who said. That it is the general Complaint of the Town, that, since the Year 1719, Malt-barns and Malt-kilns have gone to Decay, to the Number of Two, or Three, or Six, , as he believes; and he has often heard Malfters complain of the Duty: And that several of the Brewers and Retailers of Ale, to the Number of Two, have, since the Commencement of this Duty, gone out of Town, to other Parts where

the Duty did not take Place, and gave that as the Reason; but he could not give the Name of any One, or say whether they were of the most considerable, or meanest Sort.

' And, being asked whetherthere was any other Reason for the Decay of Trade; he said.

That the Smuggling Trade was another Reason given for the Decay of Trade at Inverneft; and believes the Persons who dealt in such Smuggling Trade were undone.

And, being further examined, he said.

That some of the People, who were the most considerable Dealers in Trade, have quitted the Town, by reason of a Resolution in their Affairs.

Alexander Af‘Bean being examined, said, That, since the Year 1719, he knew Two or Three Malt-barns and Kilns gone to Ruin, and thinks it was owing to their not being used: That the Duty was One of the Reasons why the Maltsters employed in those Bams gave up Malting; but does not know if it was the only one: That* his own Father is a Maltster and Brewer, and Rill continues his Business: That the Maltsters and Brewers are* generally the same Persons; and that, in this Town, he thinks there may beThirty Maltsters, and Forty Brewers: That these People who dealt most considerably in Trade, and are now failed, employed great Numbers of People in the different Branches of their Service; and their removing out of Town is a Reason for the Diminution of the Consumption of Provisions; and that the Decay of Trade was owing to the Smuggling Business.

David Munro said, That he knew the old Harbour of Inveme/s in the Year 1720: That he knew it to have had 12 Ships at a Time, of which One was of 120 Tous, but none of the rest were of that Burden; and, at another Time, saw a Ship in it of 200 Tons, but could not say whether Ihe was loaded or light: That the Tide comes into the old Harbour: and, at the furthermost End of which there is a Hole or Sluice, to receive the Exuberancy of the Tide; for that otherwise the Ships would lie upon the Keys, or be overflowed; and he has heard, that, notwithstandingthis Hole, the Keys have been overflowed: That the Soil of the old Harbour is oozy; and, so far as he heard, not apt to be turned up by the Currency of the River: That there is a Sort of Rock that* lies at the Mouth of the old Harbour; but that he knew nothing of the new Harbour, having lived at London for 16 Years last past.

And, with respect to the Opinions of Seafaring Men concerning this Harbour, he offered to produce to the Committee a Memorandum;'or Minute/of such Conver-. fation as he lately had wittfTwo Seafaring Men, whose Ships were then at Gravesend,'concerning this Harbour;

which, nevertheless, the Committee would not admit.

William Macbean being examined, said. That the Two Harbours are 80 Yards distant one from the other: That the old is nearest the Town, and an Outlet in the far End thereof, which conveys the Tide Half a Mile up the River: That the Soil of it is not apt to be turned up by the Currency of the River, so far as he has observed: That he has seen 12 Ships at a Time in the old Harbour, as near as he could judge; and the Jargeft of them of 100 Tons Burden, or 20 or 30 more; but cannot julily say above 100: And that. Nine or Ten Years ago, there was more Shipping in the old than in the new Harbour;* but said. That the new Harbour was not brought to the Perfection it is now in, till about Five or Six Years ago: That some little Repairs have been made to theold Harbour: That the Soil of the new Harbour is gravelly, and apt to be turned up by the Currency of the River.

But, in Answer to the Questions put to him severally, having said. That the new Harbour was more removed out of the Currency of the River than the old Harbour was; and that the River did not run through the new Harbour; he was again asked, How the Soil of the Harbour could be turned up with the Currency of the River ? He said, That the Flowing of the Tide might raise the Soil.

That the Petitioner is informed that a Bill is now depending in this House, intituled, An Act for exemplifying the last Will of Arthur, late Earl of Angle-fey, and for making the same Evidence in all Courts of Law and Equity in Great Britain and Ireland; and that the said German Pole having married One of the Daughters of the Lady Elizabeth Geere, who was Sifter of the said Earl, is intitled, under the Statute of Distribution, in case the said Earl shall appear to have died intestate, to a Third Part of the said Earl’s personal Estate, in Right of his said Wife, who is One of the next of Kin to the said Earl: And that the said German Pole lives One hundred Miles and upwards from London; and had no Notice, as the Petitioner verily believes, of the Bill now depending, until the Petitioner sent him Notice thereof, on the 16th of this instant March: And that Francis AnneJleykLiqmre, claims the said personal Estate, or great Part thereof, under the said Will; which Will, as the Petitioner verily believes, the said German Pole hath good Reason, and doth deiign, to litigate, as by Law he is now intitled to do, notwithstanding the Probate thereof obtained by the said Francis Annejley, in common Form; and that the Petitioner is advised. That the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will preclude the said German Pole from such Litigation of the said Will, and all his Pretensions to the said personal Estate: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pais into a Law, or that a laving Clause may be inserted therein, in behalf of the said German Pole Esquire; or that the Petitioner may have such other Relief as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into Consideration.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr and

Mr. John Bennett:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed lo the Bill, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty of Two Pennies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Penny Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer, which shall be brewed for Sale, brought into, vended, tapped, or fold, within the Town of Aberhro-thock, and Liberties thereof, without any Amendment. A Petition of the Traders in Gold and Silver Wares, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Mystery of Goldsmiths, of the City of London, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill, now depending in this House, for the better preventing Frauds and Abuses in Gold and Silver Wares, seems to be grounded upon Suggestions, as if the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Goldsmiths of the City of London had met with great Opposition and Discou-ragement in executing the Power veiled in them, of going to the Goldsmiths Shops, to assay their Gold; and that thereby great Frauds and Abuses were daily committed in the manufacturing, felling, and exporting, wrought Plate without the Hall Marks, or with counterfeit Marks (truck thereon; and likewise as if the said Wardens and Commonalty were at considerable yearly Charges, in keeping an Assay Office, Goldsmiths Hall, over and above the whole Produce arising from such Office: But that no Opposition, or Discouragement whatsoever, hath, to the Knowledge or Belief of the Petitioners, been, at any time, given to the said Wardens and Commonalty, or any of their Officers, in the coming to the Goldsmiths Shops, to assay their Gold; and that, although there may have been Frauds committed by some few Workers in Gold and SilverWares, yet, as the Petitioners are no ways culpable, or concerned therein, and they being very considerable Traders, dealing iri Gold and SilverWares, it would be, as they apprehend, exceeding hard, that the whole Mystery should labour under the Difficulties and Disadvantages, which by the said Bill, should it be passed into a Law, would be brought upon them, and the Trade in general; and that the Petitioners do not in the least question, but that, if true Accounts of the whole Produce of the Assay Office, in Goldsmith’s Hall, were to be laid before this House, for a Number of Years back, it would clearly appear, to the Satisfaction of the House, that either the Produce of the said Office greatly exceeds all the Expences yearly incident to it, or else that the Expence of the said Office,by additional Officers or Salaries, or other-ways, has been greatly increased; and that the Petitioners apprehend the said Bill to be calculated for no other end, than to give Power and bring Profit, to the Gold-finitbs Company, and to put the whole Mystery of Goldsmiths under their immediate Influence, and that, should the Bill pass into a Law, it would, in many respects, be greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, and others of the Mystery of Goldsmiths in particular, and to the Publick in general: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better preventing of Frauds and Abuses in Gold and SilverWares be read a Second time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, if they think fit;

It passed in the Negative.

That lie makes about 1,000 Ton of Bar Iron per Annum, lor the Use of the Nail Ironmongers; but at present meets with great Complaints from them, for want of a Demand for the fame: And that he has lately seen great Stocks of Nails lying in their Warehouses, more thaii what lie formerly used to do:

Ton more:

And Mr John Banijler, chief Agent to Mrs. Crozvley,

laid, Though, by the Accounts from the Custom-house, it may appear, that the Exports of wrought Iron, and Nails have for feme Years past rather increased than leffeneri; yet, he is fenlible, and l’o mult all the Dealers in Nails, that there is at present a great Decay in that Branch of Trade in particular, and the Entries at the Custom-house, he is satisfied, are very erroneous; for, since the Duty of wrought Iron and Nails exported, has been taken off', the Dealers in these Goods have not been so exatt in their Entries, nor so observant as they used to be in distinguishing Nails from wrought Iron, which formerly paid different Duties; and the Merchant often makes a great Entry, in order to forward the Loading of his Ship; the Ironmonger often makes a larger Entry than is necessary, that he may, without the Charge of a fresh Entry, indorse any larger Quantity on the Cocket, should he, before the Ship fails, receive from his Customers any further Orders; and sometimes makes a large Entry, in order to make a Figure in the Entry Paper; for the Charge of entering 20 Tons is no more than for Two Tons; and, for that Reason every Person always enters enough; and very often the Bar Iron is included in the Weight of that which is manufactured: It is common for the Ironmonger to enter Brals, Copper, Wood, and any other Goods that lie deals in, that pays no Duty, or receives a Drawback, as wrought. Irou:

That a great many Nails have been ffiipped for Two or Three Years past, by several Ironmongers in London, on their Accounts, from mere Necessity, having greater Stocks by them than they know what to do with; and those Ironmongers sometimes enter more than they ship, in order to discourage others fromlhipping: And the Dealers in Nails are now distressed, to the greatest Degree, for want of Employment; for their Workmen are ready to llarve, and are continually rising in a tumultuous manner, 50001* 1,000 of them together, threatening to destroy and pull down the Houses and Ware-houses of their several Employers, with many other Threats of the like Nature:

That England takes thrice the Quantity of Iron from Sweden, more than France, Holland, and all Europe, does besides:

That the Swedes are supplied with Iron manufactured

from Germany, and with what Cloth they want by the' Prussians and Muscovites.

II.

A Scheme, by linking Twenty thousand Pounds Paper Money, to encourage the Raising of Hemp, and the Manufacturing of Iron, in the Province of New York; with some Observations, {hewing the Necessity and Advantages thereof.

First, It is proposed, That the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds, Part thereof, be let out, on good, sufficient, real. Security, on the following Conditions, to encourage the raising of Hemp.

Secondly, That no Sum exceeding One hundred Pounds, nor less than Twenty five Pounds, be let out to any-one Person.

Thirdly, That there be paid Fiveper Cent. Interest for the First Three Years, in the current Money of the Pro- vince, on the First Day of May yearly, or within Thirty Days after.

Fourthly, That at the Expiration of the Three Years, the said Interest of Five per Cent, shall cease; and the Principal be paid back into the Treasury in Ten Years from the Expiration of the Three Years, at the Rate of Ten Pounds for every Hundred yearly, in good merchantable Hemp, of the Growth of the Province.

Fifthly, That the said Hemp be delivered to the Treasurer, or other Person to be appointed to receive the same, in the Month of April or May yearly, in no less Quantity than the full Value of One-tenth Part of the Principal; the Treasurer, or such other Person as aforesaid, giving a Receipt for the Quantity, to be accounted for by the Treasurer to the Owner, when fold.

Sixthly, That, in Default of Payment of the said Interest of Five per Cent, in Money, or of the principal in Hemp, at the respective Times before-mentioned, the Estate, given in Security, be fold, and, out of the Produce, the Principal and Eight per Cent. Interest, from the Date of the Mortgage, be paid to the Treasurer, with all Coils and Charges, and the Surplus paid to the Mortgager.

Seventhly, That, when the Hemp is delivered, sufficient Proof be made before the Treasurer, that it grew in Vol. 23.

the Province; and nqne to be received by him that is not Mamifartore well rotted, bright, and of a proper Length. of Iron in

Eighthly, That the Deliverer of each Parcel of t|ie Pknta-Hemp affix thereto, on a Ticket, his Name and Place of tl0,8 Abode.

Ninthly That the Hemp be every Year publickly fold in the City of New York, in the Owner’s Name, for ready Money, in the Month of June; and the Time and Place of Sale advertised in the NewsPapers, Three successive Weeks before the Sale.

Tenthly, That the respective Owners have Credit for the Net Proceeds of their Hemp, Two per Cent, being deducted from the Sale and Storage; and the Surplus of his yearly Payments in Ilemp be paid to him, by the Treasurer, in Money.

Eleventhly, That Three, at least, of the Justices of the Peace in each County do meet at the County House, the First Thursday in zf/>r//annually; before whom every Person in the County is to make Oath of the Quantity of Hemp by him raised in the preceding Year.

Twelfthly, That the said Justicos send to the Treasurer, by the last Thursday in April yearly, a disticCt and particular Account thereof.

Thirteenthly, And, that the Manufacture of Hemp may be carried to the greater Perfection, it is proposed.

That the following Bounties be yearly given, as a Reward to such Persons who shall excel in raising and manufacturing of Hemp, fit for the Market; viz.

To the Perfotrwho raises Haifa Ton of the best Hemp, which is to be adjudged of, and determined, on Oath, by Two or Three {kilful and judicious Rope-makers, in the City of New York, the Day preceding the yearly Day of Sale before directed, the Sum of Ten Pounds:

To the Person who raises Half a Ton of the Second best Hemp, Six Pounds:

To the Person who raises Half a Ton of the Third best Hemp, Four Pounds.

This Bounty to commence on the Payment of the First Tenth Part of the principal Money, so, as aforesaid, to be let out, and to be paid by the Treasurer yearly, du-ing the Ten Y'ears allowed for the paying the principal Money, immediately after the yearly Sale of the Hemp; provided that Oath be made, by the Owners of the said Three respective Parcels of Hemp, that the same is of the Growth of their own Farms.

Fourteenthly, It is also proposed, That, at the same time. Ten thousand Pounds, the Remainder of the said Twenty thousand Pounds, be let out at Interest, at Five per Cent, for the Three first Years; and, from thence, that the Principal be paid to the Treasury in 'fen Years, at the Rate of Ten Pounds for every Hundred Pounds, in good Iron, of the Produce and Manufacture of the Province, at the same Times and Manner, and under the like Regulations, as are before proposed for Hemp.

Put, as Iron-works require large Sums of Money to carry them to Perfection, it is proposed, That this Ten thousand Pounds may be let out in any Sum, not exceeding Pounds, and not less than Pounds,

to any One Person or Company.

The Persons delivering Iron to the Treasurer in Payment, as aforesaid, to makeOath, that the same was made at their own Works, and not by’ them bought of any Person whomsoever: This Caution will appear necessary, if we consider that One Iron-work, when it is carried so Perfection, will be capable of delivering out a great ma-nyTons yearly; and the Encouragement being intended to seton Foot many Iron-works, the Intention would be defeated, if Persons were at Liberty to repay the Money lent them in Iron, not of their own Manufacture, but purchased at other Iron-works in the Province.

Fifteenth, In case any Part of the Ten thousand Pounds, intended to encourage the railing of Hemp, should, at the Expiration of One Year, remain in the Treasurer’s Hands, for want of being let out, he may then let it out, to encourage Iroq-works, in manner before proposed.

So, on the contrary, ifany Part of the Ten thousand Pounds, intended to encourage Iron-works, remains in
