not be let out for those Purposes, at the Expiration of One Year and an Half, whatever remains in the Treasurer’s Hands is to be let out by him, for the remaining Part of the 13 Years afore-mentioned, at the yearly Interest of Six per Cent, to be paid in current Money, of the Province of New York; however, the Treasurer should have Power to call in yearly the Money so let out at Six per Cent, to the Intent that, if any Persons, during the Course of the 13 Years, should be willing to take it up, and to employ it in raising and manufacturing of Hemp and Iron, they may have it on good real Security, as aforesaid, on condition that they repay to the Treasury the whole principal Money in Hemp and Iron, as aforesaid, in equal yearly Payments, by the Expiration of the 13 Years above proposed.

Sixteenth, That the aforesaid Principal and Interest Money be applied to the Support of Government, in Ease of Trade, by lessening the Duties.

Seventeenth, and lastly. That a Tax of per Head,

be laid on all Negroes, old and young, or such other Tax on Estates, real and personal, as shall be an effectual Fund for the linking the said Bills of Credit in Years.

Whoever considers the vile Disposition of our Slaves, the small Service we have of them,' the first Costs, the Uncertainty of their Lives, and the Charge in maintaining them, compared with the low Wages of Servants in Europe,the shameful and pernicious Practice of employing them, as Carpenters, Coopers, Me. and many other Trades, by which Numbers of our People are left defti-tute of Employment, would wish we had not Oue in the Province, and would then gladly submit to any Tax laid on them, or other Discouragement to their Increase among us, as we already have, or, with little Encouragement, might quickly have, white People for its Labour and Manufacture.

The Advantage to the Planter and ManufaCurer appears openly, at first Sight, by their having the Money for the first Three Years at Five per Cent, and having Ten Years from thence to repay the Principal, without any Interest: Tis the Planter and Manufacturer who reaps the First Fruits of this great Encouragement; the Benefit to the Merchant must arise from the Progress that is made in those Works.

We need go no further than our neighbouring Colonies of Neio Jersey and to be convinced,

that fresh Meadows and Swamps are the belt and most natural Lands for Hemp; It is true. That the Expence of draining and clearing them is great; but then it is as true, that the Profit arising from them, when they are cleared and drained, will very soon and abundantly repay that Expence; not only because those Lands yield a Crop of Hemp to the Value of Ten or Twelve Pounds Sterling an Acre, but because they require no Dung; of such Lands there are enough in this Province, that now lie useless.

Nor are we wanting of Iron Ore; our Neighbours know it, and know the Goodness of it; and, to our Shame, we fee them fend their Vesselsfor it, to work up in other Colonies; while we fit still, regardless of what so highly concern us, and fee others grow rich from our Improvidence.

The raising and Manufacturing of large Quantities of Hemp and Iron is One great Encouragement to Shipbuilding; it employs great Numbers of People at home, and gives a Country Reputation abroad: Hence, in agreat measure, it is, that the Trade of that, as

well as other Branches of it, has, within these few Years, swelled to a Bulk hardly to be believed. It is Trade and Manufactures make a Country rich and populous; and, until one is encouraged, and the other set on foot, the Farmer and the Merchant will equally feel the Want of them. Let us look back, and fee what an AlterationTwenty Years has made in the Price of Wheat;

and, if we inquire into the Causes of that Alteration, we shall find them to be chiefly, if not wholly, Two; First, That the West Indies, our only certain Market for Flour, is already well nigh as fully peopled as those Islands will admit of: And, adly. That this, and our neighbouring Colonies, raise more Wheat than those Islands can con-fume: This is our present Situation; and, bad as it is, might be borne with, if it would not grow worse; but he must obstinately shut his Eyes, who does not plainly fee, that every succeeding Year will make our Condition worse; for new Settlements are made, and more will be made, in proportion to the Increase of People, and all in a View to raise Wheat, unless some other Works be set on Foot: If the Quantity of Wheat now raised be too much for the foreign Markets, all beyond that must tend to lower the Price, and reduce the Farmer to Poverty: But if these Manufactures of Hemp and Iron are set on foot, and carried a considerable Length, the Profit arising from them will be found to be so great, that the Farmer will be diverted from raising that Quantity of Wheat which now he does raise; which, of course, will enhance the Price of it; so that he will be a Gainer every Way; and we shall remove that Jealously which the Country Gentlemen of England conceive, of our raising

so much Wheat as may, in time, and as weiucrease in People, prove injurious to their Estatesat Home; whereas we have no Cause to apprehend their Jealously, but have Reason to expefik their Countenance and Encouragement, in those Two great Works of Hemp and Iron; of which I shall speak more hereafter.

The Riches of a Country consists in the Numbers of People rightly employed; and, when they are so, they become useful and serviceable to each other: Thus Tradesmen depend upon the Farmers for the Sustenance of their Families; and the Farmers upon the Tradesmen, for such Manufactures as they want: When Things are so disposed, neither one nor the other have their foie Dependence on Foreign Markets; but, by their mutual Wants, and necessary Occasions, become Markets to each other: Whatever is raised or manufactured beyond that, is exported by the Merchant. By this Order and economy. Manufactures are brought to Perfection, and the Trade and Wealth of a Country advanced; the Farmer thrives from the Demand and Consumption of what he raises; and the Manufacturer, being wholly employed in the Business of his Trade, not only carries it to an high Perfection, but maintains his Family better, and gets more Money, than if he was to employ Part of his Time in railing his own Provifl >n: Hence it is that Landed Estates in Europe are of such great yearly Value, and Manufactures so excellent in their Kind. The more Manufactures we set on Foot the better; something of every Sort is wanted, either for our own Use, or for foreign Markets; but if all Men were to be employed in One Thing, as the Farmers are at present, they would starve.

The Attempts of private Persons, how publick-spirited soever they may be/are ineffectual to retrieve the declining Trade of a Country, or to establish great and considerable Manufactures: These Things are to be hoped for only from the Publick; and we promise ourselves, that those whom we have chosen to represent us in general Assembly, will exert themselves, to the utmost of their Power, for their own, for ours, and for the fake of Pof-terity, to make this a flourishing Country: We have at present a Governor who knows our Wants; and, as his Interest is blended with ours, we may reasonably hope that he will concur with them, in whatever may promote the Trade and Prosperity of the Province: And, we af-sure ourselves, that the Assembly will lay hold on the present Occasion, which, once dipt, may belong ere it be retrieved; and, in the mean time, we shall have the Mortification to fee ourselves oppressed with Poverty, and live in Obscurity, while our Neighbours grow famous abroad, and rich and populous at home.

" The Balance of our Trade with England is now greatly against us; and will continue to be so, till we find out other Returns, which the Two Works proposed will

give

v

it Geo. II. 2i ° Martii

give us; then the Balance of Trade will take a Turn, and be in our Favour; welhall keep our Silver and Gold among us, and the Paper Money proposed to be ilruck will hold its Value.

These Works w'ill give Employment to many Hundred Families, without Fear of over-doing the Market; for England takes yearly, from Siveden only, the Value of Two hundred thousand Pounds Sterling in Iron, and from Rnjfia Seventy thousand Pounds Sterling in Hemp, which it purchases with Silver and Gold j whereas from us they woutd have both thofe Commodities in Exchange for Goods, mostly of their own Manufactures; an Advantage that carries in it an Assurance, that they would prefer our Trade to that of the North: All great Works owe their Greatness to small Beginnings; and why is it more improbable that, we should, in time, send to England those Commodities which we can raise and manufacture, than that England should, as they do, fend far abroad for those Things that they manufacture, and afterwards transport again with Advantage? Besides the Benefit mentioned, it will very much increase. our Navigation and Ship-building: For, if every Farmer in the Province improved only Half an Acre of Land in the raising of Hemp, it would, in the Exportation of it, give Employment to at leaftOne-fourth of our own Shipping: Nor can it be pretended, that we want any other Materials for Ship-building; since we have great Plenty of excellent Mads, Plank, and Timber, and as great Conveniency of Water Carriage for them, as any of our neighbouring Colonies.

The Method by which the Government of this Province is at present supported, being altogether by Im-posts on Trade, lays our Merchants under greater Disadvantages than those of our neighbouring Colonies, where they are exempt from Duties; and there cannot be a greater Discouragement to Trade, Navigation, and Ship-building, than to put our Merchants upon that unequal Foot: Nor is that all; the Farmers feel, the Consequences of it, and pay dear for their Exemption from Taxes; but are willing to impute it to any other, rather than the true, Cause; they complain of the Times, lament that the Markets are low and dull; but won’t inform themselves from whence it proceeds, though it greatly concerns them to know it: Be it known to them, therefore. That it is what I have mentioned; viz. the heavy Weight of Imposts laid on Trade, for the whole Support of Government; and, until a Remedy be applied, Trade will languid], and the Farmer feel the bad EffeCls of it: It is the Farmer’s Interest therefore to bear a Part with the Merchant; and by this Scheme, there is a Method prescribed, which opens to the Planter a Prospect of present Advantage and future Riches, and eases Trade near One thousand Pounds a Year for Three Years, and near Two thousand Pounds a Year for Ten succeeding Years.

To conclude: Let us confidently hope, that the Assembly will seriously consider what is proposed; lay to Heart the low State of the Province; and give Beginning and Strength to those things which now lieufelefs for want of their helping Hand: So will they discharge, with Honour, the great Trust reposed in them; raise the present Age to a more flourishing Condition; and deliver a grateful Memory of their Names to Posterity, with Glory and Riches.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into Consideration upon Friday Morning next.

The Petitioners then called,

Jonathan Smith Esquire, Mr. Edward AJled, Mr. John Woodioin, and Phineas Smith: Who, being severally examined, said. That the Road leading from North Jleete to Rochester is in very good Repair; and that they believe it to be one of the bell Turnpike Roads in England; and that the same is, in a great measure, owing to the prudent and good Management of the Gentlemen concerned in the Trull, and to the great Income arising from the Tolls of the said Turnpike; and that, they believed, the Tolls might be sufficient to repair the Roads to Dartford.

M r. Edward AJled, Mr. John Woodwin, and Phineas Smith, being further examined, said. That, in regard the said Road from Northjleete to Rochester is so well repaired and amended, that there will not be wanting more than Half the Money now, to repair and amend the fame, than what was formerly applied for that Purpose.

Jonathan Smith Esquire, Mr. Edward AJled, Mr. John Woodwin, and Phineas Smith, further said. That the great Road leading from the Stones End in to the City of Rochester, which lies beyond the said Town of Dartford, in the Parishes of Dartford, Stone, Northjleete, and Swanfcombe, is, in many Parts, very narrow,' and much out of Repair ;which renders it extremely dangerous for Passengers travelling through the same; several Persons having, within these few Years, lost their Lives by reason thereof.

Mr. Smith further added. That there are many cross Roads leading through the said several Parishes, and which are very bad; by which means,the Parishes have been at very considerable Charges in repairing the fame, besides the Statute-work done thereon: And that he himself has been at great Expences on that^Account, besides doing his Statute-work.

The said Mr. Smith further said, That, by reason of the great Charges the several Parishes have been at, in repairing the said cross Roads, they are not able, by their Statute-work, to repair the great Rochester Road leading through the said several Parishes.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition

And the Petitioners, to prove the fame, called the following Witnesses; vix.

Mr. Humphry Smith and \being

severally examined, said, That they were employed to survey the Fens, called Deeping Fens, and well know the same; and that in those Fens are included Pinchbeck and Spalding South Fen, ThurFen, Bourn South Fen, and Crowland Fen, alias Goggcontaining about

30.000 Acres in the Whole, whereof 10,000 Acres are called taxable Lands: That the same are, by.Two several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Reign of King C/utrles the Second, made chargeable for the effectual graining thereof:

That 5,000 Acres, other Part thereof, are the Property of some few Owners thereof, and called the Free Lands; and the remaining Part, amounting to above

15.000 Acres, are Commonable Lands.

Then the Commissioners laid before the Committee the before-mentioned Acts, one passed in the 16th and 17th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for draining of the Fen called Deeping Fen, and other Fens therein mentioned; and the other passed in the 22d Year of his said Majesty’s Reign, for settling the Draining of the Fens, called Deeping Fens.

By the First of which Acts the Commissioners of Sewers have notany Power to lay any Tax upon the Owriers and Proprietors of the said Free or Taxable Lands, un-Jess all the said Fen Lands shall be overflowed for Five Years together: In such case, they are impowered to fell those Lands, as well as the Taxable Lands, to make good all Damages that should be done thereby to that Part of the Country: And the said Mr. Smith and Mr.

Thompson said, That the Owners and Proprietors of the said Fens, have frequently met with great Difficulties, which have fr aft rated their Endeavours to preserve and keep them drained; by which means, not only the Taxable Lands but also the said Free and Commonable Lands, are almost entirely rendered unprofitable; to the gre&t Loss and Impoverithment of many of the said Proprietors and Commoners.

Mr. Thompson further said, That Captain Perry was employedTwo or Three Years by the Adventurers, as an ^Undertaker for draining the said Lands; and although above £.4,000 was therein expended, yet the same proved ineffectual; and, at this time, the much greater Part of the Level is Two Feet and'-Two Feet and a Half under Water; by reason whereof many of the Commoners are reduced to aftarving Condition.

Joseph Banks Esquire being examined, said, That several Parishes, which lie contiguous to the said Fens, have been greatly impoverished, and several Houses decayed, and many others will soon be in the same Condition; which is owing to the Level having been so long under Water, and rendered useless.

And Mr. Smith further said. That he was upon a View with the Commissioners of Sewers for the said Level, and observed, that, if the Banks which inclose the said Level were neghefted to be repaired another Year, the Navigation of the River between Spalding and Stamford would fbon be loft.

And it was agreed by all the "Witnesses, That neither the said Free and Commonable Lands, or the Taxable I.and.?, can ever be made useful, unless some new Method be taken for regaining the fame, and future Preservation thereof.

Then the Petitioners produced an Agreement, dated the 23d of February 1737; which was read.

And itappearedtoyour Committee, by the said Agreement, That the Majority of the Owners and Proprietors of the said Lands, called the Free Lands, in Number of Persons and Quantity of Lauds, have agreed to raise a Sum of £.5,000 by a Rate of 20 per Acre, upon the said Free Lands, and have executed the fame, under their Hands and Seals: And that only Christopher Clapham Esquire, who is possessed of 953 Acres; Mrs. Elizabeth Hyde, who is intitled to 380 Acres for her Life only; and

Answer to Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended his

Add re Ci. Majesty Yesterday with their Resolution 4nd Address of the 30th Day of Marchlaft: To which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz. Gentlemen,

I am fully sensible of the many and unwarrantable Depredations committed byth and you may

beaffured I will make life of the most proper and effectual Means that are in my Power, to procure Justice and Satisfaction to my injured Subjects, and for the future Security of their Trade and Navigation. I can make no Doubt but you will support me with Chearfulness in all such Measures as, in pursuance of your Advice, I may be necessitated to take, for the Honour of my Crown and Kingdom, and the Rights of my People.

A Petition of divers Gentlemen, Freeholders, and , Farmers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many other Gentlemen, Freeholders, and Farmers, in the County of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are Owners of Lands, or Tenants under Leases for Terms of Years, at full outside yearly Rents, of several Lands in the said County; which Rents are chiefly raised by Cheese, the Produce of those Lands, which the Petitioners have hitherto enjoyed the Liberty of felling to Persons well known to the Petitioners, on whose Integrity and Ability they may justly place their Confidence, and on such Terms and Credit as may bell raise and support the Price of such Cheese; and alleging. That if the Bill, now depending in the House, for altering the present Method of buying and selling Cheese in that, and several other Counties, should pass into a Law, a» it now Hands, the Petitioners apprehend it would not answer the good Ends pretended thereby; and that it will subject the Petitioners, and the Persons to whom they fell their Cheese, to greatTrouble, Charge, Hazard, and Penalties; and tending to restrain Credit, Jeflen the Number of substantial Buyers, and consequently depreciate the Value of Cheese, to the great Loss of all, and the Ruin of many, of the Petitioners and their Families: And therefore praying the House to take the Premifefr into Consideration; and that they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Part thereof, as they shall be advised; and may have such proper Relief as the Nature of their same requires.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Bill for regulating the Cheese Trade in the several Counties of England and Wales,is committed: And that the Petitioners,

if they think fit, be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

St. Leonard, A Petition of Francis Cartwright Parish Clerk, and Shoreditch, William Bewley Sexton, of the Parish of St. Leonard, Church. Shoreditch, in the County of r, was presented

to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have been lately informed, that, by an Act of Parliament, made in the Eighth Year, of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for rebuilding the Parish Church of St.Leonard, Shoreditch', in the County of Middlesex,the antient and accustomed Fees for Burials

in the said Parish belonging to the Petitioners, as Clerk and Sexton’ thereof, severally, are veiled in Trustees therein named, to be applied towards Payment of certain Annuities for Lives to be granted for railing Monies for rebuilding the said Church: And that, as the Petitioners conceive this great Loss on them, was occasioned by Mistake; and that they never gave their Consent thereto, nor knew any thing thereof, till long after the said Act had passed both Houses of Parliament, and received the Royal Assent: And that the Petitioners are informed, that in the Bill now depending in this House, for explaining and amending the said Act, there is a Clause for restoring to them their said Fees: And therefore praying the House, That the said Bill may pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved, in such Manner as the House shall think lit.

Whereas the Lords of the Committee of his Majesty’s moil honourable Privy Council, to whom his Majesty referred the Consideration of a Memorial from Richard Fitz William Esquire, Governor of the Bahama Islands in America, humbly proposing, amongst other Things, That the Right of the Soil of the said Islands should be purchased of the Proprietors, and a Power given to the Governor, for the Time being, to grant out the Lands to such People as are willing, to become Inhabitants there, under a Quit Rent to be settled by his Majesty, have this Day made the following Report to his Majesty, at this Board; viz.

The Lords of the Committee do humbly inform your Majesty, That they have long had this Matter under their Consideration, apprehending it would be greatly for your Majesty’s Service, and the Interest o Britain, That the Right of the Soil of the said Islands (houtd be vested in the Crown, in regard they are, by their Situation, most convenient for the reception of such -tish Ships as may, at any time, be sent into those Parts, for the Protection of our Trade, and of Privateers, for the Annoyance of an Enemy in Time of War. And, to that End, their Lordships had, some time since, directed the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations to treat with the Proprietors, for a Surrender thereof to your Majesty. Whereupon the said Lords Commissioners received a Signification under the Hands of Five of the said Proprietors, viz.The Duke of Beaufort, Lord Cra-

ven, Lord Berkeley, Sir John Colleton, and Robert Abdy, as One of the Executors and Devisees of Sir John Tyrrel, deceased, that they were willing to make a Surrender of their Right in the said Islands for the Sum of One thousand Guineas to be paid to each of them, clear of all Fees and Expences; reservingto themselves the Arrears of Rent that shall, at the Time of their Surrender, be due from the Lessees or Assignees of their Lease. That, as the Lord Carteret was the only Proprietor who had not signified his Consent to this Surrender,the Committee thought it necessary, before they proceeded further herein, to be informed, whether he was willing to concur with the rest of the said Proprietors; and therefore feut to Mr. Shelton, the Secretary to the said Proprietors, to wait upon the Lord Carteret, and to know his Resolution thereupon. And the said Mr. Shelton having accordingly been with the Lord Carteret, did attend this Committee, and inform them, That he had received the Lord Carteret's Directions to signify his Consent. to the Surrenderof his Right in the said Islands, upon the same Terms and Conditions offered by the other Proprietors. The Lords of the Committee hereupon proceeded to consider of the said Proposals, together with the Importance of the said Islands, to the Dominion and Trade of Great Britain in those Parts, and are humbly of Opinion, That it may be advifabie for your Majesty to accept a Surrender of the said Proprietors, of all their Right, Property, and Royalty, in and over the Soil of the Bahama Islands, for the Sum of One thousand Guineas, to be paid to each of them, clear of all Fees and Expences; upon Condition thatthey do re-linquifli to your Majesty all manner of Right to Rents, or Arrears of Rents, and to all Demands, of what Denomination soever, which they shall or may have a Claim to, at the Time of their making such Surrender of the said Islands.

And the Lords of the Committee do further humbly report to your Majesty, That having been informed that the said Proprietors had some time since granted a Lease of the said Islands for a Term of Years, Five whereof are asyet unexpired, with Power to the Lessees, or their Assigns, to make Grants of Land in Perpetuity, under a Quit Rent to be paid to the said Proprietors, originally set at Three Pence per Annum lor eac h Acre, but lately reduced to One Penny p Acre; they thought

proper to direct the Lords Commissioners lor Trade and Plantations to inquire into the fame, and to discourse with the Lessees about the Surrender of their said Lease.

Whereupon the said Lords Commissioners have represented to this Committee, That such Lease, as aforementioned, is now fubliliing: But that the Lessees have informed them, That they have hitherto granted few or none of the said Lands: And that the said Lessees have likewise informed them. That they have laid out very considerable Sums in Improvements in the said IfiaiuLs in fending over Inhabitants, Provisions, and Stores; in dislodging the Pirates who had settled themlehes there; and in defending those Islands from the Attempts of the Spaniards.

And that therefore the said Lessees hoped the said Sum would be paid to them, as should be paid to the Proprietors of the Bahamas, for the Pure-hale of those Islands.

Hereupon the Lords of the Committee beg Leave humbly to observeto your Majesty, That, although your Majestylhould be pleased to accept of the Surrender of the Proprietors Right, yet, unless the Right of tlirle Lessees be likewise purchased, your Majesty’s Governor of these Blands caunot be impowered to make any Grants of Lands to People inclined to come and settle there,during the Five Years Continuance of the said Lease; and consequently, no Improvements can be made,or thelfiaifdsltrengthened with Inhabitants,during that time: In regard where to their Lordships are humbly of Opinion that it may be advifabie for your Maj liy to cause the Right of the Lessees to be likewise purchased; and, considering that they may have been at fume Charges in making Improvements upon the said Blands, their Lordships humbly conceive, that the Sum of Two thousand Pounds will be a reasonable Consideration for the Purchase of the said Lease, and of all their Right and Demands whatsoever in and to the said Islands.

His Majesty this Day taking the said Report into . Royal Consideration, was pleased, with the Advice of his Privy Council, to approve thereof; and, judging it for the Good of his Service, and the Interest of Great Britain, that the Proposals for purchasing the Right both of the Proprietors and Lessees in the Bahama Islands should take Effect,

_ is hereby pleased to order, That she Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasurydo consider of the properell Method to complete the same.

May it please your Majesty.

Your Majesty having thought fit, with the Advice of your Privy Council, to approve of certain Proposals laid before your Majesty, by the Lords of the Committee of Council, for purchasing the Right of certain Pro prietors, and certain Lessees under them, in the Bahama Islands; and, by your Order in Council, hearing Date the ad Day of Augufllafl pall, to require us to consider

the properell Method to complete the said Purchases; we most humbly report to your Majesty,

That, to comply with the said Order, the Sums following are allowed to be paid; that is to say; to the Proprietors, namely the UuV.e of Beaufort, Lord Carteret f-ord

Craven, Lord Berkeley, Sir John Colleton, and Robert Abdy, as One of the Executors and Devisees of Sir John Tyrrel, d eceased, One thousand Guineas each, clear of all Fees and Expences, for the Purchaseand Surrender of all their Right, Property, and Royalty, in and over the Soil of the Bahama Islands, and in and to all manner of Rents, or Arrears of Rents, and to all Demands of what Denomination soever, which they shall or may have a Claim to.

We conceive, from the Nature of the respective Ef-tates and Interests proposed to be surrendered to_yo1ir Majesty, for the said Sum of Eight thou&rid):Three hundred Pounds, great Difficulties may arise, before the various Titles thereto, and the manner.of conveying the fame, can be adjusted, so as the Purchase thereof may be effectually secured to the Cjrown; but fhis.will be a Matter mol proper for your Majesty’s Attorney and Solicitor General to examine and consider, and report their Opinion to your Majesty thereupon. It seems to be agreed on all hands, that the veiling' the said Islands in the Crown will be for your Majesty’s Service, and the Interest of Great , in regard

they appear, by their Situation, most convenient ibr the Reception of such British-Ships, as may, at any time, be lent into those Parts for the Protection of our Trade, and of Privateers for the Annoyance of an Enemy in time of War.

Therefore we are not without Hopes, but that your faithful Commons, considering the Importance of the said Islands, will, upon a Motion in that Behalf, provide the Mouey for the purchase thereof, in like Manner as they did in the Year 1728, for the Purchase and Surrender of the Province of North Carolina, which1 required an Act of Parliament to make the same effectual; as, we presume, this may do.

All which is most humbly submitted to your Majesty-s great Wisdom.

Veneris, 13* OBobris;

Anno 12* Georgii IIdi Regis, 1738.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

ft is with great Satisfaction I observe, That the Temper and Moderation which I recommended to you, at the Opening of this Session, have been so well preserved through the general Course of your Proceedings; and that, from a due Regard to me and my Honour, you have avoided all unnecessary Occasions of Heats and Animosities, and made the Interest of your Country the principal Object of your Care and Consideration.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return j'ou my Thanks for the Supplies which you have so chearfully and effectually raised for the Service of the current Year. The Provision you have made to answer all Emergencies which may become necessary, in Vindication of the Honour and Interest of my Crown and People, is a great Proof of your Zeal and Concern for the Welfare and Prosperity of the Nation; and shall be employed by me in such a manner, as may belt con- duce to those Ends and Purposes for which you have so readily consented to this extraordinary Expence.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Agreeably to what hath appeared to be the concurrent Opinion of both Houses of Parliament, I have given Orders to repeat, in the strongest and most prelfing manner, my Instances at the Court of , for obtaining Satisfaction for the many Injuries and Losses sustained by my trading Subjects in America, as well as an effectual Security of their Rights for the futurei and, I hope, from the Justice and Equity of the Catholick King, to procure such Satisfaction and Security, as may preserve the Peace, and establish a free and uninterrupted Exercise of Navigation and Commerce, mutually, between the Subjects of both Crowns, pursuant to our Treaties, and the Law of Nations.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Thnr/day the Twenty-seventh Day of July next, to be then here held: And Vox. 23.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers; where the Commission was read, for the further proroguing the Parliament until day the Eighteenth Day of January next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until the Eighteenth Day of January next.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz. '

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have, upon all Occasions, declared how sensibly I have been affected with the many Hardships and Injuries sustained by my trading Subjects in America. I have the Honour of my Crown, and the true Interest of my People, too, much at Heart, to fee either of them suffer any Prejudice or Diminution, without pursuing the most proper and advantageous Methods for their real Security and Preservation.

There Considerations alone were sufficient to incite me to exert my utmost Power in vindicating and protecting ©ur undoubted Rights and Privileges of Navigation and Commerce; and nothing could add to my own Zeal in so just a Cause but the due Regard I always have to the Petitions and Complaints of my Subjects, and the Advice of my Parliament. The Wisdom and Prudence of your

Resolutions upon this great and national Concern determined me to begin with the more moderate Mea fines; and to try, once more, what Effect and Influence my friendly Endeavours, and prelfing Instanees, would bate upon the Court of Spain, towards obtaining that S itis-faction and Security which we were intitled to demand and expett: And your Assurances, to l’upport me in all Events, enabled me to proceed with proper Weight and Authority.

Thus (upported, by the concurrent Advice of both Houses of Parliament, I loft no time in making Prreparations to do myself and my People J a It ice, if the Conduct of the Court of Spain had laid us under that Necessity; and, at the same time, I did, in the strongest manner, repeat my Inllances for obtaining fuel) Justice and Reparation for the many Injuries and Lodes already sustained, and such an effectual Security for the future, as might prevent the Consequences of an open Rupture.

It is now a great Satisfaction to me that I am able to acquaintyou, That the Measures I liavepurfued havehad so good an Effect that a Convention is concluded, and ratified between me and the King of; whereby, upon Consideration had of the Demands on both Sides, that Prince hath obliged himself to make Reparation to my Subjects for their Losses,by acertaiu stipulated Payment: And Plenipotentiaries are therein named and appointed for regulating, within a limited time, ail those Grievances and Abuses which have hitherto interrupted our Commerce and Navigation in the American; and for settling all Matters in dispute, in fuel) a manner, as may, for the future, prevent and remove all new Causes and Pretences of Complaint, by a strict Observance of our mutual Treaties, and a just Regard to the Rights and Privileges belonging to each other. I will order the Convention, and the separate Articles, to be laid before you.

It hath been my principal Care to make use of the Confidence you reposed in me, in this critical and doubtful Conjuncture, with no other View, but the general and lasting Benefit of my Kingdoms; and, if all the Ends which are to be hoped for, even from fiiccelsful Arms, can be attained, without plunging the Nation into a War, it must be thought, by all reasonable and unprejudiced Persons, the most deficable Event

Gentlemen,


12 Geo. II. i Februari207

Gentlemen of the Hottfe of Commons*

I have ordered the proper Estimates to be prepared and laid before you, for the Service of the current Year. I heartily wish.That the Poflure of Affairs would have permitted me to retrench the publick Expences, for which I am obliged to demand the present Supplies. And I make no doubt but your experienced Zeal and Affection for me and my Government, and the proper Concern you have always shewn for the publick Good, will induce you to grant me such Supplies as you shall find necessary for the Honour and Security of me and my Kingdoms.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot but earned ly recommend it to you, not to suffer any Prejudices or Animofuies to have a Share in your Deliberations at this important Conjuncture; which seems, in a particular Manuer, to call upon you to unite, in carrying on such Measures as will be most conducive to the true interest and Advantage of my People.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right UfualOrders, to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall fee, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall, Hia.ll be kept free and open 5 and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Petitioners are, by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 28 th Year of the Reign of King Edioard the First, obliged to assay and mark wrought Plate, in order to ascertain

the Standard thereof: hnd the Wardens are thereby im-

fiowered to go to the Goldsmiths Shops to assay their Gold; bat that in executing this Power, the Petitioners have met with such great Opposition and Discouragement, that, oflate Years, they have not ventured to make any

any Searches at all; so that great Frauds and Abuses are now daily committed, in the manufacturing, felling, and exporting wrought Plate, without the Hall Marks, orwith counterfeit Marks, struck thereon, to the Discredit of the said Manufacture, the Prejudice of the fair Trader, the defrauding his Majesty’s Subjects, and the lessening the Duty laid on wrought Plate: And that the Petitioners have, for a great many Years past, kept an Assay Office in Goldsmiths Hall; and, towards defraying the Charge thereof, usually took Four Grains Pound Troy for assaying and marking Silver Plate; the FourGrains being about a Half-penny in Value, and the Pound Troy worth about Three Pounds Two Shillings; but, of late Years, havetaken certain Prices in Money, by Agreement with the moll confide: able Workers of small Wares, for the assaying and marking of their small Works, besides Six Grains Diet on large Plate; notwithstanding which the Petitioners are at a considerable yearly Charge, over and above the whole Produce of their Assay Office: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to provide l'uch Remedies therein, and otherwise relieve the Petitioners, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

The Copies of the said Convention, and the seperate. Articles thereunto belonging, with the several Ratifications thereof, arc bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

The Translations thereof are as follow; viz.

Translation of the Convention betwetnGreat Britain and Spain.

Whereas Differenceshave arisen, of lateYears, between the Two Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, on account of the Vjfiting, Searching, and Taking ofVessels, the Seizing of Effecis, the Regulating of Limits, and other Grievances,allegedoneachSide, aswellinthe West Indies aselfewhere; which Differences are so feriousand of such aNature, that,if Care be not taken to put an entireStop to them for the present, and to prevent them for the future, they might occasion an open Rupture between the said Crowns; for this Real’on his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and his Majesty the King of Spain, having nothing so much at Heart as to preserve and corroborate the good Correspondence which has so happily subsisted, have thought proper to grant their full Powers, viz. his Bri-tannick Majesty to Benjanun Keene Esquire, hisMiriifter Plenipotentiary to his Catholic Majesty; and his Catho^ lick Majesty to Don Sebajlian de la Quadra, Knight of the Order of St. James, Couufellor of State, and First Secretary of State, and of the Dilpatches; who, after previously producing their full Powers, having conferred together, have agreed qpon the following Articles;

Art. I.

WhereastheantienlFriendship, fodefirable andfo ne-ceffaryfor the reciprocal Intereil of both Nations, and particularly with regard to their Commerce, cannot b$ establhhed upon alaflingFoundation,unless, Care betaken not only toadjulland regulate the Fretenfions for reciprocal Reparation of the Damages already sustained; but, above all, to find out Means to prevent the hkeCaufesof Complaint for the future; and to remove absolutely, and for ever, every thing which might give Occasion thereto;

31

Convention with Spain.

Convention with Spain.

a 14 8 Februarii.A. 1738.

Jt is agreed to labour immediately* w kb all imaginable Application and Diligence, to attain so deferable an End: And, for that Purpose, there shall be named, on the Part of their Britannick and Catholick Majesties, respectively,

immediately after the Signing of the present Convention, TwoMinisters Plenipotentiaries, who shall meet at Madrid within the Space of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications, there to confer, and finally regulate the respective Pretensions of the Two Crowns, as well with relation to the Trade and Navigation in America and , and to the Limits

of Florida, and of Carolina, as concerning other Points,

which remain likewise to be adjusted; the Whole according to the Treaties of the Years 1667, 1670, 1713, 1715, 1721, 1728, and 1729; including that of the Alfiento of Negroes, and the Convention of 1716: And it is also agreed. That the Plenipotentiaries, so named, shall begin their Conferences Six Weeks after the Exchange of the Ratifications, andihall finish them within the Space of Eight Months.

Art. II.

The Regulation of the Limits of Florida and lina, which, according to what has been lately agreed, was to be decided by Commissaries on each Side, shall likewise be committed to the said Plenipotentiaries, to procure a more solid and effectual Agreement; and, during the time that the Discussion of that Affair shall last. Things shall remain, in the aforesaid Territories of Florida, and of Carolina, in the Situation they are in at present, without increasing the Fortifications there, or taking any new Polls: And, for this Purpose, his Britannick Majesty, and his Catholick Majesty, shall cause the necessary Orders to be di{patched,immediately after the Signing of this Convention.

Art. III.

After having duly considered the Demands and Pretensions of the Two Crowns, and of their respective Subjects for Reparation of the Damages ftiftaiued on each Side, and allCircumftanoes which relate to this important Affair, it is agreed, That his Catholick Majesty shall cause to be paid to his Britannick Majesty the Sum of Ninety-five thousand PoundsSterling^oraBalance which has been admitted, as due to the Crown and the Subjects of Great Britain, after Deduction made of the Demands of the Crown and Subjects of Spain; to the end that the above-mentioned Sum, together with the Amount of what has been acknowledged, on the Part of Great Britain, so be due to Spam, on her Demands, may be employed, byhlsBrilannick Majesty, for the Satisfaction, Discharge, and Payment, of the Demands of his Subjects trpon the Crown of Spain: It being ufiderstood, nevertheless, that it shall not be pretended, that this reciprocal Discharge extends or relates to the Accounts and Differences which subsist, or are to be settled, between the Crown of Spain and the Company of the Afflento of Negroes; nor to any particular or private Contrafts that may subsist between either of the Two Crowns, or their Ministers, with the Subjects of the other; or between the Subjects and Subjects of each Nation, respectively; with Exception, however, of all Pretensions of this Cfafe, mentioned in the Plan presented at Seville by the CommiCferies of Great Britain, and included in the Account lately made orrt at London, of Damages sustained by the Subjects of the said Crown; and especially the Three Particulars inserted in the said Plan, and making but One Article In the Account, amounting to One hundred Nineteen thousand Five hundred Twelve Piastres, Three Reals, and Three Quartils of Plate: And the Subjects on each Side shall be mtitled, and shall have Liberty to have Recoutfe, to the Laws 5 or to take other proper Measures for causing the abovesaid Engagements to be fulfilled, in the same manner as if this Convention did not exist.

Art. IV.

The Value of the Ship called the Wool-ball, which was taken and carried to the Port of in the Year

1732; the Loyal Charles, the Dispatch, the George, and the Prince William> which were carried to the 20

Art. V.

la reip«d> A Petition of the Cuiriers and other Dealers in Lea-

ing united ther, whole Names are thereunto IhUcribed, in *behalf of l^*UMsr* themselves, and'many others, waspresentedto-the House, And read-, fettibg forth. That, by an Act, passed in the FirftYear of the Reigo of King James the First, concerning Tanners, Curriers, Shoemakers, and other Artificers, occupying the cutting of Leather, it is, among other Things, enacted, That no Person or Persons shall buy, foil, bargain, bespeak, or take, promise to have, -exchange, or putaway, any tanned Leather not wrought and converted ijito made Wares, but only such Person and Persons as will land shall work, rind convert the (tune Leather into made Wares , and, by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of their.late Majestie’s King William and Queen Mafor explaining Part of the said recited Statute, it is enacted,'Tha^* all and every Hide, Skin, or Piece of tanned Leather, ll\aved or li-' quored, of what. Colour soever, with any lawful liquoring or dressing, and being well and truly curried, according to the Directions of the said Statute, shall be adjudged, reputed, and taken, to be the made Ware and Manufacture of the Carrier, and shall be subject to a View and Search in manner directed in the said Statute; and that it shall be lawful to and for all Leather-fellers, Curriers, Shoemakers, and all other Persons whatsoever that do deal and work in Leather, freely to bdy all-Sorts of red ^tanned Leather in any openiFainor Market, whether curried or uncurried, the same being first searched and sealed, - according to the Form of the Statutes in that same made and provided j and having so bought the fame, to fell it again to any Person' or Persons whatsoever, in their publick and open Shops, or to cut and convert the same into other made Wares, according to their . several and respective Trades: And that the Petitioners conceive the intention of the Iall-reoited Act was to make the Petitioners, among others, free Buyers and . Sellers of Hides and Skins, and to give Liberty to them to cat and fell the same in such Pieces and Parcels as are soft fit foe the respective Uses of the various Artificers dealing with them for the fame, such as Shoemakers, Sadlers, Leather Clog-makers, Collar-makers, Bellows-, makers. Chair-makers, Bodice-makers, Patten-makers, Bridle-cutters, and several others; the different Parts of One Hide and Skin being useful for distinct and different Purposes, and seldom.'worked up by any One Artificer:. And that the Petitioners have accordingly, ever since the peffing the said Act, till within these Five or Six Years, without the Ieaft Interruption, cut and fold Hides and Skins in the maimer afore-mentioned; when, by reason of fomp Doubts upon the Construction of the said Statute, several JDisputes have arisen between the Company of Cordwainers, and the Petitioners, as to the cutting and felling such Hides and Skins, And what shall be . deemed and taken to be red tanned Leather; and that -several Actions have been brought and prosecuted against feme of the Petitioners, in which Verdicts have been sometimes found fortbe Plaintiffs the Cordwainers, and sometimes for the Defendants the Curriers and Dealers in Leather; and Fourteen Actions more are brought at the Expence of the said Company, against others, several whjrfeof are now at issue, in order to binder the Petitioners, who are obliged to defend such Actions at their own private Expence, from cutting and felling Hides and Skins in such Pieces and Parcels as are roost fit for the various Artificers using the same in

their respective Occupations: That the Petitioners, the last Session of Parliament, applied to the tleufe, by Petition, for Relief in the Premiles; which was referred to the Consideration of a Committee, who agreed upon a Report,- and also came to several Refutations, which were reported, and agreed to by the Hoofe; whereupon . Leave was given to bring in a Bill to obviate the Doubts which have arisen upon the Conftrnftion of the said Act of the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary; which Bill was accordingly presented, and read the First time, and ordered to beread a Second time; but the Session was so far advanced that it did not pals into a Law: And that, without the Aid of Parliament, not only the said Actions may be prose-ented, but-many more may be brought against the Petitioners, the Defence of which will be attended with very great Expence, whereby the Petitioners will be obliged to leave off the Catting and Selling of Leather to the middling and poorer Sort of Master Shoemakers, as well as the various other Artificers working in Leather; which will not only tend to the utter Ruin of feme, and the Injury and Oppression of others, of the Petitioners, but-to the Injury and Oppression of great Numbers of his Majesty’s industrious Subjects: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill ta obviate the* Doubts, which have arisen upon the Construction of the said Act of the First Year of the Reign of King William and-Queen , intituled, An Act for explaining Part of an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, concerning tanned Leather, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet. . .*

Fraud* in Sir Francis Child reported from the Committee

Gold and whom the Petition of the Wardens and Commonalty

Wares. of the Mystery of Goldsmiths, of the City of Ijmdon, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him 10 report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners, laid before the Committee,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the 28th Year of the Reign of King Edward the First, whereby it appeared, That no Goldsmith is to make any manner of Vefibl, or other Thing, of Gold or Silver, except it be of good and true Alkty; and that no manner of Vessel of Silver is tq depart out of the Hands of the Workers, until it be assayed by the Wardens of the Craft., and marked with the Leopard’s Head; which Wardens are likewise thereby empowered to go from Shop to Shop, among the Goldsmiths to assay their Gold.

: Then the Petitioners, to prove the Frauds complained . of, called

Mr. Jofiph Ward, Allay Mailer of Goldsmiths Hall, > and Mr. Thomas Rankes, Clerk to the said Company:

Win), being fed erally examined, said, That, notwithstanding the Powers given by the before-mentioned "Aft, there had been no Searches made for the last 12 or id YeArs; and that there were no Wardens now living; tlrot: had ever made a Search; the Reason of this Dif-, Cojntf nuance of Searching Was, as they apprehended and had-heard, from the Opposition the Wardens usually met wfth in executing that Power.

And, in order to fiicw the ill Consequences arising from the Goldsmiths being thereby exempted, in a manner, from the Inspection of the Wardens of the Craft, the Petitioners called

Obadiah Weljled and Richard Vincent; who ft-verally produced to the Committee several Pieces of Plate, by them purchased, at Shops within the Cities of London and Westminster; some whereof had no Marks at all upon them; and others, as appeared by the Evidence of the

above-named Mr. Joseph Ward, Assay Mailer, had -counterfeit Marks stamped upon them. L- ,: i

The said Mr. Ward being asked, If a Mark could not be taken out of an old Piece of Plate and put into a new one, so as that the Fraud should not be discoWred ? said. It might be easily done; and, in such a manner, a£ to deceive a Person not versed in the Business; which’ his Evidence, in this Particular, was confirmed by Mr.

Weljled and Mr. Vincent. t

It appeared further, by the Evidence of Mr. Weljled and Mr. Vincent, That the several Pieces of Plate by them produced, had, lince the Purchase of them* been allayed at the Totver; and that the same had been found greatly deficient; and they gave Evidence to the Committee of the particular Deficiency of each.

Piece of Plate, which was, in some, very great, and in others less.

The Petitioners then proceeded to shew what had been the Produce of the Assay Office for some Years last past , and what the Expence of keeping it.

To which Purpose they called again,

Mr. Thomas Bankes, Clerk to the Company: Who said, That it had formerly been usual for the Company to take Four Grains per Pound Troy for allaying and marking Silver Plate; but, for several Years pall, they had taken Six Grains for large Plate, Six Pence a Piece for Sword Hilts, Three Pence a Piece for Snuff Boxes, and other final! Sums of Money for other Small Wares by the Pkce, until the 20th of 737; lince

which time they have taken only Four Grains per Pound Troy on all Silver Plate, both large and small.

He then produced an Account of the Produce and Expence of the Assay Office for 20 Years, ending the 29th of May 1737, during which time the advanced Prices were taken; whereby it appeared, on a Balance for the whole 20 Y'ears, That the Company had been in Disburse by the said Office £.950 17s. 6d. including the Rent, of the Assayers Home and the Assay Office.

And it further appeared, by the same Evidence, That, from the lft of February 1737 to the ift of February 173S, although 3,000 lb.Weight of Plate was tried at the Assay Office more than had usually been in One Year, at Four Grains per Pound Troy, yet the Produce of the Assay Office, during that Time, including the Money received for making Paper Allays, amounted only to the Sum of £.283 os. 6d.;and the Distmrfements, exclusive-of the Rent of the Assay Office, and the Assayers House, to the Sum of^.506 18r. \d.; so that the Company are

in Disburse for that Year the Sunt of £,223 ijs. lod. over and above the Rent aforesaid.

A Petition of the Company of Cordwainers in the an-tient Town and Borough of Denbigh, in the County of Denbigh, in behalf of themselves, and their Brethren, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are apprehensive that the Curriers bring in a Bill, this Session of Parliament, which was once read in the lad; which Bill, as brought in, impowers the Curriers, and all other Dealers in Leather, freely'to buy all Sorts of tanned Leather, whether curried or uncurried, and to cut and sell the same, in any small Pieces, to the various Artificers who work up the fame, and convert it into made Wares, or to’any other Person or Persons whatsoever; which Bill, the Petitioners are convinced, is calculated for the Curriers End only, and tends to the utter Ruin and Destruction of the Trade of the Petitioners in the Country, as well as in and

to encourage a Monopoly in the Curriers: And therefore praying. That the House will be pleased to take the Pre-mi fes into Consideration; and that the said Bill, so de-llru&ive to the Trade of the Petitioners, be laid slide, or otherwise, as the House shall judge bell for the Preler-vation of their Trade in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

River Lea A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and Navigation Inhabitants, of the Town of Hertford, and of the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, in the County of Hertford, and of several Farmers, Maltsters, and Barge-owners, living in or near the said Towns, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several Hundreds of other Persons, residing near to, and concerned in the Navigation on, the River Lea, running from Hertford to Ware, and from thence to the River of Thames, near the City of London; and of the Governor and Company of th e New Ribrought from Chadxoell

and Amwell to London-, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Navigation of the River Lea is an antient Navigation, and hath been very useful to the Publick, by conveying great Quantities of Grain, and other Goods, to and from the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof: And that the Petitioners the Governor and Company of the New River have usually had and taken, and Hill take, great Quantities of Water out of that Part of the River Lea, which runs from Hertford to Ware, for supplying the said Cities, Suburbs, and Liberties thereof with Water,touching which many Disputes and Controversies have arisen between the Petitioners the Governor and Company, and the Navigators, and other Persons concerned in the Navigation of the said River Lea, which have lately been accommodated, settled, and agreed; and that, although the settling of such Disputes and Differences will be of great Advantage to the Publick, by ascertaining and improving that Part of the Navigation on the River Lea running from Hertford to Ware, and will very much preserve and improve the Navigation of that Part which runs from Ware to the River of Thames, and enable the Petitioners the Governor and Company to supply the said Cities, Suburbs, and Liberties, with good and wholesome Water, and tend very much to the Increase of Trade; yet such Agreement cannot be established, and made effectual, without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying the House will be pleased to give Leave to bring in a J7

Bill for ascertaining, preserving, and improving, the Navigation of the said River Lea; and to enable the said Governor and Company the better to supply the Cities of London and WeJljninster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, with good Water.

and Candles, and bring the same from Ireland to Wales,

and there take in Coals again, and put the said Soap and-

Boats and Vessels, which they meet on the Sea Coasts,

and (there being no Waiters put on board such Ships

and Vessels) the Mailers thereof, contrary to the Laws

of this Kingdom, import and run such Soap and Candles

within the Ports of Barnejtaple, Bidefand,

in the fame, Coimtv, and publicklyfelftbefoifie af Borne*

Jtaple, Bideford, Great Torringlon, South Molton, Amd other the adjacent Parishes and Places; and, notwithstanding this Grievance hath been represented to his Ma- . jesty’s Commissioners of the Customs, and several great Seizures have been made, yet nevertheless the Maftenst of such Vessels do still industrioully apply themselves to the Importing and Running of vast Quantities of Soap and Caudles within the Ports aforesaid; and, by illegal Practices, enrich themselves in a few Years: That formerly great Quantities of Tallow were imported from Ireland into the Ports above mentioned, which brought in a considerable Revenue to the Crown; but, of late Years, and since Irish Soap and Candles have be n so clandestinely imported and run, very little or none is now imported: That, in regard the Masters of such Ships and Vessels fell the said Irish Soap and Candles at a much cheaper Rate than the Petitioners, or any other Persons who pay the Duty for the fame, can, and there being such vast Quantities of Irish Soap and Candles clandestinely imported and run into the Ports aforesaid (the Duty whereof, if duly paid, would, as the Petitioners conceive, amount unto a considerable Sum of Money every Year) the Petitioners Trade is thereby so much lessened, that it is impossible they can thereby support themselves and Families; but mull inevitably be reduced to Poverty, unless the House do consider of such Ways and Means as may for the future either prevent such a growing Evil, or that the present Duties on Soap and Candles may be taken off: And beseeching the House to take this into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as the House shall think molljuft.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

the Northern Road, lying between the Towns of Grantham and Stamford, through the Counties of Lincoln and Rutland was referred, That the Committee had exa-amined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

The Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, the Agents for the Petitioners called,

William Powell, Richard Hanks, and James Courtney:

"Who, being severally examined, said. That they were Coachmen by Occupation, and were very well acquainted with the Roads mentioned in the Petition, having frequently Occasion to travel through the same: That they had very lately passed through the said Roads, and they were so exceedingly bad and dangerous, that it was with very great Difficulty they were able to get through them at all: but seldom or never could do it without being obliged to hire some Horses to assistthem.

Solomon Clarke,a Coachman, belonging to Mr.

who usually lets out travelling Coaches, said, That he was well acquainted with the said Roads, and confirmed the Evidence given by the Three Persons above-named; and further said. That, even in the Middle of the last Summer, the Roads were so very bad, after a Show'er of Rain, that his Coach, in Company with another, was stuck; and they were forced to borrow one another’s Horses, in order so get their Coaches out of the Mire.

Sir Brownlow Skerrard said, That, to his Knowledge, the Statute-work, for some time, was done; notwithstanding which the Roads were, as above represented, exceedingly bad; and could not be put into Repair by the Statute-work. And,

John Bray said. That he believed the Statute-work was far from being sufficient effectually to amend and keep the Roads in proper Repair.

*»e cat er. fe]ves, and the rest of the Manufacturers of Leather in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, for many Years before the Year 1726, the Petitioners had^i considerable Leather Market in the said Town of Birmingham, of about Three hundred Hides, besides a proportionable Number of Calve-lkins and Kip-lkins, being commonly exposed to Sale there every Market Day; by which means the Petitioners were supplied with Leather at reasonableRates; but that,since the Year 1726, scarce Ten or Fifteen Hides have been brought to the saidMarket on OneDay, to the great Disappointment of the Petitioners: And that this Grievance is entirely owing to the Curriers within the said Town of

ham,in Number Nine, whosoreftal the Market, by buying up of all the Leather they can in the adjacent Countries, not only red tanned Leather, but also all other Sorts of Leather not manufactured by them; whereby they oblige the other Dealers in Leather to buy the same of them at an exorbitant Price: And that the Petitioners are moreover great Sufferers by the Curriers cutting and felling their Leather in small Quantities: And thatfeveral of the Curriers have of late, and since the said Year 1726, made, or caused to be made, large Quantities of Shoes and Clogs, and exposed them to Sale within the said Town of Birmingham, to the great Damage of the Petitioners: And that, if the Curriers should be enabled first to cut, and afterwards to fell. Leather in what manner they please, contrary to the Laws now exilling, it would be of the greatest Detriment to the Trade of the Cordwainers of this Kingdom in general, and in particular to the Petitioners, and endanger the total Impoverishing of Thou-fandsof Families now employed by them, as also be more expensive to thofePersons whom the Petitioners now do, or shall hereafter, supply with Shoes: And therefore praying. That the House will be pleased to take the Pre-mi fes into Confederation; and that the said Petitioners may have Leave to be heard, either by themselves or Counsel, what they have to offer against the Allegations of the Curriers; or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Commercial A Petition of divers Merchants, Planters, and others,

Disputes trading to, and interested in, the British Plantations in with Spain. America,in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners made their most humble Application to this House the last Session of Parliament, setting forth, the continued Depredations committed by the on

the High Seas of America, upon the British Shipping and Property; their barbarous andinhumanTreatment of the British Sailors, on the Taking of their Ships; and their carrying them afterwards into Slavery in Old Spain, the Spaniards making it their constantPraftice to attack and board all Briti/li Merchant Ships they met with in the American Seas, under Pretence for searching for Goods which they deemed contraband, according to their arbitrary Will and Pleasure, contrary to the Law of Nations, and in manifest Violation of the Treaties subsisting between the Two Crowns: And that, by these un-jult and violent Proceedings of the Spaniards, the Trade and Navigation to and from America was rendered very unsafe and precarious; insomuch that the Insurances had greatly risen on these Accounts only: And that the Petitioners having been heard, by their Counsel, before a Committee of the whole House, did, as they apprehend, fully make out, in Proofs, every one of the Vot. 23.

Allegations of their said Petition, to the intire and unanimous Satisfaction of the House: Upon which Application this House came to the following Resolutions:

" That it is the natural and undoubted Right of the " British Subjects to fail with their Ships on any Part of " the Seas of America, to and from any Part of his Majesty's Dominions; and that the Freedom of Navigation and Commerce, which the Subjects of Great Britain have an undoubted Right to by the Law of Nations, and by virtue of the Treaties subsisting between " the Two Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, has been greatly interrupted by the Spaniards, under Pretences " altogether groundless and unwarrantable: That, before . " and lince the Execution of the Treaty of Seville, and " the Declaration made by the Crown of Spain, pursuant thereunto, for the Satisfaction and Security of the " Commerce of Great Britain, many unjust Seizures and Captures have been made, and great Depredations " committed by the Spaniards, attended with many Instances of unheard-of Cruelty and Barbarity: That the " frequent Applications made to the Court of Spain for " procuring Justice and Satisfaction to his Majesty’s in-." jured Subjects, for bringing the Offenders to condign " Punishment, and for preventing the like Abuses for the " future, have proved vain and ineffectual, and the several Orders or Cedulas granted by the King of Spain, " for Restitution and Reparation of great Losses sustained " by the unlawful and unjustifiable Seizures and Capturesmade by the Spaniards, have been disobeyed by " the Spanish Governors, or totally evaded and eluded: " Ail which Violences and Depredations have been " carried on, to the great Loss and Damage of the Subjects of Great Britain trading to America, and in direst Violation of the Treaties subsisting between the " Two Crowns:"

" That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, humbly beseeching his Majesty to use his Royal " Endeavours with his Catholick Majesty to obtain " effectual Relief for his injured Subjects, and to conYince the Court of Spain,that, how desirous soever his Majesty may be to preserv a good Correspondence " and Amity between the Two Crowns, which can only " fubfill by a strict observance of their mutual Treaties, " and a just Regard to the Rights and Privileges belongingto each other, his Majesty can no longer suffer such " constant and repeated Insults and Injuries to be carried " on, to the Dishonour of his Crown, and to the Ruin of " his trading Subjects; and to assure his Majesty, that " in case his royal and friendly Instances for procuring " Justice, and for the future Security of that Navigation " and Commerce which his People have an undoubted " Right to, by Treaties and the Law of Nations, shall " not be able to procure, from the Equity and Friend* " ship of the King of Spain, such Satisfaction as his Majesty may reasonably expect from a good and faithful Ally, this House will effectually support his Majesty " in taking such Measures, as Honour and Justice shall " make it necessary for his Majesty to pursue."

That a Convention hath since been entered into between this Crown and that of Spain, which his Majesty has been most graciously pleased to order to be laid before this House; and the same being published by Authority, the Petitioners observe, with the utmost Concern, that the Spaniards are so far from giving up their groundless and unjullifiable Practice of visiting and searching British Ships failing to and from the British Plantations, that they appear to have claimed the Power of doing it as a Right, by having infilled, that the Differences which have arisen concerning it, should be referred to Plenipotentiaries, to be discussed by them, without even agreeing to abstain from such Visitation and Search during the time that the Discussion of this Affair may-last: That the Petitioners are under the greatest Apprehen-fions, since Spain has contended that a Point so incon-testably clear, both by the Law of Nations, and all the Treaties subsisting between the Two -Crowns, should come under Debate, that the Spanish Plenipotentiaries will be instrufted not to give it up; And if the Freedom

23* Febrmrii. 1738.

of our Navigation to and from our own Colonies should be left in Suspence, and precarious, it mult be attended with the moll fatal and pernicious Consequences to the . Petitioners, whose Persons and Fortunes will thereby be in the Power of the Spanish Guarda without any

Prospect of Relief; the Petitioners having already too severely experienced the Juliice of the Courts

and Governors, to consider them as any Security: And therefore praying. That the Petitioners may have an Opportunity of being heard; and that they may be allowed to represent to this House the great Importance of ourTrade to and from our own Plantationsin*4m<?r/ca, the clear and indisputable Right which we have to enjoy it, without being (topped, visited, or searched, by the Spaniards, on any Pretence whatsoever, and the certain and inevitable Destruction of all the Riches and Strength derived to this Kingdom from that Trade, if a Search of British Ships failing to and from the Plantations

be tolerated upon any Pretext, or under any Restrictions; or even if the Freedom of this Navigation should continue much longer in this State of Uncertainty.

And the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Citizens of London are too deeply interested in whatever affects the Trade of this Nation, not to express the utmost Anxiety for the Welfare of that only Source of our Riches; and it is with a Concern the Petitioners are unable to express, that they perceive the Trade to his Majesty’s American Colonies Hill continues exposed to thelnfults of the Spaniards; who, underun-warrantable and injurious Pretences, continue to Hop, search, and make Prizes of, Is navigating the

American Seas, in manifest Violation of the Treaties fub-ftfting between the Two Crowns; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Trade from these his Majesty’s Kingdoms to his.4mmVtf«CoIonies isof the utmost Importance, and aluioft the only profitable Trade this Nation now enjoys unrivalled by others; and that the Petitioners were

induced to hope,from his Majesty’sknown Goodness, and paternal Care of his Subjects, supported by the vigorous Resolutions of both Houses of Parliament, and the Equipment ofa very powerful Fleet, that his Majesty’s trading Subjects in the Seas of as well as in all other Pails

of the Ocean, would not only have received a full Satisfaction for their LolTes, occasioned by the Depredations of Spain, but also an undoubted Security for their Commerce, for the time to come; and that a reasonable and adequate Reparation would likewise have been Obtained for the Barbarities and inhuman Cruelties exercised by that Nation on the English Seamen, who have had the Unhappi-

ness of falling into their merciless Hands; and expressing their great Concern and Surprize to find, by the Convention lately concluded between his Majesty and the King of Spain, that the Spaniards are so far from giving up their, as the Petitioners apprehend, unjust Pretensions of a Right to visit and search our Ships iti the Seas rica, that this Pretension of theirs is, among others, referred to the future Regulation and Decision of Plenipotentiaries appointed on each Side, whereby the Petitioners apprehend it is in some Degree admitted; and that the Petitioners conceive they have too much Cause to fear, if the Right, pretended to by Spain, of searching British Ships at Sea, be admitted in any manner or degree whatsoever, that the Trade of his Majesty’s Subjects to America will become so precarious, as to depend, in a great measure, upon the Indulgence and Justice of the Spaniards, of both which they have given, for some Years pad, such Specimens, as the Petitioners think this Nation can have no Cause to be satisfied with; and expressing the Apprehensions of the Petitioners, that such a precarious Situation as this mull inevitably expose the Trade to the American Seas to continual Interruptions and Alarms, as well as to several Lodes; and that, to these unhappy Causes, the Petitioners apprehend, the present low State of the British Colonies in America may, in a great measure, be attributed; and, if the cruel Treatment of the English Sailors, whose hard Fate has thrown them into the "Hands of the Spanianis, lliould be put up, without any Reparation, the Petitioners apprehend it may be the means of deterring Seamen from undertaking Voyages to the Seas of America, without an Advance of Wages, which that Trade, or any other, will not be able to support: And that the Petitioners therefore, having laid before this House the high Importance this Trade is of to the Kingdom in general, and thisCity in particular, thought it their indispensableDuty to represent to this House the fatal Consequences of leaving the Freedom of Navigation any longer in Suspence and Uncertainty: And therefore expressing their Hope, that this House will take it into mature Deliberation, and do therein, as to the House shall seem meet.
