Bath A Petition of the Commissioners, whose Names are Roads. thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in ExecutionTwo

Acts of Parliament, one of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and the other of the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing and enlarging the Highways between the Top of Hill and the City of

Bath; and also several Highways leading to and through the said City; and for other Purposes in the said Acts mentioned; and also of several Inhabitants of the said City, and other Persons living near, and usually travelling through, the Roads leading from the Top of Old-down, alias Odd-down, to Dunkerton Bridge,; and from Bath Eafion Bridge to a Gate on the further End of Banner-down, alias Balhon; and from the Top of Claverton-doion alias Clar to New Bridge, over Camber Brook; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by the said Acts several Tolls were granted and continued, for the Terms therein mentioned, for repairing the said Highways; which the Petitioners the Commissioners finding in a very ruinous Condition, and the annual Income of the Tolls granted by thefirit-mentioned Act being not sufficient effectually to repair the fame, they were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money', in order to make the said Highways passable, and for other Purposes mentioned in the said Act; and that the Sum of 400, or thereabouts, of the Sum so borrowed, is still due; which, with the Money collected by the Tolls granted, hath been duly laid out, according to the Directions of the said Acts; and that, by reason of the excessive Weights constantly drawn through the said Highways, and some Defects in the said Act, the said Highways cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, and other Directions of the said Acts performed, and the Money due on the Vol. 23.

Credit thereof be repaid, without the Aid of a further Act of Parliament; and that the additional Roads before-mentioned, and particularly described (adjoining to Part of the Highways directed to be repaired by the former.

Acts), are, by reason of maDy heavy Carriages frequent-, ly passing through the fame, become so bad, that they, cannot, by the ordinary Course appointed by the Laws now in being for repairing the Highways of this Kingdom, be effectually amended, unless some ether Provision be made for that Purpose; and that the keeping a sufficient and well-regulated Watch in the Night-time, within the said City, will be of great Importance, and tend not only to the Preservation of the Persons and Properties of the Inhabitants thereof, but the Safety of all Persons resorting thither; and that the Petitioners* the Inhabitants of the City, conceive no effectual Provision is made, by the Laws now in being, for establishing, or well-governing, any such nightly Watch, or for the due levying or collecting any Money for defraying the necessary Charges thereof, or for enforcing a due Application, and juilly accounting for, any-Monies collected for that Purpose: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted and continued by the said former Acts; and for the effectual repairing the additional Roads aforesaid; and for the better regulating the nightly Watch within the said City, and Liberties thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Merchants trading from the Port Commercia of Liverpoole to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, I)itpun-s on behalf of themselves; and many others concerned in with Spain; that Trade, was prefehted to the House, and read; setting forth, That, upon the Application of the Petitioners, and others, to this House, the last Session of Parliament, setting forth the many Depredations committed by the Spaniards, in the High Seas of America, on British Shipping and Property; their barbarous Treatment of the British Sailors, on the Captures of their Ships; and their carrying them afterwards into Slavery in Old Spain; and the Spaniards having made it their common Practice to attack and board all British.

Merchant Ships they met with in the American Seas* under the Pretence of searching for Goods which they deemed to be contraband, or not lawful, according to their own arbitrary Will and Pleasure, for the British Merchant Ships to have on board, contrary to the Law of Nations, and in manifcli Violation of the Treaties subsisting between the Two Crowns, and thereby rendered the Trade and Navigation to and from Americd very unsafe and precarious: And that upon the Petitioners making out the Allegations in their Petitions* before a Committee of the whole House; which; as the Petitioners apprehend, they did, to the intire and unanimous Satisfactkm of the House, this House came to the following Resolutions: " That it is the natural and undoubted Right of the British Subjects to fail with their

and recommending to the Confederation of this House, whether to allow a Point so indisputably clear, both by the Law of Nations, and all the Treaties subsisting between the Two Crowns, to be brought into Question, may not be attended with the most dangerous Consequences; and, if the Spanish Plenipotentiaries should be inllructed never to give up their pretended Claim, would not leave the Trade of the British Subjects to our own Plantations in America more tinfafe and precarious: And therefore praying the House will be pleased to take into Consideration the great Importance of our Trade to and from our own Plantations in America; the clear and indisputable Right which we have to enjoy it, without being flopped, visited, or searched by the Spaniards, on any Pretence whatsoever, or left under any Restriction; or even if the Freedom of this Navigation should continue much longer in this State of Uncertainty.

Westmmilcr men, and others, Inhabitants of the Parish of St.

Church. garet, Westminster, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Parishioners, being offered to be presented to the House j

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; exprelBng the Petitioners grateful Sense of the Favour of the -House, by granting them a Bounty of Three thousand Five hundred Pounds for repairing their Parish Church and Tower; and representing to the House, That One Side of the said Tower, which -was repaired feme Years ago, which appeared fair to the Eye, and was thought to be in a Condition to (land, was, on taking down the other Parts thereof, found to be so greatly decayed, that there was an absolute Necessity to pull down and rebuild that also: And that, on examining what Repairs were necessary for the Support of that Part of the Roof over the grand or middle Isle of the said Church, which was built of Chesnut, the Whole was . found to be so greatly perished, that it seemed rather to be the Interposition of Providence, than any Strength of the Building, that prevented any Accident by its. falling in: And that, to these Two impossible to be fore- seen Accidents, it is owing, that the Petitioners have not only expended the whole Sum grauted by Parliament, but have exceeded the fame, by One thousand Five, hundred and Ninety Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Five . Pence, without having done any thing towards the Repair of the Roof over the South Isle, which is very much, if not totally, decayed: And that the Circumstances of the said Parish, by the Loss of its most wealthy apd,principal Inhabitants, and the great Number of empty Houses therein, which is fully evinced by their Land Tax last Year, which, with a Ke-assessment, amounted to Three Shillings in the Pound; and, though the whole Parish is assessed as equally as possible this Year, yet the whole Assessment produces, if all received, the Sum of Five hundred Forty-eight Pounds Six Shillings and Three Pence, less than the Quota charged on the said »5

Parish, at a time when they labour under a large Debt for their increasing Poor; make it impracticable' for the Petitioners to raise a sufficient Sum on themselves, either for the Payment of their Exceedings, or for what yet remains needful to be done to the said Church:

And therefore praying the House will be pleased, by their further Bounty, to enable them to discharge their former Exceed fogs; and to do such other Reparation to their said Church, as may make it both fit and safe to receive so august an Afferably as the Representatives of the Commons of Great when, and so often as, they shall please to honouf the same with their Presence; the Expence whereof, amounting in the Whole to the Sum of Two thousand Pounds, the Petitioners fubinit to the Consideration of . the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply

the said County of Berks; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’sTable: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Title of the aforesaid Act, passed in the Sixth Year of his present Majesty, and the Clause for continuing the same for Twenty-one Years, were read.

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr LionelRich: Who said. That the Road appointed

to be repaired by the said Act, was Fourteen Miles in ‘ Length; and, notwithstanding Nine hundred Pounds, borrowed upon the Credit of the Toll, and the annual Sum collected, have been laid out in repairing the said Road, the same is, in many Places, in a very ruinous Condition.

He also laid before the Committee, an Account, by wTiich it appeared. That, by a Computation, the annual Income of the said Toll was only £.320, the annual Expence £.iti; and that there now remains a Debt, upon the Credit of the Toll, of £.1,102. 8s. 6d.-, which Sum, he laid, could not be paid, and the Road kept in Repair, unlefo a further Term was granted, and the Toll increased.

Mr. Robert Cornish, and Mr. Thomas Hullcomb, being severally examined, said. That the Road from the Hinds Head Inn, to the Swan Alehouse, which is Two Miles in Length, is in a very bad and ruinous Condition, notwithstanding the Statute-work has been always performed upon the fame.

Mr. John Nash laid. That that Part of the Two Mile Road aforesaid, called the Wash, he, as Tenant to a particular Estate, was obliged to keep in Repair; and that the same is very often so much flooded, that Passengers are obliged to go over in Boats; but that the same has been so this 40 or 50 Years.

Mr. Vyner reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of many Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Persons, travelling from the North West Parts of the County of Lincoln, to the Wolds, or North Raft Part thereof, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them.

to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

William Garihfide said. That he knows the Road from the North-West Parts of the said County of Lincoln, unto the Wolds, on the North-East Parts thereof, leading through the several Parishes of Nettlam Field,

Lane, and Baumber Fields; and that the same is in very bad and ruinous Condition, and dangerous for Passengers to travel; and that he sent up feme Saddle-horses, and it was with great Difficulty that they passed through the fame:

That the Inhabitants of the said several Parishes have been at some Expence in repairing of the said Road: and that they were indicted by the Grand Jury; and that he was present in Court at the same time, and they pleaded they could not repair the fame, for want of proper Materials for that Purpose, having nothing butW ood and Mud to make use of, which, in a short time, made the Road rather worse than better:

That when the Road betwixt and

was inclosed, it lay in a Ridge and Furrow, and was grazing Land; and believes it is between Thirty and Forty Years since it was inclosed: And said, That, when he came that Road about a Fortnight agone, he wan obliged to go by the Fens, which is a great Way about, rather than bring his Horses ..

That it is a great Waggon Road; but, by reason of the Badness thereof. Carriages cannot pass through the fame; but, if made passable for them, he apprehends that it will be a great Advantage to the Trade of the City of Lincoln, and the several Market Towns adjacent thereto.

David Briggs confirmed the Evidence given by the former Witness, and said, That he, some time since, came over the Fens with Horses, to avoid Wragby Lane, apprehending it not safe for him to come that Way with them: And that he has often gone through Wragby Lane; and that it is the wortt Road he ever travelled in his Life-time; and that there are no other Materials but Wodd and Mud to repair the fame.

Henry Billon, being examined, said. That he knows the Roads, especially about Mintinge-, and that they are extremely bad; but that he has seen Gravel laid there, but that it was soon buried in the Clay; and that the Roads Hill continue veiy bad; and that Personsare obliged to fetch Gravel Three Miles, in order to repair the fame.

Edward Burton said, That the Roads are very bad, and impassable in the Winter Season, and scarce passable in Summer, by reason of the great Holes lying in the said Roads, where Carriages are often overthrown: And that he has heard, that the Parishes where the said Roads do lie were indicted, about Three or Four Years since; and afterwards observed Work done in the Repairs of the said Roads; but that they were soon as bad again, for want of proper Materials for the Repairs of the fame.

Thomas Cartwright said. That the Roads are very bad; but has seen Persons amending the same with Furze and Dirt; and, in a Fortnight’s time, they were as bad again as ever; and that, abontTwo Years agone, near -worth, he was stuck fail with a Coach and Six Horses; and that the Coach was in Danger to be broke to Pieces: Said, That if the Roads were repaired, it would be a great Advantage to the neighbouring Places and Towns.

John Leonard said. That he knows the said Roads, and has travelled the same severalTunes; and that they are very bad and deep; and that they have been amended in several Places; but that they were soon cut to Pieces, for want of better Materials being made use of in repairing the fame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Roads from the North-East Parts of the County of Lincoln,through Nettlam Field, Wrag by Lane,

Petitioners, and expressly contrary to the Laws in being:

And that, should the Bill, brought in by the Curriers this Session, pass into a Law, the Petitioners, who have never been heard on this Occasion, apprehend their only Trade will be laid open to the Curriers, who have a separate Trade of their own secured to them by Laws in being, and to vast Numbers of other Persons also, to the great Prejudice and Ruin of the Petitioners and their Families: And therefore praying the House,

That the Petitioners may be heard, by their Court-fel, against the said Bill, before! the same do pafsy or may have such other Relief as to the House Hia.ll Teem meet.

High Price A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereof Coal*, unto subscribed, on the behalf of themselves, and of the Glass-makers, Brewers, Distillers, Sugar-bakers, Soapboilers, Smiths, Dyers, Brick-makers, Lime-burners, Founders, and Callico-printers, and other Traders and Inhabitants in and about the Cities of and

minster, who are Consumers of large Quantities of Coals, imported from Netvcastle, and the Northern Parts of England, into the Ports of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Price of Coals at Newcastle, and other Places in the North, hath, of late,

been greatly advanced; which, the Petitioners apprehend, isowing to payingRents for Collieries not wrought; to Wharfs or Staiths being engrossed by a few; and by other Persons being prevented from bringing Coals to, and using the fame; by giving less Measure of Coals at Newcastle than heretofore; and by reason many Persons are discouraged from working their Coal Mines, for want of convenient Ways or Roads to the Staiths, which they are refused or prevented from using, renting, procuring, or having, by Methods which tend to monopolize the fame, as well as the Coal Trade: And that, -the Petitioners conceive. Coals can be afforded cheaper than they lately have been, because they are fold in the North at a much less Price for foreign Exportation, than those shipped for the Ports of Great Britain: And that, of late, great Quantities of bad and unserviceable Coals have been imported to London, and often mixed with the good, and imposed on the Consumers at the Price of the best; and the Fitters have given Certificates of a good Sort, when the Loading was mixed with different and inferior Sorts: And that divers other extraordinary Practices have, of late, been made use of by the Fitters, which together tend greatly to the Prejudice of the Navigation, and to the Oppression of the Petitioners, and other Consumers of Coals: And that, from the large Duty on Coals imported into the Out Ports of this Kingdom, being near the prime Coll of the Coals, and of those brought into the Port of London, greatly exceeding the prime Cost, and from the Smallness of the Duty upon Coals exported to foreign Parts, Coals are bought greatly cheaper in France, Holland, and Flanders, than in London and the Out Ports, whereby foreign Manufacturers are enabled to underwork the Manufacturers of Great Britain; which, if not timely prevented, will tend to the Destruction of several considerable Branches of Trade; and consequently to the Ruin of a great N umber of his Majesty’s Subjects: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Mefolved, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House Will, upon this Day Month, Vefolve itself into A Committee of the whole House, to oonfider of the said Petition.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called,

Mr; Thomas Anderson Who, being examined, said, That, in or about the Year 1722, the Church becoming very decayed and ruinous, the Parishioners caused the same to be carefully surveyed, by able and experienced Workmen, who then reported that the same was in so dangerous a condition, that it could not be repaired; and thereupon a Vellry was called, and an Order then made, for the erefiling of a Tabernacle; and which was accordingly erefited, by the voluntary Contribution of some of the Inhabitants of that Parish; and then the Pews were removed out of the Church, and placed in the Tabernacle; and a Faculty was afterwards granted by the Bishop of the Diocese, for taking down the Church, and for making Use of such of the Materials thereof, as were proper for rebuilding a new Church:

And the said Thomas Anderson further said. That, in the Year 1733, the Petitioners obtained a Brief for collecting Money, in order to defray the Expence of erefiting a new Church and Steeple; whereby, and by voluntary Subscriptions, the Sum ofj£. 1,547 19$. or

thereabouts, wascollefited and raised for that Purpose; all which Money was duly laid out and applied in erefiting a Shell of the Church, and rebuilding the Steeple,

The same Witness laid before the Committee, an Account of the Monies received and paid towards rebuilding the said Church; which Account was signed by the Churchwardens of the Parish, and approved of by a Vestry; whereby it appeared, That there was now due to several Workmen employed about rebuilding the Church and Steeple the Sum of 154. 14 That an Estimate, made by an experienced Workman, was laid before the Committee, of the Charges of making convenient Pews, and completing the Inside of the Church, and supplying the same with the necessary and decent Ornaments, and hanging up Bells in the Steeple; by which Estimate it appeared, That the Expences thereof will amount to the Sum of £. 1,200, or thereabouts, exclusive of the before-mentioned Sum of £.154. 14 s.remaining due to Workmen.

franting Annuities and otherwise, have raised several urns of Money; and the Estates so purchased by the Petitioners, have been thereby greatly incumbered, and very little Benefit hath thereby aroiie to the Petitien-' ers; and all the said Purchases are not'yet completed: And that about Three hundred thousand Pounds hath been paid in, at several Times, by the Proprietors of the Stock of this Company; and the Money Dividends which have been made amongst the Proprietors do not exceed Thirty thousand Pounds; so that the present Stock of the Petitioners hath cost the Proprietors, or those whom they represent, about Two hundred and Seventy thousand Pounds, and is, at present, of little or no Value: And that several Propofols have been made by the Petitioners, and several of their Creditors, for making a reasonable Satisfaction to the Creditors of the Petitioners, who are very numerous, and whose Debts amount to above Two hundred and Fifty thousand Von- 23.

Pounds; but the said Proposals, although agreed to by great Numbers of the Creditors, have hitherto proved inelfeftual by the Non-compliance of the other Creditors; and, in the mean time, the Petitioners, and also their Creditors, are great Sufferers, by a great Number of expensive Suits in Law an^l Equity in England and Scotland: And that the Petitioners are utterly unable to make any binding Agreement between them and their Creditors, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the said unhappy same of the Petitioners into their Consideration and to enable the Petitioners to settle with their Creditors, in such manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

That he had made an Estimate of the Charge for rebuilding the said Church; which, upon a moderate Computation, will amount to the Sum of 700, or thereabouts, to complete the same in a substantial and Workman-like manner, and make good all Damages that may be done in taking down and rebuilding the fame, and the Expence the Parish may be put to in obtaining an Act of Parliament for the Ptirpol'es aforesaid.

It appeared to the Committee, by anOrderofVellry of the said Parish, of the 12th of 1738, which was confirmed the aoth of the same Month, that Application lliould be made to Parliament to enable them to rebuild their Church; but the Sum applied for should not exceed £.2,700.

St. Nicholas Mr. Sandys reported from the Committee to whom Church at the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, principal Worcester. an(] other Inhabitants, of the Parish of St, Nicholas, in the City of Worcester, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report’the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read-, and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, in puiTuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And it appeared to the Committee, That in Consideration of the great Antiquity and ruinous Condition of the said Church, and the Inability of the Parishioners, by Collections among themselves, to rebuild the fame, a Brief was obtained in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty, for raising the Sum of £.3,873, to enable the

Petitioners to rebuild the said Church; a printed Copy of which Brief was laid before the Committee.

It further appeared by the Parish Books, produced to the Committee, That, immediately upon obtaining the said Brief, Trustees were appointed, at a general Parish Meeting of the Parishioners, to take down and rebuild the said Church; who were impowered to treat and agree with such Workmen as they lliould think fit to rebuild the fame, according to such Model as they, or the greater Part of them, should agree upon.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners called

Mr. Samuel Andrews: Who said. That, in pursuance of the Orders given at the Parish Meeting above-mentioned, the old Church was taken down, and a new Church has, since that time, been built; a Draught or Plan of the West Front and Tower of which Church he produced to, and laid before, the Committee:

That a Book, wherein are entered the Accounts of Receipts and Disbursements of taking down and rebuilding the said Church, was laid before the Committee; whereby the Sum of £.3,345 and upwards, appeared to have been expanded about rebuilding the fame; and that, by the Brief, the Sum of £.1,158. ts. 3 only had been collected, towards defraying the said Expence; but that, by the voluntary Subscriptions of several of the Parishioners, and by Levies upon themselves, the Petitioners had raised the further Sum of £.746. -]s. id. and the Sum of £.121. 19 s.3 d.was raised by the free Contributions of their Neighbours.

The Agent for the Petitioners then produced several Orders of the said Parishioners, at their Parish Meetings; whereby it appeared. That, in consideration of the Insufficiency of the said Sums, so raised and received for the Purposes intended, it was agreed and ordered, That several Sums of Money should be borrowed for the carrying on and fiuishing the said Building, amounting in the Whole to the Sum of £.1,200; and, in pursuance of such Orders so given, itappeared to the Committee, That the Sum of £.1,200 was borrowed by the Petitioners;

£.800 of which was borrowed at common Ititerest, and £.400, the Refichie thereof, was advanced by one Mrs.

Dorothy Bagley, in Consideration of granting her an Annuity of £.40 for her Life; which Agreement with Mrs. Bagley was afterwards confirmed at a general Parish Meeting; and it was also ordered. That thelnterest of the £.800, as well as the Annuity of £.40, being both raised upon the Credit of Parish Orders, should be paid by the Churchwardens of the Parish for the Time beings as the same lliould become due and payable; which Orders were accordingly complied with, and the Interest and Annuity for some Years paid, till of late some Obstruction had been made to it, by the Refusal of several Persons to pay the Rates charged upon them for that Purpose: And it appeared to the Committee, That a considerable Arrear had thereby accrued, amounting to the Sum of £.200 and upwards.

It appeared likewise to the Committee, That Mrs.

Bagley had lately agreed with the Parishioners to accept an Annuity after the Rate of £.8 per Cent, for her £.400, as well for the Arrears now' due, as for the future Payments during her Life; but that there is no Law now in being, notwithstanding the principal Part of the Pa-riftiioners are willing and desirous to affect the fame, to compel the Payment of Rates and Levies, to pay the said Annuity, and to discharge the Debt and Interest.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Inhabitants of the Parish of the City of Worcester, to raise Money for discharging

the Debts they havecontrafted in rebuilding their Parish Church: And that Mr. Sandys, Mr. Lockuood, and Sir John Rushout, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Trustees for establishing the Colony Colony of of Georgia, in America, was presented to the House, and Georgia, read; letting forth, That, by reason of the extraordinary Charge attending the military Defence of the Colony, during the continual Danger and Alarms of a Invasion, and before the Arrival of the Regiment, which his Majesty, in his great Wisdom, thought proper to fend for the Preservation of the Province, a considerable Debt has been unavoidably contracted; which, being unforeseen, could not be provided for by this House in the last Session of Parliament: And that the Inhabitants, having been taken off from their Labour in the Season for Sowing, to prepare for the common Safety, were thereby disabled from cultivating sufficient Quantities of Land for their Maintenance; and those Lands which were cultivated and sowed, by reason of a general Drought for a Year past, which has afflicted that Part of North America, have not yielded the Crops which might have reasonably beenexpected; whereby the Inhabitants do necessarily still remain Objects of Compafiioa, to be for some time longer supported by the Assistance of this House; to the granting of which, the Petitioners hope this House will be the more inclined, from the Consideration that thisColony, as the Petitioners are well assured, will, within a few Years, be found very profitable to its Mother Country, by producing several Materials for the Manufacturers of Great Britain, which are now bought from Foreigners with ready Money; and that its Situation and valuable Ports'to the Southward, are of that Importance to the Navigation of this Kingdom, and for securing the Trade of the West Indies, as to make it the constant Envy of its Neighbours; and that the Support of a civil Magistracy, the continuing the Friendship of the Indians, the encouraging the railing Produces, and other incidental Charges, are still necessary to be defrayed: And therefore praying the House to give the Petitioners such Assistance in the Premises as the House shall think meet.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ordered, That an Account be laid before the House,

shewing how the Money granted in the last Session of Parliament, for the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America, has been applied by them, towards settling and securing the said Colony,

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Freemen of the Mystery of Plumbers, of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; repre-

fenting to the House, That, in making and repairing Pumps, and Engines for railing of Water, and extiu-gui thing of Fire, they use the prime Part of strong Sole Leather, called a Butt, uncurried, which should lie well seasoned before it is put into their Work; and they find a great Convenience and Advantage in being supplied by the Curriers, and other Dealers in Leather, with such Parts thereof as are moil fit for their Purpose; which they now are, and for many Years have been, furnished with, at a moderate Price, by the Curriers, and other Dealers in Leather; the other Parts thereof, which is above Two Thirds of a Butt, being more fit for other Trades; and that, in case the Petitioners should be prevented from buying such Parts of a Butt as will bed suit their Occasions, it will not only tend to the Injury of the Petitioners, but also of those who deal with them; for, in case of a Restraint, the Petitioners would be obliged either to work up all the Parts of a Butt, in their respective Branches of Trade, or make a great deal of Waite; and, in the former Cafe, the Pumps and Water Engines will not be near so good; in the latter Cafe, will come much dearer to the Publick: And therefore praying the said Bill, now depending in the House, to obviate certain Doubts, which bavearifen upon the Construction of the Act, of the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen , intituled, An Act for explaining Part of an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of King/amis the First, concerning tanned Leather, may pass into a Law; or that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Francis Fane acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move the House, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House, for having been graciously pleased to communicate to this House the Convention, together with the separate Articles, lately ' concluded between his Majesty and the King of Spain; to express our most grateful Acknowledgments for his Majesty’s particular Care and tender Regard for the Interests of his People, in having obtained, by the said Convention, a final Adjuliment of their long depending Demands for the Lofies they had sustained, and an express Stipulation for a Payment to be made them, in a short time, upon that Account; to declare our Satisfaction in the Foundation which his Majesty has laid for preventing and removing the like Grievances and Causes of Complaint for the future, and for preserving the Peace between the Two Nations and our Reliance on his Majesty, that, from his constant Attention to the Honour of his Crown, and the undoubted Rights of his People, effectual Care will be taken, in the solemn Treaty to be made pursuant to this Convention, that the Freedom of Navigation in the American Seas may be fully feenred and established for the future; and that his Majesty’s Subjects may enjoy, unmolested, their undoubted Right of navigating and trading to and from any Part of his Majesty’s Dominions, without being liable to be stopped, visited, or searched, on the open Seas, or to any other Violation of the Treaties subsisting between Great Britain and Spain, as the only means to preserve, upon a lasting Foundation, a good Correspondence and Friendship between the Two Crowns; and that, in regulating and settling the Limits of his Majesty’s Dominions in America, in the Treaty to be made with Spain, the greatest Regard will be had to the Rights and Possessions belonging to his Majesty’s Crown and Subjecfs; and to assure his Majesty, that, in case his Majesty’s just Expectations shall not be answered, this House will, with the greatest Zeal and Cheerfulness, support his Majesty, in taking such Measures as shall be necessary to vindicate his Majesty’s Honour, and to maintain his Subjects in the full Enjoyment of all those Rights which they may justly Claim by Treaty, and the Law of Nations:

And Mr. Francis Fane moved the House accordingly.

And the Question being put, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this l louse, for having been graciously pleased to communicate to this House the Convention, together Vox, 23. '

Mr. Bevan reported from the Committee, who were Expiring appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near ex- i-avv*-piring, and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, or continued, That the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in- his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: And the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act to regulate the Price and Assize of Bread; which Act was to continue in force for three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and had further Continuance by subsequent Acts, and is now near expiring; is fit to be continued.

ReJ'olved, Thai it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Regulation of Attornies and Solicitors; which was to be in force from the ift Day of June 1720, for the Term of Nine Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and is near expiring; is fit to be continued.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Bevan and Mr. Papillon do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Agent for the Petitionerslaid before the Committee Two Acts of Parliament, theone passed in the Ninth and the other in the 1 ith Years of the Reign of his present Majesty, for building a Bridge cross the River of Thames, from the Woolstaple, or thereabouts, in the Pa-rish of St. Margaret, in the City of to the

That by the first-mentioned Act it appeared, the Commissioners therein named, or any Nine or more of them, were impowered to treat with the Owners and Occupiers of Grounds, or of such House or Houses, for the Purchase thereof, as they shouldjudge necessary, for widening the Streets leading to the intended Bridge; with several other Powers therein mentioned: t

That by the second-mentioned Act the said Commissioners, or any Nine or more of them, were impowered to dispose of such Parts of the said Grounds as they should be possessed of, over and above what may be necessary for opening and widening the Streets and Passages to the intended Bridge, to the bell Advantage; and the Monies arising thereby were to be employed in erecting the intended Bridge.

It also appeared to your Committee, by the Proceedings of the Commissioners to them referred, That Thomas Lediard Esquire had been directed to inquire into the Rents of all the Ground and Houses on each Side of Channel Row, and other Places necessary for opening a Street from the Foot of the intended Bridge to Whitehall, and another into as also what Sums

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Powers be granted to the Petitioners, in order to remove all Doubts and Difficulties concerning their purchasinjf and disposing of Ground or Houses, lying near to the Streets, Ways, and Passages, on each Side of the River of Thames, to and from the said Bridge; and also to enable them to make Ways and Passages to and from both Houses of Parliament, and the Courts of Justice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, That Leave be given to bring ina Bill, pursuant to the Resolutions aforesaid.

High price A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereof Coal*, unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and all other the Inhabitants of the Borough of Southwark, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That for several Years past the Price of Coals hath been raised to, and kept up at, so exorbitant a Degree, as to become a very great Grievance to the Petitioners inr general, and more especially to such of them who are concerned in the several valuable Branches of Trade whichare carried on within the said Borough: And that the numerous Poor within the said Borough have found, and stili feel, such an extraordinary Advance in the Price of a Commodity so absolutely necessary, to be an Oppression almost infup-portable: And that an enhanced Price hath not been the only Imposition of which the Petitioners have had reason to complain, it being remarkable, that during the time that Coals imported into the Port of London have borne a much greater Price, such Coals have likewifebeen much worse in Quality than heretofore known; and that the Petitioners are well informed, that these Grievances have arisen from Combinations entered into for that Purpose, by divers Persons who are concerned in, and are endeavouring to monopolize, the Coal Trade: And that the Provisions of the several Laws now in being having been found ineffectual for restraining such Combinations, or re-dressing the great Abuses arising therefrom, the Petitioners are apprehensive, that, unless some speedy and effectual Remedy be applied by Parliament, the Evils complained of will not only continue, but increase, to the great Detriment and Oppression of the Petitioners, and the Manu-fasturers, and the Trade of the Kingdom in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to

A Petition of the Merchants, and Planters, and others, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth the Importance to this Kingdom of the said Colonies, and the Trade thereof; and reprefen ting to the House, the present flourishing Condition of the French Sugar Settlements, and the present low Condition of the British Colonies; and attributing this surprising Alteration in the Condition of the British and French Sugar Colonies, amongst others, to the following Causes; viz. To the great Disadvantage and Inequality the British Sugar Trade lies under to that of France, from the very high Duties, both at Home and in the Plantations, on our English Sugars, compared with those laid on the French -, to the Supplies of Provisions, and other Necessaries, the French have from Ireland and North America,without which they could not fitbfift;

and to the Reftpaints the British Colonies are under, as the Laws now ftaud, (from fending any Sugars, Coffee, Cocoa, Indigo, and Ginger, to foreign Markets, before they are -first landed in Great Britain; by which Means they are Liable to the great Charge, Rifqne, and Delay, attending a double Voyage: And representing to the Houft^ That the Liberty of a direct Exportation of the Products of our Sugar Islands to the several foreign Ports in 1 Europe,is -the only Means left to regain the so-

reign Sugar Trade, and to put the British Merchants ouoe more in a Capacity of disputing the foreign Sugar Markets with the French: Andexprelfing the Hope of the Petitioners, that the great Advantage the Trade and Navigation of Great Brit am, as well as the Province of South Carolina, have received -by a Liberty of the same Nature, with regard to Rice, will be a farther Inducement to this House to grant this Liberty to our Sugar Plantations: And furtherrepresentingto tteidoufe, That another great Disad vantage thefimtpft -Sugar Setdaanots labour under arises from the Duties payable on Cocoa,

Coffee, Ginger and Rum, inported into Great Britain from the British Colonies, and the Prohibition to fell Ram in less Quantities than Two Gallons: And felting forth, That, as the Petitioners, out of a due Regard to the Sense of this House, and to the general Good of the Nation, have with great Deference, submitted to the apparent Disadvantages they labour under, by the Act against retailing spirituous Liquors in less Quantities than Two Gallons, without presuming to ask any Alteration in the fame, they are encouraged to hope, that the Duty and Excise on Rum shall be lessened: And further representing to the House, a farther great Discouragement the British Sugar Colonies labour under, from the Importation of French Sugars, Rum, and Melasses, into Great Britain and our Northern Colonies in without paying any more Duty, than if they had been of British Produce, the present Laws for preventing the same being most notoriously evaded, and by no means sufficient to remedy this Evil; and therefore representing it as a Matter absolutely necessary for the Supporting the Sugar Colonies of this Kingdom, that the Laws already made for laying Duties ou foreign Sugars, Runt* and Melasses, imported into Great Britain and America, may receive such Alterations and Additions thereto, as may be sufficient effectually to prevent all such clandestine Commerce for the future: And further representing to the House, That the Trade in Indigo, which our British Colonies had formerly so large a Share in, as to be able, not only to supply enough for our Home Consumption, but also to export great Quantities thereof to foreign Parts, is now wholly gained from U9 by the French, from whom we are under a Necessity of buying almost all the Indigo we use; the Loss of which Trade was entirely owing to the high Duties laid on this Commodity in Great Britain; and that there is too much Reason to fear the like ill Consequences may attend the present high Duties on our Sugar, Cocoa, Coffee, and Ginger; and that the Necessity we are under for Indigo is so great, that when the Trade for that Commodity was in our Hands, it was subjected to a greater Duty than it could bear; yet, that now it is entirely in the Hands of Foreigners, the Legislature has thought fit, as an Encouragement to the Importation of it, to exempt it from paying any Duty at all; and that the Sum this Nation pays yearly to IVance for Indigo, does not amount to less (as the Petitioners believe) than £. 150,000; and therefore submitting to the Consideration of the House, whether it would not be of great Benefit to the Publick, that some proper Encouragement should be given to the Planting of Indigo, so as thereby to be enabled to recover that Trade; and that such a R eduftion be made in ti«e Duty and Excise on other West India Commodities, as may preserve and promote our Trade therein: And further representing to the House the many ill Confe-queuce6 to this Kingdom, which the Loss of our Sugar Colonies must be art tended with: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises, into their most ferioqs Consideration; and to provide such ample and effectual Remedies in fnoh of the several Particulars before-named, as shall at present be thought most expedient, and as the House shall judge proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House wiH, Tomorrow Seven-night, refoflve rtfelf into a Committee of the Whole House, toconsider-of the said Petition.

And, to prove the Allegations of the fame, the Petitioners called,

Edward Norton, of the Parish of Saint Mai tin ;Who, being examined, said, That the Pavements in tire several Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, of the said Parish of St. Martin, are in a very ruinous Condition; and the Ileafon is, that the Inhabitants do little or nothing towards repairing the fame; and, when they do any thing, they do not observe a due Level: That there are Holes in the Streets, which are occasioned, frequently, by the Proprietors of the Water works breaking up the Pavements, and, when they amend them, they generally fill the Holes witliRub-bish, iuflead of Gravel, whereby the Streets, soon after, become in a very bad Condition, and dangerous for Passengers; and that, before any new-built Houses, the-Proprietors seldom remove the Rubbish in any reasonable time, which is a great Nuil’ance to the Inhabitants of the Parilli: And he further said, That the Scavengers do not do their Duty in the Parish; but, if they were obliged to do it by Law it would be of a great Service to all the Inhabitants of the said Parish.

Joshua Taylor, Thomas Middleton, Richard Dew, and John Clarke, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Norton: And Mr. John Clatkeadded further, That

the Scavengers have not a Power to collect the Money assessed; and that he loft £.20 by that means when he was Scavenger: Said further, That People who live in Courts and Alleys ofteD, in the Night-time, throw Dirt bofore such of the Inhabitants Doors as live in the publick Streets; and that, several of those Inhabitants have been indicted for the fame: And that there are several Cellars in this Parish, the Doors whereof come out into the publick Streets, which are very detrimental to many of his Majesty’s Subjects, and that their Lives are often endangered thereby.

John Newton, being caller’, and examined, as to the Parish of St. James, said, That the publick Streets,

Lanes, and Alleys, in that Parish, are not only exceeding bad before Houses uninhabited, but also before those which are inhabited; and they have no Power to oblige the Inhabitants of Houses to pay any Rate, or to force the Owners of empty Houses to repair the Pavements before their Houses: That there are very unequal Levels in the Streets, and, when the Inhabitants pave the fame, they oftener use Dirt and Rubbish, than Gravel and good Materials: That the Proprietors of the Water-works do not pave the Streets as they ought to do; and that the Pavements before such Houses as are inhabited are very feldornrepaired; and that the Custom of having Cellars into the Streets is very detrimental.

Wales's House, have laid open near Two Months together, which made it dangerous for his Highnels to go that Way in a Chair or Coach.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had di« reded him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

Mr. John Higgs was called: Who said. That he was appointed, by the said Justices, Treasurer for the County of Middlesex-, and that a Rate was made, by Order of

the said Justices, in their Sessions in April 1734, for the Faffing and Relieving of Vagrants:

That the said Rate was drawn up in the same manner as former Rates for the said Purposes have been usually drawn; he having examined and compared the same himself, with divers other former Rates:

That the said Rate was, in Trinity Term 1734, removed by Certiorari into the Court of King’s Bench, and was quashed in Hilary Term following.

Mr. Alexander Clarke, formerly High Constable for Holbome Division, being examined, said. That an Action had been brought against him by Thomas Wilbourne, a petty Constable, for Money received by him of the said Wilbourne, being Money collected on the said Vagrant Rate.

Mr. John Higgs, being again examined, confirmed the said Clat ke’s Evidence: And further said. That, in Easter Term 1735, the Court of King’s Bench was moved to grant an Information against him, for a Misdeameanour, on receiving Money, as Treasurer of the County, on the said Vagrant Rate, which had been quashed; although he had received the Money before the Removal of the said Rate by Certiorari.

Mr. Higgs further said. That au Order of Sessions was made in May 1736, for another Vagrant Rate, in the Head of that quashed in 1734; in which Order the said Justices directed the Money which had been received on the said quashed Rate, should be allowed, as Money paid on the said new Rate; and further directed him (Mr. Higgs) to lay the said Rate before Counsel; which was accordingly laid before Sir Thomas Abney, and settled by his Advice and Direction.

That the said Rate was removed into the Court of King’s Bench in Michaelmas Term 1736; and, aotwith-Voi» 23.

Handing the re was all the Care and Caution taken that could be, in the drawing up the said Order, the said Rate was quashed in Easter Term 1737.

Mr. Higgs further said, That, in January 1735, an Order of Sessions was made, for the raising the Sum of £. 200 for repairing of Brentford Bridge, then very much out of Repair, in the same manner as has been usually practised:

That this Rate was removed in Michaelmas Term 1736, and was affirmed in Michaelmas Term 1738; and that, during the intermediate Time, there had been divers Motions made in the Court of King’s Bench, and the final Determination thereof had been poflponedfor several Terms; by which means upwards of 50 had been expended out of the Money intended by the Rate to have been raised for repairing the said Bridge, and only £. 60 had been paid towards the Repairs:

That, since the affirming the said Rate, he had issued out fresh Precepts for collecting the Arrears remaining unpaid, but could not say what Money would be deficient on the said Rate.

Mr. John Higgs further said. That in July 1736, a Rate was made, by Order of Sessions, for repairing the House of Correction in Clerkenwellwhich then was, and now is, very much out of Repair: That the said Rate was removed by Certiorari, in the Michaelmas Term following; but, by the Defect of the Law, particularly with regard to this County, the said Rate could not be maintained; for that, by an Act passed in the 1 ith and 12th Year of King William the Third, intituled, An Act to enable Justices of Peace to build and repair Gaols in their respective Counties, the Justices are, upon Presentment of the Grand Jury at the Assize, Grand Sessions, or General Gaol Delivery, of the Inconveniency or Iu-sufficiency of the Gaol or Prison, im powered to agree upon a Sum for that Purpose, and charge the same on the several Hundreds and Divisions within the said County; but as there are no Assizes, Grand Sessions, or General Gaol Delivery, held for the County of no

such Presentment for the Repair of New . or the House of Correction in Clerkenwell, lying within the said County, as by the Law is made necessary, can be had.

Your Committee then proceeded to take into Consideration the several Laws relating to the Repairing of County Bridges, Gaols, and Houses of Correction; and for the Palling and Relieving of Vagrants} and beg Leave to observe, That, by an Act passed in the First Year of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act to explain and alter the Act, made in the 2zd Year of King Henry the 8th, concerning the Repairing and Amending of Bridges in the Highways, it is thereby directed, when any County Bridge is out of Repair, the Grand Jury shall present the feme so to be, to the Justices, in their respective Quarter Sessions, who are thereby impowered to assess every Parish, in such Proportion as they usually have been assessed, towards the Repair of Bridges; the Money, so assessed, to be collected and levied by the respective Constables, or other Persons, to be appointed by the said Justices in Sessions; but the said Act is entirely silent, how the Constables, in their respective Parishes, are to assess the Inhabitants; and the Sura charged on each Parish in a County is generally so small, that, in many Places, it will be impossible to make any Assessment on the Inhabitants, especially in the larger Parishes.

The Penalty laid by the said Act on the Hic !i Constables, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, ami Petty Constables, for neglectingto assess, collect, or pay, the Money as therein directed, being only 40*. is too small to make the said Law effectual, especially in large Parishes; and there is no Direction how the said Penalty shall be levied, for such Neglect of Duty.

That many Difficulties of the same Nature attend the Execution of the Act, made in the 1 ith and 12th Year of King William the Third, for building and repairing of Gaols herein before-mentioned.

It is therein directed, That the Justices in Sessions, upon Presentment of a Grand Jury of the Insufficiency or

Colfer*'.ion Inconveniency of the Gaol or Prison, and upon the Ex-01 Couty animation of able Workmen, may, by Warrant under ate», c. ^heir Han(js anc| Seals, charge, by an equal Proportion, the Sum to be levied on the several. Hundreds and Divisions within the said County; and direct the High Con-ttables, Petty Constables, Bailiffs, or other Officers, to levy and collect the same: and here, as was before observed in the same of repairing County Bridges, there is no express Direction in what manner the Assessments shall be made on the Inhabitants, in their respective Divisions.

And your Committee observe, That the Estimates, required by this Law to be made by Workmen, being yery uncertain, and seldom to be depended upon, the JuiTices cannot legally alfefs more Money than the Work shall be estimated at; and, if that should not be suficient, no Provision is made by this, or any other. Law for this Contingency, by any new Assessments, or for any Deficiency which may happen on collecting the Rate, and it is apprehended such new Assessment would be illegal; and, though it is not particularly expressed, yet it is usual, in case of the Repair of Bridges, to have an Estimate of the said Repair.

This Law is equally liable to the same Objection as that for repairing Bridges, in regard to the Suiallness of the Sum charged on each Parish; and no Penalty is, by this Law, laid on the Officers required to collect and levy the Money, for Neglect of Duty therein; the only Remedy is by Indictment, and there is noProvision made for defining the Expence of such Prosecution.

" That the Statute, made in the 7th Year of King James the 1 ft, only provides for the erecting of Houses of Correction in every County; but no Power is given by that, or any other Law, to raise Money for repairing the m.

That the Rates for railing Money formatting and relieving Vagrants, as they are to be assessed and levied in the same manner as Rates for the repairi ng County Gaols and Bridges, are liable to the same Objections; nor is there, by the Act passed in the 12th Year of Queen any Penalty laid on Collectors, High Constables, or Treasurers, for not accounting for, and paying over, the Money received by them.

That if any of the said Rates, however necessary, should be removed by Certiorari, and quashed, no Provision is made, by any Law’, for paying the Charges of defending the same; the Officers, employed in the Collection of them, are liable to Prosecutions; and, although they shall have paid the Money by them received, as the Laws direct, may be compelled to repay the same; by which means the most diligent Officers run the greatest Hazard; and the Uncertainty ofcolIeding the Rates makes Workmen very cautious in contracting for any County Work, unless for extravagant Prices,

Your Committee therefore, considering the Defects of the Laws concerning County Rates; the great Niceties, and Arid Forms, required in the making the m; the Difficulty, and evenImpradicableness,of atteffing the small. Sums charged on each Parish on the several Inhabitants;: the Want of suficient Powers in the Justices, hi many Instances, to enforce the colledingand levying of them, or of supplying, by a new Rate, the Deficiency of any former Rate; thelnconyenienciesarifingfrom the Delay, as well as the Expence of the Law, in case of the Removal of any Rates by Certiorari; and the Neqeffity there is to support and maintain County Bridges, Gaols, and Houses of Correction, and for the passing and relieving of Vagrants, and for raising the Money for the said Purposes, with the greateftEale and Certainty, and with the leaf! Charge to the several Counties; came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in being, for affelRng, collecting, and levying, the Rates for repairing of County Bridges, Gaols, and Houses of Correction, and for the patting and relieving Vagrants, are defective.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

An Act, passed in the 13th Year of Queen Elizabeth, for the bringing of the River Lea to the North Si.le of the City of London-, and also an Act, passed in the 3d Year of the Reign of King James the First, for the bringing in a fresh Stream of running Water to the North Part of the City of London; and also One other Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of the said King James,

for Explanation of the said 1 aft-mentioned Statute; were read.

That, by the first-mentioned Act, a Power is given to the Lord Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, to begin and continue the laying out of such

convenient Limits of Ground, for the Making of a Trench for the said River, at such Breadth, and in such Manner, as is and are particularly described in and by the said Act: And a Power is by the said Act given to the Lord Chancellor or Lord Keeper, for the Time being, at the Request of the said Lord Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of the said City, to appoint and authorize, by Commission under the Great Seal, Sixteen Commissioners; Four to be of the City of , and the other

Twelve to be of the Counties adjoining the River of Lea-, viz. Four of every of the Shires of Essex, and

Hertford, or some of them, not being Citizens of,

uling the Trade of Merchandize; which Sixteen Commissioners, or the Major Number of them, had thereby full Power and Authority to treat, agree, and compound, with such Numbers of Freeholders and Inhabitants of the said Counties, as to them should feemmeet and con* venient, for the Security, cleansing, repairing, and keeping, the River Lea, from such Place where the New River or Cut should have the Beginning, to the Town of IFare, in such fort as that the same should be navigable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels:

That, by the second-mentioned Act, a Power is given to the Lord Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of London, and their Successors, to make a new Trench, for conveying Water from Chadwel and Amzvell to the City of London; and to maintain the same when made: And that they might, from time to time, flop all Breaches, at theirownCharges,andsufficientlymaintainthem, and make a Recompence to the Party or Parties grieved for the Damages they should sustain by such Breaches: And that new Cut, Stream, or River, when finished, should be subject to the Commission of Sewers; and the Scouring, Cleansing, Amending, and Conservation,of the New River or Cut should be at the only Coil and Charges of the Mayor, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of London:

And that, by the Act; of the 4th of King James, the Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of the City of London, were further impowered to make a Trunk or Vault in the Earth, of Brick, or Stone, not exceeding Ten Feet in Breadth, l'or the Passage of the Water from Chadwell and Amu ell to London; which they were for ever to

maintain and preserve.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine,

Mr. Bojlock Toller: Who said. That he appeared as Agent for the Petitioners the Corporation and Inhabitants of the Town of Hertford, and also for the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, and for the Navigators on the River Lea; and that he was, about Six or Seven Yearsago, directed by those Petitioners to enquire what Right the New River Company had to take so large a Quantity of Water out of the said River Lea, as they constantly did; and, about Five Years and a Half since, he came to the Knowledge of the fame.

He also laid before the Committee a Copy of an Order of Council, bearing Date the 126 Day of September 1669; by which it appeared to your Committee, That several Disputes had formerly been between the N Com-

pany, and the Maltsters and Barge-owners of and Hertford, in relation to the Conveying of Water out of the River Lea into the New RiAnd the Matter in

Difference between them having been laid before the King and Council, in the Year 1667 and 166s, an Order was made by the King and Council; a true Copy whereof was laid before the Committee; wherein it is recited, That the Matter in Difference between the Governor and Company of the Corporation of the New River, and the Maltsters and Barge-masters of Ware and Hertford, concerning the Conveyance of Water out of the River Lea into the New River, had, by Order of the 15th of that Month, been appointed to be heard the 22d of -

tember 1669; and that the Parties concerned attended accordingly; and being called in, with their Counfel, and Two several Reports, one signed by Six of the Referret s, to whom among other things, the Matter in Difference had been, by Two several Orders of Council, of the 16th of October 1667 and the 29th of July 1668, referred to settle the fame, if they could, or otherwise make a Report to that. Board; the other signed by Fifteen Commissioners of the Sewers for the River Lea and the New River, residing in the County of Middlesex, to whom the same Matter had been also referred by the Order of the 28th of August then last; being read; as also several Depositions of Witnesses and other Evidences, and, by hearing Counsel on both Parties, as also Counsel for the City of London, in behalf of the Navigation of the River Lea, and long Debate had thereupon;

His then Majesty, taking into his princely Consideration, as well the great Use and Benefit of the Navigation of the River Lea, not only to the City of London and County of Hertford, but also to the adjacent Counties, as the Necessity of supplying the City of London with the Nero River Water, was then graciously pleased, in Council, to order,

That the Governor and Company of the River should take away their great Pipes then lying in the River Lea; and, inilead thereof, should lay Two lesser Pipes, the one of Eight and the other of Six Inches Bore, at or near the Places where the great Pipes lay; and to place and contrive them, that they might be constantly served with Water to supply the New River; and if, upon Trial, it should be found, That the Water in the River Lea would not always rife high enough to fill the said Pipes, that the Governor and Company might, and they were thereby authorized to set up and use a Turnpike or Jetty, or some other Device, to raise and force the Water to the Pipes, whereby they might be rendered most useful to the New River-, yet so as might not cause Inundation of the Meadow Groundsadjoining, nor retard or endanger the Vessels that should pass that Way: And therefore all Persons concerned were to take Notice, and to conform themselves thereunto accordingly, as they would answer the contrary at their Peril:

And Mr. Toller further said, That, when he had col-Iefted all the Fasts together, he recommended it to the Inhabitants of the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and the N av igators, to take the Opi nion of some em i nent Cou n fel; whereupon a same was stated, a Copy whereof was laid before the present Lord Chancellor, then his Majesty’s Attorney General, and another Copy before the late Lord Chief Justice Reeve; and they both advised, That, as the same was a publick Concern, proper Application should be made to the Legislature; and thereupon he waited on the New River Company, from time to time, by Direction of the Persons he was concerned for, that an amicable Agreement might be entered into.

Doctor Defeguliers, being examined, said. That, in

August 1735, he was font for into the Country, by the Navigators on the River Lea-,but did not know for what

Purpose: That, whilst he staid there, he measured the Gage or new-made Instrument, belonging to the Nero River Company, through which the whole Water passed out of the River Lea, and found that Instrument to measure Six Feet Wide and Two Feet deep, and the Top thereof to be 2S Inches above the Cill at the Water House; and then he measured the Quantity of Water below the Gage, and found that it run about 2,400 Tun in an Hour, with small Allowance for the Eddies: That, on the 28th of the same Month, he went down again; and, not trading to the First Experiment, he made several others, in the Presence of many Persons of the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and of one Mr. Mill, a Gentleman belonging to the New River Company, who also made a Calculation, and after making several large Allowances, he found the Quantity of Water diverted or taken out of the said River to be 2,100 Tun in an Hour.

He also said. That, by the Pipes which were directed to be laid down by the before-mentioned Order of Council,

12 Geo. II. 21 0 Mart295

cil, about 90 Tun of Water an Hour (according to the present Velocity of the Stream) would be taken out of the River, the Surface of the Water in the Lea being even with the Top of the Bore.

And he further said, That the [Fall of that] River is very considerable; and if a Compensation was given for scouring and cleansing the River, and for erecting of Locks, and makingother Conveniencies for the Navigation, not only that Quantity of Water which is now taken, but Half as much more might be taken, without any Prejudice to the Navigation.

Mr. Thomas Pettit and Mr. James Barge-

owners, being severally examined, said, That they had known the River Lea the one 45 and the other 47 Years; and that the Navigating of Boats and Barges is now carried on with more Expence and Delay than when they first used the River:

That tormerly they navigated to and from London to Ware in a considerable less time than they now do, and at a much less Expence; and the Reason they gave was, because the Lock-keepers cut the Weeds, which makes the Water to run quicker away, and thereby the River becomes more shallow; and great Quantities of Gravel and Stones are thrown into the River by the Weir-keepers and Millers, at the several Weirs, which occasion so many Shoals, that they cannot now pass without paying at the several Locks for Flalhes of Water, frequently, in the Summer Season, and by reason great Quantities of Water are taken out of the River, for the Use of the New River Company; and, for these Reasons, the Witnesses said, that the Navigation is become very tedious and expensive.

They also said. That the Owners of Boats and Barges, and the Navigators, had raised amongst themselves the Sum of£. 3,000 which had been expended in removing of Shoals; which, if so large a Quantity of Water had. been taken out, and such Shoals made, they should not have been at so great an Expence: And that, before the Weeds were cut, and Gravel and Stones flung into the River, the Boats and Barges, when they got below Waltham Abby, were frequently towed to Old Ford,

without anyObftruftions,or the Assistance ofany Weirs; which cannot now be done.

And they likewise laid, That there had been, in their Memory, Two Commissions of Sewers taken out, in relation to this Matter; and, during the time the Commissioners set, and executed the Powers given them by those Commissions, the Navigation was carried on much easier, and at less Expence, than at other times.

And they severally added to their Evidence, That if a Fund was established for removing the Shoals, and a con-l'tant Commission of Sewers established, it would makea double Recompence for the Water now taken out of the River by the New River Company; and that the several Nuisances complained of would thereby be remedied, and such a Quantity of Water as is now taken out could be spared.

Mr. Toller, being again examined, said, That the River Lea is divided into Two or Three Branches, between the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and unite again into One Stream again a little below Ware Mill: That the antient and right Way of navigating Boats and Barges between the said Towns was through One of the said Branches called Manifold Ditch; but the Navigation is now carried on, and has been for many Years pall, through another Branch of the said River called the Mill Stream, running to W,are Mills, and from thence through a Lock or Cillern there into the main Stream running to Ware Bridge; which Way of Navigation was, till lately, as he apprehended, precarious, and by the Consent of the Owners of Ware Mills, and might by them be flopped and prevented; but that the Company now have purchased the said Ware Mills, and the Lock belonging to the fame, with the Stream of Water runningto the fame; and did, just before such Purchase, give it under their Seal, That the Stream running to the said Mills, and through the Lock there into the main River, should, for ever after they should purchase the fame, be the indif-

A Petition of James Buchanan, of London, Merchant, and others, concerned and interested in the Ship Scipio, Alexander Mackpherson Mailer, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Ship having taken in her Cargo on the Coast of Africa, confuting of Negroes, Gold Dull, and Elephants Teeth, to the Value of Six thousand Pounds and upwards, and pursuing her Voyage from thence to the Island of Jamaica, having touched at the Island of Barbadoes, was, on the 27th Day of 08ober 1736, taken on the High Seas by a French Ship or Vessel, and carried into St. Peter's, in the Island of Martinique: And that, some time after, at the Inllance of the Director of the Customs of that Island, a Prosecution was commenced against Captain Mackpherson, Mailer of the Ship, before the Court of Admiralty there, founded on a Pretence, that Ihe was acting in Contravention to a certain Edict for settling Limits relating to unlawful Trade; and, on hearing the Matter, the Judges declared in their Decree, That it did not appear there was any Intention of carrying on an unlawful Trade; and that it was sufficiently 'proved by the said Ship’s Dispatches in due Form, that Ihe was bound to Jamaica, by way of St, Christopher's; but that, nevertheless, the Intention of the Edi£t having not been qualified by any Interpretation judicially known to them, they were obliged to conform to the express Terms of it, and therefore declared the said Ship and her Cargo duly confiscated, and that thereupon the said Captain Mackpherson appealedto thefupremeCourtof Martinique, VOL. *3.

who, upon Examination of the whole Matter, annulled the Judgment given By the Court of Admiralty, and decreed him Colls, and that he should again be put in possession of the said Ship and Cargo; and that, as the said Captain Mackpherson, agreeable to the lait Judgment, was preparing to take Possession of his Ship and Cargo, he received an Ordinance from the Intendant of me Island, which impowered the Director of the Customs to appeal from the Judgment of the supreme Court to the French King in Council; The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the i;t House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Agent for the Petitioners called,

John Poole: Who, being examined, said. That he is wCll acquainted with the several Fords usually paired over by such Travellers as go through the River Ribble, from the Township of Preston to the Township of and has known those Fords 35 Years; and, for Five or Six Years lad past, has very frequently been a Guide to such Passengers as had Occasion to go through that Part of the River:

‘ That the Fords, by reason of the great Frelhes and Tides Which lately happened therein, are so much wore, dtid become so deep and founderous, that Travellers, particularly Strangers, when such Frelhes are out, cannot, specially in the Winter Season, pass and repass

through the same on Horseback, much less with Carts and Carriages, without great Danger:

That, about Six or Seven Years since, aPerson driving his Cart, loft his Life, and some of the Horses were like-wife loft, in endeavouring to pass through the River; and since that, he has been informed, that others have had the same Fate:

That there are Ferry-boats for carrying over Horses and Passengers; but many Horses will not go into the Boats, and then they are obliged to go Three Miles round about; and Part of that Three Miles is so bad, that, in the Winter Season, it is very dangerous; and Coaches or Carriages, at that time of the Year, cannot, with any Safety, go through the fame:

That all proper Methods have been taken to make the River passable where those Fords are; but the same have proved ineffectual; and, in his Opinion, they never can be made good: That although the Ford, or Place of Passage, hath, of late Years, been changed from one Part of the River to another, for the Conveniency of Persons passing, as hath, from time to time, been thought moll iafe; yet the new Fords, where Travellers now pass, are now, by Use and Wearing, become as deep and founderous as theold ones were whendifufed; so that the Passage through this River, will, in all Probability, be entirely loft in a short time, or become so dangerous, that few Persons will venture to pass through the fame:

That, when the Frelhes and Tides are in, Pack-horses which carry Goods from Preston to Liverpoole cannot pass the Ford, but mull of Necessitygo by Walton', but the Persons who use Preston Market, rather than go near Three Miles about, frequently fwinftheirHorfes over the River; when they have often been in so very great Danger, that the Evidence has refused to guide them over, knowing the y run the Rilk of losing their Lives.

Mr. Ralph Robivfon:Who, being examined, said, He had been acquainted with the Fords in this River for 40 Years; and then confirmed the Evidence of John Poole, as to the bad Condition and Danger of the Fords, and of their being removed from one Place to another; and also as to the Badness of the Road from Preston to Liverpoole into the great common Road, which, he believed, was Four Miles about; and that that Road, in the Winter Season, cannot be passed through with Coaches err Carriages with Safety; and spoke as to the Impossibility of making the Fords good; and also as to the Danger the Persons often run who usually frequent Preston Market; and added, that one Person, about last, had

That the Road by a Place called Tardy Yate, is a high and publick Road; but, in the Winter Season, so bad, that were the several Persons, whole Estates lie on eaehSide the Road, to do double the Statute-work more than, by the Laws in being, they are obliged to do, the same would prove insufficient to repair that Road; and although feme Justices of the Peace have Estates adjoining to that Road, he never knew or heard they had ever attempted to get the same made good.
