A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, Land-owners, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Towns of Lancaster and in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and other the neighbouring Towns and Townships adjoining; and also,

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Gentlemen, Tradesmen, Land-owners, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the Towns and Hamlets of Ashton, Neither Wyerfdale, For-ton, Cleevely, Holloweth, Cabus, Nateby, Barnicker with

Bonds, and Tarnicker, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and other neighbouring Towns and Townships adjoining;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; setting fprth. That there is a Petition preferred to the House, for Leave that a Bill may be brought in for the erecting a publick County Bridge over the River Ribble, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, at a Place therein mentioned, or in any other Place, as the House shall think raoft convenient; and for raising Money upon the said County Palatine, for defraying the Expence thereof, and of repairing the fame, when built; and for such Relief in the Premises as the House should think proper: which Petition, if complied with, as the Petitioners

23

1

A. 1739.

conceive, will be very detrimental to them, and other the Inhabitants of the said County; That there is an ancient Stone Bridge, of Five Arches, over the said River Ribble, within a Mile of the Place where the intended Bridge is proposed to be built, which has always been repaired at the Expence of the County; and that the said Bridge is in good Repair, and Hands in the great Poll Road leading to the North Part of England and Scotland, and within One Mile of the Borough of Preston; which Road takes in the South-east, and great Part of the West: Side of the County of Lanca; and that, adjoining to the South End of the said Bridge, there is a Road called Walton Copp, of Half a Mile in Length, which has also been always repaired at the Expence of the County; and that, as the Petitioners conceive, the said Bridge of Five Arches is not sufficient to receive the Water of the River Ribble in the time of Floods; for that there is an hollow Way, of about One hundred Yards, laid with large broad Stones, in the said Road called Walton Copp, at the Expence of the County, to receive the waste Water of the said River, which cannot pass through the said Bridge in the time of Floods, and often makes a Stream of half or near a Yard deep: That People have been in great Danger of their Lives in riding through it; and that there is another River, called Derwent, near half as large as the said River Ribble, which joins the said River Ribble above the Place where, as the Petitioners apprehend, the new intended Bridge is proposed to be built; and that the waste Water which, in Floods, flows over the lower Part of Walton Copp, together with what comes down the River Derioent, mull pass through the new-intended Bridge; so that there will be, as the Petitioners conceive, above double the Quantity of Water more to pass through the new-intended Bridge than ever could pass through the old Bridge; and, consequently, the New Bridge, if erected, mull be Nine or Ten Arches, otherwise it mull not only occasion a Stoppage of the fresh Water in time of Floods, but like-wife lay all the Lands, for above a Mile above the said new Bridge, underWater; and also Hop the Flux of the Tide from flowing up into the Country, which will lay the In-maidhes, and other low inclosed Lands below the intended new Bridge, under Water, and endanger the drowning great Numbers of Cattle and Sheep which graze thereon; and that, in case of the least Stoppage of the fresh Water more than usual, the said> Road, called Walton Copp, will be dangerous to Travellers, and rendered almost unpayable; and that, if the said new-intended Bridge is to have Wings, and Ramparts at each End, to Hop the Water (unlefe the said Bridge be as large as above-mentioned), they will occasion a Stoppage and great Overflowing of the Water, as there is not above Three Feet of Fall between Ribble Bridge, and the said new-intended Bridge; and that there is already a Ford at Penwortham, which is moll generally palfable for Carts and Carriages, when the Waters are low, and the Tide out; and, when Floods and high Tides, there is a Ferry for Horse and Foot within a very little Distance of the said Ford; High Price A Petition of several Persons, whoseNames are thereof Coals, unto subscribed, on the behalf of themselves, and others. Proprietors of Salt-works, who are Consumers of large Quantities of Coals, imported from , and the

Northern Parts of Engla, to Lymington, the Isle of Wight, and other Parts of the County of was presented to' the House, and read; alleging, That, the Price of Coals hath not only of late been raised and kept up to a great Degree, but that they have also been much worse in Quality than heretofore, occasioned by many indirect Practices made use of by Persons concerned in the Northern Collieries, who thereby monopolize the Coal Trade, and carry on the same by unwarrantable Methods: And that very great Quantities of Salt are annually made by the Petitioners with Coals,

from whence arises a considerableDuty to that Part of his Majesty’s Revenue: And that the Petitioners being under an indispensable Necessity of consuming large Quantities of Coals, for which they pay a high Duty in manufacturing Salt, are unavoidably subjected to the Detriment and Oppression occasioned by such illegal Practices; the Confluences of which are more sensibly felt by the Petitioners, they being thereby rendered unable to carry on so beneficial a Branch of Trade upon equal Terms with the Northern Proprietors, who pay no Duty for Coals consumed in making Salt, and are exempted from the Inconveniencies arising from such Monopoly; which, if not timely prevented, will tend greatly to the Destruction of manufacturing Salt by the Petitioners, and to the Prejudice of Navigation encouraged and supported thereby: And therefore praying the House to take the Premifes into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Edinburgh A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magi ft rates. Council, Theatre. and Community, of the City of Edinburgh, was presented

to the House, and read; letting forth, That if the Bill, now depending in this House, to enable his Majesty, his Heirs, and Succefl’ors, to grant his or their Letters Patent to any Person or Persons, to act, reprefeut, or perform, or cause to be acted, represented, or performed,

’ any Interlude, Tragedy, Comedy, Opera, Play, Farce, or other Entertainment of the Stage, or any Part or Parts therein, within the City or Liberties of Edinburgh, shall pass intoa I.aw, manyInconvenienciesand Mischiefswill arise to that City, by establishing a Playhouse therein; and particularly, that the same will occasion an Expence, 1‘uch astheftnail Extent of the Wealth and Trade of that City cannot well all’ord to bear; and that the Manners of the Youth will be in great Danger of being corrupted, of whom there are great Numbers residing in that City, as being the Seat of an University, and a Place chiefly frequented for all Parts of the Education of Children of both Sexes, besides the considerable Number of Apprentices in it; and as the Parliament has already prohibited, under severe Penalties, the performing, for Gain, any Entertainment of the Stage within Five Miles of the City,

of Oxford, and Town of Cambridge; and, last of all, has prohibited the same to be acted in any Part of Great Britain, except in the City of Wcflmhijler, and in fuel*

Places where his Majesty his Heirs, and Succell'ors, shall in their Royal Persons reside, for the Time, without excepting the City of London itself; submitting to this House, if it will not be unreasonable to make an Exception of the City of Edinburgh from the general Prohibition established by the Law now in force; it being considered. That that City is entitled to the Benefit of that Law, for the same Reasons that induced the Parliament to grant a particular Privilege to the Universitiesof Oxford, and Cambridge; and that the Reasons for not excepting even the City of London from the general Prohibition stand good, and with greater Force, against making a particular Exception of the City of Edinburgh; which, as a Place of Trade and Business, is vastly inferior in Wealth and Number of Inhabitants to London, and, as the Seat of an University and a Place of Education, is in the like Circumstances with the City oiOxford and Town of Cambridge: And therefore praying the Floufe, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Principal and Professors of the Uni- Edinburgh verfity of Edinburgh was presented to the House, and Tneuti«. read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed.

That the said Bill is depending in this House, and that, they reckon themselves bound, as having the Inllruftion of Youth in the liberal Arts and Sciences, and their Im-. provement in Religion and Virtue particularly committed to their Care, to represent to this House, that whatever may be said of the Innocence and Usefulness of Theatrical Representations when the Pieces represented are perfectly cliafte and moral, and the Representation is performed in a decent Manner; the Petitioners cannot but be apprehensive, that the Reverse of this may be expected, from a general Allowance to act any Interlude, Comedy, Farce, or other Entertainment of the Stage, while there arefo many loose anddifiblute Pieces of that Sort in the English Language, and the Choice is left to such as, either from their own Taste, or in Compliance with the vicious Relish of the Multitude, are likely to choose such Performances as have the most direct Tendency to corrupt the Morals of the Audience, especially those of the younger Sort; and that the Petitioners are greatly confirmed in this Apprehension, from the Observation they have made of the pernicious Eflefts the Stage has ever had in that Place where the Performances have been frequent, and the Access to them near; and that, instead of being a virtuous or improving Entertainment, it has been a plentiful Source of Idleness and Debauchery, efpeeially among the Youth; insomuch that many Gentlemen of that Place, who, from an Opinion founded upon general Theory, and the Observation of antieut Times of Greece, were at first Favourers of a Stage there, have, from seeing the bad Efleft it has had, come to be quite of another Mind; and that the unhappy Influence of Playhouses, in such Places as are Seats of Universities, has been made appear, to the Satisfaction of the Legislature; for which Reason t hey have been lately discharged by Act of Parliament in or near Oxford and Cambridge: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Dean of Guild of and his Edinburgh

Council, and the other MerchantsandTraderswithin the Theatre, said City, and Liberties thereof, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. P E TITI ON of the Merchants andothers of the Port of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; representing, That the Port of Lancaster is very advantageously situate for the Importation of Irish Wool and Bay Yarn, being on the North-West Coast of this Kingdom, and nighest to the Towns of Leeds, Halifax, and Wakefield,the most considerable Places for the

Woollen Manufacture in the North Part of this Kingdom: And that the Wool produced in that, and the other Northern Part of this Kingdom, is naturally very coarse; and that the Irish Wool, being generally of a finer Sort, will be very properand fuitableto mixthere-with, and will greatly tend to improve the said Manufacture: And therefore praying, That the Liberty of importing of Irish Wool and Bay Yarn may be extended to that Place.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. St. John reported to the House, That her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales had been attended with the congratulatory Meffageofthis House, on the increase of the Royal Family, by her Royal Highness being happily delivered of a Prince: And that her Royal Highness was pleased to return the following Answer:

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, the' Agent for the Petitioners produced, and laid before the Committee,

Two Acts of Parliament, onepaffed in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First for amending the several Roads therein mentioned, leading from the City of Bristol-, and the other passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, to explain and amend the aforesaid Act: That it appeared, by the said Acts, Provision is made for amending the Road leading from the City of Bristol, through the Parish of Bitton, in the County of Gloucester, to Buckle Brook, in the Parish of Kelfon, in the County of set:

But that neither of the said Acts have yet been, or are likely to be, put in Execution for amending that Part of the Road which lies in the Parish of Kelfon, between Buckle Brook aforesaid, and Coombes Brook.

Then one Mr. Richard Helfom was called as a Witness; and being examined, as to what Condition the last-roentioned Road was in at this time, said, That it is now in a very ruinous Condition; which was occasioned by many heavy Carriages, loaden with Brass and other Goods, frequently pasting through the fame, as it is the high Road for Waggons, commonly called Tranting Waggons, usually travelling to and from the Cities of London and Bristol.

And the Witness further said. That the Inhabitants of the Parish of Kelfon have been at very great Expences, and constantly performed their 'Statute-work; yet that has proved not sufficient to put this Road into good Repair.

Upon the Whole, it appeared to the Committee, That the Road mentioned in the Petition cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, unlei's lomefurther Provision be made for that Purpose.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee ' to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted and given by Two Acts of Parliament, one of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and the other made in the Seventh Year of iris late Majesty King George the First, for repairing, amending,

Importation A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and and Exporta- principal Inhabitants, of the Town and County of Poole, tion of Wool. wag presenteti to the House, and read; complaining of the Decay of the Woollen Manufacture in the Towns and Counties adjacent to the said Town and County, and of the Discouragements and Disadvantages which the Towns and Counties adjacent to the said Port have, for many Years pad, laboured under, for want of having a Liberty of importing Wool, and Woollen Yarn, from Ireland, into that Port, and having the Duty of Four Pence per Stone, pow payable on all Wool exported from Ireland, taken off; and representing to the House the Reasonableness and Necessity, That the Importation of Wool and Woollen Yarn, into England, may not be confined to a few Ports on the North Side of this Kingdom, where very little Wool is made use of; but that the other more considerable trading Ports, on the Southern and Eastern Sides of this Kingdom, may have also the Benefit of the Importation of Wool and Woollen Yarn, from Ireland, in registered Ships, extended to them* and particularly the said Portnf; so that the whole Kingdom may become a proper Market for the fame: And therefore praying the House for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

/ APctition of the Sugar Refiners in the City of London, Carrying and Partsadjacent, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Petitioners con- Jhnfvlmi'ies flantly give Employment to a great Number of Trades, to foreign such as Blacksmiths, Coppersmiths, Plumbers, Back- I’ans. makers, Bricklayers, Carpenters, Potters, Coopers, Tallow-chandlers, Stationers, and others, besides a great Number of menial Servants, who depend for their Subsistence on this Manufacture; and likewise consume very large Quantities of Coals, which pay a very considerable Duty to the Publick, as well as greatly increase the Navigation of this Kingdom: And that, for Three Years last part, the whole Produce of the Sugar Plantations have been taken off the Hands of the Proprietors, at very high Prices; and had the Importation of Sugars been much larger, they had not wanted Purchasers; for, notwithstanding the Importation of Sugars to the Port of London,the last Year, amounted to upwards of Sixty thousand Hogsheads, being, upon a Aledium, the usual Quantity annually imported for same Years palt, many Sugar-houses are now unemployed, for want of a sufficient Supply of Sugar at Alarket: And that, lliould the Bill, now depending in this House, for granting a Liberty to carry Sugars, of the Growth, Produce, or Alanuiafture, of any of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America, from the said Colonies, directly to foreign Parts, in Ships built in Great Britain, and navigated according to Law, pal's into a Law, the Quantity of'Sugars imported into Great Britain will necessarily be much less; and conseqnently the Price of Sugars will be higher at the Expence of the Confnmers, and to the Dccrease of the Publick Revenue; and as the Prices of refined Sugar will advance in proportion to the Price of Alufcavados, it will occasion not only less Consumption of this Commodity, as well as of several other Commodities which pay Duties to the Crown, but will prevent the Exportation of any refined Sugars to foreign Countries, to the great Lois of the Nation, and of the Petitioners, and all others concerned in the manufacturing of Sugars in this Kingdom, by enabling Holland and Hamburgh, who are already supplied with Alufcavado Sugar cheaper than Great Britain, to be supplied still cheaper, and to supply every other Country in Europe, much cheaper than Great Britain will be able to do, with the Manufactory of refined Sugars: And that, by the Liberty alked, the Difference of Price between the Alarkets of Holland and Hamburgh and the Alarket of Great Britain will be so great, as that it will probably be a Temptation to the Running of manufactured Sugars into this Kingdom, to the farther great Lofsof the Petitioners in particular, as well as the Nation in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Bill may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty being restrained by the Laws now in being from making rrovision for his younger Children, out of the Hereditary Revenues of the Crown, in such manner as his Royal Predecessors have usually done; and being desirous, That competent Provisions may be made for the honourable Support and Maintenance of his dearly beloved Son the Duke of Cumberland, and of his dearly beloved Daughters the Four young Princesses, his Majesty hopes. That he shall be enabled, by Art of Parliament, to grant an Annuity of Fifteen thousand Pounds per Annum to the Duke of Cumberland, and his Issue, and an Annuity of Twenty-four thousand Pounds per Annum to the Four Prince lies; to take effert after his Demise: And recommends the Consideration thereof to this House.

Treaty with Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the Denmark. House, That he had a Menage from his Majesty to this House, signed by his Majesty: And that he had received his Majesty’s Commands to lay before this House,

Copy of the Treaty with Denmark, 14 th March, N. S.

173S-Q; and Tranllation thereof.

And he presented the said Vlelfage, together with the said Copy and Trauflation, to the House.

And the said Message was read by Mr. Speaker, all the Members being uncovered; and is as followeth; viz.

George R.

His Majesty being truly solicitous for the Peace and Welfare of these Kingdoms, and desirous to contribute, as far as in him lies towards preferring the publick Tranquillity, and the Balance of Power in Europe, hath concluded with the King of Denmark aTreaty, agreeable to that, which expired in 1737; an<^ has ordered the same to be laid before this House, that he may be enabled to make good the Engagements which he hath thereby entered into.

And, as Events may happen, during fitch time as it may be impossible for his Majesty to have the immediate Advice and Assistance of his great Council, upon any Emergency, arising from the prefect Postureof Affairs in Europe, which may nearly concern the Honour, Interest, and Safety, of these Kingdoms; his Majesty hopes he shall be enabled and supported by his Parliament, in making such further Augmentation of his Forces, either by Sea or Land, as may become absolutely necessary; and in concerting such Measures as the Exigency of Affairs may require; and whatever Expence shall be thereby occasioned, shall be made in as frugal a manner as is possible; and an Account thereof shall be laid before this House the next Session of Parliament.

Ordered, Nemine Contradicente, That his Majesty’s said most gracious Message be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And the Title of the said Copy and Tranllation being read;

Ordered, That the said Copy and Tranllation be referred to the said Committee.

The Copy of the said Treaty is bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

And the Tranllation thereof is as follows; viz.

Translation of the Treaty with dated at

Copenhagen, 14th March 1739.

A 1^x9.

Be it known to all, to whom it appertains. That his Majesty the King of Great Britain, on one Side, his Majesty the King of Denmark and the

other, having considered. That, in the present Situation of the Affairs of Europe,their reciprocal Interests require,

That the antient Fiicndship and Confidence which has been at all times cultivated between their Majesties and their glorious Ancestors, to the great Advantage of the-Two Nations, should be renewed and llrengthened by drifter Ties, and by a new Treaty of defenlive Alliance; their Majesties have thought lit to charge reciprocally their Ministers; that is lo say; his Majesty the King of Great Britain the Sienr Walter his Miniller re-

fident at his Danijh Majesty’s Court; and his Majesty

the King of Denmark and of Norway, his Privy Coun-fellors of his Council, the Sieur Ivar Ro/enkranfz Lord of Rnfcnhalmand of Ryegaard, Knight of the Order of

the Elephant; the Sieur John Ixmis de Iloljlcin, Lord of Wreile Clojler, Knight of the Order of , his

first Secretary of State of the Danish Chancery; and the Sienr John Sigmund de Schulin, Knight of the Order of

Dannebrog, his First Secretary of State for foreign Affairs, and of the German Chancery; being provided with the necessary full Powers to confer thereupon; who* after having exchanged their full Powers, have agreed upon the Points and Articles following;

Art. I.

There shall beafincere Amity, and a most ftriftUnioa, between their Majesties, their Successors and Heirs, Kingdoms and Subjects, in such manner, that the one-shall consider the Interests of the other as his own, and shall faithfully employ himself to promote them as much as possible; and to prevent and keep ofl’fromeach other, mutually, all Trouble and Damage.

Art. II.

To this End, it is agreed, That all the preceding Treaties of Peace, Amity, Guaranty, Navigation, and Commerce, without excepting any, shall be taken to be renewed and confirmed by this present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses; and they shall have the same Force as if they had been here inserted, Word for Word, as far as there shall have been no Alteration made therein by the present Treaty.

Art. III.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having desired, That his Majesty the King of Denmark would hold in Readiness a Body of his Troops for the Service of his Brilannick Majesty, in case the Good of his Kingdoms and Dominions should require that Succour, his Majesty the King of Denmark has been willing to agree thereto; promising and engaging, by virtue of this Article, to hold in Readiness for that Purpose, during the Space of Three Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this present Treaty, a Body of Six thousand Men; that is to say, One thousand Horse, and Five thousand Foot, provided with the necessary General Officers and Subalterns, fitly mounted and armed, in a Condition to march, for the Service of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Two Months after Requifitiou shall have been made, or sooner, if it be possible; unless there be need of them for the immediate Defence of the Kingdoms and Dominions of his Brilannick Majesty; in which case they shall march immediately after the Requisition has been made; and the said Troops shall take the Oath of Fidelity to his Brilannick Majesty when they shall have passed the Frontiers of the Territories belonging to the Crown of Denmark, [without Prejudice to that which they have taken to his Majesty the King of Denmark]; his said Danish Majesty however retaining the Disposal of all the Polls that shall become vacant in that Corps; and the Administration of Justice in it remaining regulated in the same manner as it was practised in that which went into the Service of and Holland, by

virtue of the Treaty of 1701.

Art. IV.

Ashis Danish Majesty isen gaged to fend; uponOceafions that may arile, considerable Succours to other Powers,

- his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to pay to his Majesty the King of Denmark, without any Abatement or Delay,.an annual Subsidy of Two hundred and Fifty thousand Crowns Banco, during the Time that the Troops shall l»e at the Charge of tfte Treasury of his Majesty the King of Denma which Subsidy shall commence from the Signing of this present Treaty, and shall be continued to the F,xpiration,of the ThreeYears above mentioned: But when these Troops shall actually be taken into the Pay of his Majesty the King of Great tain., his Majesty the King of Denmark shall then be contented with an annual.Subsidy of One hundred and Fifty thousand Crowns Banco; j pjjpch Subsidy shall continue during the whole time that the said Troops shall be in the Service,of his Majesty: The Payment of the pne and of the other shall be maderegularly* every Quarter, in the Town of Hamburg, to such Persons as shall be authorized by his Majesty the King of Denmark to receive it: But if his Majesty the King of Great Britain lets the abqyesaid Three Years pass, without demanding the Body of Six thousand Men, his Majesty the King of Denmark shall not be any longer obliged, after that, to furniili the fame, and the Subsidy z shall entirelly cease, at the same time, at the End of those

Three Years, unless the Two contracting Kings agree otherwise concerning it.

Art.;

His Majesty the King of Great Britain shall take upon himself the Pay and Entertainment, as,well ordinary as extraordinary, of the O fficers, Horsemen, and Foot Soldiers, of that Body, from the Day they shall begin their March for his Service; and this Pay, both ordinary and ext raordinary, shall be regulated upon the same Foot with that of the Troops, made over by

the Treaty of 1701; and it shall be put into the Hands of the Danish Commissaries, without any Abatement or Ilftninution, to make the Distribution thereof; but if it should, by Misfortune, happen, that any Regiments or Companies of the abovesaid Corps lliould come to be ruined or destroyed, in the Whole or in Part, his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall cause to be paid, without Delay, to the Officers of the said Body of Troops, the Charges of the necessary Recruits, for putting the Regiments or Companies speedily again in a good Condition; and these Recruits shall be, in like manner, regulated upon the Foot of those that were furnished to the Officers of the Danish Troops, by virtue of the Treaty of 1701; to the end that this Corps may always be preserved and sent back one Day in as good Condition as it was received.

Art. VI.

His Britannick Majesty shall be at Liberty to keep, this Corps in his Service all the Time of the Duration of this Treaty, in order to make use of it wherevqr he shall have Occasion; provided it be not either in , nor upon the Fleet, nor to be transported, in the Whole, or in Part, beyond Sea, after it is come once out of the Territories of his Majesty the King of Denmark, except for the Defence of the Kingdoms of Great Britain and t. Ireland.; in which same these Troops shall wholly enjoy the same Pay which the English Troops enjoy: And, when his Majesty the King of Great hall be

desirous of fending back the said Troops, he shall acquaint his Majesty the King of Denmark with it Three Months before-hand; and shall cause to be paid to them a'Month’s Wages for their Return.

Vol. 23.

Art. VII.

In case his Majesty the King ot lliould be attacked or troubled in the PolVeftion of his Kingdoms,

Dominions, Lat1ds, Provinces, or Cities, his Britannick Majesty promises to fend the said, Body of Troops speedily back to him, paying them a Month’s Wages for their Return; and to give h\s Danish Majesty,. besides, all the Assistance, by Sea and by Land, that the same shall require; which Assistance shall be continued to him till he shall have obtained a good and advan-geous Peace: As his Majesty the King of Denmark, on his Part, promjfes. That, in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain should be attacked or troubled, as is abovesaid, he will give him immediately all the Assistance, by Sea and by Land, that the same shall require; which Assistance shall, in like manner, be continued to hiqri, until he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace: In case, contrary to all Expefla-tion, a War should break out in Europe, the Two con* trafting Kings reciprocally engage not tomoleft, in any fort whatsoever, the Liberty, of Commerce of their respective Subjects.

Art. VIII.

In order to make this Alliance and Union so much the more perfect, and to leave the Parties no kind of Scruple as to the certainty of the Assistance which tliqy are to expect from each other, it is expressly agreed, That, for judging hereafter whether the same of this Alliance exists or nor, it shall be sufficient, that either of the Parties be actually attacked by Force of Arms, without that Party’s having before used open Force agaiull him who attacks.

Art. IX.

This Treaty shall last for the Space of Three Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing it; and, if their Majesties think fit tp continue, prolong, or change, it, that Matter shall be treated of Three Months before it expires, according to the Exigency of the Cafe.

Art. X.

The Ratifications of this Treaty shall be exchanged at Copenhagen, within Two Months after the Signing, or sooner, jf it bepoffible.

In Witpefs whereof, We, the under-written, being furnished with the full Powers of the most serene Kings of Great Britain and of Denmark and Nonoaii, have, in their said Names, signed the present Treaty, and have caused our Seals to be set thereunto. Done at Copenhagen, the 14th Day of March, N. S. 1739.

That, within the Memory of most of the Petitioners, the Price of Wool is fallen near One Half; whereby the Tenants, who pay the feme Rents as when Wool was dearest, or greater, are disabled from holding their Farms, without a proportional Y . able

able Abatement of Rent; or to discharge the great Arrears that are owing to their Landlords: And that, by importing Wool from Ireland, the Price of ool

mult not only be reduced Hill lower, but great Part thereof will not be saleable at all, the Growth of that Commodity being already too great for the Market: And that the Petitioners do not conceive how the taking off the Duties on Irish Yam, and increasing the Number

of Ports, as intended by the Bill now before the House, can be a Means to prevent the Exportation of Irish Wool, or Woollen Manufactures, to foreign Parts; or why as effectual Methods may not be taken to prevent such Exportation, whilst those Duties continue, and the Ports which give Opportunities of exporting are fewer; but that the Petitioners apprehend, That, as the taking off those Duties will lower the Price of Wool in,

so it wtH advance the Value of Wool in , and

consequently bring the Englishi and Irish Lands to an Equality, though the Rent now paid for the one is double to the Rent paid for the other; and, whilst it invites the Irish Tenants to turn their Lands to the keeping of Sheep, which will discourage the Linen Manufacture there, it will oblige the Tenants in ’, in order to

make their Rents by Corn, which they wiH not be able to make by Wool, to plough up their Sheep Walks and Failures, and thereby ruin the Farmers here 5 and that the Price of the Wool itself is so incohsiderable in all Manufactures, that the reducing it will undo the Grower, without any Benefit to the Manufacturer, or even bringing it cheaper to Market, as the Trade is now managed; it being well known, that Woollen Goods fell as dear now as when Wool was double the Price; though all Necessaries of Life are much lower noW than they were at that time, and the Manufacture rather worse than better; and that, if the Petitioners for the Bill may themselves be believed, now that Wool is the cheapest, the Trade is in the utmost Decay; which shews, that as the Greatness of the Price of Wool has not been tlte Grievance, so neither will a Reduction of it be the Remedy; and that, the Petitioners apprehend, it would plainly appear, had they time to make a proper Application to the House, that if the Bill, now before the House, shall pass into a Law, it will bring down the Rents of all Englijk Lands, or starve the Tenants, and such of the Poor as live by Spinning, whose Wages, since the Importation of Irish Yarn, are already lessened One-

third; and will be an Advantage only to a few Mailer Workmen, Merchants, and Factors, who, under the Pretence of a publick G ood, seek only to amass to themselves great Estates, by oppressing the Body of the People, whole Labours are the Foundation of the Trade itself, and the Support of the Nobility and Gentry of the Kingdom: But that the Petitioners hope the House will fiud Means for satisfying the reasonable Desires of the One, without ruining the other; and for encouraging the WouHen Trade in general, by allowing all who contribute thereto, from the Grower to the Exporter, a reasonable Share in the Profit that is to be made thereby.

My Lords and.Gentfemep,

The Dispateh you have given to the publick Bufi- The King’s uefe that has been under your Consideration, makes, it Speech, proper tqput an End to this Session of Parliament, and to give you that Recess which the Seaibn of the Year requires.

You have so. Cully declared your Sentiments, as well with regard to the pall Conduct of Spain, as to the Measures that might become necessary to be pursued, in consequence of any Part which that Court might afterwards take, and enabled me to act, in all Events, as the I lonour and Interest of my Crown an,d Kingdom, foall require, that no Inconvenience can arise from the imme<-diate Want of your further Afliftanpe, during the Recess of Parliament. And I shall so entirely rely upon the Affurances ypu ha,ve given me, with so much Zeal, and Unanimity, and upon your effectually supporting me, in following the concurrent Advice of bptfi Houses of Parliament, that I will not be wanting in my Endeavours to vindicate and maintain our undoubted Rights, and tq answer the just Expectations of my People.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the necessary Provisions you have made for the Service of the Current Year, in so ample a manner. The extraordinary Supply which you have granted me towards augmenting my Forces, by Sea and Land, is such a Proof of your Aueftion and Confidence in me, and of your con ft ant Attention to the Service of your Country, that Icannotenough commendthis. feasonable Care of the Welfare and Safety of tire Kingdom.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am persuaded itisunnecessary for me to recommend to your serious Considerafian, the fatal Consequences that may threaten a Nation divided within itself, inflamed and milled by all the wicked Arts and Insinuations that Msdice and Fallhood can fuggeil. It is too obvious what Advantages our common Enemies wait to take from the Heats and Animofities, that, under groundless Pretences, are industriously fomented and spread throughout the Kingdom. Let all who profess themselves zealous Asser-t-ors of the Rights and Privileges, Laws and Liberties, of their Country, and of the Protestant Religion, tinder the present Establishment, unite, in the Defence of these ineltimable Blefiings: Let the Honour, Prosperity, and Safety, of the Kingdom, become One common Gause, and reconcile all civil Discordsand Divisions, that, by your Unanimity, you may disappoint the only Hope? and vain Expectations of our Enemies.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The present Posture of our Affairs has obliged me to call you together, at this time, sooner than has been usual of late Years, that I may have the immediate Advice and Assistance of my Parliament at this critical and important Conjuncture. I have, in all my Proceedings with the Court of Spain, acted agreeably to the Sense of both 1 loufes of Parliament; and therefore I can make no

Doubt, but I shall meet with a ready and vigorous Support, in this just and necessary War, which t he repeated Injuries and Violences committed by that Nation upon the Navigation and Commerce of these Kingdoms, and theixObftinacy, and notorious Violation of tin* most solemn Engagements, have rendered unavoidable.

I have augmented my Forces by Sea and Land, pur-fuantto the Power given trie by Parliament; which I have done with all the Moderation that the Security and Defence of my Dominions, the Protection of our Trade, and the necessary Means of dilifefling and annoying our Enemies in the most fenfibie Parts, would admit: But as these Services will be various and extend ve, they mud inevitably be attended' with great Expences, and some Inconveniencies; which I allure myself w ill be sustained with Satisfaction and Cheerfulness, in pursuing such Measures as the Honour and Interest of mv Crown and Kingdoms, and the general Resentment of an injured and provoked Nation, have called upon me to undertake.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Officers to lay before you . Eltimates for the Service of the ensuing Year, and like-wife Accounts of the extraordinary Expences that have been made this Year, in pursuance of the Power given me by Parliament. And as, in the Prosecution of this War, a Number of Soldiers, to serve on board the Fleet, may be requiftte, I have judged it proper, that a Body of Marines should be raised; and have direeled the F.ftinvates for this Purpose to be likewise prepared, and laid before you: And I cannot doubt, from your known Affection to my Person and Government, and your Zeal for the Satiety, Prol'perily, and Glory, of these Kingdoms, but you wiil grant me such effectual Supplies, and with such Dispatch, as may forward and give Spirit to our Preparations, and enable me to carry on the War with Vigour.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Heats and Animosities, which, with the greatdt Industry, have been fomented throughout the Kingdom, have, I am afraid, beenOne of the chief Encouragements to the Court of Spain to hold such a Conduct towards Us, as to make it necessary to have Recourse to Arms; and the unhappy Divisions amongst my Subjects are the only Hopes of the Enemies to my Government: But whatever Views and Projects they may form upon this Rupture, and what advantages soever Spain may vainly promise itself from any Circumstances in the present Situation of Affairs, it is in /our Power* by the Blessing of God, to defeat the one, and disappoint the other. Union among all those who have nothing at Heart but the true Interest of Great Britain, and a becoming Zeal in the Defence of my Kingdoms, and in support of the common Cause of our Country, with as general a Concurrence in " carrying on the War as there has appeared for engaging in it, will make the Court of Spain repent the Wrongs they have done us; and convince those who mean the Subverlion of the present Establishment, that this Nation is determined, and able, both to vindicate their injured Honour, and to defend themselves against all our open and feeret Euemies both at home and abroad.

the King's Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House Speech, for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to express

ourentire Satisfaction in his Majesty’s Declaration of War against the Crown of Spain; a War which the repeated Violences and Depredations committed by that Nation upon the Trade and Commerce of these Kingdoms, the notorious Violation of their most solemn Engagements, and their obstinate Refusal of making Reparation for pall Injuries, and of giving Security against the like for the future, have rendered just and unavoidable; to acknow-lege, with all possible Duty and Gratitude, our Sense of his Majesty’s Wisdom and paternal Care of his People, in making use of the Power granted him by Parliament for the Security and Defence of these Kingdoms, for the Protection of our Trade, and for distressing and annoying our Enemies in the most sensible and effectual manner; and to assure his Majesty, That nothing shall divert or deter us from sustaining, with Satisfaction and Cheer-fidnefe, any extraordinary Expences or Inconveniencies that may attend the various and extensive Services which his Majesty shall find necessary to undertake, in vindicating the Honour of his Crown, in asserting the Rights ' of his People, and in procuring Justice to an injur ed and provoked Nation; and that, in defence of his Majesty’s Kingdoms, and in support of the common Cause of our Country, we will grant to his Majesty such effectual Supplies, and with such Dispatch, as may forward and give Spirit to his Majesty’s Preparations, and enable his Majesty to carry on the War with Vigour; and that we will ' endeavour to heal the unhappy Divisions, which have too long prevailed among his Majesty’s Subjects, and, by our Union and Harmony, to defeat and disappoint all the ,vain Projects, Hopes, and Expectations of his Majesty’s open and feeret Enemies both at home and abroad.

Mr. Henry Archer reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and lie read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as foltoweth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne, and to express our entire Satisfaction in your Majesty’s Declaration of War against the Crown of Spain; a War, which the repeated Violences and Depredations committed by the Spanish Nation upon the Trade and Commerce of these Kingdoms, the notorious Violation of their most solemn Engagements, their obstinate Refusal of making Reparation for past Injuries, and of giving Security against the like for the future, have rendered just and unavoidable.

It is with the highest Sense of Duty and Gratitude we acknowledge your Majesty’s Wisdom and paternal Care of your People, in making use of the Power granted to your Majesty by Parliament, for the Security and Defence of these Kingdoms, for the Protection of our Trade, and for the distressing and annoying our Enemies in the most sensible and effectual manner; and we beg Leave to af-sure your Majesty, That nothing shall divert or deter us from sustaining, with Satisfaction and Cheerfulness, any extraordinary Expences and Inconveniencies.that must inevitably attend the various and extensive Services which your Majesty shall find necessary to undertake, in vindicating the Honour of your Crown, in asserting the Rights of your People, and in procuring Justice to an injured and provoked Nation.

And we beseech your Majesty to accept the strongest and most affectionate Assurances, that, in Defence of your Majesty’s Kingdoms, and, in Support of the common Cause of our Country, we will raise such effectual Supplies, and with such Cheerfulness-and Dispatch, as will forward and give Spirit to your Majesty’s Preparations, and enable your Majesty to carry on the War withVigour. Voi. 23.

And your dutiful Commons, being, truly fenGble of the fatal Consequences of intestine Heats and Animoftties, will, with a Zeal becoming the Repfefentatives of the People in Parliament, endeavour to compose those unhappy Diviftons which have too long prevailed among your Majesty’s Subjects; and we do allure your Majesty,

That nothing shall be wanting, on our Part, to restore to the Nation that Union and Harmony, which may effectually defeat and disappoint all the vain ProjeCls,

Hopes, and Expectations, of your Majesty’s opeu and secret Enemies, both at Home and Abroad.

The said Address, being read aSecond time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House. i Bejolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House. '

Condition,

A Motion being made. That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the-Crown, to make out a new Writ, for electing a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of in the

room of the Right honourable Harry Grey Esquire, commonly called Lord Grey, now Earl of Stamford;

The House was moved, That the Journal of the House of the th Day of November 1692, and of the 12th Day of November 1694, in relation to several Orders of the' House, for ilfuing Warrants to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out new Writs for the Elections of Burgelfes, in the room of Sir Henry Capell, Charles Lord Henry Herbert Esquire, and Richard Lord Colchester, might be read:

And the same was read accordingly.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ, for electing a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Leicester, in the room of the Right honourable Harry Grey Esquire, commonly called Lord Grey, now Earl of Stamford, called up to the House of Peers.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, humbly to lay before him, as the Advice of this House, That he would be pleased to give Directions, That the Body of Marines intended to be raised, may be done in the most frugal manner, and put upon the least expensive Establiffiment, by having as many private Men, and as few Officers, as the Nature of the Service will admit; Economy, at first setting out, being absolutely necessary to enable us to support his Majesty in the vigorous Prosecution of this War; and, as Draughts from the present Regiments of Foot, which are all equally proper to be employed either by Land or by Sea, will be attended with the lead Expence, as well as be most expeditious for any immediate Service, humbly to recommend that Method to his Majesty, in tender compassion to his People, already burthened with many heavy and grievous Taxes; and to allure his Majesty, whenever he shall judge it necessary to increase the Corps from whence such Draughts are made, that his faithful Commons will most readily enable him to do it; being fully convinced, that their Safety and all that is dear to them, consist in the Preservation of his Majesty, and the Protestant Succession;

The House divided.

ReJ'dyed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of Four Shillings in the Pound be raised, in the Year 1740, upon Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offices, and personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed; and that a proportionable Cess, according to the Ninth Article of the Treaty of Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of William Mitchell Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, at the last Election of a Knight of the Sliire to serve in Parliament for the County of Huntingdon, in the room of the present Duke of Manchester, the Petitioner and Charles Clarke

Esquire flood Candidates: That, at the Time of such Election, the said Mr. Clarke was not qualified, according to Law, to fit and vote in the House of Commons, as a Knight of the Shire for the said County; and that therefore the said Election and Return of the said Mr. Clarke is void: That, notwithstanding the Premises aforesaid, the said Mr. Clarke is returned, in prejudice to the Petitioner, who was duly elected a Reprefen tat ive for the said Countyr and therefore ought to have been returned accordingly, instead of the said Mr. Clarke: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioner such Relief as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard, at the Bar of this House, upon Monday the 14th Day of January next.

Hockliffe, fTT'.HE Lord Sidney Beauclerk reported from the Comarc. Road! X mittee, to whom the Petition of the several Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, of the Counties of Bucks and Bedford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition} and had directed him to report the fame, as.it. appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Agent for the Petitioners called,

Mr. James Hall, Mr. Robert Colett, and Mr. John Hoare: Who, being severally examined, said, That they are well acquainted with the Road leading from the End of Hockliffe, in the County of to Stoney

Stratford, in the County of Bucks, which is commonly called the Walling Street Road, about Fourteen Miles in Length, and is the antient Poll Road between London and West Chester, and leads through several Townships and Parishes in the said Counties, and particularly mentioned in the Petition; and that many Parts of the same Road are, by reason of the many heavy Carriages frequently passing that Way, become so bad, that, in the . Winter Season, the same is dangerous for Travellers; and several Horses have been so mired, that some of them have been killed by drawing them, out of the founderous Places:

And they further fin'd, That the Inhabitants of several Parishes, through which the Road leads, have con* stantly done their Statute-work; and several of the Parishes have raised Eight Pence in the Pound; notwithstanding which, several of the Parishes have been indited, by reason of the badness of the Road, and fined; which Fines they have paid, and the Money hath been laid out in amending of this Road; all which hath not proved near sufficientto repair the fame) and that, so much having been laid out on this publick Road, the Repairs of the other Highways have been neglected.

And the said Mr. Colett added to his Evidence, That in regard the Road is so very bad, the Owners of the fe* >5

Decembris. . A. 1739.

veral travelling Waggons, who frequently pass through the fame, have agreed to pay, and do pay, Six Pence per Waggon every, time they pass that Way, to be applied towards the Repair of the Road; and appointed him to receive the same; which lie has received for Three Years past; and the Money arising thereby amounts to about Seventy Pounds Annum; which has been duly applied accordingly;

And the Three Witnesses before named said further.

That Materials proper for repairing this Road lie Five Miles Distance from some Parts thereof, and will colt about Five Shillings per Load; so the Inhabitants of the several Parishes are not able effectually to repair such Parts of the Road as lead through such Parishes.

And it appeared to the Committee, upon the examination of all the Witnesses, That the Road cannot be sufficiently repaired, and kept amended, unless some further Provision be made for raising Money for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road between Hockliffe, in the County of Bedford, and Stony Stratford, in the County of Buckingham :And that the Lord Sidney Beauclerk, Mr. Hampden, and Dr. Butler, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Commissioners for building a Bridge Westminster cross the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to Bridge, the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; fettingforth, That the Petitioners are, by an Act passed the last Session of Parliament, impowered to open, make, design, and lay out, such Ways, Streets, and Pafl’ages, as they shall find proper to make, on each Side the River Thames, to and from the intended Bridge, the Courts of Juliice, and both Houses of Parliament; and to agree for, and purchase, such Houses and Ground, within certain Limits by the said Act prescribed, as they shall find necessary for them to be possessed of for that Purpose; and that the Petitioners have proceeded to carry the several Powers granted them by the said Act, into Execution; but that certain Difficult ies have occurred in the Performance thereof, for want of sufficient Powers to enable and oblige several Persons, interestedjn Estates within the said Limits, to convey the same to the Petitioners, and effectually to secure the Consideration-money, for the Purchase of such Estates, and the Produce thereof, to the several Persons entitled thereto; and that the Petitioners have, in the building the said Bridge, and purchasing Houses and Grounds within the Limits prescribed them, for making and opening Ways, Streets, and Passages, expended and contracted for great Part of the Monies hitherto granted them for the said Purposes, notwithstanding the y have proceeded with the utmost Care and Frugality; and therefore find themf. And the Counsel were called in:

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded in their Evidence, in Support of their Construction of the "Word " Commonalty," in the last Determination of the 1 louse, concerning the Right of electing Burgesses for the said Borough made the 9th Day of June 1660:

And the Report from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, made the 3 ill Day of , in the First

Year of the Reign of King William and Queen touching the Election for the said Borough, and the Resolution of the House thereupon, was read:

And a Copy of the Indenture of Return of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, dated the 30th Day of July 1698, made by the Mayor and Commonalty of the said Borough, under their Common Seal, was produced and read.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member examined several Witnesses, in order to prove, That Freeholders have, by Usage, voted at Elections of Members to serve m Parliament for the said Borough; and that,at the last Election, both Parties agreed. That the Freeholders had a Right to vote:

And then the Counsel for the Sitting Member were further heard, and summed up their Evidence:

And the Counsel for the Petitioner were heard, by way of Reply.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That, in the last Determination of this House, of the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, made the 9th Day of June, in the Year One thousand Six hundred and Sixty, which is as followeth, " That the " Mayor and Commonalty of have Right to

" elect Members to serve in Parliament for that Borough it appears to this House, That the Word Commonalty," therein mentioned, extended to the Freemen only of the said Borough:

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out, after the Word " Freemen," the Word " only," and inserting the Words * and Free- holders," in (lead thereof:

And the Question being put. That the Word only" Hand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Then the main Question being put;

Resolved, That in the last Determination of this House, of the Right of Election of Membeis to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, made the Ninth Day of June, in the Year One thousand Six hundred and Sixty, which is as followeth. That the Mayor and Commonalty of Plymouth have f( Right to elect Mem hers to serve in Parliament for that " Borough"; it appears to this House, That the Word " Commonalty," therein mentioned, extended to the Freemen only of the said Borough.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again called Vo l,23.

in; and, being acquainted by Mr. Speaker with the said Resolution, were again directed to withdraw.

Then the Sitting Member acquainted the House, That the Word " Commonalty," mentioned in the last Determination of this House, of the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Plymouth, being declared by this House to extend to the Freemen only, of the said Borough, he would not give the House any furtherTrouble.

And then he withdrew.

And the Question being put, That John Rogers Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That Charles Vanbrugh Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon.

A REPORT of the Commissioners of Greenwich Hospital, as to what Money has been received from the Derwentwater Estate, in the Year 1739; and of their Proceedings in carrying on the said Building:

In Obedience to the Directions of an Act, passed in the First Session of this present Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates, forfeited by the Attainders at' James late Earl of Derwenlwater, and of Charles Radcliffe;

Requiring the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Grecmoich, to contract and agree with able and sufficient Tradesmen, Artificers, or other Persons, for finiffiing and completing the said Royal Hospital in a workman-like and substantial manner, on the easiest and most reasonable Terms, according to the Plan laid before the House of Commons in the said Session of Parliament; and to lay their Proceedings therein before his Majesty, aqjl both Houses of Parliament, respectively;

The Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital do humbly report as followeth;

j£* S‘ d.

There has been received, between the 31st December 1738, and the 30th of November 1739, out

of the Rents and Profits of the Estate - 4,000 -

As to their Proceedings in carrying on the Building: ——

The Governor’s Kitchen and Scullery are quite finished. The Walls of the Brewhouse, and great Reservoir, are quite up, and covered in.

In Queen Anne’s Court, Two Partition Walls, and Two Stacks of Chimneysare carried up from Bottom to Top of the Building; a great Part of the lower Story is arched, Two Floors are put in, Two Reservoirs for Water made, a Stone Staircase, with Iron Balluftrade, is carried up from Bottom to Top, and great Part of the Attick and Metzonian Stories are floored andwainfeoted.

In Queen Mary's Court, a great Quantity of Earth and Rubbish is dug and carried ayay; the Walls of the Chapel are quite up, Balluftrade and Roof put on, and covered in; the Tower at the West End of the Chapel iscarried up to the Base of the Columns that carries the Dome: the Colonnade, on the West Side of the Court, is far advanced; in the East and South Sides of this Court, Piers of Stone are carried up, great Part of Two Stories are arched, and Four large Reservoirs for Water, with Pipes for them, are made.

The Expence of which, brought to an Account in September last, and paid, has amounted to - 19,768 — - —

Kensington, Mr. Henry Archer reported from the Committee, to kc. Ry»ds. whoih the Petition of the Freeholders, Landholders, Churchwardens, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Kensington, in the County of whose Names are

thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of several of thelnhabitants of the Parish of and others usually

travelling through the said Parish,were referred, That the Committee had examined the Matters of the saidPetitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place: and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House,examined the Matter of the said Petitions:

And, to prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, the Petitioners called

Mr. Richard O/good: Who, being examined, said, That he had known the Road mentioned in the Petition Twenty Years, which is a publick Road, and the Chelsea Stage Coach frequently pafl'es that Way: That it is in so ruinous a Condition, that he is now obliged to use Six Horses to draw a Carriage which formerly lie had drawn with Two; and that he apprehends the Reason of such Decay to be, the great Number of heavy Carriages, loaden with Gravel, continually passing through the fame, to amend the Roads directed to be repaired by the Bill depending before the House: And that it was impossible for the said Road to be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law.

Being further examined, he said, That the Difficulty of passing the Road is the Reason why several Houses at Bromptonare unoccupied: And that the Farmers and Gardeners cannot carry the Produce of their respective Farms and Grounds to , or any other Market,

unless the Road be amended.

Mr. Smith confirmed the foregoing Evidence: And added further, that the Parish of Kensington raises 9 s. on every House, towards the Repair of the said Road; and that it is impracticable to go from his own House without paying at some Turnpike; and that he is determined to leave the House where he now resides, by reason of the Badness of the Road.

Mr. Bird said. That he was Churchwarden of the Parish of Kensington in the Years 1729 and 1730: That there is a Composition paid by the Inhabitants of that Parish of £.35 a Year, to the said Turnpike; and that all’ the Road mentioned in the Petition lies in the Parish of Kensington.

Mr. Jenkins said, That his Dwelling-house is situate upon Part of the said Road, which is so ruinous, that when he has attempted to take a Hackney Coach, upon his Return home from London, he has frequently been refused by the Coachmen, so soon as he informed them whither he proposed to go: That he has been an Eye-witness of Coaches and Chaises being overturned before his Door, where the Road is so narrow that it is impossible for Two Carriages to pass the one by the other; which occasions daily Quarrels, and thereby endangers the Lives of the Passengers.

Mr. Joseph Griffin, Surveyor of the Highways for Kensington in the Year 1731, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Bird, with regard to the Composition of 35 a Year, paid by the Inhabitants of Kensington to the Turnpike: And further said. That the Roads, unprovided for by the Bill, and to be repaired by the Statute-work, are about Four Miles in Length; and that, during the time he acted as Surveyor, he laid 300 Loads of Gravel on it; which was given, and Part of the Expences for digging and carting was paid for by a voluntary Contribution; and that the Statute-work was insufficient for the Repair of the said Roads.

And the Witnesses severally agreed. That the Road mentioned in the Petition is a publick Highway; and that the Reason of its being in so ruinous a Condition was.

the heavy Loads of Gravel continually passing through the fame, for repairing the Roads directed to be amended by the Bill.

In order to prove the Allegations of the Second Petition, the Petitioners called

John Hutchins-. Who said, The Road intended to be repaired did not exceed in Length Three Furlongs and Sixteen Perches; and is now in a very ruinous Condition, notwithstanding the voluntary Contributions of several Gentlemen.

Mr. Upton confirmed the aforesaid Evidence: And added, that he apprehends the Road to be a publick one; and that it is very much frequented, though very dangerous to Passengers.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Firli, for repairing the Roads in the Parishes of Kensington, and Fulham, and other Parishes therein mentioned, in th©

County of Middlesex, is committed, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, for repairing the Road from the Sign of the Bell, at Brompton, to the>

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Na- Dan vigation of the River Dun,in the County of under Navigation,

their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by several Acts of Parliament, are impowered to make the said River Dun navigable, in Inch manner as by the said Acts isexprelTed; and that, in doing the fpme, the Petitioners have already expended upwards of Twenty-four thousand Pounds, and made a good Navigation from Rotherham to Wilfick House: And representing to the House, That in the said River Dun, between Wilfick House, and Fishlock Ferry, there are several Shallows, which make the Navigation thereof so imperfect, that in Neap Tides, or dry Seasons, Boats or Vessels cannot pass, to the great Discouragement of Trade, by Loss of Time in the Conveying of Goods up and down the said River; and that the improving the Navigation thereof will be for the Publick Good, and a great. Encouragement to the Manufactures of Iron, and more convenient for the Carriage of Cheese, Lead, Coals, Lime, Stone, Timber, and all other Goods, M ares, and Merchandizes, and will very much tend to the Increase of Watermen and Seamen, and be a means to preserve the Highways, and very advantageous, by employing the Poor: And therefore praying, That this House will give Leave, 'That a Bill be brought in to improve the Navigation of the River Dun, from Wilfick House in the Pai ilh of Barnby Dun, in the County of York, to Fishlock Ferry, in the same County.

The Lord Sundon reported from the Committee to Westminster whom the Petition of the Commissioners for building a Bnd*‘ Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of WeJI-minster, to the pppofite, Shore, in the County of Surry, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in Support of the Allegations therein contained,

The Agent for the Petitioners laid before the Committee an Act, passed in thelall Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act to enlarge the Powers of the Commissioners for building a Bridge, SCc.; whereby it appeared, That the Petitioners, as is alleged in their Petition, were impowered, to open, make, delign, and lay out, such Ways, Streets, and Passages, as they shall find proper to make on each Side of the River Thames to and from the intended Bridge, the Courts of Justice, and both Honfes of Parliament; and also to agree for, and purchase, such Houses and Ground, within certain Limits by the said Act prescribed, as they should find necessary for them to be possessed of for that Purpose.

It appeared likewise to the Committee, upon Perusal of the said Act of Parliament, That, agreeably to the Representation of the Commissioners in their Petition, several Inconvenienciesand Difficulties, and fuchascould not easily be got over, consistently with Justice, must necessarily arise in the Exercise of the Powers already vested in the Commissioners: And further, That, in order to carry on the Work intended by the said Act effectually

several other necessary Powers were wanting--Some

lostances of these Defects in the late Act the Committee have thought proper to lay before the House; which are as follows;

In the case of litigated Titles to Houses or Ground, judged necessary by the Commissioners to bepurchased, it appeared to the Committee, That the Direction in such Cases prescribed by the Act is. That, after Damage and Recompence shall have been assessed and awarded by the Verdict of a Jury and the Determination of the Commissioners had thereupon, it shall be lawful for the Commissioners to pay the Money, so awarded for the Purchase of such Estate, into the Bank of ,or, at the Request

of the Person in Possession of the Premises, to place it out -in the Funds; there to remain until the Matters in Dispute between the Parties interested thonld be settled and adjusted, or the Title cleared, to the Satisfiiftion of the Commissioners: But no Provision is made in the said Act, that the Interest of the Purchase-money, so placed in the Funds, should, in the mean time, be applied to the Use of the Person in Possession of the Estate at the time of such Sale, in like manner as the Rents and mesne Profits of the Estate, during fuchDispute, would have been applied; whereby it appeared to the Committee, an Injury would be done to Persons in such Circumstances as diverted of an immediate Interest in an Estate, without any Equivalent substituted in itg stead.

So likewise in the same of Femes Covert, possessed of Estates in their own Right, and of Wives having Right of Dower, it appeared to the Committee, That the Execution of the Powers veiled by the late Act in the Commissioners might be attended" with very great Hardship as well as Injury; for the Act in general provides for the Sale of all Estates, and for the Payment of the Money; but there is no Restraint in such Cases by the said, Act upon the Husbandfrom retaining the Purchase-money, so paid, to his own Use; so that the Right of the one, or the other, may be defeated, at the Will of the Husband.

The Inconveniencies hitherto Hated arise from the Powers as now vested in the Commissioners; but the Committee likewise observe Inconveniencies, that may arise from the Want of some Powers that seem fit to be lodged in the Commissioners.

It appears, by the Clause in the late Act, which, to prevent the Retarding of the Publick Good, takes off the Disability that wouldotherwise lie uponFeoffees inTruft, and others, to sell and convey such Houses and Ground as the Commissioners should judge necessary for the carrying on their Work, that, in such Cases, on Refusal of the Parties concerned to promote the general Good, a Jury is to be appointed, in such manner as other Juries; who are to inquire of, and assess, such Damage and Recompence as they shall judge fit to be awarded to the Owners and Occupiers of such Houses and Ground so refuting to sell the same: And that, in consequenCe of such Assessment, upon Payment or Tender of the Sums so awarded, or, in case of Refusal, upon Payment thereof into the Bank of England, for the Use of the Parties interested, the Commissioners are impowered to pull down and dispose of such Houses and Ground for the Purposes of the Act: But the Committee observe. That after all the Steps regularly taken as prescribed in the Act, although the Commissioners themselves are quieted in the Possession of the Premises so converted and disposed of, yet may their Labour, in some measure,still be frustrated or hurt, at lead, as there is no Power any where Jpdged to compel the Owners or Occupiers of such Houses or Ground to convey the same to the Commissioners; By which Means, as the legal Estate is not by such Verdict veiled in them, the Commissioners are disabled from letting or disposing of such Houses or Ground as they shall be possessed of, over and above what is necessary, in the manner (intended by the Act) that they shall find moll advantageous.

The Committee likewise observe. That there is a great Defect in the Act, with regard to the Method of Proceeding in such Cases by the Jury, in order to the Assessment of Damages; there being no Power in the Commissioners to compel the Owners or Occupiers of such Houses or Ground to produce their Deeds and Writings til! after the Jury shall have set a Value upon the fame; which mull necessarily leave! the Judgment of the Jury, as to the Value of such Estates, subject to many Errors, for Want of proper Lights, and therefore should have been prior to the Assessment.

The Committee further observe. That it might be proper to extend the Manner of Conveyance by Bargain and Sale inrolled, to the Estates of Femes Covert, and to give it, in that Cafe, as in others prescribed by the

Act, the Force and Effect of a Fine and Recovery---

And likewise, that it would be of great Use and Convenience, after the Inrolment of such Bargain and Sale, to bar all Claims that should not be made within a limited Time.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners proceeded to Hate to the Committee the Surplus of the Monies already granted by Parliament, and the further Expences necessary for finishing the intended Works: For which Purpose,

MR. Hampden reported from the Cortunittee to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose ' Names are thereunto subscribed, living near, and usually travelling through, a Lane, commonly called Tyburn Lane, leading from the great Oxford Road to the great Western Road, near Hyde Park in the Parish of

St.George, Hanover Square, in the County of was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in ht the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of file said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called

Mr. John Carter: Who, being examined, said, That be knows the Lane, commonly called Tyburn Lane,\e*ding from the great Oxjord Road to the great Western 24

yanuarii. 1739.

Road, near Hyde Park Corner, mentioned in the said Petition; and that the same is an antient Road; but is become so ruinous and bad, that, in the Winter Season, it is almost impassable for Carts and Carriages; and that the same cannot, by the Laws now in being, be amended, and kept in any Sort of Repair, so that Coaches and Carriages may travel through the same with Safety: And he further said. That, in the Year 1732, the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square (wherein the said Lanelies) was indicted, by reufon of the Badness thereof; and that he has known Five Carts overturned of a Day: And he further said, There is a Turnpike at each End of the Lane; one whereof was erected by the Trustees for repairing Kevfinglon Road, and the other by the Trustees for repairing the Roads from St. Giles's Pound to Kilburn

Bridge; but neither Set of the Trustees repair any Part of the said Lane, although the Parishioners pay, in lieu of Statute-work for the said Parish, One hundred Pounds per Annum to the Trustees for repairing of the Kenfing-

ton Roads, and Seventy Pounds per Annum to the Trustees for repairing the Roadsfrom St. Giles’s Pound.

Benjamin Berioick, Surveyor of the Highways, belonging to the Parish of St.George, Hanover- Square, being called and examined, confirmed the Evidencegiven by John Carter :And said further. That the Parish is always in Debt, upon account of several extraordinary Sums of Money expended on their Roads.

Mr. Simon Parry, Vestry Clerk to the said Parish of St. George, Hanover Square,being called and examined,

said. That the said Lane is almost iinpafiable in the Winter Season, and very dangerous for Travellers, notwithstanding that the Parishioners, some Years have laid out One hundred and Fifty Pounds on that Lane; and that the Parish hath, for Twelve Years last past, paid to the Trustees for repairing Kensington Roads One hundred Pounds per Annum, and Seventy Pounds per Annum to the Trustees for repairing the Roads leading from St. Giles's Pound,in lieu of Statute-work; but neither Sett

of the Trustees have repaired any Part of the Lane.
