Ordered, That the said Estimate and Account do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Supply. Mr. Francis Fane, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That {it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-three thousand Four hundred and Twenty-nine Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for railing and maintaining Two thousand and Forty Men, Officers included, to be added to the Six Regiments of Marines, for the Year 1740.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two thousand Four hundred and Fifty Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Six-pence, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining one Company of Invalids, to be forthwith raised, and for making an Addition of Twenty Men to each of the Four Companies of Invalids, raised in 1739; in all to

One hundred and Eighty-one Men; for the Service of the Year 1740.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Three hundred Forty-seven Pounds Six Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, for Out-pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year 1740.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Colony of A Petition of the Trufiees, for establishing the Colony Georgia. Qf Georgia in America, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by the Affiltance granted in the last Session of Parliament, have been enabled, not only to defray the extraordinary Charge which attended the Military Defence of the Colony during the continual Danger and Alarms of a Span if h invasion, and before the

Vol. 23.

Arrival of the Regiment which his Majesty most graciously sent over for the Preservation of that Province; but also to assist those industrious Inhabitants, who have been taken off from their Labour to prepare for the common Safety, or deprived of their Crops by the late general Drought in that Part of North America; and to defray the necessary Expences of Georgia, to Lady-day next, with a Surplus towards the further settling and improving the said Colony: That though the Inhabitants are now protested, and thereby can, with Safety, go on with Cultivation, for raising their own Provision, yet the Petitioners find it requifiteto assist those who are industrious, towards obtaining the other Necessaries of Life, until, by their producing Materials for the Manufactures of Great Britain, they shall receive the Benefits arising by those Produces the Petitioners encourage them to raise, which are now bought from Foreigners with ready Money: That the said Surplus, towards the further settling and improving the Colony from Lady-day next, will not besufficient to defray the Expence of the Support of a civil Magistracy, continuing the Friendship of the Indians, encouraging the raising Produces, and other Charges, for the ensuing Year: That the Petitioners are enabled, by credible and sufficient Witnesses, atpresent in London, tomakeappear to the House, the Convenience

and Capacioufness of the Harbours and Ports in Georgia, the Safety of Navigation along the Coast, the Goodness and Value of the Silk already produced there, and the well-grounded Expectations of raising other beneficial Produces, as soon as the House shall please to take into Consideration the Utility of this Province to the Trade and Navigation of Great Britain, as well as the Security which it. gives to the other Provinces upon the Continent of America: And therefore praying the House to take the PremifesintoConsideration, and grant the Petitioners such Aififtance as the House lha.ll think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ordered, That an Account be laid before this House, fheu'inghow the Money, granted in the last Session of Parliament for the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America, has been applied by them, for the further settling and improving the said Colony.

Sir Miles Slapylton reported from the Committee, to nun whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation. Navigation of the River Dun, in the County of York, under their Common Seal, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof.

The Petitioners produced Three Acts of Parliament,

One passed in the 12th, and another in the 13th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and the Third in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second; by which last mentioned Act the said Company were impowered to make the said River Dun navigable, in such manner as by the said Act is expressed.

And then the Petitioners called,

Sir. Joseph Steers, who wasTreasurer to the said Company for several Years: And he, being examined, said,

That the Proprietors of the Navigation have 150 Shares at £. 165 each Share, which amount to the Sum of £.24,750: And that Sum hath been expended in making good the Navigation from Roto Wilfick be-

fideTwo Years Income; which he computed to amount to £.900per Annum. And that the Navigation is so good, that Four Men can do as much Work in the River as Six in the Itiver Eyre and Colder: And he furthersaid, That the Income of the Navigation was let to Mr.

.RroadJiead, Mr. Crips, and Mr. for the Term of

14 Years; and, for the first Seven Years of that Term, they paid after the Rate of £.1,200 per Annum, and for the remaining Seven Years £.1,500 per Annum: And all farther Sums advanced by the Company were, for the first Seven Years, to be at the Rate of Five Pounds per Cent, per Annum, and, for the remaining Seven Years, to be after the Rate of Six Pounds and One Quarter per Cent, per Annum: And he also said, That there are Three Bridges erected over the Dutch River, or Nero River, which are to be maintained and repaired at the Expence of the Company, during the said Term of 14 Years; and that the Company have expended, within these last Two Years, on the Bridges£.700 and upwards: And he being alked. Whether he knew what Books of Accounts are kept by the said Lessees ? He laid, he did not know what Books were kept by them: And he further said, That he apprehends, the Lell'ees have the same Powers assigned over to them that the original Proprietors had: And being asked, Whether he knows, that there has been any more charged for Carriage of Goods than there was before the Income of the Navigation was let ? he said. He did not know there was, or ever heard of any Complaint of Goods being charged more for Carriage than when the Navigation was in the Company’s Hands: He laid. That there were Books kept by the Company before the Income of the Navigation was lett; but were kept very incorrectly; and that, he believes, was one Reason of letting a Lease of the fame; but that most of the Books belonging to the Company are now in the Hands of Mr. Radford of Sheffield.

And the said Mr. Steers, being further examined as to the Shallows in the River, said. That, last January, he, with several others, viewed the River between Wilfick House and Fishlock Ferry :wherein they found several

Shallows, which make the Navigation very imperfect; and that on a Shallow on Ba Boat stuck fast, though at that time there was a Frelh in the River; aftd a Boatman then present said, That that Boat would continue there till a bigger Frelh or a Spring Tide came; and that he has had a Boat ltick on the Shallows Four, Five, or Six Days, to the great Discouragement ' and Hindrance of Trade, and Loss of Time, in carrying of Goods up and down the River: And the said Mr. Steers further said. That the Sheffield Factors, when stinted in Time, are obliged to carry their Goods, at a yery great Expence, by Land Carriage, and put them on board below Slainforth Shallow: and that, if they miss the Opportunity of Ships going off from Hull to foreign Parts, they not only lose the Year’s Trade, but is a great Detriment and Disappointment to the Merchants abroad: And he further added, That the Vessel which stuck on the Shallows, last January, was about 20 Ton; but did not know what Draught of Water the Vessel drew; but Boats which generally ply on that River draw from Two Feet Four Inches to Three Feet Two or Three Inches Water; and that Vessels, in dry Seasons, con-fiantly (tick on the Shallows; and, at that time, there is not above Eight or Nine Inches Water: He further* said, That Vessels of 40 Tons do sometimes happen to come from Fishlock to Stainforth, in the Height of strong Tides; but that it is uCiial for Vessels of 40Ton to lall constantly from below Fishlock to Hull in Spring Tides. The said Mr. Steers, being alked, What Quantity of Tons have been carried on the River in One Year? he said, He could not tell; but said. That the Duty thereof amounted to about £.900 per Annum; and that the Navigation never exceeded that Sum while Ihe same was in the said Proprietors Hands.

And the said Mr. Steers further said, That Goods are carried from Sheffield to Tinjley by Land, which is about Two Miles and upwards; and, in the Winter Season, that Road is almost impalpable; and that the same cannot, by the Laws uow in being for repairing of Highways, be amended, and kept in any sort of Repair; and, if the same was amended, it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the said Town of Sheffield, and enable the Traders to carry their Goods at a much less Expence at all Times of the Year.

Mr. Richard Ellison, being called and examined, confirmed all the Evidence given by Mr. Steers, as to the Navigation and the Badness of the Roads from Sheffield to Tinjley: And further said. That* many Matters of Vessels throw their Ballad into the River; which, if it could be prevented, would be of great Service to the said Navigation, and keep the River open and clear: And the said Mr. Ellison said. That the Sum,

of Three thousand Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds would repair and complete the new-intended Navigation, pay the Expence of making One Lock; the Cut whereof would be about Two Miles long, and above Eight Feet deep; and also complete the Building of Three Bridges over the said Cut and River: And he further added. A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Clergy, Gen«- Medway tlemen. Freeholders, and other principal Inhabitants, N"vlgatlon of the Counties of Kent and Sussex whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act passed in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King Charles the Second, reciting, that making the River Medway, and all Rivers, Streams, and Water* courses falling the reinto, in the Counties of Kent and Sussex, navigable, had been found, upon View, to be feasible, and would be of great Use, for the better and more easy and speedy Portage of Iron Ordnance, Balls,

Timber, and other Materials, in Places adjacent, made, forged, and provided, for his Majesty’s Service, at all Times, and moreespecially at such Times and Seasons. in the Year, as the same could not otherwise be brought out of those Parts, and would be advantageous to the Inhabitants, and all others concerned, as well for Carriage of the Commodities aforesaid, as of Wood, Com, and Grain, Hay, Hops, Wool, Leather, and all other Provisions growing and accruing from thence, as also of Coals, Lime, Stone-wares, and all other Necessaries and Commodities to be carried thither, whereby Commerce and Trade would be much increased, and the publick Weal advanced; it was therefore enacted, That it should be lawful for certain Persons therein named, to make the said River and Streams running the reunto navigable, in such manner as by the said Act is appointed; and Commissioners were also therein appointed, with Power to determine proper Satisfaction to all Persons, Bodies politick or corporate, for any Damage to be by them sustained, by cutting, digging, or otherwise damnifying their Lands and Tenements, in making the said River and Streams navigable, with a Power for appointing new Commissioners, in the stead of those dying or refilling to act; but that although the making the said River and Streams navigable would have been not only of great Use to the Publick, but also very beneficial to Trade and Navigation, and a great Improvement of the Estates of the Inhabitants of the said Counties of Kent and Sussex,through which the said River and

Streams run; yet, for Want of Money to carry on so great an Undertaking, the said Act was not carried into Execution; and the several Persons authorized thereby to make the said River and Streams navigable, and the several Commissioners therein named, being all lince dead, without any proper Successors appointed in their stead, in manner as by the said Act is directed, the Petitioners apprehend the Powers in the said Act cannot now be otherwise enforced than by the Aid of this House; and that the making the said River and Streams navigable, at this time, would be of as much, if not greater Utility to the Publick, as well as to Trade in general, than it w ould have been at the time of passing the said Act, by reason that the Timber growing in the Weald of Kent and Sussex, through which the said River and Streams run, of which there are now very great Quantities, is allowed to be the best in this Kingdom for the Use of his Majesty’s Navy; but, by reason of the Badness of the Roads in those Parts, the same cannot be conveyed to any Market,but at a monstrous Expence; insomuch that Timber contracted for sometimes lies Two, sometimes Three, Years, before it can be removed' from the Places where the same is felled; all which could, with great Ease, and at a moderate Expence, be conveyed to his Majesty’s Dock Yards of Chatham, -

Mr. Edward Inge, being examined, said. That he travelled the Road in August last, and then found the fame, in many Places, in a very ruinous Condition, particularly between the End of Dunchu Town, and a

Mr. Caleb Copfon was called; and, being examined, said, That he travelled the Road in December last, and confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Inge, as far as it related to the Badness of the Road: And Mr. Copfon added to his Evidence, That the further End of the Towq of I Meriden was in a very ruinous Condition.

And he being alked, What Part of the Road he took to be the Bottom of Meriden Hill? he said. That there is a Water runs at the Bottom of the Hill, and runs as far as a House called the Red Lyon Inn in; which

House he always apprehended, and believes, to be at the Bottom of Meriden Hill.

That an Account was laid before the Committee of the yearly Produce of the Tolls, and also of the Expences annually; whereby it appeared that the Income was, oue Year with another, about 500l.;

and that the necessany Expences annually was 100l. or thereabouts; and the Interest of the before-mentioned Debt was 100 I. per Annum more: So it appeared to the Committee, That the Overplus of the Money arising by the Tolls, would not be sufficient to amend and keep the Road (which is about Twelve computed Miles in Length) in good Repair, and pay off the Debt aforesaid.

MR. Rowney reported from the Committee to whom

the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Roads from the Top of Stoken Church to Enjlow Bridge, and the Road leading from Wheatly Bridge through the City of Oxon, by Begbrooke, to New cock, in the County of Oxon (except the Mile Way on each Side of the said City); and of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, and other Persons living in, near, and usually travelling thrpugh, the* said Roads; and also the Road leading from, an House, commonly called the Croivn Ale House, to the Turnpike erected'on Stoken Church Hill; was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as follows;

The Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And it appeared to the Committee, That, by the Act above mentioned, several Tolls, as is alleged in the Petition, were granted for the amending of the said Roads, which were to take place, and have continuance, only fropn and after the 20th Day of April 1719, for and during the Term of 21 Years; so that the said A ft expire* on the 20th Day of April next.

It appeared likewise to the Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. Edward Clerk, That, in pursuance of Power* granted by the said Act, considerable Sums of Money had been borrowed on the Credit of the said Toll*, which,.together with the Tolls collected, had beeu

duly applied to the amending of the Roads; and that the Money so borrowed had been all paid off.

Stephen Solesbury, John Morris, and John Stone, Surveyors of different Parts of the Road directed by the said Act to be repaired; who all concurred in Evidence with regard to the Badness of the Roads in their several Dif-trifts, before the passing of the late Act, and f he present good Condition of them; the Insufficiencyof the'Statute-work to keep the same in good Repair; and, consequently, the Necessity of the further Alhftance of Parliament, in continuing some Tolls for that Purpose.

It appeared likewise to the Committee, by the Evidence of John Bartlett, That the Road leading from the

Crown Ale House to the Turnpike now erected on Stoken Church Hill (about Half a Mile in Length, and not included in the Roads directed by the Act above mention-to be repaired) is in a very bad Condition; and that, though it is so situated that Persons travelling through the same contribute greatly to the Support of the Turnpike on Stoken Church Hill, yet not the least Benefit arises from thence to the Road, there being no Provision in the late Act for the Repair of it.

He further said, That the Statute-work had been constantly done on the said Road, and found very ineffectual.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing and making more effectual an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Roads from the Top of Stoken Church Hill to Enfo Bridge, and the Road from Wheatley Bridge through the City of Oxon, by Begbrook, to New Wood/lock, in the County of Oxon (except the Mile-Way on each Side of the said City); and for repairing the Road from the Crown Ale House to the Turnpike on Stoken Church Hill aforesaid: And that Mr. Rowney, Mr. Packer, Sir James Dafiwood, Dr.

Butler, and Mr. Herbert of Oxford, do prepare, and

bring in, the fame.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called; viz.

the Use of China, instead of Silk, would be a

great Saving to the Nation in the prime Cost abroad, the usual Price of the f\ueft Italian raw Silk being from Fourteen Shillings to Sixteen Shillings, and of Eight

Shillings and Six Pence; but that the Silk, through the Expence of the Voyage, Risk, and Duty, comes dearer to this Market than Italian raw Silk does: That all Sorts of Italian raw Silk now pay One Shilling and Five Pence and One Tenth Part of a Peny per great Pound, and China raw Silk paysThree Shillings and Nine Penceand Forty-fiveofOne hundred Parts ofaPenny per great Pound; which great Difference in the Duty near deprives us of the Use of it, almost amounting to a Prohibition; so that, was the Duty on China raw Silk reduced to the same with that on Italian raw Silk, such a

Misfortunes, another strong Mole, called the Merchants Key, was built, forae Years since, at a great Expence, which effectually securesthe Ships in Harbour from being drove out to Sea, as they used to be:

That the Harbour has been deepened from time to time, at a great Expence, by blaliing and cutting up the Rocks and Stones which lie under the Sand and Mud, that in some Places it has been deepened Seven or Eight Foot, in most Parts Three or Four Foot:

That there is now at Spring Tides Seventeen Foot Water for the lower Tire of Ships in the Harbour, and Ten Foot at Neap Tides; but that the biggeit Ships, when ioaden, drawing Fourteen Foot Water, do not float above Six or Seven Hays at the Spring, and then are neapt, and block up the others, so that few Ships can get out at the NeapTides; but the Pier being above 150 Yards from Low-water Mark, where the Tide rises near Thirty Foot at SpringTides, it is proposed to erefct another Pier there, and also a new Mole, to make a convenient Place for Twenty or more of the biggest Ships to lie in Safety, to fail at Neap Tides, as there will be 28 Foot Water at SpringTides, and 21 Foot at Neap Tides, which isFourFoot more than they have within the other Pier at Spring Tides; by this means also there will be Water for Ships to come in at any time, from Halfflood to Half-ebb, which they can uow do only at or near high Water; by which means many Ships are now call away on lhatCoaft: That, as these Improvements of the Harbour have been making since the former Acts of Parliament for the Harbour, the Trade of the Place, the King’s Revenue, and also the Ships, thg new Buildings of the Town, and also the Inhabitants, have been gradually increasing; and that every Year upwards of 30 Sail trade to Virginia, and above 20 Sail to Norway.

and that the Proprietors of the said Hundred and Fifty Shares were, by the said Act, incorporated by the Name of the Company of Proprietors of the Navigation of the River Dun, and empowered to do all such Acts, and to take such Duties, as the Two Corporations, who were the former Proprietors, might have done by virtue of the former Acts j and that in the said Act was contained a Clause, that a Committee of the said Proprietors, chosen in such manner as is directed by the said Act, should have Power to raise and fall the several Lock Dues payable to the said Proprietors, as they should judge to be moll to the Advantage of the said Proprietors, and of the Trade of the said River, so as the said Duties should not be raised higher than they were settled by the said Acts: And alleging, That the said Committee have neglected to execute the Power veiled in them, as aforesaid, and have either never made any Regulation of the Rates to be taken, or have done it in a secret and unequal manner; and that the Rates taken are not such as are beneficial to the Proprietors, or to the Trade of the said River, butunequal and injurious to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners are informed, That by the Bill now depending before the House, for the more effectual improving the Navigation of the River Dun,from a Place called Wilfick House, in the Parish of Barmby Dun, in the County of York, to in the same County, it is intended not only to subjeci the said Navigation to further burthensomeDuties, under the Pretence of defraying the Expences necessary to the carrying on the said Undertaking, whereas the Rates which they are already empowered to take are more than sufficient to defray whatever Sums may be necessary for the perfecting the said Undertaking; but also to raise the same in an unequal and oppressive manner, exempting some Persons, and charging others; whereby the Interest of the Petitioners will be greatly prejudiced, as well by dellroying their Market, as by lowering the Value of the Produce of their Estates: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against so much of the said Bill; and that the House will give such farther Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, upon their said Petition, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Inllruftion to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That jt be an Inllruftion to the said Committee, That they have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

An Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King the Eighth, intituled, An Act concerning the Bridge of Staines, was read; by which it appeared, that the Chancellor of England {or the Time being, or Keeper of the King's Great Seal, and their Successors, had Power to depute and appoint Two, Three, or Four more Persons, of the Town and Parish of Staines, to take and receive the Toll and Custom, ufedforTime immemorial to be paid, as well for Carts and Horses laden with Merchandize, and other Stuff, carried over and upon the Bridge of the said Town, as of Barges coming underneath the said Bridge, and to employ the same in repairing the said Bridge, and also a Causeway extending from the said Town to the Town of Egham, in the County of Surry; and to render a yearly Account thereof to the said Chancellor or Keeper for the Time being, or before such Perforts as he should depute and appoint, between the Feasts of St. Michael the Archangel and All Saints.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners laid before your Committee an attested Copy of an Act, passed in the 39th Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act for the betterMaintenance and well Keeping of Staines Bridge and Egharrt Causeway, being the Highway from

London unto the West Parts of England-, by which it appeared, that the Chancellor of England for the Time being, or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, and their Successors, have the Deputation and Assignment of Four Persons, whereof Two to be of the Town or ParifTi of Gainey aforesaid, and the other Two of the Tow n or1 Parilli of Egham aforesaid, and the said Four to take and receive, by themselvesor their Deputy or Deputies; the Toll and Custom usually paid for passing over and going under the said Bridge, and to employ the same upon the Reparation and Making of the said Bridge and Causeway; and thereof to yield Account to the said Chancellor or Keeper of the Great Seal for the Time being, or before such Persons as heshall depute and assign,yearly, between the Feasts of St. Michael the Archangel and Saints; and, by Default of the Four Persons aforesaid in gather-' ing, or not well employing, the said Toll, the Chancellor or Keeper of the Great Seal for the Time being hath Power to inflid a Penalty upon them, or any of them, in whom such Default shall be found, as aforesaid, not exceeding Ten Pounds; the same to be levied by Distress, by such Person or Persons as shall be nominated by the said Chancellor or keeper of the Great Seal for the Time being, and to be employed for maintaining the said Bridge and Causeway.

Mr. Daniel Atwick, being examined, said, That the Tolls and Duties payable for passing over, and going under, the said Bridge, was farmed at ^.63 per Annum.

That the Charge to the Land Tax was at ;£.6o per Annum-, which, at Two Shillings s. d. in the Pound, amounts to - - - 6 — —

That the Poors Rate was Six Pence in the Pound; and generally Three, and sometimes Four Rates in a Year; and that the Remainder was not sufficient to amend, maintain, and support the said Bridge and Causeway in good Order and Repair.

Mr. PhilipStone, Bridge-matter, being examined, said.

That Part of the said Bridge was repaired Iaft Year, during which time a Ferry was set up, and about Fourteen or Fifteen Pounds per Week taken from Passengers patting over the said Ferry, which has not as yet been accounted for; and that other Parts of the said Bridge was at present very much out of Repair.

Mr. Fi-'ancis Brown, Carpenter, said, That the great Arch of the said Bridge was so much decayed, that it was not safe for Carriages to go over the same; and that Part of the said Bridge, on that Side the great Arch which stands next Middlesex, is also much decayed, and will want rebuilding in about Six or Seven Years.

A Petition of several of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, for the City and Liberty of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, in Obedience to his Majesty’s Command, in pursuance of an Addrefe of this House, the Justices for the said City and Liberty have considered of the proper Means to put the Statute for regulating the Measures and.Prides of Coals in Execution; and that, for that Purpose, they sent for several of the principal Retailers of Coals, living within the said City and Liberty; and representing to the House the Refult of their Enquiry; That they find the Ibid.Retailers now fell their Coals for Three Pounds Twelve Shillings the Chaldron, since they have been obliged to pay Fifty Shillings in the Pool, Thirteen Shillings for Carriage, and other Charges for Metage, Wharfage, and Loading, amounting toTwo Shillings and Eight Pence more, besides the Second Charges they are at in re-delivering them to their Cullomers; and that it appeared there were not above Seventy-feveu Chaldrons

Vol. *3-

remaining in the Hanclsof Nine of the principal Dealers who attended the Petitioners (Two of whom had none); and that they all allured the Petitioners, That they were very certain all the rest of the Retailers in Westminster together were not Matters of the like Quantity ;.apd that Mr. Fin linfonparticularly declared. He had, with

great Difficulty, procured some Coals, on Wednesday the Thirteenth of this instant February; but was obliged to pay Fifty-six Shillings in the Pool, and take them without the Ingrain, which, he said, he could not fell under Three Pounds Fifteen Shillings the Chaldron, without Loss; and that it appeared to the Petitioners, That the Retailers had not hitherto fold for more than One Shilling and TenPence toTwo Shillings the Bushel, and for lefstill very lately; that, at the Beginning of the Frqft, they took no more than One Shilling and Four Pence the Bushel; and that their Price was always governed by that taken in the Pool; and that they have not charged for their Coals, during all the hard Weather, more by the Buftiel (in favour of the Poor) than they have fold for by the Chaldron; and that the Retailers all declared. They did believe, from the best Enquiry they could make, there were not Coals in the River, or on Shore, sufficient to supply the Town for a Fortnight; and that the great Wages paid for able Seamen, which have been raised from Thirty Shillings to Five Pounds and Five Pounds Ten Shillings the Voyage; the Restrifitions in the Protefitions granted to the Colliers, in which they are allowed but One able Seaman to an HundredTons; the impressing Men out of the Colliers in coming up the River; and the excessive Price of the Carriage, occasioned by the miserable Condition of the Streets; have unavoidably raised the Price of Coals, particularly in Westminster; and that the Retailersalfo observed, That, from the Deficiency of the Quantity of Coals brought this Year into the Port of Landau, and all their Stocks being exhausted, the Town cannot be supplied next Year, un-leis these Difficulties are speedily removed: And further representing to the House, That, on due Consideration of the Afit, passed in the ifith and 17th Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for regulating the M eafares and Prices of Coals, they apprehend they have no Jurisdifition to settle the Prices of Coals, which is thereby given to justices of the Peace for Counties only; but that, in case they had Jurisdifition, they could iK»t, as that Law now Hands, enforce it, for the Reasons following; for that the Statute gives no Power to the Justices to oblige any Retailer of Coals to appear before them, nor to examine him on Oath, or to produce his Books or Accounts, or to compel his Servant or other Personto give Evidence on Oath, whereby it might appear what Price he paid for his Coals, and what were the Charges accruing thereon; and that great Difficulties would arise in settling the Price (as Retailers cannot be compelled to.answer on Oath) in Cafes where several Parcels of Coals have been bought at different Times and Prices, and heaped together; and that no Penalty is laid on Persons felling at a higher Rate than what is settled by the Justices, nor any Directions given to publifti the Price; and when the Price is settled, if the Retailer refuses to comply with it, the Provision made for Entrance into his Wharf or House by Force, is so worded, that they cannot think it safe, either for themselves or Officers, to execute what is required of them; and further observing, That should the Retailers, by any future Afit, be subjefited to the Jurisdifition of the Justices of the Peace, the Petitioners apprehend it will be impossible for them effectually to reduce the exorbitant Price of Coals, and answer the good Intentions of the Legislature, if it shall be in the Power of any Set of Men, by Combinations, or any other Artifices, to fix what Price they please on Coals in the Pool, or at the Pits, whence the Cities of London and Westminster are supplied: And praying such Relief in the Prenul’es as to the House tliall seem meet.

Petitioners having received the Directions of the Honfc, to take care, That the Scavengers keep the Streets free and open from all Nuisances, and that there may be no Obstructions to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from the House of Commons, find themselves obliged to lay the following Reasons before the House, why they are not capable of doing what is required of them: That by the Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of Kin glVilliamand Queen Mary, forcleanfmgthe Streets, there is no Penalty laid either on the Scavengers or Rakers, for not carrying away the StreetDirt: That the Justices being obliged to appoint such Persons as have most Voices or Hands at Parochial Meetings, the Inhabitants suffer great Losses and Inconveniencies by the Appointment of improper and insufficient Scavengers: That the Scavengers may agree on what Terms, and with what Rakers they please, without any Power given either to the Justices or Inhabitants to interpose: That, in Consequence of these Agreements, the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, the Scavengers in some Parishes have received Poundage of the Rakers for employing them, and in others, for a Sum of Money, wholly made over the Rate to the Rakers, and, at the End of the Year, have refused to give any other Account than their Receipts; by which means the Parishes have been defrauded of any Surplus on their Rates, the Scavengers have had no Regard to the Interest of their Parish in making their Contracts, and the Rakers, being under no Controul, are notoriously negligent in the Discharge of their Duty: That many Losses and Inconveniencies happen from the Scavengers not being compellable to give any Accounts of their Receipts and Payments, or (however insufficient they may be) to pay over the Money into safe Hands, till after the Expiration of the . Year: That under the present Laws the Scavengers cannot be restrained from paying the Rakers, though they do not their Duty: which the Justices apprehend to be One great Cause of their gross Neglect; but that was a Power given to flop Payment till the Rakers had effectually cleansed the Streets, the Petitioners imagine, it would have a better Effect, and be as strong an Inducement to them to do their Duty as any Penalty that should be laid upon them: That the Petitioners, as Justices, have no Power to remove the Nuisances and Obstructions in the Streets, and can proceed only by Indictment, as any other Person may do; which is very dilatory and expensive; and no Provision is made for defraying the Charges: And further representing to the House, That, for many Years past, great Difficulties have arisen in the Execution of the Act, passed in the 12th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, relating to Vagrants, which are so well known, as to make it unnecessary to enter into the Particulars; and that they find by Experience, they cannot cure the Grievance, so justly com-lained of, until some more effectual Provision is made y the Wisdom of Parliament: And further representing to the House, besides the Defects already mentioned, the Difficulties and Discouragements the Justices of the Peace lie under in executing these and other Acts of Parliament, from the many Niceties and Forms of Laws, wherein, if they happen to bemiftaken(as thegreateft Lawyers have often been), they are as liable, in many Cafes, to Actions, as if they had acted contrary to their Duty; and that this still.. the greater Hardship, as there are no Forms of Convictions, Rates, Orders, or Warrants of Distress, settled and approved of, under which they might act with more Security: And praying such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. 15

Accounts being required to be taken daily of the Earnings of the Coopers, moll of whom are paid by Piecework* to secure the Crown against Watte of Time, it was found impossible for One Clerk to attend that Service, and keep Up the many Books required for entering the Cooperage Affairs in due Methods, to state the Accounts quarterly, as of late Years practised; and the great Increase of the Numbers of Coopers this Winter rendered it absolutely necessary to allow another extra Clerk.

Upon a general Application from the Clerks under the Officers of the Victualling at the Out-ports, setting forth the great Ihcrease ... of all Necessaries for Life, of late Years, whereby their small Salaries afforded, but the meanest SubsistenCe for themselvesand Families, the Lords of the Admiralty, by Order, 8th February 1732, directed an Increase of £.10 a Year to be made to Seven Clerks at Portsmouth, Seven at Plymouth, and Three, at

Chatham, for their better Support, and an Encouragement to their executing the Business and Trust reposed in them with Diligence and Fidelity.

A Petition of John Fletcher, as well on the Behalf of Protection of himself and others his Copartners, Owners, and Proprie- Collieries, tors of certain Coal-works or Collieries, in the County of Derby, as on behalf of others. Owners and Proprietors of Collieries in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioner, and his Partners, and those under whom they claim, have been at great Expence in making Soughs, and other expensive Works, for the better and more convenient carrying on and working their said Collieries; the Benefit whereof, as the Petitioners apprehend, they have the Sole Right to enjoy, which nevertheless will be enjoyed by other Persons who have not contributed t.o any Part of the Expence; and the Petitioner, and his Partners, and other Proprietors of Collieries, under the like Circumstances, will be thereby and otherwise injured in their Properties, in case the Bill for further and more effectually preventing the wilful and malicious Destruction of Collieries and Coal-works, which the Petitioner is informed hath been presented to the House, passes into aLaw, in the Manner, in which it is at present penned: And therefore, as well on the Behalf of himself, and his Partners, as on behalf of the Owners and Proprietors of Collieries in this Kingdom, praying the House to take their same into Consideration; and that he and they may be heard, by their Counsel against the said Bill, before the same passes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Henry Archer reported from the Committee appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: And the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for punishing such Persons as shall wilfully and maliciously pull down or destroy Turnpikes for repairing Highways, or Locks or other Works, erected by Authority of Parliament, for making Rivers navigable; which was to continue in Force, from the 24th Day of June 1728, for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued for Five Years, and from the 24th Day of June 1732, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued for Five Years, from the 15th Day of May 1735, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Relief of Debtors, with respect to the Imprisonment of their Persons; which was to continue in Force for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and was explained and amended by an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his present Majesty; and which, by another Act, made in the

Eighth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued until the 24th Day of March 1740, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for reviving and amending an Act, made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act to prevent Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Weirs upon the River of Thames Westward; and for ascertaining the Rates of Water Carriages upon the said River; which was to continue in Force, from the First Day of May 1730, for the Term of Nine Years, and from thence to the End of the then next 9eflion of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Greenland Fishery; which was to continue in Force, from the 25th Day of December 1731, for the Terra of Nine Years; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the further Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, carried on by his Majesty’s British Subjects; which was to continue in Force during the Continuance of an Act, passed in the 5th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Greenland Fishery; is near expiring and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests; which was to continue in Force, from the 24th Day of June 1726, for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was explained, amended, and further continued for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for reviving an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty’s Subjects to and from the East Indies-, and for the more effectual prevent-ingall his Majesty’sSubjectstradingthither under foreign Commissions; which was to continue in Force, from the First Day of May 1732, for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for further encouraging and regulating the Manufacture of British made Sail Cloth; and for the more effectual securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail Cloth imported into this Kingdom; which was to continue in Force, from the 24th Day of June 1736, for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better preservation of his Majesty’s Woods in America; and for the Encouragement of the Importation of Naval Stores from thence; and to encourage the Importation of Mails, Yards, and Bowsprits, from that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, as relates to the Premiums upon Malls, Yards, and Bowsprits, Tar, Pitch and Turpentine; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

And he further said} That in dry Seasons there is not Water sufficientto supply the Navigation, and the Mills on the said River; by reason the Canals cut by the Shallows, and put into the deepest Head of Waters lying above the Mills, and the frequent navigating through those Cuts, will make a Deficiency of Water to the Mills, till supplied by Rain.or Frefhes; which Scarcity happens One or Two Months at a time; and, if large Quantities of Coals should be navigated down the River, the Trade for Goods on the same mull be detrimented: That the Millers are often obliged to collect Water for to work their Mills One or two Months at a time in the Year; but believes, for about Six Months in every Year, there may be Water sufficientto carry down any Quantityof Goods; and believes 20,000 Chaldron of Coals may go down every Year, without Damage to the Navigation.

Mr. Henry Fox, according to Order, reported from Encouraging the Committee of the whole House, who were appointed Seamen t to consider of Heads of a Bill for the further and better voluilteer-Encouragement of Seamen to enter voluntarily into his Majesty’s Service, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House'; which he read iu his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a voluntary Register of Seamen will be of great Utility to this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Register shall extend to all the Dominions of the Crown of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Fraternity of Trinity House of Deptford Strand be intruded with the Management of the said Register, with Power of appointing inferior Officers and Servants necessary for the Execution of the said Trust.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a pertain Sum of Money be paid to every Marti who is willing to register.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every registered Man shall be obliged to give an Account of the Place of his Abode to the Register Office.

Resolved, That it vb the Opinion of this Committee,

That the registered Men shall be divided intoClafles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a yearly Pension be allowed to every registered Man who shall be disabled in Fight, over and above such Allowances as are now given; and a yearly Pension to every Widow of a registered Man llain in Fight, over and above the present Allowances made to fuchWidow; and if the Party leaves any Children, that each of them have ayearly Pension, until theyarrive at the Age of Fourteen.

Resolved,

13 Geo. It. 13° Martii.

499

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every registered Man he exempted from paying the King’s, or Parish Taxes, Or serving in any Parish Offices, or serving in Or contributing towards the Militia.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That none be preferred to be petty Officers in Any of his Majesty’s Ships but registered Men.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion Of this Committee, That all petty Officers in Merchants Ships, As Boat-fvvains, Gunners, Sic. be chosen out of registered Men.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Men, who shall register themselves, do retriain oO the Register no longer than to a certain Age.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Men who shall have continued on the Register to a certain Age, do enjoy all the Advantages of registered Men during Life.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all registered Men shall have the Preferenbe of being admitted into Greenwich Hospital.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Captains, or Commanders of his Majesty’s Ships of War, who shall be applied to in foreign Parts, 'shall take on board any registered Men, and the Men so taken on board shall, from that time, be deemed Part of the Ship’s Company, and receive Wages accordingly.

Resolved, That it is 4he Opinion of this Committee, That registered Men be allowed to go into the Merchants Service, when the Service of his Majesty shall not require them; and that the proper Officers do give them Certificates for the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That registered Men be entitled to receive their Wages

o o

in certain Proportions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Seamen, now absconding in foreign Parts, or at Home, on account of Running of Goods, who shall enter on board any of his Majesty’s Ships, and claim the Benefit of this Register, shall be entitled to their Pardon, except Persons who have been concerned in actual Murder.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all registered Men who shall be summoned to appear on board any of his Majesty’s Ships, and shall neglect or refiife to do the fame, shall be subject to be punished as D' ferters.

ResolvedrThat it. is the Opinion of this Committee, That all foreign Seajnen, who shall claim the Benefit of Ibis Register, shall be entitled to all the Rights and Privileges of natural-born Subjects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trustees of Charity Schools for the Education of Boys, shall be obliged to put forth Apprentice to the Sea Service, Inch as shall find Mailers willing to take them.

Resolved, That it is (he Opinion of this Committee, That registered Men shall wear some honorary Mark of Diilinciion.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Register Office be obliged to give an Account to the Lord High Admiral, or the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral, for the time being, of all the Men that shall be registered.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Register Office shall, on the Receipt of an Order from the Lord High Admiral, or the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral, for the time being, for any Number of Men contained on the Register, issue out their Orders for the said Number of Men, to appear according to the Order directed to them, as aforesaid.

The Order of the Day being read, for Edward Lijte Privilege- — Esquire, a Member of this House, to attend this House suspendin^i in llis Place; Member 8

And the House taking Notice; that he did not attend fro*1* it-According to the said Order;

And the Serjeant at Arms attending this House being called upon to give an Account of the Service of the said Order;

The Messenger who was Ifent to serve the said Order was called in, and acquainted the House, That he went with the said Order to the House of the said Mr. in Red Lyon Square, but found the same locked up; and was informed by the Neighbours, that the Goods were rembved, and that they thought Mr. Life was gciio beyond Sea: That afterwards he went to Monies Court, in Hampshire, the House of the said Mr. Life, and there being no Servant of Mr. Life there, he left a Copy of the said Order with a Person, who laid he was retained by Dr. Burton to take care of the Gardens there: That then he went to the Sheriff of the County; and delivered the original Order to him; and that he has since beeii informed by several Persons (One of them Mr. Life's Steward) who have received Letters from him of a late Date, that lie was at Montpelier in France-, and that he was also informed by another Person, that Mr. Life dismissed his Servants at Dover, and told them he was going abroad, and did not know whether he should eveir return to the Kingdom again.

And then the said Messenger withdrew.

Then the Petition of Cacilius Calvert Esquire (which was presented to the House upon the 28th

Day of February last, and ordered to he upon the Table) was read; letting forth, That Edward Life Esquire, a Member of this House, did, in the Year 1733, fell to the Petitioner an Annuity of Four hundred Pounds, to be issuing and payable out of his Estates in the Counties of Southampton, Wills, Dorset, and Somerset, for the Petitioner’s Life; and accordingly the said Mr. Life, to secure the Payment thereof, did, by certain Deeds, dated the 27th and 28th Days of September 1733» charge his said Estates, in the said Counties, with the Paymetit of the said Annuity to the Petitioner, and his Assigns, during Ins Life, in such manner aS in the Deeds is mentioned and expressed; and that the said Mr. Life not paying the said Annuity according to his Agreement for that Purpose, the Petitioner did, in Michaelmas Term last, exhibit his Bill in the Court of Chancery against the said Mr. Life, and others, who lay claim to the Estates; and that the said Mr.

Life,being a Member of this House, is entitled to the Privilege thereof; and therefore the Petitioner cannot now proceed according to the Rules of the Court; he being Party to the said Bill: And, in regard the Petitioner is likely to be a great Sufferer, by not knowing where to apply to the said Mr. fife, praying. That the Petitioner may be at Liberty to proceed against him in such manner as he shall be advised, notwithstanding any Privilege he may be entitled to as a Member of this House.

taking Port* Montague:

Bello. Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed upon an Address to his Majesty: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence'of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The said Address was read; andisas follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and in Parliament assembled, do congratulate your Majesty on the glorious Success of your Majesty’s Arms in the West Indies, under the Command of Vice Admiral Vernon, by entering the Port and taking the Town of Porto Bello, and demolishing and levelling all the Forts and Caltles belonging thereto.

This Enterprize, so wifely concerted, and so bravely conducted, cannot fail of giving the utmost Joy to all your Majesty’s faithful Subjects, since it also rds the moll reasonable Hopes and Expectations, that, by the Blelling of God upon your Majesty's Councils and Arms, it may be attended with other important Advantages, and highly contribute to the obtaining real and effectual Security of those just Rights of Navigation and Commerce belonging to your Majesty’s Subjects; for the Preservation of which your Majesty entered into this necessary War.

The laid Address being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by adding, after the Word " thereto," at the End of the First Paragragb, the Words " with Six Ships of War " only}"

And the Question being put. That those Words be there inserted;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Tellers for the Noes, j £}r; } 3«.

Mr. Walpole reported from the Committee who were Prohibiting appointed todraw upReafons, to be offered to the Lords ('ommefre* at a Conference, for disagreeing to such of the Amend- sPa,a-ments,made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for prohibiting Commerce with Spain, as this House hath disagreed to That the Committee had drawn up Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

To the First Amendment, made by your Lordships; to the Bill, intituled, An Act for prohibiting Commerce with Spain, the Commons do agree.

To the Second Amendment, made by your Lordships, in Press 1. L. 20. of the said Bill, whereby the Word " June," is directed to be left out, and the Word May" to be inserted instead thereof, the Commons disagree:

Because they apprehend, That if the Prohibition of bringing in Spanish Goods was to take place the First of May, many Persons who have Goods on the Way front Spain, which have been long since bought and paid for, may be too much straitened in Time, considering the Uncertainty of Winds, as well as the Difficult^ the Merchants maybe underof getting Ships to load their Goods in Minorca, or at Gibraltar, that are fit to run without Convoy; and the Delay that may happen by other Shi ps waiting for Convoy, which is the more to be regarded, on Account of the heavy Penalties, which, by this Bill, are inflicted on importing such Goods after the Time limited; which your Lordships feein feniible of, by the Provision in Clause A; which the Commons have disagreed to, for the Reasons after-mentioned.

To the 3d Amendment; made by your Lordships,-in P. 2. L. 2. of the said Bill, whereby the Word " Foreign," is directed to be inserted alter the Word " Port," the Commons disagree;

Because the Prohibition of importing Spanish Goods would be thereby restrained to such Goods as thou Id be imported from some foreign Port or Place, and t-Onfe-questly there would be no Prohibition of importing into

this

To the next Amendment, made by your Lordships, being ClauseA, the Commons disagree:

Because they think it better that the Prohibition should take place absolutely, in all his Majesty’s Dominions, at the same time, than to give Leave to bring^anj/ftGoods from Minorca or Gibraltar to Great Britain after the Prohibition has taken place, upon Proof being made, before the Commissioners of the Customs, of the Goods being imported into Minorca or Gibraltar before the 26th of February; which may occasion th^ Law to be evaded, and would lay all Importers of such Goods, who do not live in or about the Cities of London and minster, under great Difficulties.

To Clause B, and the rest of the Amendments, made by your Lordships, to the said Bill, the Commons do agree.

forth. That the late general Embargo, and that laid on or about the Second of February last, which now continues, has been a very great Loss and Discourageroent to the Trade of these Kingdoms, by lessening the Exports thereof, besides a great Loss to the Merchants, in having their Goods and Effects lie perishing on board their Ships many Months in the River , and else-

where in his Majesty’s Dominions: That these great Losses and Hardships have been borne by the Sufferers with the greatest Cheerfulness, upon account of a Necelfity there might be to supply his Majesty’s Ships of War with Mariners, for the Defence of the Nation in general a gain ft the common Enemy: That the Embargo upon Ships navigated by Foreigners has been taken off some time fmce, while that on the British iscontinued: which encourages many Persons to load their Goods and Merchandize upon such foreign Ships only, and not upon the al-

though they are much preferable for Defence and Security incarrying them to Ports beyond the Seas, than thofeShips manned with Foreigners: That, if the said foreign Ships are permitted to be the only Carriers of the British Merchandize, while our own Ships must lie rotting in the River, our Navigation, which always has been esteemed lb valuable to the Nation, the Merchants and Traders, will meet with such Discouragement that in few Years more it maybe greatly lessened: That the great Number of Ships which usually go upon the Fishery,

Whale Fishery, and to Virginia, Sec. generally proceed upon theirfeveral Voyages about this Season of the Year; and it is well known the great AdvantagesthofeBranches of Trade have been of to Great for many Years

past: That several Merchants and Owners of Ships have Applied, in the usual manner, to the Lords of the Admiralty for Protections, and Leave to proceed on their Voyages with their Ships and Loadings; many of the said Ships have been loaden and ready to go to Sea several Months, with very valuable Cargoes of Woollen Goods and Products of these Kingdoms, some of which are of a perishing Nature: That their Lordships have acquainted several Merchants, who have applied to them at their Board, That it was required of all Masters of Ships who wanted the Embargo to be taken off, in order to go to Sea, that each Ship must provide a certain Number of Mariners in proportion to what they carry, for the Use of his Majesty’s Ships of War; and, unless the Merchants complied with those Terms they would not be permitted to have any Protection, or used Words to that or the like Effect: That such very severe Terms and Precedents as are now proposed, the Petitioners are wholly unacquainted with; and are humbly of Opinion, That if the present Embargo iscontinued only till the Merchant scan supply a sufficient Number of Mariners for the Men of War, it will be such a Discouragement to our foreign Trade, and the Navigation of these Kingdoms in the Merchants Service, that it is not possible to be performed or supported, the great Expence and Charge upon each Man, to be paid by way of Premium, for his entering on board a Man of War, may amount to more than Ten Pounds per Man, besides the high Wages on account of the War; and, if this Practice is to be encouraged and established in future, the Crimps, and their Landlords, who are Seamens Advisers, may raise the Premium to what Price they please, and in time stagnate the whole Maritime Commerce: And that it is the humble Opinion of the Petitioners, That such a Method will prevent Seamen from ever entering on board his Majesty’s Ships, while the Merchants are obliged to supply them, at such an exorbitant Premium: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves or Counsel, upon the said Petition; and grant that such Provision'may be made, in future, to encourage the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House; and that the

Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard by themselves before the said Committee;

The House divided.

The House according to Order, proceeded to take p,..... into Consideration the Report made, of the Conference Commerce* with the Lords, upon Monday last; and the Reasons given with Spain, by the Lords for infilling on Two of the Amendments, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for prohibiting Commerce with Spain, to which this House had disagreed, were read; and are as follow j viz.

The Lords do infill on their ad Amendment made to the Bill, intituled, An Act for prohibiting Commerce with Spain, in Press 1. L. 20, of the said Bill, whereby the Word " May" is directed to be inserted, instead of

the Word "June-,"to which the Commons disagree:

Because their Lordships apprehend, That should there be a Liberty granted of importing into his Majesty’s Dominions, any Goods or Commodities of the Growth or Product of Spain, till the First Day of June next, it would be a great Prejudice to this Kingdom, since an Opportunity may be thereby given of importing large Quantities of Goods contrafted for after the Prohibition of Commerce, on the Part of Spain, and which mull therefore be paid for in ready Money; whereby the Balance of Trade may be turned to the Prejudice of Great Britain; and great Advantages will arise to the King of Spain, and his Subjects, during the Time of

actual

13 Geo. II. x 7" — 18° Apritis.

S23

actual War with that Crown; which will, as the Lords conceive, be in a great Measure prevented by the said Amendment.

The Lords do not infill on their 3d Amendment in Pr. 2. L. 4, of the said Bill, whereby the Word " Foreign" is directed to be inserted, before the Word " Port j to which the Commons disagree.

The Lords do infill on their Amendment Clause A; to which the Commons disagree:

Becanfe it did appear to their Lordships, by the Account given by the Merchants at the Bar, that aim oft all the Effects of the English Merchants, contracted for in Spain, were either in Minorca, Gibraltar, or at Sea, in their Way to England, on or before the 26th Day of February last, the Time limited by the said Clause for the Arrival of such Goods at Minorca or Gibraltar: And the Lords conceive that no Inconvenience! can arise by indulging the Merchants to the 24th Day of June, for bringing home such Goods, since, by the said Clause, they are required to make Proof that the said Goods were actually imported into Minorca or Gibraltar, and there landed, or loaded on board some Ship or

Vessel, on or before the said 26th Day of February; and the Method prescribed for making this Proof is agreeable to what has been formerly practised in Cafes of the like Nature, except that in this same the Proof is, for the greater Security, required to be made before the Commi (Boners of the Customs, inllead of the Barons of the Exchequer; but no greater Difficulty will be thereby oe-cafioned to the Importers, who do not live in or about the Cities of London and Westminster, than was thought reasonable in the Act 3° Si, 40 Anna, Cap. 13. Sed. 3, and besides, it will be very practicable for them to fend up their Proofs to be produced, and laid before the Commissioners of the Customs.

For the Reasons above mentioned the Lords apprehend, That no Inconvenience can happen from the said Clause, and from the Prohibitions not absolutely taking place in all his Majesty’s Dominions at the same time.

A Petition of Francis Wilks and Christopher Kilby Esquires, Agents for . Province of Massachujfets Bay in New England, for and in Behalf of the said Province, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That in the Year 1730, when Jo Esquire,

the present Governor of the said Province, first came to his Government, each Year to 1741 was charged with a Debt, in Bills of Credit, that had been before that time issued to answer the Exigencies of Government of between Sixteen and Seventeen thousand Pounds, commu-nibus Annis, occasioned by a long and distressing War with the Indians; and that all the Bills emitted since that time to defray the growing Charge of the Province, have beeh laid on the Years preceding 1742, by means whereof the last Year 1739, and the present Year 1740, and succeeding Year 1741, are each charged with the heavy Burden of Sixty-eight thousand Pounds, one Year with another; besides about Forty-five thousand Pounds Principal and Interest, which is to be speedily drawn in, for the closing the several Province Loans: And further representing to the House, That, by reason of the heavy Charges of the Province, and the Scarcity of the Money, the People there have met with great Difficulty in the Payment of their Taxes, and in carrying on their Trade and Business; there being no other Medium of Commerce among them but their Paper Currency; the fmallQuantities of Silver and Gold, which are from time to time imported, being applied for the Payment of the Manufactures of Great Britain, which are expended in great Quantities in this Province; and that the Paper Currency in all the British Plantations being now under the Consideration of this House, and the Petitioners being intruded by the said Province to take care of their Interest, in all Matters that may arise here by which the Interest of the said Province may be any ways affected, conceive it their indispensable Duty to represent to the House the present distressed Condition of the said Province, for want of a new Emission of Paper Currency; which they do not desire, but upon providing sufficient Funds to secure the sinking and calling in the fame; and which, should they be prevented from doing, the Province must necessarily be thrown into the utmost Disorder and Confusion, the ’ Government be without’any Support; the Forts and Garrisons remain in a defenceless Condition, and wholly unprovided with warlike Stores; and the Province be unable to equip suitable Vessels of War to guard their Coast and their Trade; and Commerce be ruined and undone: And therefore, as the Resolutions to be taken by this House upon this Affair may greatly affect the Interest of the said Province of the Maffachnfets Bay, praying, That the Petitioners may be heard in relation to the State of the Paper Currency in New England, before this House comes to any Resolution thereon.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Papers presented to this House upon the Twenty-eighth Day of March last, from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, concerning the Paper Currency, and the Rates of Gold and Silver, in America, from the Year 1700 to the present Year, and then ordered to lie upon the Table; and to whom the several other Papers concerning the said

Vol. 23.

Paper Currency, tlrid the said Rates of Gold and Silver American Coin, presented to this House the Fifteenth Day of this Paper ihstant April, from the Commissioners for Trade and Currency. Plantations, and then ordered to lie upon the Table,

Wefe referred; be received: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Mr. Francis Fane, according to Order, reported from the Committee, the Resolutions which they had direfiled him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table.

Then Christopher Kilby Esquire, One of the said Petitioners, was called in.

And the Resolutions of the said Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That -it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for af-Certaining the Rates of foreign Coins in her Majesty’s Plantations in America,hath not been duly observed, as it ought to have been; by means whereof many indirect Practices have grown up, and various and illegal Currencies have been introduced in several of the said Colonies and Plantations, contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act, to the Prejudice of the Tradj of his Majesty’s Subjects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the creating and issuing Paper Bills of Credit in the British Colonies and Plantations in America, by virtue of Acts of Assembly there, and making it obligatory on all Persons to take such Bills of Credit in Payment for all Debts, Dues, and Demands, hath frustrated the good Intentions of an Act of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for ascertaining the Rates of foreign Coins in her Majesty’s Plantations \n America; and hath been a great Discouragement to the Commerce of this Kingdom, by oncafioning a Confusion in Dealings, and lessening of Credit in those Parts.

And then the said Christopher Kilby Esquire w’as heard.

And then he withdrew.

The First Resolution of the said Committee, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, Nemine conlradicente.

Mr. Francis Fane acquainted the House, That he was directed by the said Committee to make a Motion, with respect to the said Resolution.

And he moved the House accordingly. 1

Resolved, Nemine conlradicente. That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to require and command the respective Governors of his Colonies and Plantations in,

effectually to observe his Majesty’s Royal Inftrnftion di-resting them, that the Act of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for ascertaining the Rates of foreign Coins in her Majesty’s Plantations in America, be punctually, and bona fide, observed and put in execution, according to the true Intent and Meaning of the said Act.

Mr. Francis Fane also acquainted the House, That he was directed, by the said Committee, to make another Motion, with respect to the said Resolution.

And he moved the House accordingly:

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, that he will begraciously pleased to issue his Royal Proclamation, to settle and ascertain the Rates and Proportion at which all foreign Gold Coins shall be accounted, received, taken, or paid, in any of his Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in America.

After which his Majesty was pleased to make a most The King* gracious Speech to both lloufes of Parliament; as fol- Speetn, loweth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Zeal which you have shewn for the Support and Prosecution of the just and necessary War in which I am engaged, is a fresh Proof of your Concern for the Honour and Interestof my Crown and Kingdoms.

As this great and national Undertaking is the principal Object of our Attention and Expectations, so the Justice of our Cause, and the Success which hath hitherto attended my Arms, gives us the moll reasonable Hopes,

That by the Continuance of the Divine Afliliance we may fee a happy Ilfuc of it.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you for the efi‘e6tual Supplies which you have granted me for the Service of the current Year. The best Return I can make is to allure you. That they shall be duly employed to the Purposes for which they tvere given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have-formerly recommended to you Union amongst yourselves, as being highly conducive to the carrying on this great Work with Honour and Advantage, and to the more speedy obtaining of all possible Justice and Sa-tisfaclionfromtheCrownof Spain, for themany grievous Injuries fullered by my Subjects, and effectual Security for the Freedom of our Commerce and Navigation for the future. I do now earnefily exhort you to promote and extend that Union in your respective Countries.

Let the Support of the common Cause of the Nation prevail to attain this desirable End. Our Enemies mull . already have been made sensible, in some Degree, of the,

Weight of our just Resentment. They fee my Kingdoms in such a Posture of Defence, as mull render all Attempts from them, without Encouragement from amongst ourselves, vain and desperate. They fee the Trade and Navigation of my Subjects protected, as far as the Nature and Circumstances of a maritime War will pofiibly admit, and at the same time the moll valuable Branches of the Spanish Commerce greatly interrupted, and subjected to many Difficulties and Losses. From these - happy Effects of my early Endeavours, and your ready Concurrence at the firftEntrance into the War, I cannot but hope that the Preparations which I am now making for carrying it on in the most proper Places and in the most vigorous and effectual Maimer, will be blessed with Success equal to our just Expectations.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the Third Day of June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the Third Day of June next.
