the most proper Places, and in the most vigorous and effectual manner. For this Purpose strong Squadrons were got ready and ordered to fail upon important Services both in the West Indies and Europe, with as much Expedition as the Nature of those Services and the Manning of the Ships would admit. A very conGderable Body of Land Forces was embarked, which is to be joined by a great Number of my Subjects raised in' America; and all things necessary for transporting the Troops from hence, and carrying on the designed Expedition, were a long time in Readiness, and waited only for an Opportunity to pursue the intended Voyage.

The several Incidents which have happened in the mean time have had no Effect upon me but to confirm me in my Resolutions, and to determine me to add Strength to my Armaments, rather than to divert or deter me from those just and vigorous Methods, which I am pursuing, for maintaining the Honour of my Crown, and the undoubted Rights of my People.

The Court of Spain, having already felt some Effects of our Uefentment, began to be sensible, that they should be no longer able alone to defend themselves against the Efforts of the British Nation. And if any other Power, agreeably to some late extraordinary Proceedings,should interpose, and attempt to prcscribe or limit the Operations of the War against my declared Enemies, the Honour and Interest of my Crown and Kingdoms mull call upon us to lose no Time in putting ourselves into such a Condition, as may enable us to repel any Insults, and to frustrate any Designs formed against us, in Violation of the Faith of Treaties. And I hope any such unprecedented Steps, under what Colour or Pretence soever they may be taken, will inspire my Allies with a true Sense of the common Danger, and will unite us in the Support and Defence of the common Cause.

The great and unhappy Event of the Death of the late Emperor opens a new Scene in the Affairs of , in which all the principal Powers may be immediately or consequentially concerned. It is impossible to determine what Turn the Policy, Interest, or Ambition, of the several Courts may lead them to take in this critical Conjuncture. It shall be my Care ItriCtly to observe and attend to their Motions, and to adhere to the Engagements I am under, in order to the Maintaining of the Balance of Power, and the Liberties of and in Concert with such Powers, as are under the same Obligations, or equally concerned, to preserve the publick Safety and Tranquillity, to act such a Part, as may bell contribute to avert the imminent Dangers that may threaten them.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons.

I have ordered Estimates to be prepared and laid before you, for the Service of the ensuing Year: It is always with Regret that I ask any extraordinary Aids of my People; but what I have already mentioned, must be sufficient to satisfy you, that some Augmentations will be necessary, not only for carrying on the present War with Vigour, but aTfoto put ourselves in a Condition of being prepared for such Events as may arise in this new and uncertain State of Europe: I therefore depend on your experienced'Zeal and Affection for me, and my Government, your Concern for your own Safety, and the Support of the Common Cause, to grant me fuen effectual Supplies as may be requisite for these great Ends.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Scarcity of Corn which has happened in many Countries of Europe has induced several Pow’ers to make extraordinary Provisions to obviate the ill Effects of that Misfortune: And though in many Parts of this Kingdom the Harvest has proved more favourable, yet common Prudence calls upon us to provide, as far as may be, against the Approach of such a Calamity: Beiides, in our present Circumstances, it would be an incxcufeable Neglect to fuflerour Enemies to be supplied with any Kind of Provisions from my Dominions, and that, even at the Hazard of my own Subjects being drftreffed. Let me therefore earnestly recommend it to you to consider of some good Law to prevent this growing Mischief.

The Difficulties which have been found in manning the Fleet by the usual Methods hitherto practised, demonstrate the Want of some parliamentary Remedy. I must therefore press it upon yon, to l.»fe no Time in making such Provisions, in this respect, as, whillt we are engaged in a War, in Defence of the Commerce and Navigation of this Kingdom, may enable the Publick to avail ilfelf of those great Numbers of Seamen which make so valuable a Branch of our Strength.

The Importance of these Considerations is so apparent, that I need use no Arguments to convince you of the Necessity of the utmost Unanimity and Dispatch in your Proceedings.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That at humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to acknowledge, with Duty and Gratitude, his Majesty’s great Regard for the Honour and Interest of these Kingdoms, in equipping such strong Squadrons of Men of War, and erubarkiUg a Body of Land Forces, to be joined, and {Lengthened by a considerable Number of his Majesty’s Subjects raised in America, in order to carry on tf»e YV ar in those Parts in the most vigorous and effectual manner; to express our most dutiful Sense of his Majesty’s Firm-ness and Resolution, in not suffering himself to be diverted or deterred, by any Incidents, from pursuing the just and vigorous Measures in which he is engaged, for maintaining the Honour of htsCrown, and the undoubted Rights of his People; and to allure his Majesty, that tins House will Hand by and support his Majesty against all Attempts made in Violation of the Faith of Treaties, or tending to prescribe or limit the Operations of the War against his Majesty’s declared Enemies; and that we will, with great Cheerfulness, grant his Majesty such effectual Supplies, as shall be necessary, not only for carrying on the present War with Vigour, but also to put his Majesty in a Condition of being prepared for such Events as may arise from the new and uncertain State of Affairs in Europe; and that we will lose no Time in considering the most proper Methods of remedying the great Mif-chiefs that may'arise from the Scarcity of Corn, or from suffering our Enemies to be supplied with any Kind of Provisions from any of his Majesty’s Dominions; and that we will take such Measures as shall be thought most reasonable and practicable, to enable his Majesty effectually to man his Royal Fleets, for the Defence of the Kingdom, for the Security of the Trade and Navigation of his Majesty s Subjects, and for carrying on the War with Vigour; - -

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Refolded, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Refolded, That if it shall appear. That any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Refolded, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Refolded, That if shall appear, That any Person hath given false Evidence in any Cafe, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Refolded, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elc6tion$ of Members tp serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Refolded, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall fee, or be informed of, to be in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting: And that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Post Mailer General.

Ordered, That when any Letter, or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame, and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

?uire is returned a Burgess for the said Borough: Which ndenture of Return, being by him, and the said Town Clerk, compared with a Draught of a Counter part thereof, prepared by the said Town Clerk, was found to agree therewith; and that thereupon, by virtue of the said Deputation, he put the Sheriff’s Name, and Seal of his Office, to the said Counter-part; and executed the same for the said Sheriff; and requested the said Town Clerk to convey the said Writ and Return to the Clerk of the Crown.

Mr.Bromley reported from the Committee, appointed Add rest on Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his the King’* Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address sPeech-accorrlingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

Most gracious Sovereign,

We your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, humbly beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on your safe and happy Return to these your regal Dominions; and to return ourfincere Thanks for your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Your faithful Commons, with Hearts full of Duty and Gratitude, cannot but acknowledge your Majesty’s great Regard for the Honour and Interest of these Kingdoms, in equipping such strong Squadrons of Men of War, and' embarking a Body of Land Forces, to be joined and strengthened by a considerable Number of your Majesty’s Subjects raised in America, in order to carry on the War in those Parts in the most vigorous and effectual manner.

We at the same time beg Leave to express our most dutiful Sense of your Majesty’s Firmness and Resolution, in not fullering yourself to he diverted or deterred, by any Incidents from pursuing the just and vigorous Measures in which your Majesty is engaged, for maintaining the Honour of the Crown, and the undoubted Rights of your People: And we assure your Majesty, that this House will itand by and support your Majesty against all Attempts made in Violation of the Faith of Treaties, or tending to prescribe or limit the Operations of the War against your Majesty’s declared Enemies.

Your dutiful and loyal Commons will, with the utmost Cheerfulness, grant your Majesty such effectual Supplies as shall be necessary,not only for carrying on the present War with Vigour, but also to put your Majesty in a Condition of being prepared for such Events as may arise from the new and uncertain State of Affairs in Europe.

Your Majesty’s Tenderness and Concern for the Ease and Welfare of your Subjects, in recommending to the Consideration of Parliament the great Distress that may arise from the Scarcity of Corn, calls upon us in the strongest manner, to lose no Time in taking the most proper and effectual Methods of avoiding those great and dangerous Mischiefs, which so apparently threaten us, and of not suffering our Enemies to be supplied with any Kind of Provisions from any of your Majesty’s Do-, minions.

We will also take such Measures as shall be thought most reasonable and practicable to enable your Majesty effectually to man your royal Fleets, for the Defence of the Kingdom, for the Security of the Trade and Navigation of your Majesty’s Subjects, and for carrying on the War with Vigour.

The said Address, being read aSecond time, was,upon the Questionput thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleasure when he will be attended by this House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, The King’s take into Consideration his Majesty’s most gracious Speech to tm Speech tQ both Houses of Parliament. considered.

A Petition of the Merchants ofwhole Names E'cportatioa dre thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and #fCom. others residing in, and trading to* Ireland, -

land, the Provinces of New England, New York, the Jerseys, Pensylvania, Maryland, Virginia, North and South Carolina, and the British Sugar I/lands, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by the Exports of Provisions from Ireland, and the Northern British Colonies in America, to the English Sugar Islands, a very great and valuable Trade is carried on, without which those Islands will not be able to subsist, their whole Dependence for a constant Supply of Victuals, being thereon: That since the Exportation of Rice from Carolina directly to Portugal hath been admitted, and the Merchants trading to and from have

fallen into the Method of clearing their Ships with Rice* designed for the Markets of Holland, Hamburgh, 8Cc. at an Out Port in the English Chanel, the Planters of that Grain have greatly increased their Plantations, and* by rendering it very cheap in Europe, have obtained the supplying the Dutch and German Markets therewith, which heretofore had it from the Mediterranean:

That the Benefits arising to Great Britain from these Branches of Trade are very great, particularly in employing a large Number of Shipping, whereby Sailors are increased, and the many Tradesmen dependent oil Navigation supported: And that if any Stop be put to that Course of Business, which is necessarily carried on by his Majesty’s Subjects, from one Colony or Plantation to another, for their mutual Support, and from America to Europe, in return for those Goods and Ma<-nufactures which we fend them from these Kingdoms, and which they cannot pay for, but by the Returns of what they produce, the Petitioners conceive it may tend to destroy the bell Branch of Trade we have now left; and that it will be, in its Consequences, ruinous to Navigation, and to many Thousands of his Majesty*'s Subjects: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel,against the Bill to enable his Majesty to prohibit, for a Time to be limited, the Exportation of Corn, and other Provisions* out of Great Britain, Ireland, and his Majesty’s Colonies and Plantations in America.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petition- ers be heard, by themselves, upon their said Petition, if they think fit, before the said Committee.

Vol. 23.

Majesty and the King of Sweden, as Landgrave of Cassel', signed, Westminster, 9 May 1740: And also,

Translation of a Treaty with the King of Sweden, as Landgrave of tiqffe Cassel, q May 1740.

And the Titles of the said Papers were read.

The Copy of the said Treaty is bound up with the other Papers of this Session j

And the Translation thereof is as follows; viz.

Be it known unto those whom it shall appertain, That his Majesty the King of Great Britain on one Side, and his Majesty the King of Sweden, as Landgrave of Hesse, on the other, having considered, that, in thepre-sent Situation of the Affairs of Europe, their reciprocal Interests require, that the antient Friendship and Confidence which has beenat all times cultivated between their Majesties, and their glorions Anceliors, with a mutual Advantage, should be renewed and strengthened by stricter Ties, and by a new Treaty of a defensive Alliance, have thought fit to charge their Ministers, that is to say, his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Philip Lord Hardioicke, his Chancellor of Great Britain, Spencer Earl of Wilmington, President of his Privy Council,

Holies Duke of Nexccastle,one of his principal Secretaries

of Stale, William Lord Harrington, the other of hiS principal Secretaries of State, and Sir Robert Walpole^ Knight of the most noble Order of the Garter, First Commissioner of his Treasury, and Chancellor and Under Treasurer of his Exchequer; and his Majesty the King of Sweden, in Quality of Landgrave, the Sieur Alt, his Counsellor of Legation; being provided with the necessary full Powers to confer thereupon; who, after having exchanged their full Powers, have agreed upon the Points and Articles following:

Article I.

There shall be a sincere Amity, and a most Ariel Union, between their Majesties, their Successors, and Heirs, and Subjects, in such a manner, that the one shall consider the Interests of the other as his own; and

7 A shall

Treaty with King ot Sweden*

550 5* Decembris. A. 174a.

shall faithfully employ himself to promote them as much as possible, and to prevent and keep off from each other mutually all Trouhie and Damage.

Article II.

To this End it isagreed, that all the preceding Treaties, chiefly those of Guaranty, shall be taken to be renewed and confirmed by this presentTreaty.in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses; and they shall have the same Force as if they had been [here] inserted Word for Word, as far as they are not derogated from by the present Treaty. Article III.

His Majesty the King of Great , having desired

that his Majesty the King of Sweden, as Landgrave of lleffk, would hold in Readiness a Body of his Hessian Troops, for the Service of his Britamfick Majesty, in case the Good of his Kingdoms and Dominions should require that Succour, his Majesty the King of Sweden has been willing to agree thereto, promising and engaging, by virtue of this Article, to hold in Readiness for that Purpose, during the Space of Four successive Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this present Treaty, a Body of Six thousand Men; that is to say, Twelve hundred Horse or Dragoons, and Four thousand Eight hundred Foot, provided with the necessary general Officers and Subalterns, fitly mounted and armed, in a Condition to march for the Service of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Two Months after Requifi-tion shall have been made, or sooner, if it be possible, unless there be need of them for the immediate Defence of the Kingdoms and Dominions of his Britannick Majesty; in which case they shall march immediately after the Requisition has been made; and the said Troops shall take the Oath of Fidelity to his Britannick Majesty, when they shall have passed the Frontiers of Hejje, without Prejudice to that which they have taken to his Majesty the King of Sweden as Landgrave; his said Majesty, be-lides retaining the Disposal of all the Posts that shall become vacant in the Corps, the Administration of Justice being reserved to him likt wife.

Article IVth.

Ashis Swedi/h Majesty will be engaged in several considerable Expences for remounting and putting in a Condition the above-mentioned Corps, his Majesty the King of Great Britain, to assist him therein, promises to pay to his Majesty the King of Sweden, for every Horse-man fitly armed and mounted Fourl'core Crowns, and for every Foot Soldier Thirty Crowns BanCo; qne Half immediately after the Signing this Treaty, and the other Half when the Troops shall be delivered. Besides, his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to pay to his Majesty the King of Sweden, without any Abatement or Delay, anannual Subsidy of Two hundred and fifty thousand Crowns Banco, during the Time that the Troops shall be at the Charge of the Treasury of his Swedish Majesty; which Subsidy shall commence from the Signing of this present Treaty, and shall be continued to the Expiration of the Four Years above, mentioned; but when those Troops shall actually be taken into the Pay of his Majesty the King, of Great Britain, his Majesty the King of Sweden, shall then content himself with ah annual Subsidy of One hundred and fifty thousand Crowns Banco; which Subsidy shall continue during the w hole time that the said Troops shall be in the Service of his Britannick Majesty; the Payment of the one and the other shall he made regularly, without Abatement, and every Quarter, in the d own of to the

military Chest of his Swcdijh Majesty, authorized for the Receipt of it.

Article Vth.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain charges himself

with the Pay and Entertainment, as well ordinary as extraordinary, of the Officers, Ilorfemen, and Foot Soldiers, of that Body, from, the Day they shall begin their March for his Service; and this Pay, both ordinary and extraordinary, shall be regulated upon the same Foot with that of the llcjjuui Troops, made over by the Treaties ofi 702, Articles Five and Six, and of 1726, Arti-Sij jJicd Iron* the Tranllmion ^relented to thulioulc*

cle Six; and it shall be put into the military Chest, with* out any Abatement or Diminution, to make the Distribution thereof; but if it should by Misfortune happen, that any Regiments or Companies of the abovesaid Corps should come to be mined or destroyed, in the Whole, or in Part, his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall cause to be paid, without Delay, to the abovesaid Chest, the Charges of the necessary Recruits and Remounts for putting the Regiments or Companies speedily again into Condition; and these Recruits and Remounts shall be in like manner |regulated upon the Foot of those that were furnished to the Officers

by virtue of the Treaty of 1702, Art. Five; to the end that the Corps may always be preservgd and sent back One Day in as good Condition as it was delivered. Article Vlth.

His Britannick Majesty shall be at Liberty to keep this Corps in his Service, all the time of the Duration of this Treaty, in order to make use of it where-ever he shall have Occasion, provided it be not upon the Fleet, nor beyond Sea, after it comes once out of the hereditary Dominions of his Swedi/h; except however for the Defence of the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland-, in which case these Troops shall enjoy, in all respects, and without any Restriction whatever, the same Pay and Emoluments which the Troops enjoy;

and when his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall have a mind to lend back the said Troops, he ilia.ll acquaint his Majesty the King of Sweden with it Three Mouths before-hand; and shall cattle to be paid to them a Month’s Wages for their Return, furnishing them the necessary Transport Ships gratis. It is like-wife agreed, that the said HTroops shall not be employed either against the Kingdom of Sweden itfelfi or against any of the Provinces belonging to it.

Article Vllth.

In case his Majesty the King of Sweden should be attacked, or troubled in the Possession of his hereditary Dominions, his Britannick Majesty promises and engages to fend the said Body of Troops speedily back to him,paying them not only a Month’s Wages, but furnishing them also gratis the Transport Ships that shall be requi-

site for their Return, and togive besides to his Yavdi/ft Majesty, as Landgrave of Hejfe, all the Succour of Troops which the same shall require; which Assistance shall be continued to him till he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace, as his Majesty the King of,

in the Quality of Landgrave, on his Part, promises like-wife,that in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain should be attacked, or troubled in his Kingdoms, States, Countries, Provinces, or Towns, he will give him like-wife all the Assistance that the same shall require; which Assistance shall in like manner be continued to him, until he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace.

Article Vlllth.

In order to make this Alliance and Union so much the more perfect, and to leave the Parties no kind of Scruple, as to the Certainty of the Assistance which they are to expert from each other,* it is exp rest Iv agreed, that, for judging hereafter whether the same of this Alliance, and of the stipulated Succour, exists or not, it shall be sufficient that either of the Parties be actually attacked by Force of Arms, without that Party’s having before used open Force against him who attacks him.

Article IXtli.

This Treaty shall last for the Space of Four Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing it; and if their Majesties think fit to continue, prolong, or change it, that Matter shall he treated of Three Mouths before it expires, according to the F.xigency of the Cale.

Article Xtli.

The Ratifications of this Treaty shall be exchanged at London, within. Two Months after the Signing, or sooner, if it be possible.

In Witness whereof, Wc, the underwritten, being ftirnillied with the full Powers of the most ierene Kings of Great Britain, and oi Sweden, have iigtied the present

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

The Petitioners produced the Act of Parliament, made in the 12th Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, mentioned in their Petition; whereby it appeared, That several Tolls and Duties were granted, and made payable, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, commencing the ill Day of June 1726, for repairing and amending the said Roads.

Then Mr Roger Gay thor tie, Treasurer to the Trustees,

and Mr. John AJklon, Surveyor of the said Roads, being

severally examined, said. That, at the Time the said Act passed, the Roads before mentioned were in a ruinous Condition, and, in many Parts thereof, in the Winter Season, dangerous to Palfeugers: And Mr. Gaychorne further said, That the said Road being so very bad, both at and since the Commencement of the said Act, the 20

Decembris. A. 1740.

Trustees, in order to make the same palfable, were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money; and that there is a Debt of £.6,500 remaining due on the Credit of the said Act.

And the Witnesses further said. That, since the Commencement of the said Act, there hath been £.3,711, or thereabouts, expended in paving several Parts of the said Road; particularly at Hay and James Street, and in Kensington Town.

And they added, That the Money borrowed, together with the Tolls and Duties collected by virtue of the said Act, had been duly applied towards repairing the said Roads, and that great Progress hath been made therein j but, by reason of the excessive Weights and Carriages continually passing, the Roads cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, for the Accommodation of Travellers, and the Money remaining due, with the Interest thereof, be repaid, unless the Term, Tolls, and Powers, by the former Act granted, be enlarged and continued, and the said Act made more effectual.

In order to prove the Allegations of the other Petition^ the Petitioners called Mr. Richard Osgood: Who, being examined, said. That the Road leading from the Re// at Brumpton to the End of Sehvood's Lane, hading to the Queen's Elm, and from the End of Lane so the

William Morice Esquire, being examined, said. Mr. Upton,being examined, said. That the Road

Mr. Simon Parry, being examined, said. That the Right of nominating a Minister or Curate to the said Chapel is claimed, as well by the Wear of Rofthern, as by the principal Inhabitants of the aforesaid Five Townlliips or Hamlets; but that the present Minister was, as he believes, about Fifty Years ago, named by the Inhabitants to officiale, in the said Chapel; and Once in every Year Two or Three of the Inhabitants of the said Townships or Hamlets, at the Requeil of such Minister, coiled Contributions towards his Maintenance and Support: That the said Minister, as the Witness believes, was formerly not entitled to any certain Maintenance or Provision, except the yearly Stipend of £.5 Gs. 8 dpaid him by the Vicar of Rofthern, and the Surplice Fees; lor which Sum the Vicar infills that he has the Right of nominating the Minister to officiate in the said Chapel.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-three thousand Seven hundred and Eleven Pounds Eight Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to his Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the fame, to make good the Deficiency of the Duty of Twelve Shillings per Barrel on Sweets or Wines made from British or foreign Fruit or Sugar, at Michaelmas 1739, to anf-wer Three Pounds per Centum per Annum Interest on Five hundred thousand Pounds charged thereon.

which areltill, for that reason, so much drank by People of inferior Rank, notwithstanding the Act lately made for restraining the excessive Use thereof: And further representing to the House, That Spirits

drawn from Malt only, are more wholesome than such as

are now uftially drawn from unmalted Com mixed with Malt, which is so mixed in the Proportion of Seventy Quarters at least of unmalted Corn to Thirty Quarters of Malt: And further alleging, That with the Grains of unmalted Corn, now used in brewing and preparing spirituous and other Liquors, Distillers and others do feed and fat a great Number of Hogs; which would otherwise be better fed and fatted in the Country by Farmers, or would necessarily consume a great Quantity of Peas and Beans, and coarse Corn mixed with Grains, if the said Distillers and others were obliged to use malted Corn only: And therefore, in behalf of themselves, and many others, thus prejudiced by the Use of unmalted Corn, which also tends so much to the Diminution of the publick Revenue, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give Relief to the Petitioners, by enforcing the said Laws heretofore made for the Consumption of malted Corn, or by such other Means as to the House shall seem meet.

14th January 1740-1.

In Obedience to the Directions of an Act, passed in the First Session of this present Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of Denventivater, and Charles Radcliffe;

Requiring the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, to contract and agree with able and sufficient Tradesmen, Artificers, or other Persons, for finishing and completing the said Royal Hospital in a workmanlike and substantial Manner, on theeafielt and most reasonable Terms, according to the Plan laid before the House of Commons, in the said Session of Parliament; and to lay their Proceedings therein before his Majesty, and both Houses of Parliament, respectively;

THE Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital do humbly report as followeth;

s. d.

There has been received, between the ill of December 1739, and the 3°^ of 1740, out

of the Rents of the Estate - -- 3,720 o o

As to their Proceedings in carrying on the Building:

In Queen Anne's Court,

Apartments for Two Captains arc completely finished, and a large Drain made from the South Pavilion of this Court to the great Sewer on the East Side of the Hospital.

The Paving of the Upper Gallery is laid, and the Mezzanine and Attic Stories of the South Pavilions are near finished.

In Queen Mary's Court,

The Body of the Colonnade is wholly laid, and near covered in; the vaulted Arches of the Hall, under the Chapel, and those under the Dome, are finished; the vaulted Arch over the great Kitchen, and great Part of that over the First Story of the East and South Buildings, are also completed; a large Drain is made from the Middle of the South Building of this Court to the great Sewer on the East Side of the Hospital; greatest Part of the Earth is dug out, and carried away, from the East Colonnade, and the Upper Stories of the North East and South Pavilions of this Court are near finished; and, in the Mezzanine and Stories of the East and South Buildings, the Salhes and Frames are put in, and glazed.

A subterraneous Passage is made from the Colonnade of King William's Court to the new Brew-house; and a large Well is dug, and finished; a new Engine is made, and Pipes carried up from it to the great Reservoir, which contains One hundred Tons of Water; and is designed to serve Two Stories of the whole Hospital; the said Reservoir is lined with Lead; and a large Main is carried from it through the fubterraneousPassage to the West Colonnade, from whence Branches are to be carried into the several Courts and Apartments of King Charles's and King William's Buildings.

The great new Copper in the Brevvhouse is set; and a large leaden Pipe is laid from it through the subterraneous Passage to the West Colonnade; which Pipe is to serve the DiningHalls with Beer.

The new Brewhouse is also very near finished.

All which Works were brought to Account in September last, and amounts to the Sum of Eleven

thousand One hundred Seventy-three Pounds and Eleven Pence - - - - 11,173 o if

The ordinary Works and common Repairs, with Allowances, amounts to the Sum of One thousand Nine hundred and Seven Pounds Nine Shillings and Nine Pence - - - - 1,907 9 9

Total - 13,080 10 8

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, there was produced the last Will and Testament of the honourable William Steu art, late of the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square, in the County of Esquire,

dated the 31st Day of May 1726; by which it appears, That he bequeathed the Sura of 5000l. of Irish Money, to b& laid out and applied. Ten Vears after his Deceaie, in building and endowing a School in the said Parish of St. George, in such manner as his Executors should think fit: And appointed his Wife Elizabeth Steuart, and his Nephew James Steuart, Executors; who have duly proved the said Will.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the said Executors, being defiirous to carry the said Will into Execution, applied to the High Court of Chancery for that Purpose; in pursuance of which a Decretal Order was made by the said Court (which was produced, dated the Ilth Day of August 1736), in a Cause wherein John Willes Esquire, then his Majesty’s Attorney General, at the relation of Dennis Rond Esquire, and James Spilman Esquire, Churchwardens of the Parish of St. George, were Plaintiffs, and the said James and Henry

Rowe Esquire, and Elizabeth his Wife, late Elizabeth Steuart, were the Defendants: By which it was ordered. That the Sum of 4,484 I.6s. id. of lawful Money of Great Britain, being the Amount of the said 5,000l. Irish Money, should be laid out in the Three per Cent. Annuities, in the Name of the inxdjames Steuart, Henry Rowe, and Elizabeth his Wife, who should declare the Trull thereof, subject to the Order of the said Court: And that, until such time as a Piece of Freebold Ground could be purchased, to erect the said School upon, the Produce of the said Annuities should be accumulated, for the Benefit of the said Charity: And that as soon as a Piece of Ground could be found, to erect the said School upon, the said Trustees should, with the Appro-4

bation of the said Court, erett a School thereon; and that Twenty Boys of the said Parish of St. George should be therein taught to read and write, and be clothed, at the Expence of the said Charity.

It appeared like wile, by the Mailer’s Report (which was also produced, dated 18th March 1-36.) That the said Trustees did, in Obedience to the find Decree, lay out the said Sum in the ptirehaft: of Three per Cent. Annuities; and by tli ir Deed Poll have severally declared, That the said Three per Cent. Annuities now Hand in their Names, upon Trnft, to be subjefrl to such Order as the said Court should hereafter think lit to make or pronounce touching the fame.

Henry Rowe Esquire acquainted the Committee, That the Trustees have endeavoured to ptm-hase Freehold Land in the said Parish, to erect the School upon; but have not been able to procure any for that Purpose: For which Reason they made Application for a Faculty, to erect a School npou the Church Wall, in-llead thereof: but that some of the Inhabitants of the said Parish obtained a Prohibition against it.

Mr. Simon Parry, Vestry Clerk of the said Parish,

produced the Minute Book of the said Vestry; by which it appeared, That, on the 30th of x 740,

an Agreement was entered into, between the Trustees and the Churchwardens, Vestry, and principal Inhabitants, of the said Parish, to consent to transfer and pay the said Annuities to the Governors and Guardians of the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Chidren, in Consideration that they should receive Twelve poor Boys of the said Parish, being under the Age of Three Years, and maintain them: And, so often as any Vacancy shall happen in the said Number of Twelve, that such Vacancy shall be filled up by other poor Boys of the said Parish.

Mr. Herman Verelfi, Secretary to the said Governors and Guardians, produced Minutes of a General Board, dated the 31st of December last; whereby it appeared. That the said Governors and Guardians consented to the before-mentioned Agreement.

Upon the Whole, it appeared to the Committee, That all the Parties concerned have consent. d to the said Agreement; which will be more beneficial to the Parish of St. George, than if the said School had been built and endowed according to the said Decree, and will answer thecharitable Intentions of the said Tellator; but that the same cannot be carried into Execution without the Aid of Parliament.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Sports- Horse-men, and Breeders of Sporting Horses, in the North rac,nS Riding of Tork/hire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend themselves nearly affected in their Properties, by an Act, made the last Session of Parliament, to prevent the excessive Increase of Horle-racing, as the same Afl seems to tend to the intire Extirpation of Ilorfe-racing in this Kingdom, and eonfequently to the Ruin of the Breed of the most useful Horses for the Saddle; the Petitioners, as well as most of their Tenants, being Breeders of Horles for the Saddle, which they annually vend, upon account of their Blood, for considerable Sums; and that, should that antient and Royal Diversion of Horle-racing be wholly suppressed, the Blood of all good Horses, which our Ancestors have improved at a very great Expence, still superior to those of all our neighbouring Nations, w ill be totally neglected, since there is no other Method of proving them so well as by racing; and that, if no Plate or Prize was suffered to be run for under the Value of Forty Pounds, it would, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, answer the good Intention of the late Afl, by taking away above Five hundred Prizes yearly, and leave a tolerable Liberty for proving the Breed of Horses, at a moderate Expence; and expressing the Hopes of the Petitioners, that they may be at Liberty to run for any Prize, any Weight, at Newmarket or Black as the Peti-

tioners have been informed was intended by the House -and that they may not be obliged to lay such heavy' Weight upon their Horses, till they are past Six Years old, or arrived at their full Strength, as by the said late AQ: is prescribed (King’s Plates excepted): And therefore praying. That the House would please to take the Premises into Consideration; and grant the Petitioner's such Redress and Relief therein, as shall seem most reasonable and convenient.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. A Petition of several Merchants, Captains, and Mailers of Ships, as also of several Mathematicians, whole names are thereunto subscribed; on behalf of tiiemselves, and others concerned in Trade and Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; letting, forth, That by an Art of Parliament, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for providing a publick Reward' for such Person or Persons as shall discover the Longitude at Sea, the Commissioners appointed by the fame Art are impowered to apply any Sum or Sums of Money, not exceeding Two thousand Pounds, for making Experiments of any Proposal or Proposals that 10

shall be made to them for the Discovery of the Longitude: That it is absolutely necessary, to the making the Discovery useful at Sea, that the Longitude and Latitude of the chief Ports and Head-lands on the Coasts of Great Britain and Ireland, and the Dominions thereof, should be first determined more exartly than has hitherto been done; in order to which Determination, some Progrels has been therein already made, with good Success, at a considerable Expence; and that although the fixing the Longitude and Latitude of such Ports is absolutely necessary for making the Discovery useful, yet some Doubts have arisen, Whether by the Words of the said Art of Parliament the said Two thousand Pounds, or any Part thereof, can be applied for this Purpose: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the explaining and amending the said Art, l'o that the same may fully answer the Intention of the Legislature for making the said Discovery. 1

Otdered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition.

APetition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Merchants, Tradesmen, and others. Inhabitants of the Towns and Neighbourhood of Wakefield and Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, together with the several Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Towns of Pontefract and Knottingley,in the said Hiding, already have petitioned this House, praying that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road leading from the Town of Wakefield aforesaid, through several Villages, to Wee-land, in the said Riding, in fitch Manner, and by such Methods, as to the House should seem meet; and further letting forth, That the Road leading from the Town of Halifax aforesaid, to the said Town of Wakefield, passing over a certain high, iieep, and dangerous Hill, commonly called Halifax Bank, and through the Villages of Lightclife, Ilightown, and De, in the said Riding,

being the most frequented Road for the Carriage of "Wool, Cloth, Woollen Manufactures, dying Wares, Groceries, Corn, and other Sorts of Merchandize and Commodities, made or consumed in that populous and trading Part of the Country, is, at all Times of the Year, very deep in some Parts thereof, and, in the Winter Season, very dangerous, and aimost impassable; and that the Inhabitants of the several Towns, Town- ships, and Parishes, through which the last mentioned Road leads, cannot, by the Laws now in being relating to Highways, effectually repair the fame; and that, as the Petitioners conceive, the Repairing of the said Road betwixt the said Towns of Weeland and Wakefield, will be of great Advantage to the Inhabitants of the aforesaid Towns of Wakefield, Halifax, and Knot-

tingley; and likewise the continuing the repairing the same Road from Wakefield to Halover the said

Hill, and through the Villages aforesaid, will be highly advantageous, not only to the Inhabitants #f and Halifax aforesaid, but to all the trading Towns and Places adjacent, by rendering the several Roads to and from the aforesaid Places, convenient for all forts of Carriages, and thereby reduce the Charges thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given tb bring in a Bill, for repairing the Road betwixt the Towns of Wakefield and Halifax aforesaid, in such Manner, and by such Methods, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Painters of Fan Mounts, in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, in behalf of themselves, and all other the Paiuters of Fan Mounts in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read { felting forth, That the Number of Persons, employed, in painting of Fan Mounts was very great, and daily increasing, till about Three Years ago, when several Persons procured Copper-plates for the Printing of Fan Mounts, by which Means many of the Artifis are reduced to the utmost Distress, for Want of Employment, and others of them find their Business greatly decreased: That One Engraver, and Two Painters, are able to furnish more printed Fan Mounts in a Month’s Time, than this Kingdom makes use of in a Year; and One Person, employed in the walhing of these printed Fan Mounts^ will colour more in Three Days than One Painter can paint in a Quarter of a Year; that, by the Introdu6lion of printed, instead of well-painted Mounts for Fans, the Art of painting Fan Mounts, which was brought to great Perfection, is greatly discouraged; and the Exportation of Fans with painted Mounts, which brought into this Kingdom a large Sum of Money annually, almost intirely loft to Great Britain: And therefore, in Consideration of the Premifes, inordertogiveEmploymentto such aNum-ber of Persons, who have been bred up to the painting of Fan Mounts, and for preserving so valuable a Branch of Business to this Kingdom, praying the House to grant the Petitioners such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Read and Mr. Robert Read, being severally examined, said, That the whole Level contains about 4,500 Acres of Fen and Low Grounds, about 2,500 Acres whereof are commonable Lands, and the rest are Lands called Severals; and that the greatest Part of the said Level is w ithin the Manor of Waterbeach cum Denny, and the rest within the Parishes of Wicken,'Stretham, and Thetford.

Navigation, whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Clothiers, and otherlnhabitants of the Towns, Townships, Chapelries, and Precincts, of Halifax, d Rip-

ponden, in the West Riding of the* County of , was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is < as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the saidtPetition, an Act, made in the Tenth and Eleventh Year of the Reign of King William the Third, for making and keeping navigable the Rivers Aire and Colder, in the County of York, was produced.

Then Mr. John Eyes, Surveyor, being examined, said. That the River Colder was, by virtue of the said Act, made navigable to the Town of Wakefield: That he had surveyed the said River from Wakefield to Ealand, and found it capable of being made navigable thereto; a Plan of which Improvement in the Navigation of the said River he laid before the Committee.

Being further examined, he said, That the Navigation might easily be continued by the Brook Mouth to

habble Bridge, and so further up the River called Halifax Brooke, to the Town of Halifax:

That great Numbers of the Inhabitants of the Town and Parish 6f Halifax, and Parishes adjacent, are employed in the Woollen Manufactory; which would be greatly encouraged by continuing the Navigation to lifax, the present Price of Land Carriage betwixt Halifax and Wakefield being 15 per Ton; which might be reduced by Water Carriage to 9s. per Ton, Lock Dues included.

Being asked. Whether Goods could not be brought cheaper by Land Carriage than by Water, according to the Calculation of 9V. per Ton, provided the Roads were effectually repaired

He answered, That the Water Carriage would be much cheaper, though the Roads were ever so well repaired.

Mr. James Alderfunsaid. That, by Computation, aboveSixty thousand Inhabitants of the Town and Parish of Halifax are employed in the Woollen Manufactory, and in the several Parishes adjacent above double that Number: That, this great Manufactory would be much benefited by continuing the Navigation from Wakefield to Ealand, and so on to Halifax, as the Price of the Carriage of their Wool, to he manufactured, and their manufactured Goods, would be reduced at lead One Third: That all the Wheat brought from Wakefield, for the Supply of that populous Part of the Country, does now cost them 3*. a Quarter, reckoning Eight Bushels to the Quarter; which by Water would be brought to them f<»r 15<f. or at most for i8d. a Quarter, Lock Dues included:

That the Persons concerned in the said Manufactory are obliged to fend their Goods to Leeds and Wakefield, to be baled; which is a great Detriment to the said Goods, by packing and unpacking, and a Charge to the Manufacturer, at least double to what it would be, if he had an Opportunity to bale his Goods at home; which he might do if the River were so made navigable.

And being alked. If the Expence of Land Carriage . would not be lower than Water Carriage, if the Roads betwixt Halifax and Wakefield were sufficiently repaired

He said. That in his Opinion, the Roads could never be repaired, and made so easy for Carriages, but that the Price of Carriage by Land would \>enear a Third Part more than it would be by Water; and that, was it possible to make them as level and as good as any Turnpike Road in the Kingdom, the Carriage by Water would be ftiH cheaper than it would be by Land.

from thence by the Brook Mouth to Salter-h abble Bridge, and so further up a River called Halifax Brooke, to the Town of Halifax: And that Sir Mi Stapyllon and Mr. Cholmley Turner do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And offered to present to the House a Petition of the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia, in America.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House, to do therein as they shall think proper.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by the Surplus remaining in their Hands at Lady-day 1740, out of the Money granted in the Year 1739, and by the further Assistance granted in the last Session of Parliament, have been enabled to defray the Expence of aCivil Magistracy; to preserve the Friendship of the neighbouring Indians immediately bordering ou the Settlements in Georgia-, to encourage the raising Produces; and to bear the Charges of settling and improving the said Colony, to Lady-day 1741: That several Highlanders, settled at Darien, in Georgia, who entered voluntarily into his Majesty’s Service against St.AuguJline,having been killed or taken at

Fort Moofa, the Residue of them desire to have that Loss supplied by more of their Countrymen; and the Saltz-burghers, settled at Ebcnczer, in Georgia, have applied for their Settlement to be enlarged with others of their Countrymen, who are desirous lo join them at Ebenezer; the Inhabitants of both which Settlements in Georgia are an industrious andufeful People, and highly deferv-ing of Encouragement; and that the Beacon at Tybee, which has been of great Service to the Navigation along the Coast of Georgia, is in a ruinous Condition by tem-peftuous Weather, and requires an immediate Repair; and that their being several Servants in Georgia, whose Times of Service are almost expired, the Petitioners are under an Obligation to assist them in their beginning to VOL. 23.

Mr. Daniel Booth, being examined, said, That he is very well acquainted with the Quality of Silk,

which, in its Nature, is a fine glossy Silk, and greatly improves the Manufactures here; but that there is very little of it in Town, though greatly wanted: That, ever since the Declaration of War against Spain, the said Silk has borne an extravagant Price; and that he is very well assured, that the Importation of Messieurs Porter, Bourdieu, and Defmarette's Silk, now lying at Mar-feilles and Leghorn, will be of great Advantage to the Si/k Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Glonceft«r Colonel Selwyn reported from the Committee to whom "Waterworks, the Petition of the Mayor and Corporation of the City of

Gloucester, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition1, Mr. James Rogers, being examined, said, That the City of Gloucester is of late Years become very populous; and that the Inhabitants are subject to many Inconveniencies for want of a suficient Quantity of good and pure Water for their necessary Occasions, they being at present obliged to have Water brought to their Houses in Carts, or upon Sledges, from the River, which is at all times very dirty, and not fit to be made use of in many Instances: That there are Pumps in the said City, but the Water is of a hard nature; and that formerly an Engine was employed to throw the Water into the City from the River, but that the same has not been used for Two Years pad.

Mr. Joseph Andrews, being examined, said. That there are fresh Springs on or near a Hill called Matjton's Hill, otherwise Robin Hood's Hill, about a Mile and an Half distant from the City, from whence a suficient Quantity of good Water may be conveyed for the Use of the Inhabitants, which will be of great Advantage to the said City; but that the same cannot be completed without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better supplying the City of Gloucester with fresh Water: And that Colonel Selwyn and Mr. do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Resolution of the House of the 4th Day of December, in the Seventh Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, made upon Consideration of the Merits of an Election for the said Borough, was read; whereby it was resolved.

That such Persons as had, within Two Years last, received Kendrick's Charity, or any other annual Charity, distributed in the said Borough, bad not a Right to vote in Elections of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for ' the said Borough.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner examined several Witnesses, and produced Evidence, in order to disqualify such Voters for the Sitting Member as had received a Proportion of that Charity within Two Years before the last Election for the said Borough.

Then they examined several Witnesses, and produced Evidence, in order to establish the Votes of several Persons who were rated, and tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, but were rejected by the Mayor; and also of several other Persons, who were proposed to the Over-seers of the Poor, to be put upon the Rates, as fit to be rated, but were rejected by them; and who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, and were rejected by the Mayor.

Differing The Lord Baltimore reported from the Committee, of the to whom the Petition of j'everai Merchants, Captains, Longitude. an(] \|aflers of $()ips; as also of several Mathematicians, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the , Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at

the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

By an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for providing a publick Reward for such Person or Perfousas 111 all discover the Longitude at Sea, the Commissioners therein appointed were impowered to apply any Sum or Sums of Money, not exceeding Two thousand Pounds, for making Experiments of any Proposal or Proposals that should be made to them, for the Discovery of the Longitude.

It appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of Mr. Charles Middleton an Mr. the

First of which Tenons has used the Sea Eight-and-thirty Years, and the latter Forty Years, That they had by Experience found the Latitude of the North Foreland to be erroneous in most, of the Charts, or Sea Maps, in some Thirty Minutes, and iu other Twenty Minutes, and the Longitude still more erroneous.

That the Latitudes and Longitudes to the Northward of Newcastle, particularly the I lies of Orkney, and the moil northern Parts of Britain, are very false; which, the Examinants apprehend, is the Occasion of many Ships being loll upon the northern Coalt; and which they conceive to be very prejudicial to Navigation, and particularly to those Ships which are obliged to come North about:

That the Longitude and Latitude of the South Foreland, though more correct than the North Foreland, is

Voj.. 23.

not so exactly laid down as might be; and that the fixing the Longitude and Latitude of both those Places, as likewise of many Headlands in the Channel, particularly the Bill of Portland, the Lizard, and also the Klands of Sicily, out of the Channel, would be of general Service to the Navigation of this Kingdom.

The Reverend Mr. Whiston,being examined, said,

That he had been at ^.300 Expence in buying Inftrn-ments, and employing proper Persons, to find the Longitude and Latitude of several Places, particularly the North and South Forelands, and Duand that Persons were employed in finding the same at Beachy Head; and that he had received £. zoo and upwards, by voluntary Subscriptions of several Persons of Quality and Distinction, towards carrying on the said Undertaking:

That lie had applied to the Commissioners, appointed by the above-mentioned Act, for so much of the Sum of Two thousand Pounds therein mentioned, for making Experiments at Sea, as tlie CommissionersIhouId think a reasonable Recompence; but that some Doubts have arisen, whether any Part of that Sum could he appropriated as a Recompence for the finding out, and better ascertaining, the Latitude and Longitudes o Headlands and Havens, although the Examinant thinks the same very necessary and advantageous to the Navigation of this Kingdom; and that, in the First place, if the Longitude at Sea flmuld be fully discovered, it would be absolutely necessary, that the Latitude and Longitude of the Place gone from, and also the Latitude and Longitude of the Place to be gone to, should be described as exactly as possible.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain so much of an Act, passed in the Twelfth 'Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen intitu-

led, An Act for providing a publick Reward for such Person or Persons as shall discover the Longitude at Sea, as relates to the making of Experiments of Proposals for discovering the Longitude at Sea: And that the Lord Baltimore, Sir John Barnard, and Mr. tre, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Graziers, Wool-growers, Gentlemen, ciandertme and others, concerned in Romney Marfi, in the County Export of of Kent, and Places adjacent, whose Names are there- Wo°* unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and many others, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the several Acts of Parliament, which have been made to prevent the Exportation of Wool to foreign Parts, are, in a great measure, ineffectual; and that there has been a constant Decrease, for Twenty-twoYearspaft, in the Price of that Commoditj', from Ten Pounds to near Four Pounds the Pack; which, the Petitioners apprehend, could not have happened if the Woollen Manufacture in this Kingdom had not been greatly diminillied; the Decay whereof has already leffened, and mult very soon to a great Degree, inevitably reduce, the Value of valt Numbers of Estates in this Kingdom, and at the same time carry immense Riches to those neighbouring Countries, who have too successfully of late rivalled us in the Woollen Manufacture; and that, as the Petitioners have been informed, the French cannot work up their own Wool into Cloths proper for the foreign Markets, wilhout mixingOne Pack of British or Irish Wool with Two of their own; which makes

the Petitioners hope, that, if effectual Methods could be found to prevent the French from having any Wool from Great Britain or Ireland, they would not, for the future, be able to undersell his Majesty’s Subjects in the foreign Markets: And further repreienting to thelloufe,

That a Law to oblige the Owners of all Wool, Ihorn in GreatBrilainov Ireland, to register the fame, and not permit it to be conveyed from the Place of itsGrowth to any other Part of the Kingdom, but by Lund Carriage, till it be manufactured, seems to the Petitioners to be the most likelyWaytopreventtheExportationofWoolout of these Kingdoms: And therefore praying the House to.take the Premises into Consideration; and give such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet. 1

By ai\ Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of King William and Qtieen Mary, for the encouraging the Diddling of Brandy and Spirits from Corn (which recites, That, by an Act, made in the Parliament held in the Fii'lt Year of their Majesties Reign, intituled, An Act for prohibiting all Trade and Commerce with France, all Brandies, Vila:, and Spirits, were prohibited to jbe imported into this Kingdom, and that good and wholeibme Brandies, Aqua and Spirits, might be made and drawn from malted Corn, it appeared. That, ibr the Encouragement of the making of Brandies, llrong Waters, and Spirits, from malted Corn, and for the greater Consumption of Corn, and the Advantage of Tillage in this Kingdom, a Duty of One Penny only ivas imposed on every Gallon of low Wines of the First Eitraction, drawn and made from Drink brewed and made of kny Sort of malted Corn; and the several Duties of Eight Pehbe, Twelve Pence, and Three Pence, were imposed upon every Gallon of such low Wines made or drawn from the several other Materials therein mentioned; and that several Provisions were made, for obliging all Distillers to draw their low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesome Drink, made of malted Corn entirely, Without any Mixture of any Meddles, Waflt, or 'l ilts, or other Materials whatsoever; and for the further Encouragement of Distillers, and others, to draw and make Spirits or Brandies from malted Corn, and expott the fame, a Drawback upon Exportation was allowed, of ThreePence for every Gallon of Brandy or Spirits made and drawn from Drink brewed from malted Corn, without an}' Mixture with any other Materials; which said Act continued in force till the 25th Day of December 169.5.

By another Act, made in the Seventh and Eighth Year of the Reign of King William, the said several Duties, and the said Provisions, with the Allowance of the said Drawback, were continued until the 23th Day of March mm.

By another Act, made in the Twelfth and Thirteenth Year of the Reign of King William the Third, several liew Duties on low Wines, or Spirits cif the First Extraction, were imposed; which were to have Continuance Until the 25th Day of March 1706: And by this Act the like Drawback was allowed upon Exportation of Spirits or Brandy made from malted Corn only', us was allowed by the former Acts.

By an Act, made in the Third and Fourth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne,the Duties imposed by the last mentioned Act, and the several Powers, Directions, Penalties, Forfeitures, Clinics, Matters, and Things, thereby provided, settled, and cllablithed, for the better railing, levying, recovering, or paying the Duties thereby imposed, or for making any Drawbacks, Repayment, or Allowances, upon Exportation, were farther continued until the 24th Day of June 1710; and from thence were further continued by another Act, made in the 5th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne; and have since been made perpetual by another Act, made in the First Year of his late Majesty’s Reign.

By an Act, made in the Sixth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for the better Encouragement of Spirits drawn from Corn i n0GreatBritain, a Drawback upon Exportation is allowed of £.4. i8r. o for every Tun of such Spirits; and for every Tun of Spirits draw’n from Barley, Malt, or other Corn, the Bounty of /.i. tos. o d.is also directed to be paid to the Exporter of the fame, when Barley is Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter, or under.

Mri Stephen South, Brewerj being examined, said, That, in July 1739, lie went to a Diliiller’s near -ford, and that at One Malli Tun lie saw them work unmalted Corn with C.orn malted; which they mixed in the Proportion of Four Parts unmalted to One malted: That then lie went to Two Mills, which ground Corn for Distillers; and at One he saw Three hundred Quarters of Barley, and likewise several Sacks of ground Corn j both Wheat and Barley unmaltedj and at the other he saw divers Quantities of Barley- as good as any ever made use of for Malt.

Mr. William Oram and Mr. Ralph Porter, Mallfters, being severally examined, said. That Seventy-five Quarters of Barley weigh as mueh as an Hundred Quarters of Malt; and that an Hundred Quarters of Barley will produce an Hundred and Five Quarters of Malt: And the Jaft-mentioned Witness added. That Six Bushels of Barley are generally equal in Weight to One Quarter of Malt; though lie has had Barley which has not weighed, so much as the like Quantity of some Malt.

Mr. SayerNeal, Distiller, being examined, said, That he followed that Business Twenty Years, and has gone through the several Branches thereof: That Distillers ule a great Deal of Corn, as good as any sold at Bear -That sometimes they use-the middling, but cannot make use of the word Sort of Barley; especially if it be not found: That having mixed Ten Quarters of Malt with the like Quantity of Meal (Tw o Quarters w hereof were Wheat, and the rest Barley), they produced Three hundred and Sixty Gallons of Spirits; and that the Spirits produced from Eight Quarters of Malt mixed with Twelve Quarters of Meal (Two Quarters whereof are Wheat, and the Remainder Barley) run a greater Lengt li by Two Gallons upon each additional Quarter of Meal, tiian they would do if drawn from Malt onl y:

That Twenty Quarters of raw Corn (Three Quarters whereof are Wheat Meal, and the other Seventeen Barley) mixed with Five Quarters of Malt, will produce Font-hundred and Eighty-five Gallons of proof Spirits:

That. Coni distilled, whereof Three Parts is Meal and One Malt, will produce Two Gallons of Spirit on each Qilarter more than Corn distilled, whereof Three Parts is Malt, and One Meal; and that more Wort is drawn from it iu proportion as the Quantity of Meal is larger.

That if Distillers were obliged to use malted Coni in -tirely the Consumption of Corn would increase in the Proportion of betweenTweuty and Thirty' Quarters in every Hundred:

That Malt may be made of the word Sort of Bariev, provided it be found; and, when it comes to the K.ihi it is mnch cleaner than if unmalted, and will produce *£ cleaner Spirit, though not run so great a Quantity.

Being allied, What Price lie would give for Bariev, of which Malt sold at 2os. per Quarter is made? He* an fwered, About 15J. 6d. or 1 6s.

And one Mr. Porter, a Maltster, being asked the Question, said, That the Charge of Malting isTwo Shillings per Quarter.

The Examinant Neal further said, That he never knew intire Meal brewed without Malt; becanfe, if* there was no Malt to save the Com, it would be iin-possible to malli it, it being of a gluey Substance.

Being examined, as to the Difference in the Quality of Spirits drawn from Corn, and of those drawn from Malt, he said. That the Spirit extracted from raw Corn is stronger, and more foul, than that produced from malted. Corn: That it has not so clean a Flavour, and wants more cleansing by Fire: That the latter is better for the Consumer, and would be more for the Benefit of the Com-poundersin general, though they were to give more for it: as it would find a Market abroad, and credit the Exporter: That the best Corn will produce the be it Spirits; mut That the Spirits extracted from Corn ami Malt, mixed in equal Proportions, are clearer; but do not run so great a Length as when there is a greater Proportion of unmalted Corn.

With regard to the Number of Hogs fed by the Distillers, and the Manner of their being fed;

The said Mr, Neal, being examined, said. That he has had Six or Seven hundred Hogs at one time; which he fed with the Grains and Wadi from the Still; That they are, by that means, fed much cheaper than the Farmers are able to feed them; and they will gain in Value by their Feeding i. c. 6d. per Week; but that he does not think the Carcasses of such Hogs so proper for Salting, as those fed by the Farmers:

ThatDillillers could not fat Hogs, if they were obliged to use malted Corn only; and that the Fatting of them by Farmers inuft necessarily consume a greater Quantity of Corn, as well as add much to the Gooduefs of the Hogs:

That Hogs fed with Pollard are better than those fed by the Distillers.

Mr. Harveftlikewife said. That the Distillers usually

That the Petitioners are apprehensive, thaL in case a Bill brought into this House, for repairing and enlarging the Roads from the Town of Selby, in the West Riding of the County of York, to the Town of Leeds and from thence, in Two several Branches, one through Bradford and Horton, and the other through Hozvlino and WibJ'ey, to the Town of Halifax, in the same Riding, should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will he thereby much aggrieved by the Tolls and Duties thereby to be laid, and made payable, for amending the Road proposed to be amended by the said Bill, as well in regard fa much of the same Road, as lies within their Township, wants no repairing, for the Purpolts of the said Bill, it being already a good Wheel Carriage Road, as that the Prices of Corn coming to their Market will be thereby enhanced; and the Coals, from a Colliery of the Right honourable the Lord Visconnt Irxoen, in the Parish of Whilkirk, adjoining to the said Parish of Leeds, will be thereby, inelfeft, prohibited to be brought to Leeds:

And therefore, the Premises considered, and in regard the Petitioners have been in no Default of repairing their Roads, lying between Selby and Bradford, aforesaid, and the subje.'ting the Coal brought to Leeds, from the said Colliery, to the said Tolls and Duties, must greatly affect the Woollen Manufacture at Leeds, and make the same go dearer to foreign Markets; praying. That the Inhabitants of Leeds, their Cattle and Carriivgesof all K’uds, and all other Cattle and Carriages, laden or empty* ana going to load, or returning empty from loading ol Coal or Corn, to or from Leeds, may be exempt from Payment of any Tolls or Duties to be laid, or made payable, by the said Bill; and that no Turnpike Gate or Bar may be erected on the said Road, fb proposed to be amended, in Leeds,or at any Place in the said Road, between Bradford and Leeds, nearer to Leeds than the Stone Pillar Handing in Kirkftall,in the said Parish; or at any Place in the said Road between Tweeds and Selby, nearer to I^eeds than the Stone Pillar called

Hallon Dial, in the Parish of L, nor at the Place last mentioned; and that the York Road may lie open for all Cattle and Carriages to pass without Payment of any Toll or Duty; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as to the House thall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Merchants of , and

others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and great Numbers of Merchants, Traders, and other Inhabitants, in the Province of the setts Bay, in America,was'presented to the House, and

read: setting forth. That while his Majesty and this House have exerted their Authority and utmost Cate, not only to prevent the Increase of Paper Money in America, but even to fink apd discharge what has already issued under the public Authority, by virtue of Act# of Assembly there, John Coleman Esquire, and a very great Number of private Persons, in the sets Bay, his Associates, have, without any Authority, assumed a Power to erect themselves into a Company or Society there, by the Name of the Land Bank, and have chosen and appointed Directors, Treasurers’ and Officers, to carry on the same under large yearly Salaries, avowedly for the Purpose of issuing Paper Bills or Notes, to a very large Amount, to be redeemable Twenty Year# hence, or at some other remote Distance of Time; and haveactually issued out their Notes, and, by their Numbers and Influence, endeavour to force a Currency for the fame: and this, notwithstanding that the most considerable Inhabitants in the Mass Bay in due time opposed such Scheme, and petitioned the General Assembly there to discountenance and suppress that pernicious Project; and notwithstanding that his Majesty’s Governor, with the Advice of the Council there, by publick Proclamations, did discourage the fame; so that, by means of the said Land Bank, the Quantity of Paper Money there is greatly increased, and many Frauds, Losses, and Prejudices, are likely to ensue to the Petitioners, and others, if not timely prevented; and that several of the Petitioners have humbly petitioned his Majesty in Council, for Relief against the said Coleman's Scheme, and the Lords of the Committee of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, and the Lords Commissieaers for Trade and Plantation's, to whom the Petition has been referred, have concurred in Opinion, That that Scheme was of dangerous Tendency, and fit to be suppressed as speedily and effectually as possible; and have given all the Orders that were possible for them to give, that the Governors should continue in the mean time to discourage the said Scheme; and that, although the said Co/e/aan’s Scheme would here in Great Britain be an high Offence, and attended with heavy Punishments, and might easily be suppressed, as being within the Act of the Sixth Year of his late Majesty King George the First, Chapter the 18th, Sections l|, 19, 20,yet his Majesty’s Attorney and Solicitor General, to whom the Method for. prosecuting the Persons concerned in the lajd Schpme was in the course of the said Petition referred, have reported their Opinion, That that Act does not extend to America; and that nothing can effectually be done to put a Stop thereto, but by the Interpolation of a positive Law; so that, notwithstanding all the Endeavours used by the Petitioners, without the Aid of Parliament, no Remedy can be had against those Persons, who have already presumed to set on foot this fraudulent Project;. but all the Care taken by his Majesty, from, time to time, and his repeated -Royal Orders and Instructions on the Head of Paper. Money, as well as the Care and Inquiry of this House, will be totally evaded and eluded, and many other Persons may take upon themselves also to set on foot other like Projects in America: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to hear the Petitioners, by their Counsel; and that the said Act of Parliament, of the Sixth Year of his late Majesty King George the First, may be extended to the British Plantations in America, by express Words, with properClauses and Powers, and with such Penalties, Forfeitures, and Disabilities, on all Persons offending Vol. 23.

against the fame, or with such other Refief in the Premises as to the House fha.FI seem proper.

St. Botolph A Petition of Thomas Kynaston, Clerk, Impropriator of without Aid- the Rectory Impropriate of St.Bwithout gate Church, in the City of London, and County of was

presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Indenture dated on or about the 23d of December 170 6, Samuel Brewfterthe younger, Esquire, Impropria-

for or Owner of the said Rectory Impropriate, and Sarah his Wife, did, with other Persons, Parties thereto, demise certain Grounds, Parcels of the said Rectory, to the then Churchwardens of the Parish of St. Botolph, to hold to them, and their Successors, for Five hundred Years; and the then Churchwardens, for the Considerations mentioned in the said Lease, for themselves, and their Successors, for the Time being, did covenant and agree, that they should and would, from time to time, during that Term, pay and discharge all such Sums of Money as then were, orfhould or might be, rated or assessed on the said Samuel Breufter, his Heirs or Assigns, or on the Rec-

tory Impropriate of the said Parish,-or ontheTythesor Profits belonging to the fame, for or in respect of any Poor's Rates, or parochial Duties or Dues (Aids to the Crown excepted), and should and would indemnify the said Samuel Brewster,his Heirs and Assigns, of and from the same: That, in the Year 1728, the Petitioner purchased the Fee and Inheritance of the said Rectory Impropriate, and hath ever liuce strictly kept the Covenants contained in the said Lease on his Part: And that, if the Bill to enable the Parishioners of the Parish of St.Botolph without Aldgate, in the City of London, and County of Middlesex, to rebuild the Church and Steeple of the said Parish, should pass into a Law, as it is now drawn, the Petitioner apprehends, that he will thereby be made liable to contribute towards the Expence of pulling down and rebuilding the said Church and Steeple, notwithstanding the before-mentioned Agreement stipulated between the Parties, as aforesaid,of which the Petitioner

hopes he shall have the Benefit: And therefore praying,

That he may be heard by his Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as will affect him; or that he may have such other Relief in the Premifes, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, if he thinks fit, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

to the House, and read; complaining of the Decay of the Woollen Manufacture in the said Town; the Cause whereof, as the Petitioners apprehend, is the fending Wool to France, and other foreign Parts, from England and Ireland, which the Petitioners have the greater Reason to believe, because in those Years when France was lately afflicted with a contagious Distemper, and their Trade thereby flopped, the Manufacture of the ^own of Colchester was near double to what it hadTjeen for many Years before, or hath been at any Time since, and more gainful to the Parties dealing in it, though the Price of Wool was then also considerably higher: And therefore. praying Relief.
