Mr. Walpole accordingly reported from the said Committee the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts is greatly prejudicial to the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in being are not sufficient to prevent the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts.

Resolved \That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a publick Regiller of the Wool grown in Great Britain and Ireland is the most effectual Method of preventing the Exportation thereof to foreign Parts.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, Nemine contradicente.

The Second and Third Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Walpole also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to direct the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, during the Rccefs of Parliament, to prepare a Scheme for the Registering the Wool of Great Britain and Ireland, to be laid before this House the next Session of Parliament:

And he moved the House accordingly.

A PETITION of the Mayor an(l Commonalty of the Clandestfae City of York was presented to the House, and E*{^y^n read; complaining of the Decay of the Woollen Manufacture in that County, arising, as the Petitioners conceive, from the Exportation of Wool to France; and representing to the House, That a Law, to oblige all Owners and Manufacturers of Wool to register the same in the Parishes in which they relide, by Per Ions independent, and under no Influenc e, chargeable with a certain Sum, to be paid only by those who export it without its being completely manufactured, seems, to the Petitioners, to be a most effectual Remedy to this great Evil:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Pr. a. L. 28. Before " Provided," add Clauses marked

A and B.

A: ‘’ And whereas, by the Default or Neglect of Persons employed in suffering Common Recoveries, it has happened, and may happen, that fuel) Recoveries are " not entered on Record; whereby Pnrchafers, for a ira-V luable Consideration, may he defeated of their just " Rights: For Remedy whereof, be it further Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That when any Person or " Persons hath or have purchased, or shall purchase, for " a valuable Consideration, any Estate or Estates in Lands,

Tenements, or Hereditaments, whereof a Recovery " or Recoveries is, are, or were, necessary to be suffered,

" in order to complete the Title such Person and Persons, and all claiming under him, her, or them, having " been in Possession of the purchased Estate or Estate*

" from the time of such Purchase, shall and may, after " the End of Twenty Years from the time of such Purchase, produce in Evidence the Deed or Deeds making

" a Tenant

law concerning Common Recoveries.

684 17 ' Marti \ 1740.

a Tenant to the Writ or Writs of Entry, or other " Writs for fuflering a common Recovery, or common " Recoveries; and the Deed or Deeds so produced, the Execution thereof being duly proved, shall, in alt " Courts of Law and Equity, be deemed and taken as " a good and sufficient Evidence for such Purchaser and " Purchasers, and those claiming under him, her, or " them, and that such Recovery or Recoveries was or '* were duly suffered and perfected, according to the " Purport of such Deed or Deeds, in case no Record " can be found of such Recovery or Recoveries, or the " same should appear not to be regularly entered on " Record. Provided always, That the Person or Per- fons making such Deed or Deeds, as aforesaid, and " declaring the Uses of a common Recovery or Recoveries, had a sufficient Estate and Power to make a " Tenant to such Writ or Writs, as aforesaid, and to " suffer such common Recovery or Recoveries.

B: " And whereas it has frequently happened, That " the Deeds for making the Tenant to the Writs of " Entry, or other Writs for fuflering common Reco- veries, have been loft, or that the Fines or Deeds' " making the Tenants to the said Writs have not been " levied or executed till after the Judgment given in " such Recoveries, and the Writs of Seisin awarded, by reason whereof great Doubts have arisen, whether such

Recoveries, for want of proper Tenants to the Writs, " are good and effectual in Law j to prevent such " Doubts for the future, and in order to render common " Recoveries more certain and effectual, be it Enabled, by the Authority aforesaid, That every common Recovery, already suffered, or hereafter to be suffered, " shall, after the Expiration of Twenty Years from the " time of the fuflering thereof, be deemed good and " valid, to all Intents and Purposes, if it appears, upon " the Face of such Recovery, that there was a Tenant " to the Writ, and if the Persons joining in such Recovery had a sufficient Estate and Power to fuflier the " fame, notwithstanding the Deed or Deeds, for making " the Tenant to such Writ, should be loft, or not appear. And be it further Enabled, by the Authority " aforesaid, That, from and after the Commencement of " this Act, every Recovery, already suffered, or hereafter to be suffered, iba.ll be deemed good and valid, " to all Intents and Purposes, notwithstanding the Fine, or Deed or Deeds, making the Tenant to such Writ, should be levied or executed after the Time of " the Judgment given in such Recovery, and the Award of " the Writ of Seisin, as aforesaid; provided the same appear to be levied or executed before the End of the " Term in which such Recovery was suffered, and the *' Persons joining in such Recovery had a sufficient Estate, " and Power to suffer the fame, as aforesaid."

To prove the Matter of the fftid Complaint, the following Witnesses were examined, on the Part of the Complainant:

Edward Gibbs said, That lie occupies a House and

Land in the Parish of Kensington, of which the Widow of the late Sir George Saunders was formerly Owner: That upon her Death, which happened about a Year and a Half ago, the Witness was informed, by one Mr.

Jeremy,who then and before received the Rent for the said House and Land, That Mr. Revell was his Landlord; and that he accordingly went to pay his Rent to Mr. Revell, at the Victualling Office; but he, being then very busy, had not time to receive it:

That about Six Weeks before the Day he was examined at the Conrimittee, One Sarah Colby, who pretended to be the Owner of the said House and Land, with Two other Persons, came to the Witness, and demanded

?offefiion thereof; which he refused to give: and that, wo Days after, the again demanded the fame; and the Witness then told her, Mr. Revell was his Landlord, and that he kept Possession for him: Whereupon she, with one Jones, an Attorney, and his Son, and one William Warren, a Sheriff’s Officer, entered the said House by Force:

That Warren, with a large Stick or Piece of Wood, broke in at the Window; and, having let in the said Sarah Colby, Jones, and his Son, catched up the Witness’s Wife in his Arms, and told her. She shoutd go out first.

Afterwards the Examinant heard the said Jones direct the said Sarah Colby to walk over Three Fields, m order to her taking Possession thereof; Part of which Fields belong to Mr. Revell, and are occupied by the Witness: That, having thus got Possession, they asked the Witness to attorn Tenant to Mrs. Colby; and gave him good Words to persuade him thereto; but threatened, at the same time, in case of his Refusal, to turn him out immediately, and remove all his Goods: At which he, being terrified, did con Cent to attorn; though otherwise, he said, he would not, having always looked upon himself as Mr. Revell's Tenant.

Maria CdlherinaGibbs, Wife of the said Edward Gibbs,

said. That the Day on which the before-mentioned Persons came to demand Possession was the /9th of aryItfft: That the First time they came they demanded to be let into the House; which the Witness refilled, and fattened the Door; but that Warren broke the Sash of the Windows; upon which she took up a Spit, and of-posed his Entrance:

That about an Hour after, they came again, and Warren opened the C^fement, split the Shutter of the Window; and, having got in, opened the Door, and let jn Mrs. Colby, Landen Jones, his Son, and another Person; and that Mrs. Colby walked over the Groulild which the Witness’s Husband rented of Mr. Revell.

Being asked. If they produced any Writ ? she said, They fhevved her a Paper, which they called a Warrant from the High Sheriff of the County.

Being asked, Why she refused them Entrance? she said, It was, because her Husband and she looked upon them-, selves to be Tenants to Mr. Revell, and had been so informed by one Mr. Jeremy, who used to collect the Rent of the Premises fbrthe late Lady Saunders', and that the last Rent her Husband paid was paid to the said Jeremy.

Jefeph Orchard said, That about Six Weeks before the Day he was examined at the Committee, Mrs. Gibbs called him to come to her Assistance, when Five Persons, Four Men and One Woman, attempted to break into Gibbs's House:

That he saw One of the Persons take up a Piece of Timber, and attempt to break open the Door; and that afterwards he saw the same Person break open the Shutter of the Window, and s Wife run at him with a Spit.

Mr. Speaker also reported. That his Majesty was The King1* afterwards pleased to make a most gracious Speech Sp«>ch from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of rePorte^-which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which lie read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

At the Opening of this Section I took Notice to yon of the Death of the late Emperor, and of my Refutation to adhere to the Engagements, I am under, in order to the Maintaining of the Balance of my Power, and the Liberties of Europe, on that important Occasion. The Assurances I received from you, in return to this Communication, were perfectly agreeable to that Zeal and Vigour which this Parliament has always exerted in the Support of the Honour and Interest of my Cro wn and Kingdoms, and of the common Cayfe.

The War, which has since broke out, and been carried on in Part of the AujlrianDominions, and the various and extensive Claims which are publickly made on the late Empe»or's Succession, are new Events, that require the utmost Care and Attention, as they may involve all Europe in a bloody War, and, in consequence, expose the Dominions of such Princes as shall take Partin Support of the Pragmatick Sanction, to imminent and immediate Danger. The Queen of Hungary has already made a ltequisition of the Twelve thousand Men expressly stipulated by Treaty; and thereupon I have demanded of the King of Denmark, and of the King of Sweden, is Landgrave of Hesse Cassel, their respective Bodies of Troops, confiftijig

Things, many Incidents may arise, during the Time when, by reason of the approaching Conclusion of this Parliament, it may be impossible for me to have your Advice and Assistance, which mav make it neceflaty for me to enter into ftiil larger Expences for maintaining the Pragmatick Sanction. Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I mull recommend it to you to grant me such a Sup» ply as may be requisite for these Ends; and the just Concern and Readiness which I have constantly found in you to make all necessary Provisions for the publick Good, and our common Security, leave me no room to doubt of the same good Dilpofitieu and Affection in this Instance.

That the Sum of Forty-four thousand Five hundred Sixty-nine Pounds Eight Shillings and One Peny be granted to his Majesty, for what remains payable of the Subsidy for the Six thousand , taken into his Majesty’s Pay to the 25th of December 1741, pursuant to the Treaty, dated the 14th of March 1739, N.S.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty, six thousand One hundred Fifty-seven Pounds Nineteen Shillings and One Peny Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying several extraordinary Expences and Services incurred Anno 1740, and not provided for by Parliament.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Fifty-three thousand Nine hundred Ninety-five Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining a Regiment of Foot, raised in America for his Majesty’s Service, confiding of Thirty-six Companies, for the Service of the Year 1741, commencing the 25th Day of December 1740, inclusive.

8. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eleven thousand Six hundred Eleven Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining the Charge of several Officers appointed by his Majesty to go with the Forces on board the Fleet in the Expedition under the Command of the Right honourable Lord Calhcart, for the Year 1741.

9. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousandTwo hundred Seventy-seven PoundsTen Shillings,be granted tohis Majesty, for maintaining the Charge of the StaffOfficers appointed by his Majesty to attend the Hospital established for the Service of the Expedition under the Command of the.Right honourable Lord Cat heart, for the Year 1741.

10. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That aSum, not exceeding Twenty-nine thousand Three hundred Pounds Seven Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, for reduced Officers of his Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year 1741.

11. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand One hundred Twenty-six Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for paying of Pensions to the Widows of such reduced Officers of his Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines as died upon the Establishment of Half-pay in Great Britain (and who were married to them before the 25th Day of December 1716, for the Year 1741.

12. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Two hundred Forty nine Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Four Pence Thiee Farthings, be granted to his Majesty, to make good the Loss sustained by several Merchants, and by the Officers commanding the Six new-raised independent Companies of Foot in the Istand of Jamacia, by the Failure of Mr. Henry Popple, appointed by his Majesty Agent to the said Companies.

13. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Eight hundred Sixteen Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Four Pence Three Farthings, be granted to his Majesty, to make good the Loss sustained by Richard Fitzwilliam Esquire, Captain of an independent Company of Foot in the Istand of Nero Providence, on account of the Pay of the Company under his Command, by the Failure of the said Henry Popple, appointed by his Majesty Agent to the said Company.

14. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred and Fitly Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to make good a Idol's sustained by the Receiver General of , by the

Failure of the said Henry Popple.

15. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds he granted to his Majesty, for the resettling and re-ellahliftiing the unhappy Sufferers of the Province of South Carolina in the late dreadful Fire at Charles Town.

Royal Assent A Message from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, to Bills. Gentleman Usher of the Biack Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to give the Royal AlTent to the several publick and private Bills following; viz.

An Act for granting to his Majesty the Sum of One million out of the Sinking Fund: and for applying other Sums therein mentioned, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-one; and for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon Coals used in Fire Engines for drainingTin and Copper Mines in the County of Cornwall; and for appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament; and for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer Bills, Lottery Tickets, and Orders, loft, burnt, or otherwise destroyed; and for giving further Time for the Payment of Duties omitted to be paid for the Indentures and Contrafts of Clerks and Apprentices:

An Act for the Encouragement and Increase of Seamen; and for the better and speedier manning his Majesty’s Fleet:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot part with this Parliament, without publickly returning you roy Thanks for the many eminent Instances you hare given me of your Fidelity and Affection to my Person and Government, your fixed Resolution to maintain the Protestant Succession in my Family, and your unshaken Adherence to the true Interest of your Country. You have, with the moll becoming Spirit and Firmness, exerted yourselves in vindicating and defending the Honour of my Crown, and the undoubted Rights of Navigation and Commerce belonging to my Subjects; and enabled me to revenge those Wrongs and Jnfults, which, contrary to the Faith of Treaties, had been committed against both. In so critical a Conjuncture, you have supported the national Credit, and llrengthened the Hands of my Government, to a Degree exceeding the Expectations of those who wished well to us, and to the manifeil Disappointment of such as envied our Prof-perity. At the same Time you have demonstrated to all the World, that Great Britain is in a Condition not only to defend herself, but also to afford a due Support to her Allies, and the common Cause of Europe. As such a Conduct mull give a lasting Reputation to this Parliament, so it will be the Subject of Emulation to those which shall come after it.

I will immediately give the necessary Orders for calling new Parliament. There is not any thing I set so high a Value upon as the Love and Affection of my People,

in which I have so entire a Confidence, that it is with' great Satisfaction I fee this Opportunity put into their Hands, of giving me fresh Proofs of it in the Choice of their Representatives.

On the present Establishment depends the Continuance of our excellent Constitution in Church and State; and in this Constitution consists the Security of the present Establishment: Nothing can hurt the one, that will not, in proportion, undermine and weaken the other.

For my Part, the uniform Preservation of bot i i, and the Maintenance of the religious and civil Rights of all my Subjects, have been, and ever shall be, my conflaot C ire.

Those who distinguish themselves by persevering in tlit fe Principles, shall always find my Countenance and Favour; and, by invariably pursuing these wife and lionelt Measures, we may entertain the best grounded Hopes, that, under the Protection of the Divine Providence, the Happiness of Great Britain will be perpetuated to Posterity.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

[Parliament Prorogued.]

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the 12th Day of May next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the 12th Day of May next.
